column1: As usual
column2: the Governing Council devoted part of its meeting to an exchange of views on recent economic
column3: monetary and financial developments. This discussion took place against the background of conflicting messages. Clearly
column4: on the one hand
column5: the data on the economic situation in the United States and Europe
column6: especially in the euro area
column7: mainly indicate a continuation of real GDP growth
column8: though possibly at a somewhat slower pace. On the other hand
column9: however
column10: the global macroeconomic environment has deteriorated. In particular
column11: the number of signs suggesting that the world economy will slow down in 1999 is increasing. At the same time
column12: uncertainty in the financial markets has been heightened by news of the near collapse of a large hedge fund
column13: losses by individual financial institutions
column14: and the large movements in world equity
column15: bond and foreign exchange markets.

column1: In the view of the Governing Council
column2: in responding to recent economic developments and current market conditions
column3: it is of the utmost importance that proposals inspired by policy activism that do not take due account of the complexity of the issues at stake are avoided. This would only contribute to compounding the uncertainties which underlie the prevailing global financial market volatility. Against this background
column4: the Governing Council is of the view that proposals for a reassessment of capital controls as an acceptable policy option
column5: or recent calls for world-wide
column6: uniform interest rate reductions
column7: are inappropriate as they do not address the very nature of the problems. At the same time
column8: the Governing Council considers structural improvements at the global level to be warranted. These should focus
column9: in particular
column10: first on enhancing the transparency of both the public and private sectors; second
column11: on strengthening domestic banking systems
column12: primarily in emerging markets and economies in transition; and
column13: third
column14: on improving financial crisis prevention and management
column15: in particular through the increased involvement of the private sector. A number of proposals have already been developed on these issues
column16: which should now be finalised with a view to their early and forceful implementation.

column1: In addition
column2: the Governing Council stressed that such structural improvements at the global level would have to be accompanied by sound policies at home. In this respect
column3: given the size of the euro area and its global role
column4: it is of crucial importance that price stability - and hence a climate conducive to growth and employment - should be maintained in the euro area. Achieving this will also be of vital importance for the world economy as a whole.

column1: With this in mind
column2: the Governing Council reviewed the monetary
column3: financial and macroeconomic situation in the euro area.

column1: First
column2: the Council discussed the monetary situation with reference to preliminary data on the basis of the new harmonised reporting system for money and banking statistics. Once internal work has been completed
column3: these monetary statistics will be made available to the public. When looking at various definitions of broad money
column4: our preliminary data show broadly similar and stable annual growth rates of between 3 and 5% in 1997 and the first half of 1998. According to our initial analysis
column5: these data do not appear to signal inflationary pressures arising from money at this juncture. However
column6: given the preliminary nature of the new data
column7: caution should be exercised with regard to their interpretation.

column1: Second
column2: as regards other financial indicators
column3: although long-term interest rates have risen recently
column4: they are still at low levels by historical standards and the yield curve has levelled off relative to the situation some months ago. A substantial part of developments in bond markets during recent months reflects a ""flight into quality"".

column1: Third
column2: the Governing Council discussed the broad outlook for prices in the context of the overall macroeconomic environment. With respect to price developments
column3: international factors continued to exert downward pressure. HICP rates in the euro area fell to 1.2% in August after having remained unchanged at 1.4% from April to July. This mainly reflected a decline in energy prices
column4: which were almost 4% lower in August than a year earlier
column5: and in other commodity prices. For the euro area as a whole
column6: price pressure as indicated by industrial output prices and labour costs also remained modest. In 1999 average inflation in the euro area is expected to remain subdued
column7: according to the projections available.

column1: Fourth
column2: considerable difficulties are encountered in precisely assessing and quantifying the impact of recent international developments on prices and
column3: equally

column5: which reached 0.6% in the first quarter of 1998
column6: has slowed down somewhat in the second quarter. We need to await the release of more complete and thereby more reliable data for the euro area as a whole before a final view can be taken. Other recently released data on industrial production
column7: the volume of retail sales and passenger car registrations appear to point to continued growth. This view is also supported by EC survey data

column1: The Governing Council welcomed recent interest rate reductions by a number of euro area national central banks. As a result
column2: euro area-wide three-month interest rates have now reached a level of 3.8%
column3: which implies a decrease of around 15 basis points since the end of August. These changes underline the fact that the process of the convergence of central bank interest rates in the euro area
column4: which is to be concluded by the end of this year
column5: is clearly under way. The Governing Council considered further interest rate convergence towards the lower end of the current range prevailing in the euro area as being appropriate
column6: given our current knowledge of monetary trends and the prospects for price developments and taking account of an environment characterised by risks of downward pressures. The Governing Council will continue to monitor closely monetary
column7: financial and economic developments within the euro area with a view to determining the appropriate level of money market interest rates for the euro area.

column1: Meanwhile
column2: the Governing Council will continue to monitor closely fiscal intentions in the euro area Member States. The structural budgetary positions in several Member States are still far from being close to balance or in surplus as required by the Stability and Growth Pact. Therefore
column3: these Member States are not yet sufficiently prepared to enable automatic stabilisers to function in the event of a slowdown in real GDP growth
column4: while still respecting the 3% reference value set out in the Treaty and ensuring a decline of debt ratios at an appropriate pace. Moreover
column5: in a number of Member States
column6: against the background of a still favourable and partly better than expected growth performance
column7: short-term budgetary targets appear not to represent structural improvements.

column1: In addition to the review of economic developments
column2: a number of decisions were taken with regard to various aspects of the preparatory work for Stage Three. First and foremost
column3: let me turn to the issue of the monetary policy strategy. I can inform you that at today’s meeting the Governing Council reached agreement on the main features of the stability-oriented monetary policy strategy that the ESCB will pursue in Stage Three of Monetary Union.

column1: Before explaining our decision on the strategy
column2: let me emphasise certain important characteristics of the environment in which the single monetary policy will operate as of next January. Of most concern to the ESCB are some uncertainties which will inevitably arise as a result of the move to Stage Three. These relate
column3: in particular
column4: to the way in which the transition to Stage Three of Monetary Union will affect economic behaviour and institutional and financial structures in the euro area. They also relate to statistical issues.

column1: Against this background
column2: the Governing Council has chosen a distinct monetary policy strategy
column3: one that reflects the special circumstances it faces at present. This strategy will ensure continuity with the successful strategies pursued by participating national central banks in recent years
column4: while taking into account - to the extent needed - the unique situation created by the transition to Monetary Union.

column1: With this context in mind
column2: the Governing Council today agreed on the main elements of the stability-oriented monetary policy strategy of the ESCB. These elements concern:

column1: the quantitative definition of the primary objective of the single monetary policy
column2: price stability;

column1: a prominent role for money with a reference value for the growth of a monetary aggregate; and
a broadly-based assessment of the outlook for future price developments.
First
column2: let me stress that
column3: as mandated by the Treaty establishing the European Community
column4: the maintenance of price stability will be the primary objective of the ESCB. Therefore
column5: the ESCB’s monetary policy strategy will focus strictly on this objective.

column1: In the interest of transparency and in order to give clear guidance with regard to expectations regarding future price developments
column2: the Governing Council of the ECB has agreed to announce a quantitative definition of price stability. In this context
column3: the Governing Council of the ECB has adopted the following definition: ""Price stability shall be defined as a year-on-year increase in the Harmonised Index of Consumer Prices (HICP) for the euro area of below 2%"".

column1: Let me emphasise the fact that price stability is an objective which is to be maintained over the medium term. The current rate of HICP inflation in the euro area is in line with this objective.
Three features of this definition should be highlighted:
first
column2: the HICP is the most appropriate price measure for the ESCB’s definition of price stability. It is the only price index that will be sufficiently harmonised across the euro area at the start of Stage Three.

column1: second
column2: by defining price stability using the HICP ""for the euro area""
column3: the Governing Council of the ECB makes it clear that it will base its decisions on monetary
column4: economic and financial developments in the euro area as a whole. I should like to emphasise the fact that the single monetary policy will adopt a euro area-wide perspective; it will not react to specific regional or national developments.

column1: third
column2: this definition is very much in line with most current definitions adopted by national central banks in the euro area.

column1: Furthermore
column2: the statement that ""price stability is to be maintained over the medium term"" reflects the need for monetary policy to have a forward-looking
column3: medium-term orientation. It also acknowledges the existence of short-term volatility in prices which cannot be controlled by monetary policy.

column1: In order to maintain price stability
column2: the Governing Council of the ECB agreed to adopt a monetary policy strategy which will consist of two key elements.

column1: Deviations of current monetary growth from the reference value would
column2: under normal circumstances
column3: signal risks to price stability. The ESCB will assess how best to counter these risks. However
column4: the concept of a reference value does not imply a commitment on the part of the ESCB to mechanistically correct deviations of monetary growth from the reference value over the short term.

column1: The relationship between actual monetary growth and the pre-announced reference value will be regularly and thoroughly analysed by the Governing Council of the ECB; the result of this analysis and its impact on monetary policy decisions will be explained to the public. The precise definition of the reference aggregate and the specific value of the quantitative reference value for monetary growth will be announced by the Governing Council of the ECB in December 1998.
However
column2: while the monetary aggregates contain important and relevant information for monetary policy-making
column3: monetary developments will not constitute a complete summary of all the information about the economy that needs to be known for an appropriate monetary policy to be set.

column1: Thus the Governing Council will systematically analyse all the information available regarding the prospects for
column2: and the risks to
column3: price stability in the euro area as a whole.

column1: This strategy underlines the strong commitment of the Governing Council of the ECB to its primary objective and should facilitate the achievement of this overriding goal. It will also ensure the transparency of the ESCB’s decision-making and its accountability. Based on its strategy
column2: the Governing Council of the ECB will inform the public regularly and in detail about its assessment of the monetary
column3: economic and financial situation in the euro area and the reasoning behind its specific policy decisions.

column1: This strategy is designed to avoid giving the impression that monetary policy responds ""mechanistically"" to deviations from a single target or changes to a specific variable. The monetary policy strategy that has been selected by the Governing Council of the ECB signals that monetary policy in the euro area will be determined in a manner which will maintain price stability
column2: responding to new developments in or disturbances to the economy in an appropriate manner which is consistent with this overriding objective.

column1: The strategy therefore offers a clear and transparent framework within which the Governing Council of the ECB will be able to assess and present monetary policy decisions.
Please note that the main features of the strategy are also summarised in a press release to be distributed to you.

column1: The Governing Council has also agreed on the approach to be used for estimating the number of euro banknotes to be printed before the launch date of 1 January 2002. The quantity of euro banknotes to be printed will be determined by the number required to replace the stocks of national banknotes in circulation (launch stocks) in the participating EU Member States together with the volume of the logistical stocks needed to ensure that the banknote changeover operates smoothly. It is currently estimated that up to approximately 13 billion euro banknotes will need to be printed before the issue date for the eleven participating Member States. This estimate will be updated regularly as we approach 2002.

column1: Let me start with the Governing Council's discussion on recent economic developments and the decisions that the Governing Council has taken today in the field of monetary policy.

column2: there was consensus that some of the risks identified earlier

column1: Turning to financial indicators
column2: euro area capital markets underwent a correction in February
column3: which was mainly linked to spillovers from the United States and Japan. This followed a decline in long-term interest rates in January which had brought bond yields in the euro area to the lowest levels seen since the late 1940s. The euro area yield curve shifted upwards across the entire maturity spectrum during February. Let me also recall that the nominal effective exchange rate of the euro area in early March stood around 1% below its level on 1 February and around 4% below its starting level on 4 January 1999.

column1: Let me start with the Governing Council's discussion of recent economic developments and the decisions that the Governing Council has taken today in the field of monetary policy. After an in-depth review of recent monetary
column2: financial and economic developments
column3: the Governing Council decided that the interest rate for the ECB's main refinancing operations will

column5: be set at 2.50%. In addition

column1: Let me report in some more detail on the reasons for which the Governing Council
column2: in the context of the ECB's monetary policy strategy
column3: deemed it appropriate to lower interest rates.

column1: As regards monetary developments in the euro area
column2: the acceleration of monetary aggregates seen in January 1999 was partly reversed in February. The 12-month growth rate of M3 declined from 5.6% in January to 5.2% in February. This largely reflected a slowdown in the high pace of growth of overnight deposits
column3: presumably reflecting the unwinding of the influence of some special factors related to the start of Stage Three and the introduction of the euro. As the February figures were somewhat higher than those observed in late 1998
column4: the three-month moving average of M3 growth covering the period from December 1998 to February 1999 still increased by 0.2 percentage point to 5.1%. The Governing Council does not regard current monetary trends as constituting a signal of future inflationary pressures
column5: taking into account that the rate of growth of M3 is still close to the reference value of 4½% and considering that it may to some extent mirror the specific environment related to the start of Stage Three.

column6: it appears unlikely that HICP increases will be out of line with the Eurosystem's definition of price stability.

column1: The Governing Council reviewed the main monetary
column2: financial and other economic indicators in line with its monetary policy strategy. As a result of its examination it decided not to change the ECB interest rates. The interest rate on the main refinancing operations of the Eurosystem will thus remain 2.5%. In addition
column3: the interest rate on the marginal lending facility will continue to be 3.5% and that on the deposit facility has been kept at 1.5%.

column1: Let me give you some details about our latest assessment of the monetary policy stance and thereby explain the decisions taken today.
With regard to monetary developments in the euro area
column2: the three-month moving average of M3 growth
column3: covering the period from March to May 1999
column4: increased slightly to 5.2%
column5: from 5.1% in the three months up to April. Consequently
column6: M3 growth remained above the reference value of 4½%. The major contribution to the rise in M3 growth in May came from overnight deposits. With the exception of repurchase agreements
column7: marketable securities included in M3 also experienced higher growth.

column1: The annual growth rate of total credit to euro area residents rose in May
column2: from 7.3% in April
column3: to 7.9%. The pick-up in credit growth was visible both in loans and in securitised lending and occurred in respect of credit to both the private sector and the general government. The growth of loans to the private sector rose to 10% in May
column4: stimulated by the further decline in bank lending rates. Taken together with the high pace of growth of the most liquid components of M3
column5: this evidence supports the view that households and firms in the euro area do not currently face liquidity constraints. In the view of the Governing Council
column6: this situation is not seen as threatening price stability at present. However
column7: a reassessment may be appropriate if money and credit growth increase further.

column1: Turning to financial market indicators
column2: we have seen a significant upturn in long-term interest rates in the euro area since the end of May. This development was certainly affected by the continued increase in bond yields in the United States over the same period. More recently
column3: however
column4: domestic factors have probably played a more important role in the determination of domestic bond yields than was previously the case. These factors include financial market perceptions of more evidence pointing to a further strengthening in economic activity in the euro area during the year
column5: accompanied by a modest pick-up in inflation expectations from the low levels seen in recent months. The more positive market sentiment regarding the prospects for euro area output growth has also been reflected in a narrowing over recent weeks of the relatively wide differentials between US and euro area bond yields. Exchange rate developments do not yet reflect these very same factors.

column1: As we have said on earlier occasions
column2: the Governing Council believes that the euro is firmly based on internal price stability and therefore
column3: has the clear potential to achieve a stronger external value. The Governing Council reaffirmed its view at today's meeting that the monetary policy of the Eurosystem will safeguard the euro's internal purchasing power and will thereby support its international value.

column1: The prospects for a more broadly based and sustained recovery in the world economy have become stronger. The outlook has improved further
column2: in particular in relation to expectations of continuously strong growth in the US economy and some tentative indications that the prolonged decline in activity in Japan may have come to a halt. In addition
column3: recent developments in economic and financial indicators for the emerging market economies suggest that a recovery is under way in South-East Asia. Moreover
column4: to the extent that the Kosovo conflict may have had a negative impact on economic sentiment in a number of countries
column5: its end has eliminated a risk to the outlook for economic developments in the euro area. As recent developments in Latin America indicate the outlook has improved only moderately.

column1: With reference to developments in economic activity in the euro area
column2: some important data have been released since our last meeting. Most notably
column3: Eurostat has now started to publish euro area national accounts data which are based more closely on data compiled in accordance with the new ESA 95 methodology. According to these estimates
column4: the quarter-on-quarter rate of real GDP growth increased to 0.5% in the first quarter of this year
column5: compared with 0.3% in the previous quarter. At present there is insufficient experience with regard to the properties of the new ESA 95 data
column6: in particular their susceptibility to revision
column7: and some caution should therefore be exercised when interpreting the most recent developments in real GDP growth. However
column8: further evidence supporting the view that growth will recover in the course of this year is also provided by the recent development of other indicators of economic activity. Following successive declines
column9: the level of industrial production appears to have stabilised in the months up to April. Given the developments in industrial confidence up to June
column10: it would appear that the trough was reached at the end of the first quarter. This points to a turning-point in activity in the industrial sector. At the same time
column11: household sector demand patterns appear to be broadly unchanged
column12: as indicated by a still high level of consumer confidence. Therefore
column13: while the signs of recovery are still modest and are not yet reflected in labour market developments
column14: recent data appear to confirm the outlook for a continued improvement in the course of this year. The Governing Council considers it necessary that other policy areas make a decisive contribution to bolstering confidence in the euro area's growth potential
column15: particularly by means of firm structural reform measures to enhance the sustainability of public finances and the efficiency of labour and product markets.

column1: Looking at the latest developments in consumer prices
column2: the annual rate of increase in the Harmonised Index of Consumer Prices (HICP) fell to 1.0% in May
column3: down from 1.1% in April. While energy prices
column4: which had caused the rise in the overall HICP rate in the previous two months
column5: continued to exert some upward pressure
column6: this was more than offset by movements in other components. A lower rate of increase was recorded in May for both processed and unprocessed food prices and for services prices. Hence the decline in the overall HICP rate was also reflected in the HICP rate excluding the two more volatile components - energy and seasonal food. These developments have to be seen partly in the context of a one-off base effect resulting from country-specific increases in indirect taxes which occurred last year. Against this background
column7: the expectation remains that over the next few months the rate of price increases will tend to edge upwards
column8: mainly reflecting the increase in energy prices.

column1: In conclusion
column2: the outlook for the maintenance of price stability in the euro area remains favourable and in line with the Eurosystem's definition of price stability. The Governing Council therefore decided to maintain the prevailing levels of the ECB interest rates. At the same time it noted that the sustained growth of monetary and credit aggregates
column3: the slight improvement in output growth in early 1999
column4: the expectation of a strengthening in economic activity in the course of 1999 and a further acceleration next year all indicate that any upward pressures on prices will have to be monitored very carefully.

column2: in line with its monetary policy strategy. As a result

column7: inter alia
column8: the signs emanating from index-linked bonds issued in the euro area

column1: Developments in the world economy continue to show signs of improvement. Growth in the US economy continues and some positive economic signals have been recorded for Japan. While the outlook for stronger growth in the global economy is also supported by recent developments in other regions
column2: notably South-East Asia
column3: some risks remain
column4: primarily in relation to the strength of the recovery in Latin America.

column1: As regards economic activity in the euro area
column2: industrial production data up to June point to a further improvement in output growth in the second quarter of this year
column3: as has already been indicated by various survey data. Moreover
column4: available evidence in terms of retail sales data and consumer confidence
column5: while somewhat more mixed
column6: suggest broadly sustained consumption growth. These developments are consistent with recently published forecasts
column7: which foresee an upturn in economic growth in the course of this year. The downside risks pertaining to these projections have tended to recede and real GDP growth might eventually turn out to be somewhat higher than currently forecast.

column1: As generally expected
column2: consumer price increases
column3: as measured by the Harmonised Index of Consumer Prices (HICP)
column4: picked up in July
column5: with the annual rate of change rising from 0.9% in June to 1.1% in July. This effectively reversed the downward movement in the overall HICP rate

column10: at this stage we also expect this further increase to level out below the ceiling we have defined as being compatible with price stability over the medium term.

column1: In conclusion
column2: the prospects for a sustained economic upturn in the euro area are good
column3: as are the chances of continued price stability. However
column4: we remain vigilant taking into account the upward risks to price stability. In particular
column5: with a view to conducting a thorough assessment of the risks to price stability in the medium term
column6: the increase in monetary growth over recent months and the high growth rate of credit to the private sector need to be monitored very carefully. In addition
column7: the short-term upward pressure on consumer prices
column8: which stems from the increase in oil prices over recent months and the lagged pass-through of developments in the exchange rate
column9: have to be taken into account. If accompanied by continued wage moderation
column10: these factors alone should not be expected to threaten the current outlook for price stability. Accordingly
column11: the results of the wage bargaining round for the year 2000 will play a particularly important role for the further assessment of price developments in the euro area.

column1: The only way to prolong a non-inflationary recovery
column2: and hence to substantially re-absorb the still very high unemployment
column3: is for all responsible parties to act decisively
column4: in the near term
column5: to increase flexibility in the labour
column6: product and service markets. This would also be the best way to allow the economy to take full advantage from the present stance of monetary policy.

column1: Taking all this information into account
column2: the Governing Council decided to maintain the prevailing ECB interest rates. In addition
column3: it stressed that low inflation and therefore low interest rates should encourage higher investment
column4: helping to prevent the emergence of capacity constraints during economic expansion. At the same time
column5: the expected improvement in economic activity offers greater opportunities to cut fiscal deficits further and to enhance structural reforms. Indeed
column6: the creation of this virtuous circle depends on all policy-makers playing their part.

column1: Let me now give the floor to the Vice-President to introduce three additional topics

the Vice-President and I are here today to report on the outcome of today's meetings of the Governing Council of the ECB

column1: The outcome of today's discussion was that the Governing Council has decided to leave the prevailing ECB interest rates unchanged. The interest rate on the main refinancing operations of the Eurosystem will thus remain 2.5%. In addition
column2: the interest rate on the marginal lending facility will continue to be 3.5% and that on the deposit facility has been kept at 1.5%.

column1: The Governing Council conducted an intensive discussion of the current monetary policy stance in which it was concluded that the balance of risks to price stability remains on an upward trend.
With regard to monetary developments in the euro area
column2: the three-month average of the 12-month growth rates of M3 for the period June to August 1999 increased to 5.6%
column3: from 5.5% in the three-month period ending in July 1999. While a good deal of caution is required when interpreting short-term monetary developments
column4: it should be noted that the 12-month growth rate of M3 has displayed an upward trend during 1999. The high growth of M3 seems to be related to the low level of opportunity costs of holding monetary assets
column5: particularly the most liquid components. Furthermore
column6: the gradual improvement in the real economic situation may have fostered the expansion of M3.

column1: Credit to the private sector also continued to expand at a fast rate in August 1999
column2: namely 10.7%. Since the start of Stage Three credit to the private sector has been expanding at rates of around 10%. Developments in credit growth in August tend to confirm that the demand for loans remains strong
column3: supported by low bank lending rates
column4: indicating that euro area residents do not face borrowing constraints.

column1: On balance
column2: the Governing Council believes that monetary conditions
column3: especially the sustained growth of M3 in excess of the reference value
column4: signal a rather generous liquidity situation in the euro area.

column1: Long-term nominal interest rates in the euro area continued to increase in September. While it is likely that this increase is related to expectations of a recovery of activity in the euro area
column2: expectations of increasing inflationary pressure may also play a role.

column1: The more favourable expectations for economic development in the euro area are partly connected with a further improved outlook for the world economy
column2: as is also reflected in the recent upward revision of the forecast for world growth by the IMF. The growth of the US economy continues to be strong
column3: and in Japan economic indicators are now more clearly pointing towards an improvement in economic activity. In addition
column4: in some Asian countries the recovery in growth appears to be taking place somewhat earlier than expected. Notwithstanding individual downside risks in the countries I have just mentioned and a more general uncertainty regarding the recovery in Latin America
column5: the world economy seems to be set for higher growth.

column1: As regards economic activity in the euro area
column2: some important data have been released since we last met. A first estimate by Eurostat for real GDP growth in the second quarter of 1999 points to slightly lower quarter-on-quarter growth compared with the first quarter of this year. However
column3: these data do not appear to impinge on the view that there is an upturn in growth in the course of this year. In fact
column4: industrial production data for the period up to July confirm the gradual improvement of recent months
column5: and various survey data suggest that there was a further strengthening of output growth in the industrial sector over the summer months. Evidence for the consumer sector continues to point to broadly robust consumption growth. The outlook for a continuing improvement in overall activity therefore remains favourable.

column1: In line with our expectations
column2: the annual rate of change in the Harmonised Index of Consumer Prices (HICP) saw a further rise in August 1999 to 1.2%
column3: up from 1.1% a month earlier. This upward movement was mainly caused by the ongoing increase in oil prices. Some counterweight came from a decline in unprocessed food prices and from a lower rate of increase in services prices. Largely reflecting this development in services prices
column4: the HICP rate excluding more volatile components - namely energy and seasonal food - declined to 0.9% in August
column5: having risen to 1.0% in July. Oil prices continued to increase further in September and
column6: given the relatively short time of pass-through to consumer prices
column7: expectations of further increases in the overall HICP rate in the coming months have become firmer.

column1: In conclusion
column2: monetary and credit developments indicate that continuous close attention must be given to upward risks to price stability. In the light of the medium-term orientation of the Eurosystem's monetary policy
column3: the rising trend of M3 growth calls for great vigilance on the part of monetary policy. The recent increase in oil prices will continue to impose additional upward pressure on the HICP. Seen in isolation
column4: the increase in energy prices should have only a temporary effect upon consumer price increases
column5: but it is essential that this effect does not trigger wage claims which prove incompatible with price stability in the medium term.

column1: Against the background of the medium-term outlook for a sustained acceleration in economic activity
column2: decisive structural reform is warranted in order to prevent early upward pressure on prices. In fact
column3: the Governing Council sees a strong case for enhancing structural reform in labour and product markets. The anticipation of an expected cyclical improvement should not lead to a weakening of efforts in this regard
column4: but rather it should be used as a welcome opportunity to make convincing progress. This
column5: together with continued wage moderation and fiscal adjustment in line with the Stability and Growth Pact
column6: would greatly facilitate the monetary policy task of maintaining price stability in an environment of stronger growth.

1999-11-04;1;Ladies and gentlemen
the Vice-President and I are here to report on today's meeting of the Governing Council of the ECB.

The outcome of today's meeting was that the Governing Council has decided to increase the ECB interest rates. The forthcoming main refinancing operations of the Eurosystem will be conducted as fixed rate tenders at an interest rate of 3.0%
column2: starting with the operation to be settled on 10 November 1999. This increase implies an upward adjustment of 50 basis points from the rate of 2.5% applied to previous such operations. In addition
column3: the interest rate on the marginal lending facility will be increased from 3.5% to 4.0% and that on the deposit facility from 1.5% to 2.0%
column4: both with effect from 5 November 1999.

column1: Overall
column2: on the basis of prospective developments
column3: the Governing Council considers that today's decision will counter the upward trend of the balance of risks to price stability. This decision will therefore contribute to sustaining non-inflationary economic growth in the euro area over the medium term.

column1: The main argument for raising the interest rates was the fact that since around the beginning of the summer the balance of risks to future price stability has gradually been moving towards the upside. In fact
column2: the economic situation in spring 1999 had given rise to concern about downward risks and had led to a precautionary interest rate reduction by 50 basis points on 8 April 1999. However
column3: the current economic environment is far more favourable. Moreover
column4: several indicators
column5: including monetary growth
column6: suggest that there is ample liquidity in the euro area. Inflation rates are expected to increase gradually in the months ahead
column7: mainly as a result of the increase in energy prices earlier this year working its way through to consumer prices. The latest data on industrial producer prices confirm this pattern. Over the medium term
column8: however
column9: it is important to prevent the availability of ample liquidity from translating into upward pressure on prices. In particular
column10: an increase in interest rates now should help to counteract further liquidity growth over the medium term and contribute to maintaining inflation expectations safely below 2%.

column1: With regard to the perception that an increase in interest rates now would endanger the resumption of economic growth
column2: the Governing Council is of the opposite opinion. A timely rise in interest rates will avoid the need for a larger increase in interest rates later and
column3: hence
column4: will contribute to stronger growth over an extended period of time.

column1: Concerning the size of an increase in interest rates
column2: against the background of a fundamentally changed situation
column3: the precautionary interest rate reduction made in April 1999 is no longer justified. Furthermore
column4: today's move by 50 basis points appeared to be the best way in which to avoid uncertainties regarding the future course of monetary policy. In addition
column5: such a move is expected to contribute to reducing any uncertainty premia potentially prevalent in financial markets and also to help to contain a possible increase in volatility in money markets towards the end of the year. Under these circumstances
column6: the alternative of moving by less than 50 basis points now and examining the need for an additional step later on could potentially introduce unwarranted uncertainty for the period ahead.

column1: Let me now provide you with more detailed information on monetary
column2: financial and other economic developments
column3: and thereby further explain the decisions taken today.

column1: With regard to monetary developments in the euro area
column2: the monetary data up to September 1999 reinforced the view that M3 growth is on a rising trend. The three-month average of the annual growth rates of M3
column3: covering the period from July to September 1999
column4: was 5.9%
column5: which is almost 1½ percentage points above the reference value of 4½%. This deviation from the reference value has steadily increased during 1999. The strong growth of the most liquid components of M3 is particularly noteworthy
column6: suggesting that the very low level of interest rates favoured the strong growth of monetary aggregates. The pick-up in economic activity is likely to have further stimulated M3 growth. Credit to the private sector also continued to expand rapidly in September 1999
column7: at a rate in excess of 10%. The demand for loans remained strong throughout the first three quarters of 1999
column8: supported in particular by the low level of bank lending rates and the ongoing economic recovery. Overall
column9: these developments indicate a generous liquidity situation in the euro area.

column1: Euro area financial market developments over the past few months confirm the general change in economic conditions and perspectives for the euro area by also anticipating an acceleration of economic growth. This is reflected in the rise in government bond yields and the associated pronounced steepening of the yield curve since spring 1999. Today's decision should contribute to firming financial market expectations of stronger growth without increasing inflationary pressures.
With regard to economic activity itself
column2: current information indeed continues to support the view that there is an ongoing strengthening in the euro area. The outlook for the world economy remains positive; this mainly relates to the sustained growth of the US economy
column3: but also to the apparent strengthening of the recoveries in South-East Asia and Japan. Most recent data releases for the euro area suggest an acceleration of real GDP growth rates in the second half of this year. This is indicated by confidence and survey data
column4: as well as by production data for the industrial sector extending into the third quarter of the year. Therefore
column5: the prospects for a continued improvement in output growth remain good.

column1: Concerning consumer prices
column2: in September 1999 the annual rate of change in the Harmonised Index of Consumer Prices (HICP) was 1.2%
column3: that is to say unchanged from August 1999. On the one hand
column4: upward pressures related to the surge in oil prices in recent months and to the rate of change in prices for seasonal food. On the other hand
column5: in September the increases in both services prices and prices for non-energy industrial goods were more moderate than in August. Countervailing price movements of such a kind may possibly continue in the coming months
column6: while expectations remain that there will be some overall upward movement in the HICP rate in the short term
column7: which will mainly be linked to energy prices.

column1: In conclusion
column2: the downside risks to price stability have disappeared. Instead
column3: monetary developments
column4: together with the accumulating evidence of improved economic prospects
column5: confirmed the view expressed earlier by the Governing Council that the balance of risks to future price stability has gradually moved towards the upside. This assessment argued in favour of adjusting the interest rates within the context of a monetary policy stance which is conducive to maintaining price stability over the medium term.

column1: Containing inflationary expectations in a forward-looking manner is decisive for ensuring sustainable growth in GDP and employment. This would be greatly facilitated if individual member countries were to make convincing progress in the structural reform of the labour and product markets
column2: which
column3: over the medium term
column4: would enhance the euro area's production potential and thereby curb upward pressure on prices as the recovery proceeds. Together with fiscal consolidation in the context of the Stability and Growth Pact and the necessary moderate wage developments
column5: such reforms could make a crucial contribution towards transforming the current cyclical upswing into a process of longer-term non-inflationary growth.

column1: Let me first report that the Governing Council decided to confirm the reference value for monetary growth
column2: namely an annual growth rate of 4½% for the broad aggregate M3. This decision was taken on the grounds that the components underlying the derivation of the first reference value in December 1998

column4: have remained unchanged.

column1: As before

column3: with the next review to take place in December 2000.

column1: Against this background
column2: the Governing Council wishes to emphasise that the trend growth potential of the euro area could be considerably enhanced by structural reform in the labour and goods markets. The Eurosystem's monetary policy strategy would take such changes into account
column3: as appropriate. The derivation of the reference value of 4½% is an expression of a medium-term-oriented approach. The generous liquidity situation in 1999 will have to be borne in mind.

column1: The ECB will issue a press release today providing some background information on the review of the reference value carried out today by the Governing Council. The press release will also recall the role of the reference value within the Eurosystem's monetary policy strategy.

column2: this time including a review of the most recent forecasts and projections. After this examination
column3: the interest rate on the main refinancing operations of the Eurosystem was left at 3.0% and the interest rates on the marginal lending facility and on the deposit facility were maintained at 4.0% and 2.0% respectively.

column1: Allow me to outline the main elements of our assessment of the latest information on monetary
column2: financial market and other economic developments.

column1: With regard to monetary developments in the euro area
column2: the data up to October 1999 - which still refer to the period before our decision to raise interest rates - confirmed the picture of a generous liquidity situation in the euro area. column3: covering the period from August to October 1999
column4: was unchanged at 6.0%
column5: and thus stood 1½ percentage points above the reference value of 4½%. The growth of the most liquid components of M3 remained very dynamic. In addition
column6: the annual growth rate of credit to the private sector continued to exceed 10%. As we have noted on previous occasions
column7: these monetary and credit developments are considered to have been driven mainly by the low level of interest rates
column8: as well as by the pick-up in economic activity in the euro area.

column1: The initial reaction of euro area financial markets to the Eurosystem's monetary policy move of last month was favourable. In particular
column2: this was signalled by the continued decline in long-term government bond yields and the immediate substantial reduction in market uncertainty regarding the evolution of future long-term interest rates. Later in November
column3: long-term bond yields in the euro area began to rise again gradually
column4: in connection with developments in international bond markets and favourable expectations for world growth.

column1: Indeed
column2: the global economic outlook remains positive
column3: and the view that the world economy is set for higher growth appears to be shared by the major international organisations. At the same time
column4: the expectation that growth differentials between the main economic regions will narrow in the course of time is widespread. While real GDP growth in the United States is generally expected to ease
column5: it is expected to accelerate in the euro area. Overall
column6: relatively wide growth differentials between the major world economies will give way to a more balanced scenario
column7: thereby underlining the potential for the euro to appreciate.

column1: With regard to developments in economic activity in the euro area
column2: the latest data confirm a strengthening of growth in the course of the second half of 1999. In particular
column3: production growth in the industrial sector saw a further upturn in the third quarter and various survey data suggest that this will continue in the final quarter. All available projections indicate that this upward momentum will lead to an acceleration in real GDP growth
column4: from around 2% this year to close to 3% in both 2000 and 2001.

column1: Consumer price increases
column2: as measured by the Harmonised Index of Consumer Prices (HICP)
column3: have recently resumed their upward trend
column4: as expected. In October the annual rate of change in the overall HICP was 1.4%
column5: up from 1.2% in September and August owing to higher price increases for food and non-energy industrial goods. The impact of higher oil prices on energy prices in the HICP
column6: which had accounted for most of the upward pressure since June 1999
column7: was countered in October by more moderate increases in other energy components. Some additional counterweight to the upward movement in goods prices came from a further moderation of increases in prices in the services sector. In general
column8: the overall upward trend is expected to continue until early 2000 as a result of the increase in oil prices since spring 1999. Forecasts available suggest that price increases will nevertheless remain below 2% in the course of 2000 and 2001. However
column9: the actual developments will very much depend on the behaviour of a number of factors

column12: these relate to
column13: inter alia
column14: the behaviour of money and credit aggregates

column17: main factors are linked to the effects of deregulation and liberalisation.

column1: In conclusion
column2: the current monetary policy stance should ensure a sustainable expansion of non-inflationary economic activity in the euro area. In line with its monetary policy strategy
column3: the Governing Council will remain vigilant with regard to any risks to price stability arising either from domestic or from external sources and act in a timely manner.

column1: Let me now give the floor to the Vice-President to introduce some of the additional topics we discussed during our meetings.

column1: The Governing Council today conducted its regular examination of the current outlook for price developments and the risks to price stability in the euro area. column2: covering the period from September to November 1999
column3: was 6.0%

column2: as we have already noted
column3: it is clear that they were able to weather the century date change without encountering any major problems. column2: note was taken of the fact that activity in the world economy is continuing to gain momentum as projections for world output growth have been revised upwards recently. This mainly reflects the sustained and high level of growth of the US economy

column3: which is similar to the situation observed in previous months. The annual rate of change in the overall HICP was 1.6%

column10: in particular
column11: that it does not trigger second round effects such as excessive wage claims. Indeed
column12: stability-oriented behaviour is urgently required.

column2: the available indicators confirm our previous analysis and assessment on the overall situation as regards the risks to price stability. Against this background
column3: we remain both confident and vigilant.

column3: price and cost increases - including oil and non-energy commodity prices as well as producer prices - have been larger and more protracted than foreseen earlier and hence indicate risks of ""second round"" effects. Such risks
column4: which are of a more enduring nature
column5: are further increased by the fact that the international environment is showing continuous signs of improvement and the prospects of a cyclical upswing in the euro area are very strong. Indeed
column6: internal and external factors reinforce one another and thereby contribute to intensifying the growth of the real GDP of the euro area. The depreciation of the euro which we have witnessed is contributing to increases in import prices.

column1: Timely and appropriate monetary policy adjustments should ensure that these risks are kept under control
column2: so that risk premia in financial markets will be diminished. The Governing Council's determination to counter threats of inflation should assure wage negotiators that the prospects for price stability remain favourable. In fact
column3: it will be important to ensure that wage settlements themselves do not constitute a threat to price stability in the medium term.

column1: Starting with the first pillar

column1: Turning to the second pillar
column2: long-term nominal interest rates signal increased expectations of a lasting upswing in the euro area economy. Between the end of December 1999 and the end of January 2000 ten-year government bond yields in the euro area increased further to reach the highest level observed since late 1997.

column2: activity is also accelerating in other industrialised countries and the recovery is strong in both Asian and Latin American emerging market economies.

column3: and larger and more protracted commodity and producer price increases are heightening the risk of second round effects. Against this background it is crucial for wage negotiators to be able to rely on the maintenance of price stability in the medium term.

column1: The Governing Council conducted its regular examination of the outlook for price developments in the euro area. After reviewing the evidence available from both the first and the second pillar of the monetary policy strategy of the Eurosystem
column2: the Governing Council decided to maintain the interest rate on the main refinancing operations of the Eurosystem at 3.25% and the interest rate on the marginal lending facility and that on the deposit facility at 4.25% and 2.25% respectively
column3: i.e. at the levels determined a month ago. The Governing Council also concluded that the balance of risks to price stability in the medium term remains on the upside. These upside risks will need to be monitored and assessed continuously in order to ensure that timely action can be taken
column4: if and when required.

column1: The main elements of our assessment of the latest information on monetary
column2: financial market and other economic developments are as follows.

column1: Starting with the monetary indicators covered under the first pillar of the monetary policy strategy
column2: the three-month average of the annual growth rates of M3 for the period from November 1999 to January 2000 was 5.7%
column3: compared with 6.0% in the last quarter of 1999. The reduction was determined by a base effect
column4: since the monthly increase in M3 in January 1999 was exceptionally strong
column5: reflecting the special environment at the start of Stage Three of Economic and Monetary Union. At the same time
column6: the annual growth rate of credit to the private sector remained high
column7: at 9.5% in January 2000. Overall
column8: the prolonged deviation of M3 growth from the reference value of 4½%
column9: especially when seen in conjunction with the dynamic growth of credit
column10: indicates that liquidity conditions in the euro area remain generous.

column1: With regard to the second pillar
column2: as usual
column3: the Governing Council examined a broad range of indicators. Starting with long-term nominal interest rates
column4: there was little change in the course of February. The yield curve remained relatively steep
column5: thus indicating expectations of strong economic growth in the period ahead.

column1: Such expectations are partly based on the favourable outlook for the world economy. A key element underlying this positive outlook is the fact that the US economy is continuing to grow at a high rate
column2: but the strong recovery and the acceleration of growth in other areas also support this view. The strongest level of performance is currently being recorded in emerging market economies in South-East Asia
column3: while the broad outlook in Japan remains uncertain.

column1: There is also further evidence that economic activity in the euro area continued to expand strongly after the third quarter of last year. While euro area estimates for the fourth quarter of 1999 are not yet available
column2: data for individual Member States point to continued robust output growth. In addition
column3: area-wide industrial confidence increased further around the turn of the year and consumer confidence remained at the high level reached in the last two months of 1999. The cyclical upswing should extend well into 2000 and continue thereafter. This is also confirmed by available forecasts
column4: which point to real GDP growth of slightly over 3% in 2000. As for 2001
column5: the economic expansion in the euro area is generally expected to continue at a similar pace.

column1: Developments in the exchange rate of the euro
column2: which do not reflect the underlying strength of the euro area economy
column3: remain a cause for concern. Their upward impact on import prices is having a negative effect on the price climate and is thereby increasing the risks to price stability in the medium term.

column3: the upward movement has continued. In January 2000 the annual rate of HICP inflation was 2.0%

column7: on an annual basis
column8: reached 12.0% in January. Excluding the more volatile components
column9: namely energy and seasonal food
column10: HICP inflation in January increased slightly to 1.1% on account of somewhat higher price increases for non-energy industrial goods.

column8: developments in monetary and credit aggregates will need to be analysed continuously in order to assess upward risks to price stability. Second
column9: in view of the improving economic conditions

column11: developments in the exchange rate and in oil prices will play a major role.

column1: I should like to take the opportunity of this special meeting to take stock of where we stand 15 months after the start of Monetary Union. In January 1999 the euro was successfully launched as the single currency for 11 Member States of the EU. As a result of very careful conceptual and technical preparations
column2: both the monetary policy-making process and the implementation of monetary policy have functioned efficiently right from the start.

column1: The challenges involved in setting up a central bank for a currency area as large as the euro area have been enormous. The Eurosystem - which comprises the European Central Bank and the 11 national central banks of the countries which have adopted the euro - has met these challenges with success. This would not have been possible without a strong willingness to co-operate on the part of the actors involved. I should like to take this opportunity once again to thank all the members of the Governing Council and the staff of the Eurosystem for this.
From the start
column2: we had extremely productive and open discussions in the Governing Council on monetary policy issues. In this respect
column3: our monetary policy strategy has provided a very useful framework within which to organise our thinking. In our discussions there has always been a clear understanding
column4: based on the Treaty
column5: that the single monetary policy can only focus on maintaining price stability in the euro area as a whole. This is based on the simple fact that in a monetary union
column6: there is only one monetary policy
column7: and this must be directed to a single objective. As laid down in the Treaty
column8: each member of the Governing Council is therefore well aware that he or she is not a representative of a country or central bank but acts in a personal capacity in deciding the appropriate conduct of monetary policy for the euro area as a whole.

column1: The move to the single currency and the introduction of the euro were based on a degree of convergence towards price stability in participating countries that few observers would have predicted some years ago. In 1999 the average rate of consumer price increases in the euro area as a whole was among the lowest recorded since the Second World War and
column3: remained fully consistent with price stability. At the same time
column4: Monetary Union does not mean perfect identity of economic conditions in all parts of the euro area. The experience of all larger currency areas shows that some differences in regional price developments and also in regional output growth may exist.

column1: As differences in national or regional developments cannot be addressed by the Eurosystem
column2: they require
column3: whenever necessary
column4: country-specific responses. This means
column5: in particular
column6: responsible national wage settlements and appropriate national fiscal policies aimed at counteracting specific national problems. In addition
column7: reforms addressing rigidities in labour and product markets and aiming at enhancing labour and capital mobility are the tools to ensure that market mechanisms will play an increasingly important role in limiting the scope for divergent developments in the euro area.

column1: The single monetary policy offers a great opportunity to maintain price stability in the euro area and to create the conditions needed for sustained economic growth. Currently
column2: the prospects for strong economic growth in the euro area are very favourable - indeed
column3: more favourable than they have been for many years. Economic activity in the euro area strengthened markedly in the second half of 1999 and this upswing is expected to continue through 2000 and beyond. Available forecasts point to real GDP growth of slightly over 3% in 2000 and 2001
column4: reflecting both the favourable external environment and strong domestic demand. In line with this positive outlook
column5: employment is expected to increase further and unemployment to come down in this context.

column1: The Governing Council today conducted its regular examination of the outlook for price developments and the risks to price stability in the euro area. Following this review
column2: the Governing Council decided to maintain the interest rate on the main refinancing operations of the Eurosystem at 3.5% and to keep the interest rates on the marginal lending facility and on the deposit facility at 4.5% and 2.5% respectively.

column1: Allow me to give you an overview of the main elements of our assessment of the latest information on monetary
column2: financial market and other economic developments.

column1: Let me start with information in relation to the first pillar of our monetary policy strategy. No new monetary data have been released since the last meeting of the Governing Council
column2: which was held in Madrid on 30 March 2000. The annual growth rate of M3 in February 2000 was 6.2%. This implied a small increase in the three-month moving average of annual M3 growth
column4: from 5.8% recorded for the three-month period from November 1999 to January 2000. M3 growth thus remained around 1 1/2 percentage points above the reference value of 4 1/2%. The picture of generous liquidity conditions in the euro area is also confirmed by the continued strong annual rate of growth of loans to the private sector
column5: which stood at 10.5% in February.

column1: With regard to economic developments in the euro area
column2: following strong growth of real GDP in the second half of 1999
column3: most recent production and survey data suggest that the economic expansion also remained strong in early 2000. In particular
column4: both consumer and industrial confidence have now reached levels which are close to the highest observed since the mid-1980s. This picture of strong growth of domestic demand supports the favourable outlook for economic growth in the euro area as depicted in recent forecasts. The positive prospects for euro area activity also benefit from the strong cyclical upswing in the world economy
column5: which has become more broadly based across industrial and emerging economies and which is expected to continue in the years to come.

column1: The exchange rate of the euro does not reflect the ongoing improvement in domestic fundamentals in the euro area economy. In nominal effective terms
column2: the euro was around 4% lower in mid-April than at the beginning of the year and approximately 14% below its level in the first quarter of last year. Until reversed
column3: this development will put upward pressure on import prices and will continue to affect the risks for price stability in the euro area.

column3: to a large extent
column4: from the combined effects of both oil price and exchange rate developments. The annual rate of change in the HICP rose to 2.0% in February 2000
column5: from 1.9% in the previous month. The rate of inflation on producer prices also rose further in February 2000
column6: mainly in connection with rising prices for intermediate goods.

column2: namely that the oil price increases which we observed until March will partially unwind in the course of the year. At the same time
column3: it is most likely that the complete upward impact on consumer prices via import and producer prices of the oil price and exchange rate developments in recent months has not yet materialised. Against this background

column5: before falling back to lower levels.

column2: however

column1: The Eurosystem will remain vigilant in assessing upside risks to price stability and will take appropriate action if and when required. A forward-looking monetary policy which responds to risks to price stability before they materialise will avoid the need for a costly stabilisation of inflation at a later stage. Such a forward-looking approach is clearly also the best contribution monetary policy can make to ensuring the sustainability of the process of economic growth.

This phase of economic growth in the euro area will offer a great opportunity to make further progress in bringing down the high level of unemployment in the euro area. An important means of achieving this will be continued wage moderation
column2: which
column3: in turn
column4: will also help to contain inflationary pressure. This notwithstanding
column5: as I have stressed repeatedly in the past
column6: the key to achieving a sustainable reduction in the level of unemployment will be structural reforms in the euro area
column7: including a lowering of the tax burden and an improvement in the fiscal expenditure structure. Only when labour markets are more flexible and competitive pressures are high will it be possible to prevent bottlenecks from triggering upward pressures on prices at a relatively early stage of an economic recovery.

column1: Fiscal policy has to play its part in this context. The favourable economic prospects will lead to higher tax revenues. In line with the Stability and Growth Pact
column2: it is not opportune to use these extra revenues for higher spending. Now is the time to speed up fiscal consolidation in order to help to reduce further the debt-to-GDP ratios in the Community and to approach more quickly fiscal budgetary positions in surplus or balance.

column1: Let me now give the floor to the Vice-President to present some of the additional topics discussed today by the Governing Council.

column3: such arrangements cannot be regarded as a substitute for two years' participation in ERM II. column4: it should be clearly understood that a common accord would have to be reached on the central parity against the euro.

column1: With a view to further enhancing the ECB's transparency policy
column2: the Governing Council has today decided to publish all non-confidential legal instruments governing the relationship between the ECB and the euro area national central banks in the Official Journal of the European Communities. column1: The Governing Council conducted its regular examination of the outlook for price developments and the risks to price stability in the euro area. The interest rate on the main refinancing operations of the Eurosystem was left at 3.75% and the interest rates on the marginal lending facility and the deposit facility were maintained at 4.75% and 2.75% respectively.
Allow me to give you an overview of the main elements of our assessment of the latest information on monetary
column2: financial market and other economic developments.

column1: In March 2000 the three-month average of the annual growth rates of M3 - covering the period from January to March 2000 - rose to 6.0%
column2: compared with 5.9% in the period from December 1999 to February 2000. Consequently
column3: M3 growth remained 1 1/2 percentage points above the reference value of 4 1/2%. The annual rate of increase in credit to the private sector also rose
column5: compared with 10.4% in the previous month. These figures confirm our earlier assessment
column6: namely that liquidity continued to be ample in the euro area in early 2000.

column1: As regards economic developments
column2: recent information confirms the very positive outlook for strong growth in the euro area. All available indicators and forecasts seem to point to a phase of continued economic growth
column3: following the upturn observed in the second half of 1999. Industrial production rebounded in February and this
column4: together with further increases in capacity utilisation and industrial confidence up to April
column5: suggests an ongoing strengthening in industrial activity. In addition
column6: with consumer confidence remaining at an all-time high and unemployment continuing to decline
column7: the recent strength of private consumption should be sustained. Looking at the world economy
column8: the upturn in growth has become more broadly based
column9: pertaining to both industrial and emerging economies
column10: and most forecasts indicate that current growth differentials between economic areas are in the course of narrowing.

column1: Notwithstanding the strong growth performance and favourable outlook for euro area economic activity
column2: the exchange rate of the euro has continued to decline over the past few weeks and has thereby moved further out of line with the increasingly positive economic fundamentals of the euro area
column3: as well as international balance of payments positions.

column1: In March consumer price inflation
column2: as measured by increases in the Harmonised Index of Consumer Prices (HICP)
column3: rose to 2.1%
column4: up from 2.0% in the previous month. This was due to developments in both oil prices and exchange rates. A moderation in 12-month inflation rates can be expected in the course of 2000
column5: reflecting the decline in oil prices from around mid-March and base effects dampening the increase in inflation rates compared with the same month a year earlier. However
column6: what matters for monetary policy are the trends underlying the outlook for price stability in the medium term. In this respect
column7: the depreciation of the exchange rate of the euro
column8: until it is reversed
column9: will increase the risks to price stability in the medium term. These risks have to be taken seriously in the light of the current strong upswing. Other important factors which will have a crucial impact on the outlook for price stability over the medium term are a continuation of currently moderate wage developments
column10: a further fiscal consolidation in line with the Stability and Growth Pact and the further implementation of structural reforms in product and labour markets.

column1: Over recent months the risks to price stability in the medium term have clearly continued to increase. This assessment has been supported by the information from both the first pillar and the second pillar of the Eurosystem's monetary policy strategy. With regard to the first pillar
column2: strong growth of money and credit throughout 1999 and the pronounced expansion of money and credit aggregates over the first four months of 2000 have strengthened the view that liquidity conditions are ample. As for the second pillar
column3: in a phase of strong growth upward risks to price stability currently relate mainly to the spillover of rising import prices to consumer prices
column4: owing both to the lagged effects of the exchange rate depreciation and to rising oil prices. In fact
column5: most inflation forecasts have been revised upwards over recent months. This is a matter of concern. Today's increase in ECB interest rates is a decisive step to address these upside risks to price stability and it will contribute to the continuation of non-inflationary growth in the euro area.

column1: Allow me to give you a more detailed overview of the main elements of our assessment of monetary
column2: financial market and other economic developments.

column1: Let me start by addressing the latest monetary developments in the euro area. The three-month average of the annual growth rates of M3
column2: covering the period from February to April 2000
column3: was 6.3%
column4: i.e. significantly above the reference value of 4 1/2%. Thus
column5: the most recent M3 data confirm that the liquidity situation in the euro area continues to be very generous. M3 growth deviated from the reference value in 1999 and growth rates increased further in early 2000. This picture of very generous liquidity conditions in the euro area is complemented by the rapid expansion of credit to the private sector
column6: which remained close to or above 10% throughout 1999 and exceeded 11% in April 2000. Taken together
column7: such developments would clearly point to upside risks to price stability over the medium term
column8: if not counteracted in time.

column1: Turning to the second pillar
column2: we have to consider economic and financial market developments as well as consumer price developments.

column1: Looking at economic developments
column2: the outlook for growth in the euro area has improved markedly over the past few months. Overall
column3: indicators for economic activity released since the end of last year point to continued strong growth
column4: following the upturn in real GDP growth in the second half of 1999. All the forecasts currently available from major international organisations and private institutions now project real GDP growth to be above 3% this year and next year
column5: which is significantly higher than expected at the end of last year. This positive outlook reflects favourable domestic and external conditions for growth. On the domestic side
column6: expansion of private consumption and investment should benefit
column7: in particular
column8: from ongoing employment growth and higher rates of capacity utilisation. Domestic demand is also supported by high business and consumer confidence. On the external side
column9: the upturn of growth in the world economy appears to be stronger
column10: faster and more broadly based than was expected at the end of last year. Hence
column11: euro area exports should remain strong.

column1: Financial market developments also support the view that the economic expansion in the euro area is set to continue at a fast pace. Moreover
column2: the exchange rate of the euro appreciated at the end of May and in the first few days of June
column3: also reflecting expectations that robust economic growth will continue in the euro area. Notwithstanding the recent appreciation of the euro
column4: the extent and duration of its previous depreciation will still exert upward pressure on consumer prices.

column1: Against this background
column2: the outlook for consumer price developments had become less favourable prior to today's meeting. In April 2000 inflation - as measured by the Harmonised Index of Consumer Prices (HICP) - was 1.9%
column3: following 2.1% in March. In the immediate future
column4: the strong rise in oil prices in May 2000 is pointing to renewed short-term upward pressures. Looking further ahead
column5: all available forecasts for consumer price inflation for this year and next are now higher than they were at the end of 1999. Current projections of a rate of inflation of around 2% in 2000 and 2001 are clear warning signals.

column1: In conclusion
column2: with today's decisions the Governing Council has acted in a forward-looking manner in order to contribute to the maintenance of favourable conditions for a lasting
column3: non-inflationary economic expansion. This should help other economic actors to rely firmly on the maintenance of price stability in the medium term. They are also called upon to contribute to price stability and growth by means of appropriate wage settlements compatible with employment growth
column4: structural reform and fiscal consolidation. At the current juncture
column5: they are especially encouraged to press ahead with structural reform
column6: and governments are particularly urged to avoid a pro-cyclical loosening of fiscal policies. This is particularly important in those countries where there is a risk of overheating.

column1: The Governing Council conducted its regular examination of recent monetary and economic developments and their implications for the risks to future price stability in the euro area. Subsequently
column2: it decided to keep the interest rates on the Eurosystem's monetary policy instruments unchanged. Thus the minimum bid rate in the main refinancing operations of the Eurosystem was left at 4.25%
column3: and the interest rates on the marginal lending facility and the deposit facility were kept unchanged at 5.25% and 3.25% respectively.

Current bond market yields continue to show market expectations of a period of sustained economic growth in the euro area. At the same time
column2: the accumulated depreciation of the exchange rate of the euro remains a cause for concern and has to be taken into account in the assessment of the risks to price stability.

column1: Overall
column2: the outlook for price stability will be affected by several factors
column3: which will need to be monitored carefully. First

column1: Let me now give the floor to the Vice-President to say a few words about other issues discussed by the Governing Council.
