column2: I should like to address the euro banknote-related issue concerning the determination of the number of banknotes to be printed before the launch date of 1 January 2002. The latest forecast shows that there will be a need to put 14 billion euro banknotes into circulation
column3: compared with last year's estimate of 13 billion. The increase can be attributed to three main factors: a higher than expected figure for national banknotes in circulation
column4: which forms the basis of estimates of the launch stocks; a higher forecast for the use of low-denomination banknotes; and a somewhat slower than previously expected development in the use of electronic money.

column1: Second
column2: the Governing Council also had an exchange of views on recent developments in the EU banking industry. The discussion was based on preparatory work by the Banking Supervision Committee. The Governing Council is well aware that the current process of consolidation is no longer confined to small and medium-sized banks - as it was in the past - but that now it also covers the larger banks at the national level and cross-border mergers and alliances are on the increase. The role of the euro as a factor encouraging this process of consolidation via further integration of money and capital markets is important. The consolidation process is welcome in general since it allows efficiency gains to be achieved in the banking sector. On the other hand

column1: The Governing Council of the ECB today conducted its regular examination of recent monetary and economic developments and their implications for the risks to future price stability in the euro area. Subsequently
column2: it decided to keep the interest rates on the Eurosystem's monetary policy instruments unchanged. Thus
column3: the minimum bid rate in the main refinancing operations of the Eurosystem was left at 4.50%
column4: and the interest rates on the marginal lending facility and the deposit facility were kept at 5.50% and 3.50%

column1: Allow me to give you an overview of the main elements of our assessment of the latest information on monetary
column2: financial market and other economic developments.

column1: As regards the developments in the context of the first pillar of the monetary policy strategy of the ECB
column2: no new monetary data have become available since our decision taken on 31 August 2000 to raise the main ECB interest rates. After having increased at a very strong pace in the first quarter of 2000
column3: M3 growth has been showing some signs of moderation over recent months. This moderation has mainly been a consequence of lower growth in the most liquid components of M3
column4: which bear little or no remuneration
column5: indicating that the monetary policy measures taken since November 1999 are gradually feeding their way through. At the same time
column6: the average of annual M3 growth rates for the period from May to July 2000
column8: continued to deviate on the upside from the reference value of 4 1/2%. In the context of the robust expansion of economic activity
column9: continued ample liquidity conditions would constitute a risk to price stability.

column1: Turning to the second pillar
column2: real GDP growth in the euro area
column3: according to first estimates published by Eurostat today
column4: reached 3 3/4% (on an annualised basis) in the first half of 2000. Currently available forecasts predict that growth will remain above 3% next year. The strength of the euro area's economic expansion in the past few months is in line with these forecasts. In fact
column5: recent indicators suggest that
column6: following the period of acceleration
column7: the economic expansion may now have settled at a high rate of growth. The overall level of confidence has remained at
column8: or close to
column9: record highs in recent months. Moreover

column11: these factors should underpin the growth of private consumption and investment

column1: The positive outlook for the euro area is also supported by external developments. The outlook for growth of the world economy
column2: and thus for growth of euro area exports
column3: has remained favourable. Forecasts of world growth have consistently been revised upwards over the past few months.

column1: Expectations of a period of sustained economic growth in the euro area can also be found in euro area bond markets. Overall
column2: longer-term bond yields in the euro area have shown a very high level of stability in the course of this year

column1: The annual rate of increase in the Harmonised Index of Consumer Prices (HICP) was 2.4% in July 2000. Recent consumer price developments in the euro area have been very much influenced by the strong rise in oil prices and the depreciation of the exchange rate of the euro.
While monetary policy cannot address short-term developments in prices
column2: it is imperative for monetary policy that medium-term upward pressure on prices be contained. The risk that the current pressure on the HICP might spill over onto costs and prices determined in the domestic economy must be taken seriously. This holds true in particular in the context of the favourable prospects for economic growth.

column1: The Governing Council reacted to this picture by raising the main ECB interest rates at its meeting on 31 August 2000. This step followed a series of interest rate increases implemented since November 1999. The Governing Council will continue to remain alert to emerging risks to price stability.
It is a matter of fact that recent oil price increases have caused the terms of trade of the euro area to deteriorate
column2: and thus have also reduced real income. This loss of real income cannot be avoided for the economy as a whole. Attempts to shift the burden of this loss within the economy will risk endangering the continuation of a non-inflationary growth process.

column1: For the maintenance of price stability
column2: it will be particularly important
column3: in the current phase of strengthening economic growth
column4: that wages continue
column5: on average
column6: to grow at rates compatible with the objective of price stability. Any attempt for wages to catch up in reaction to recent oil price increases would be highly detrimental to the current favourable growth prospects
column7: since monetary policy would need to react to the resulting upward pressure on prices.

column1: Governments also have to play a role in order not to convey the false impression that the costs stemming from the increase in oil prices could be avoided by relaxing budgetary policies. This would not be in line with the needs of establishing budget positions in balance or in surplus and would complicate the fostering of tax reforms conducive to a stronger growth potential of the euro area.

I should also like to reiterate that the prospects for a stronger potential for growth in the euro area will depend very much on progress made in enhancing the flexibility of labour and goods markets in the euro area. Although reform efforts in several countries have been heading in the right direction
column2: there is still much to be done when looking at the area as a whole.

column3: with the objective of sustaining price stability in the euro area over the medium term. column4: there is still no decisive evidence that measurable and lasting increases in productivity growth in the euro area would warrant a significant upward revision in the assumption for trend potential growth. This notwithstanding

column6: the Governing Council will carefully monitor further evidence with regard to an acceleration of productivity growth in the euro area. The Governing Council also wishes to emphasise that potential output growth could be strengthened by further structural reforms in the labour and goods markets. Naturally
column7: the ECB's monetary policy will take such changes appropriately into account. The ECB will issue a press release today to provide some background information on the review of the reference value carried out by the Governing Council.

column1: The Governing Council also conducted its regular examination of monetary and economic developments and their implications for the maintenance of price stability in the euro area. column1: The Governing Council conducted its regular examination of monetary and economic developments and their implications for the maintenance of price stability in the euro area. The decision to keep interest rates unchanged reflects the Governing Council's assessment that the risks to price stability in the medium term now appear more balanced than at the end of last year. Factors which might pose upward risks to price stability in the medium term are still present and as such will be subject to ongoing close monitoring.
Let me elaborate on this assessment. Starting with the first pillar of the monetary policy strategy of the ECB
column2: monetary data for December 2000 confirmed the gradual moderation of the growth of monetary aggregates which has been observed since the spring of last year. According to the latest data
column3: the three-month average of the annual growth rates of M3 in the months from October to December 2000 stood at 5.0%
column4: which was slightly lower than the average of 5.1% recorded for the period from September to November 2000. Therefore
column5: after the recent slowdown in monetary growth
column6: the risks to price stability from the monetary side have become increasingly balanced. Caution still needs to be exercised
column7: however
column8: given the continued dynamics in credit growth to the private sector and the upward deviation of M3 from the reference value in the past.

column1: Turning to the examination under the second pillar
column2: broadly similar indications are emerging
column3: as inflationary impulses resulting from previous developments in oil prices and the external value of the euro are gradually diminishing.

column1: As regards economic activity
column2: uncertainty concerning the external environment for the euro area has increased
column3: mainly related to signals that the slowdown in growth in the United States may be more significant than earlier expected. This is likely to result
column4: directly and via a spillover to other regions
column5: in some deceleration of growth in the world economy. World real GDP growth
column6: which in 2000 posted its strongest performance for many years
column7: may therefore moderate in 2001 but will still remain at an acceptable level.

column1: This deceleration will clearly have some dampening effects on euro area net exports. The euro area is a large economy where exports of goods and services amount to around 17% of GDP only. Economic activity in the euro area is therefore determined mainly by domestic factors. Overall
column2: the fundamentals of the euro area remain broadly favourable. While
column3: as recently published data show
column4: real GDP growth slowed somewhat in the second half of last year
column5: the level of business and household confidence has remained high
column6: supported by
column7: inter alia
column8: high degrees of capacity utilisation and ongoing unemployment declines. Moreover
column9: real income in the private sector will benefit from lower oil prices and from the reductions in direct taxes in 2001. Hence
column10: while downside risks to real GDP growth exist
column11: growth is very likely to continue at a reasonably robust pace.

column1: Developments in the euro area bond markets are in line with this outlook for economic activity. Moreover
column2: inflationary expectations implied by bond yields confirm that the financial markets expect current levels of consumer price inflation to be temporary
column3: and price stability to be maintained in the medium term. This assessment may also have been reinforced by the recent moderation in oil prices and the movement of the euro exchange rate in the period since the end of October 2000.

column1: Lower oil prices and the appreciation of the euro have already produced some effects on price developments. In December 2000 the annual rate of increase in the Harmonised Index of Consumer Prices (HICP) declined to 2.6%
column2: from 2.9% in November. A confirmation of recent developments in oil prices and the euro exchange rate would contribute to a further downward adjustment of overall HICP inflation in the period ahead. Over the near term
column3: this process may be slowed down by the delayed impact of past import price increases and possibly also by some transitory further food price rises caused by the current health issues associated with beef consumption. It may therefore take some time for HICP inflation to move back below 2%.

column1: Notwithstanding the assessment that the risks to price stability are now more balanced
column2: there are still factors posing upside risks which therefore require continued attention. These are mainly related to potential second-round effects on wages of the past increases in import prices
column3: as well as to bottlenecks and shortages in labour markets. For the medium term
column4: it remains paramount that wage developments remain moderate.

column1: In addition
column2: it is crucial that structural adjustments continue. This requires sustained labour market reforms
column3: continuing liberalisation of product markets and further integration in the financial services sector
column4: all of which will expand economic activity and increase employment. It is equally important that further progress be achieved in the area of fiscal policy reform
column5: with continuing progress in fiscal consolidation through limits in public spending growth
column6: allowing both a reduction in remaining budget deficits and an alleviation of the fiscal burden on corporations and households without threatening or slowing the progress in fiscal consolidation.

column1: Overall
column2: the existence of the euro and the single monetary policy has provided the euro area with an institutional setting which leaves it significantly less exposed to external influences. Within the euro area the maintenance of price stability over the medium term
column3: together with further progress on structural reforms
column4: will provide an important contribution to the achievement of sustained non-inflationary economic growth and will thereby also support a further solid and sustainable expansion of the world economy.

column1: The Governing Council conducted its regular examination of monetary and economic developments and analysed their implications for the maintenance of price stability in the euro area. It decided to lower the key ECB interest rates by 25 basis points. This reduction is to be seen as an adjustment of the level of interest rates to somewhat lower inflationary pressure over the medium term. On the basis of the information available
column2: this is the appropriate level of interest rates to ensure that the euro area economy will be able to maintain price stability and thereby to contribute to sound economic growth over the coming years. In order to explain today's monetary policy decisions in some more detail
column3: let me share with you our assessment of the information provided under the two pillars of the ECB's monetary policy strategy.

column1: As regards the first pillar
column2: also taking into account the latest available information
column3: monetary developments no longer pose a risk to price stability. M3 growth has been on a gradual downward trend since spring 2000
column4: reflecting the increase in the key ECB interest rates which occurred in the period from November 1999. The three-month average of the annual growth rates of M3 was 4.8% in the period from January to March 2001
column5: which is close to the reference value of 4 1/2%. In the past few months
column6: some slowdown in credit aggregates has also been visible. In addition
column7: as already stated on several occasions
column8: there have been indications that the monetary growth figures are distorted upwards by non-euro area residents' purchases of negotiable paper included in M3. This has now been confirmed by clear evidence
column9: and the magnitudes involved are significant. As regards holdings of money market fund units/shares by non-euro area residents
column10: on which we now have solid statistical data
column11: the distortion has become more sizeable over recent months and currently amounts to around half a percentage point. In addition
column12: there have been non-negligible upward distortions to the annual growth of M3 as a result of non-euro area residents' holdings of other marketable paper included in M3
column13: for which precise statistical information is currently being developed. The ECB will keep the public informed about ongoing developments in these categories of M3. As these factors can be broadly identified
column14: the information content under the first pillar is ensured. Taking into account these upward distortions
column15: as well as all information from the first pillar
column16: it can now be concluded that there is no longer a risk to price stability over the medium term emanating from the first pillar.

column1: As regards the second pillar

column3: however
column4: requires continued monitoring of growth trends and wage developments
column5: in particular.

column1: The Governing Council has to focus on the outlook for price stability in the medium term as only this perspective allows for the time lags for monetary policy to work its way through the economy. The information under the first pillar indicates that price stability can be maintained over a medium-term horizon. The information under the second pillar indicates that upward pressure on prices can be contained. The Governing Council will continue to monitor wage developments as well as external and domestic demand trends. The picture from the two pillars taken together is positive. At the same time it underlines the need to remain vigilant.

Fiscal policy will have to continue the consolidation process in line with the Stability and Growth Pact and the commitments made in the context of the stability programmes. The avoidance of inflationary pressures on a permanent basis in an environment of solid growth requires that governments and social partners implement decisively the structural measures in labour and product markets that are essential for lifting the growth potential of the euro area.

column1: As usual
column2: we conducted our regular examination of monetary and economic developments and analysed their implications for the maintenance of price stability in the euro area. The Governing Council decided to keep the key ECB interest rates unchanged. It considers that the current monetary policy stance remains appropriate and should bring inflation back in line with price stability in the medium term. Maintaining a favourable perspective for price stability is the best contribution monetary policy can make to fostering economic growth over the long run.

column1: The Governing Council conducted a comprehensive examination of recent monetary and economic developments in order to assess the prospects for the maintenance of price stability in the euro area over the medium term. It concluded that the information which has become available since the Governing Council meeting of 8 November confirmed our expectations and thereby also the forward-looking decisions taken over the past few months by the Governing Council. Against this background
column2: the Governing Council decided to keep the key ECB interest rates unchanged. The Governing Council continues to consider the current level of key ECB interest rates appropriate.

column1: Starting with the analysis under the first pillar of our monetary policy strategy
column2: the three-month average of the annual growth rates of M3 rose to 6.8% in the period from August to October 2001. This was significantly above the medium-term reference value for annual M3 growth of 4 ½%.

column1: We confirmed this value of 4 ½% today in our annual review of the reference value. This decision was taken on the grounds that the evidence continues to support the medium-term assumptions underlying the derivation of the reference value
column2: namely those for trend potential output growth of 2-2 ½% per annum and for a trend decline in M3 income velocity of ½-1% per annum in the euro area. We will issue a separate press release today providing further background to the confirmation of the reference value.

column1: In comparing current developments with the reference value we have to keep in mind that the reference value is a medium-term concept. Short-run movements of M3 may stem from a number of temporary factors and do not necessarily have implications for future price developments. For this reason the Governing Council made it clear already in 1998 that the announcement of the reference value does not entail a commitment on the part of the ECB to correct mechanistically deviations of monetary growth from the reference value. Rather
column2: developments of M3 are thoroughly analysed by the ECB
column3: in conjunction with other monetary indicators and information from the second pillar
column4: in order to ascertain their implications for the risks to price stability over the medium term.

column3: investors have shifted their portfolios towards liquid and relatively safe short-term assets included in M3. column1: At today's meeting
column2: the Governing Council continued its comprehensive examination of monetary
column3: financial and economic developments and assessed new evidence that has become available over the past few weeks. Our conclusion was that while risks to price stability over the medium term remain tilted to the upside
column4: recent evidence sends mixed signals. Against this background
column5: the Governing Council decided to leave the key ECB interest rates unchanged.

column1: As regards the analysis under the first pillar of our monetary policy strategy
column2: the three-month average of the annual growth rates of M3 increased to 7.5% in the period from March to May 2002
column3: from 7.4% in the period from February to April. While there was some normalisation of M3 growth in early 2002
column4: M3 dynamics have strengthened again recently. This development may partly reflect renewed portfolio shifts into M3 instruments
column5: related to the recent increase in overall financial market uncertainty. However
column6: more fundamental factors
column7: such as the low opportunity cost of holding money and the economic recovery in the euro area have also driven monetary expansion in recent months. In addition
column8: the rate of growth of loans to the private sector has been recovering. While due caution in interpreting recent short-term monetary developments is warranted
column9: it is a matter of concern that there is significantly more liquidity available in the euro area than would be needed to finance sustainable
column10: non-inflationary economic growth.

column1: Concerning the second pillar
column2: the latest data confirm that a gradual recovery in real GDP growth in the euro area is under way. Information from several surveys and leading indicators for the second quarter of this year point to somewhat higher real GDP growth rates than in the first quarter. Looking ahead
column3: an ongoing strengthening in both domestic and foreign demand continues to be the most likely scenario. The conditions for further recovery in the euro area remain in place. There are no major imbalances in the euro area and financing conditions are very favourable. At the same time
column4: there is continued economic growth outside the euro area. However
column5: in view of recent financial market developments
column6: the uncertainty surrounding the strength of the economic upturn – both outside and inside the euro area – has not diminished over recent weeks.

column1: Turning to price developments
column2: Eurostat's flash estimate indicates that annual HICP inflation fell from 2.0% in May to 1.7% in June. However
column3: it is too early to interpret this fall as a sign of receding upward pressure on prices
column4: given that HICP inflation excluding the more volatile items of energy and unprocessed food prices has remained high throughout the first half of this year
column5: reflecting in particular trends in services prices. Moreover
column6: it is to be expected that overall HICP inflation rates will fluctuate around 2% in the coming months.

column1: The strengthening of the euro exchange rate should have a moderating effect on inflation. However
column2: it is difficult to quantify the size and establish the timing of this effect. For price stability to be maintained on a sustainable basis it is crucial that the high wage increases resulting from recent negotiations in some regions do not spread across the euro area
column3: not least because this would have negative consequences for competitiveness
column4: employment growth and consumption.

column1: Overall
column2: the strengthening of the euro exchange rate is a new factor suggesting a potential for lower inflation rates. However
column3: other factors – in particular monetary developments and wage trends – do not indicate a moderation in price pressures. Monetary policy therefore needs to remain vigilant as regards the key factors determining the outlook for price stability over the medium term.

column1: Regarding fiscal policies in the euro area
column2: we have seen some worrying developments in the past few months. Against this background we call upon all member countries to honour the commitments made to achieve budgets that are close to balance or in surplus by 2003-04
column3: in compliance with the framework of the Stability and Growth Pact. This is necessary in order to maintain and further strengthen confidence in the policy framework of the euro area and to establish fiscal positions in all countries that allow automatic stabilisers to operate efficiently without endangering sound fiscal positions in the longer term. Moreover
column4: governments are encouraged to push ahead with reforms relating to the size and structure of public expenditure and revenue
column5: which will also create room for tax cuts and absorb the fiscal costs of population ageing.

column1: In the field of structural reforms allow me to refer briefly to the adoption of the Broad Economic Policy Guidelines. If implemented in a determined manner
column2: structural reforms will contribute to expanding the euro area's potential for non-inflationary growth and to reducing its high level of unemployment.

column1: At today's meeting

column1: As regards the analysis under the first pillar of our monetary policy strategy
column2: the three-month average of the annual growth rates of M3 was 7.3% in the period from May to July 2002

The recent strength in M3 growth partly reflects both the low opportunity cost of holding money and renewed portfolio shifts into M3 in an environment of financial market uncertainty. In this context
column5: monetary trends need to be assessed with caution. From a longer-term perspective
column6: there is concern that more liquidity is available in the euro area than would be needed to finance sustainable
column7: non-inflationary economic growth. However
column8: at this juncture
column9: there is less risk that excess liquidity will translate into inflationary pressure
column10: given the environment of subdued demand. The trend in the growth of loans to the private sector also seems to point in this direction.

column1: Concerning the second pillar
column2: the latest data confirm a modest recovery in real GDP growth in the euro area in the first half of this year. In the second quarter of this year real GDP growth is estimated to have grown by 0.3% quarter on quarter
column3: following upwardly revised growth of 0.4% in the first quarter. In contrast to the first quarter
column4: developments in demand appear to have been more broadly based
column5: as activity was supported by private consumption
column6: export growth and inventories. However
column7: overall domestic demand growth remained subdued as a result of the protracted weakness of investment.

column1: Looking ahead
column2: the most likely scenario is that of ongoing
column3: albeit modest
column4: growth in real GDP in the second half of this year
column5: with growth rates in line with potential growth in 2003. This delay in the acceleration of economic activity in the euro area broadly corresponds with the world economic outlook
column6: given that the expected pace of the recovery has been scaled down over recent months. Sharp declines in stock prices are having negative effects on consumer and investor confidence. Consequently
column7: the strength of the upturn in economic activity has become more uncertain
column8: both inside and outside the euro area. At the same time
column9: however
column10: the conditions for a stronger economic recovery in the euro area remain in place. On the domestic side
column11: private consumption should particularly benefit from lower inflation and improved real disposable income

column13: the gradual recovery of the global economy is also expected to continue. Nevertheless
column14: risks to the economic outlook
column15: both inside and outside the euro area
column16: need to be monitored closely.

column4: its first decline in 2002. Eurostat's flash estimate for August

column1: Overall
column2: subdued aggregate demand and the strengthening of the euro should contribute to lower inflationary pressure. At the same time
column3: other factors – in particular monetary developments
column4: but also wage trends and oil price developments – might pose risks to price stability in the medium term and therefore need to be monitored closely.

column1: Regarding fiscal policies in the euro area
column2: flood-related costs should lead to a review of priorities and a reallocation of expenditure. In addition

column4: it seems to be more warranted than ever to call on member countries to remain committed to the Stability and Growth Pact. Countries with sound fiscal positions should safeguard their achievements
column5: while countries with remaining imbalances must avoid deficits in excess of 3% of GDP and implement determined policies in order to progress towards budgets close to balance or in surplus. This is essential for maintaining and further strengthening confidence in the policy framework in the euro area and for establishing fiscal positions in all countries that allow automatic stabilisers to work efficiently without endangering sound fiscal positions in the longer term.

column1: We have reviewed monetary
column2: financial and economic developments and have incorporated new information into our assessment. Overall
column3: the current monetary policy stance remains appropriate to preserve a favourable outlook for price stability in the medium term. Consequently
column4: we have kept our key interest rates unchanged. Their low level should help counterbalance the negative effects on economic activity that currently stem from the high degree of worldwide uncertainty and should
column5: thereby
column6: contribute to a sustainable economic recovery in the course of 2003. For the time being
column7: we still assume that the high degree of uncertainty will decline in the course of this year. However

column11: and the euro area in particular.

column1: Turning to the analysis under the first pillar of our monetary policy strategy
column2: the three-month average of the annual growth rates of M3 declined to 6.9% in the period from October to December 2002
column3: from 7.1% in the period from September to November 2002. The continued strong monetary growth reflects an ongoing pronounced preference for liquidity in an environment of high financial
column4: economic and geopolitical uncertainty. However
column5: it also mirrors the low level of short-term and long-term interest rates in the euro area.

column1: Although liquidity remains ample
column2: it is unlikely at this stage that it will give rise to inflationary pressures
column3: given the current economic environment and the expectation that some of the portfolio shifts will be reversed once the financial market uncertainty diminishes. This assessment is also supported by the continuing moderate growth of loans to the private sector.

column1: As regards the information under the second pillar
column2: economic activity in the euro area remained subdued around the turn of the year
column3: as suggested by recently published data and survey information. These indications are broadly in line with previous expectations which suggest a gradual increase
column4: starting in the second half of the year
column5: in real GDP growth rates to levels close to potential. Whereas the appreciation of the euro over recent months may contribute to dampening export growth to some extent
column6: the price competitiveness of euro area companies remains favourable in a medium-term perspective and export growth should benefit from the expected recovery of the world economy. Therefore
column7: recent exchange rate movements should not fundamentally affect the main scenario for the economic outlook.

column1: At the same time
column2: several factors contributing to the general climate of uncertainty are still in place. In particular
column3: investors remain risk averse against the background of ongoing geopolitical tension. Further turbulence in the oil markets could have a negative impact on economic activity throughout the world and
column4: thereby
column5: also on euro area employment. These concerns are also weighing on consumer confidence. Finally
column6: the accumulated macroeconomic imbalances give rise to uncertainty about the strength of the recovery in other major economies. Taken together
column7: there remain downside risks to the outlook for euro area economic activity.

column1: Considering price developments
column2: according to Eurostat's flash estimate

column1: Beyond the immediate future

column4: should reduce inflationary pressures. The most likely outcome remains that inflation will fall and eventually stabilise at a level below 2% in the course of 2003. column5: the indications for this are still mixed

column4: economic and geopolitical uncertainty. Although liquidity remains ample

column1: 2003-06-05;1;"Ladies and gentlemen
column2: the Vice-President and I will now report on the outcome of today's meeting of the Governing Council of the ECB.

column1: Following a comprehensive economic and monetary analysis
column2: we have concluded that the outlook for price stability over the medium term has improved significantly since our last decision to lower interest rates in March. As a result
column3: we have decided to reduce our key interest rates by 50 basis points. This decision is in line with our monetary policy strategy
column4: including the aim of maintaining inflation rates below but close to 2% over the medium term. At the same time
column5: this interest rate reduction takes into account the downside risks to economic growth. The Governing Council will continue to monitor carefully all factors which are relevant to its assessment.

column1: Let me explain our assessment in detail.
In the context of our economic analysis
column2: the latest data releases on real GDP growth have confirmed that economic activity in the euro area remained subdued in the first quarter of this year. This outcome also reflects the negative impact of the Iraq crisis on both the global economy and the euro area. However
column3: the survey evidence for April and May does not suggest an immediate improvement after the resolution of this conflict and is at best mixed. Accordingly
column4: economic growth in the first half of 2003 is likely to be very weak
column5: and expectations for annual average economic growth for this year and for 2004 have had to be scaled down.

column1: Nevertheless
column2: we still expect a gradual strengthening of real GDP growth in the course of 2003
column3: which should gather more pace next year. All available forecasts as well as recent financial market reactions seem to reflect a similar assessment. The main factors supporting this outlook are both external and domestic in nature.

column1: On the external side
column2: the expected upturn in extra-euro area demand should compensate for the dampening effect of the appreciation of the euro. Evidently
column3: the significant and rapid appreciation of the euro over recent months will dampen external price competitiveness. However
column4: the current level of the euro's real effective exchange rate
column5: and thereby the competitive position of euro area exporters
column6: is very close to longer-term averages. Thus
column7: when put into perspective
column8: current euro exchange rate levels are in line with economic fundamentals and with our interest in a strong and stable euro.

column1: On the domestic side
column2: private consumption growth should recover further from the second half of 2003 onwards. This would reflect the growth in real disposable income supported by positive terms of trade effects and lower inflation rates. Moreover
column3: there are no significant imbalances in the household sector as a whole that would hinder such a recovery. At the same time
column4: the contribution of investment to growth is likely to remain more modest
column5: although an improvement in the global economic environment and the historically low level of interest rates should contribute to an upswing.

column1: The Governing Council is conscious of the continuing downside risks to economic growth. Notably
column2: risks stem from the past accumulation of macroeconomic imbalances outside the euro area
column3: and there are ongoing concerns with regard to the SARS virus. In addition
column4: some uncertainty remains as to the extent of the adjustment still needed in the euro area corporate sector to enhance productivity and profitability. This could also have an impact on employment growth and thus private consumption.

column1: Given this environment
column2: the outlook for price developments has become more favourable. Following Eurostat's flash estimate of the inflation rate for May of 1.9%
column3: annual inflation rates are expected to hover broadly around this level for the remainder of this year and to fall significantly in 2004. This assessment is based on the assumption of favourable import prices
column4: reflecting both generally stable oil price developments and the higher exchange rate
column5: as well as lower domestic price pressure in the context of a moderate economic recovery. In particular
column6: wage growth is expected to remain broadly stable. Coupled with productivity gains
column7: this should therefore result in a moderation of unit labour costs.

column1: In the context of our monetary analysis
column2: we saw persistent strong growth in the broad monetary aggregate M3. Consequently
column3: the euro area economy has continued to accumulate liquidity significantly above the amount needed to sustain non-inflationary growth.

column1: There are
column2: however
column3: several considerations which counterbalance concerns that this ample liquidity will lead to inflationary pressures over the medium term. In particular
column4: monetary developments continue to be fostered by portfolio shifts
column5: reflecting a sustained preference on the part of investors for liquid and secure assets. This is confirmed by evidence from both the components and counterparts of M3. Indeed
column6: loans to the private sector increased at a much more moderate pace than M3. Moreover
column7: higher monetary growth was accompanied by a much lower net acquisition of foreign equity by non-MFI euro area residents
column8: also implying portfolio reallocations away from riskier assets. Consequently
column9: the portfolio shifts that have affected M3 growth over the past two years should unwind over time. Finally
column10: the perspective that economic activity will remain moderate reduces the likelihood of excess liquidity giving rise to increased spending. Nevertheless
column11: one has to bear in mind that monetary growth is also supported by the low level of interest rates. Therefore
column12: monetary developments need to be closely monitored with respect to their implications for price stability over the medium to long term.

column1: Summing up our economic analysis
column2: it currently appears that inflation rates should decline to below 2% over the medium term
column3: following recent movements in the exchange rate of the euro and given the sluggish growth performance of the euro area. Our monetary analysis indicates that the strong expansion of M3 should not for the time being adversely affect this outlook. Hence
column4: cross-checking the information from the two pillars leads us to conclude that the outlook for price stability over the medium term has become more favourable.

column1: Let me at this point comment on the debate about the hypothetical risk of deflation. As far as the euro area is concerned
column2: it should be recalled that inflation has been hovering around 2% for quite some time and that there are currently no forecasts indicating any deflationary risks. The ECB's monetary policy aims at inflation of below but close to 2% over the medium term. In this respect
column3: inflation expectations should remain well anchored at this level
column4: irrespective of shorter-term developments in prices. At the regional level
column5: a period of relatively low price increases or even price level declines will improve a region's competitiveness within the currency area. Within a monetary union
column6: deflation is not a meaningful concept when applied to individual regions.

column1: At this juncture
column2: it may be particularly warranted to stress that monetary policy cannot by itself generate lasting and sustainable growth and employment in the euro area. This can only be achieved by appropriate structural measures that address fundamental weaknesses and tackle urgent adjustment requirements. In this respect
column3: fiscal policies have a great potential for fostering confidence and thereby supporting activity
column4: even in the short run. Establishing a well designed medium-term consolidation strategy in those countries currently struggling with increasing fiscal imbalances would make a major contribution in this direction. This would imply comprehensive and growth-friendly measures including
column5: in particular
column6: a courageous reform of the structure and level of public expenditure. Curbing spending growth would eventually also create further room for manoeuvre to address future pressure arising from pension systems and scope for future tax cuts. Procedurally
column7: it is crucial to underpin the fiscal policy framework with a decisive and consistent implementation of the rules of the Treaty and of the Stability and Growth Pact
column8: and rigorous monitoring and peer pressure amongst Member States.

column1: By the same measure
column2: bold structural reforms in the labour and product markets would not only increase the euro area's growth potential and enhance its ability to better withstand external shocks
column3: but it would also eliminate a great deal of the uncertainty currently overshadowing long-term planning and perspectives. This
column4: in turn
column5: would also have positive effects over the shorter term. In particular
column6: renewed momentum in the process of structural reform would foster consumer and investor confidence and thereby greatly facilitate spending and investment decisions in the euro area.

column7: counteracting the effects of the loss of price competitiveness. On the domestic side

2003-11-06;2;Ladies and gentlemen

Today marks the first time that I had the honour and the pleasure of chairing the meeting of the Governing Council of the ECB. I am delighted to now proceed with our well-established practice of real-time communication and to report on the outcome of our meeting
column2: together with the Vice-President.

column1: Following our regular economic and monetary analysis
column2: we have decided to leave the key ECB interest rates unchanged at their low levels. Overall
column3: we anticipate some further stickiness of inflation rates in the shorter term
column4: while the medium-term outlook for price stability remains favourable. Against this background
column5: we continue to judge the current stance of monetary policy as appropriate. At the same time
column6: we see additional signs of a gradual economic recovery in the euro area. We will carefully monitor all developments that might affect our assessment of risks to price stability.

column1: Let me now explain our decision in more detail.
Starting with the economic analysis
column2: new data and other information show that the recovery of the world economy is clearly making progress. Also for the euro area
column3: the indicators are increasingly pointing towards some improvement in economic activity in the second half of this year. For the time being
column4: this is primarily reflected in business surveys and leading indicators
column5: but we expect that forthcoming data on euro area production and demand will confirm that a gradual recovery has started.

column1: Taken together
column2: we see further confirmation of our main scenario of a gradual improvement in economic activity this year
column3: and a broadening and strengthening in the course of 2004. This assessment has received support from recently published forecasts of official and private sources
column4: as well as from developments in financial markets. Externally
column5: the expansion of global economic trade and real GDP growth should counteract the changes in the effective exchange rate of the euro
column6: which is back to its level of early 1999. Domestically
column7: the conditions for investment should improve further
column8: given the continued adjustment efforts of firms to enhance productivity and profitability
column9: the low level of interest rates and generally favourable financing conditions. Moreover
column10: private consumption should benefit from real disposable income growth
column11: fostered by positive terms-of-trade effects stemming from the past appreciation of the euro.

column1: The short-term risks to our main scenario appear to be balanced. Over a longer horizon
column2: we remain concerned about the sustainability of global economic growth being undermined by persisting imbalances. This relates
column3: in particular
column4: to the sustainability of public finances and to external imbalances in some regions of the world.

column1: Recent inflation rates
column2: measured by the HICP
column3: developed broadly as anticipated. The annual rate of inflation was 2.1% in October
column4: according to Eurostat's flash estimate. It thus remained unchanged from August and September. When looking ahead over the shorter term
column5: it appears that inflation rates may continue to hover around this level for several months to come and
column6: hence
column7: may not fall as quickly and strongly as had been expected up to the summer. Three factors can be identified as contributing to this stickiness of inflation rates. First
column8: in the remainder of 2003 and early 2004
column9: unprocessed food prices could imply some limited upward pressure as a consequence of this summer's heat wave. Second
column10: oil prices remain higher than expected
column11: owing to political uncertainties in the Middle East. Last but not least
column12: in the course of 2004
column13: planned increases in indirect taxes and administered prices in some euro area countries will have an upward impact on inflation.

column1: However
column2: when taking into account more lasting factors
column3: we continue to expect inflation rates to moderate over the medium term and to develop in line with price stability. This expectation is based on the assumption that wage developments will not be affected by the current inertia of inflation rates
column4: and will remain moderate in the context of a gradual economic recovery. Moreover
column5: the past appreciation of the euro should continue to dampen price pressures. These views are also reflected in recently released forecasts. At the same time
column6: inflation expectations warrant close monitoring.

column1: Turning to the monetary analysis
column2: after an extended period of strong M3 growth
column3: liquidity in the euro area remains ample
column4: despite a certain slowdown in monetary expansion over recent months. This situation of persistently more liquidity than is needed to finance non-inflationary economic growth reflects past portfolio shifts
column5: precautionary savings and the low level of interest rates. The low level of interest rates also supported the annual growth of loans to the private sector
column6: which fluctuated between 4½% and 5% in recent months. At the current juncture
column7: the accumulation of excess liquidity is not of concern for price stability
column8: given the economic outlook. However
column9: if it were to continue in conjunction with a significant strengthening of economic activity
column10: it could lead to inflationary pressures in the medium term.

column1: Cross-checking the information from the two pillars
column2: our economic analysis indicates that the medium-term outlook for price stability remains favourable
column3: in the context of a gradual economic recovery and moderate import price and wage developments. In view of the economic situation
column4: the strong monetary expansion should not
column5: for the time being
column6: be seen as adversely affecting this outlook.

column1: Fiscal developments and the Stability and Growth Pact are now at a critical point at which the credibility of the institutional underpinnings of EMU must be maintained. The Treaty and the Stability and Growth Pact provide an appropriate framework for ensuring fiscal discipline
column2: within adequate bounds of flexibility. The deficit reference value of 3% of GDP
column3: which is laid down in the Maastricht Treaty itself
column4: is the nominal anchor for the rules and procedures governing fiscal policies in the EU. This anchor must not be placed in doubt.

column1: Fully abiding by the rules and implementing them in every respect has very solid economic justifications
column2: and is not a mere procedural matter. Upholding trust in the soundness of public finances enhances confidence of all economic agents and thereby contributes to sustainable growth in consumption and investment. Stability and growth are thus not conflicting objectives
column3: but rather reinforce each other – a fact which is very well captured in the title of the fiscal framework called the ""Stability and Growth Pact"". Concerning recent developments in the context of the excessive deficit procedure
column4: it is the view of the Governing Council that the proposals of the Commission push the room for interpretation of the rules and procedures to the limit. As regards future decisions
column5: which are expected in the course of November
column6: the Governing Council strongly urges each institution and government concerned to live up to their responsibilities. It is the overall credibility of the fiscal framework and
column7: hence
column8: the prospects for economic growth in the euro area that are at stake.

column1: Fiscal consolidation plans are best placed within a comprehensive and credible medium-term strategy. This requires strong emphasis on structural expenditure reforms and the adaptation of public pension and health systems to the challenges arising from the ageing of the population. Moreover
column2: structural reforms in the labour and product markets are needed to allow a better allocation and utilisation of capital and human resources
column3: and to enhance the euro area's growth potential. The Governing Council strongly supports current efforts by a number of governments in this direction and also encourages social partners to fully commit themselves to the objective of making the euro area a more dynamic and innovative economy.

column2: the Vice-President and I will now report on the outcome of today's meeting of the Governing Council of the ECB.

column1: Following a comprehensive economic and monetary analysis
column2: we concluded that the monetary policy stance remains appropriate to preserve price stability over the medium term. Accordingly
column3: we left the key ECB interest rates unchanged at their low levels. While annual inflation rates are likely to fluctuate around 2% over the coming months
column4: a gradual and limited decline should take place later on. We also noted that the economic recovery in the euro area has started and that confidence has strengthened further. We will continue to carefully monitor all developments that might affect our medium-term assessment of risks to price stability.

column1: We also discussed the potential implications of the deeply regrettable developments at the ECOFIN Council meeting on 25 November. As we already stressed in our statement on the same day
column2: these developments risk undermining the credibility of the institutional framework and the confidence in sound public finances of Member States across the euro area. Let me add that a credible fiscal framework is key not only to stability but also to growth
column3: and is a precondition for low risk premia in financial markets to be preserved.

column1: I shall now explain our assessment in more detail.
In the context of our economic analysis
column2: the latest data releases confirmed that economic activity in the euro area has picked up. Real GDP growth in the third quarter reflects the strong momentum of the world economy
column3: which we assume will continue next year.

column1: We expect that domestic demand will start improving. Private consumption should be supported by positive terms-of-trade effects due to the past appreciation of the euro. With the usual lag
column2: it should also profit from an increase in employment growth. Business investment is expected to recover gradually
column3: mainly helped by an expansion of external demand
column4: the low level of interest rates and generally favourable financing conditions. Moreover
column5: it should increasingly benefit from the adjustment efforts of the corporate sector to enhance productivity and profitability.

column1: Taken together
column2: we look forward to a gradual recovery in euro area economic growth over the next quarters
column3: leading to a broader and stronger upswing in the course of next year and the year after. The risks to this scenario appear to be balanced. Over a longer horizon
column4: we remain concerned about the sustainability of global economic growth being undermined by external imbalances in some parts of the world economy.

column1: Concerning prices
column2: the latest information is in line with earlier expectations. According to Eurostat's flash estimate
column3: annual HICP inflation was 2.2% in November
column4: following a rate of 2.0% in October. Similar rates have prevailed for most of this year and this inertia of inflation rates at around 2% is likely to continue in the coming months. Due to adverse food price developments
column5: the evolution of oil prices and planned increases in indirect taxes and administered prices
column6: inflation rates will fall neither as quickly nor as strongly as was expected earlier in the year.

column1: However
column2: when assessing price trends over the medium term
column3: a number of factors should dampen inflationary pressures. First
column4: given the past appreciation of the euro
column5: import prices should contribute to this effect. Second
column6: domestic cost pressures should remain moderate. In particular
column7: wage growth should be contained in the context of a recovery which
column8: for the time being
column9: is expected to remain gradual. Provided that wage moderation can be preserved
column10: which is indispensable for fostering employment
column11: a cyclical recovery in productivity tends to dampen growth in unit labour costs

column6: oil prices
column7: exchange rates
column8: wage developments and fiscal measures. Therefore
column9: elements of risk to the outlook for price stability need to be kept in mind. In this respect

column11: and other indicators have remained broadly unchanged
column12: inflation expectations warrant close monitoring.

column1: Turning to the monetary analysis
column2: M3 growth has been very strong over the past two years
column3: reflecting portfolio shifts
column4: precautionary savings and the low level of interest rates. The low level of interest rates has also supported the growth of credit demand. In our assessment

column7: for the time being
column8: the economic recovery is only gradual. However
column9: should high excess liquidity continue to prevail once there is a significant strengthening of economic activity

column1: In summary
column2: the economic analysis indicates that the main scenario for price developments in the medium term continues to be in line with our definition of price stability. This picture is confirmed by cross-checking with the monetary analysis.

column1: Turning to fiscal policies
column2: I have already mentioned that we expressed deep regret following the ECOFIN Council meeting on 25 November. Furthermore
column3: we stressed our support of the Commission's views on the ECOFIN Council's Conclusions. We also took note of the commitments made by France and Germany to correct their excessive deficits as rapidly as possible and at the latest by 2005. Moreover
column4: we noted that the ECOFIN Council stands ready to take a decision under Article 104(9)
column5: on the basis of the Commission recommendation
column6: should the two governments fail to act in accordance with their own commitments. We strongly urge the governments concerned to live up to their responsibilities. Confidence in the soundness of public finances is essential for sustainable growth in consumption and investment.

column1: The overall fiscal framework of the Stability and Growth Pact remains of central importance and should be fully respected. The same applies to the requirement to avoid excessive deficits
column2: laid down in Article 104 of the Treaty
column3: and to the reference values of 3% and 60% for the deficit and debt-to-GDP ratios respectively
column4: specified in the Protocol on the excessive deficit procedure annexed to the Treaty. These are the foundations for trust and confidence in EMU.

column1: Trust and confidence are also crucial in the context of structural reform. Enhancing the competitiveness of the euro area
column2: in particular in labour and product markets
column3: increasing the efficiency of the tax systems and ensuring the sustainability of social security schemes all foster a better allocation and utilisation of capital and human resources. There is no doubt that measures in these respects improve the growth perspectives of the euro area. However
column4: in order to foster confidence in the shorter term
column5: convincing assurance must be given that these challenges are indeed being tackled in a decisive manner and that clear action is being taken. While some progress has been made
column6: the Governing Council strongly encourages governments to accelerate the implementation of structural reforms and also calls upon social partners to fully commit themselves to the objective of making the euro area a more dynamic and innovative economy.

column1: Following our regular economic and monetary analysis
column2: we continue to judge the current stance of monetary policy as appropriate to preserve price stability over the medium term. Accordingly
column3: we have decided to leave the key ECB interest rates unchanged at their low levels. The available indicators point to an ongoing economic recovery in the euro area. This assessment has not fundamentally changed. Although recent exchange rate developments are likely to have some dampening effects on exports
column4: export growth should continue to benefit from the dynamic expansion of the world economy. Import price developments in the euro area should become somewhat more favourable
column5: thereby helping to contain inflationary risks. We will continue to carefully monitor all developments that could affect our assessment of risks to price stability over the medium term.

column1: Let me now explain our decision in more detail.
Starting with the economic analysis
column2: recently available indicators confirm that world economic growth is progressing. For the euro area too
column3: the latest information on production and confidence is consistent with an ongoing recovery in economic activity
column4: and the momentum for growth should strengthen in the course of 2004. This assessment is supported by all available forecasts from official and private sources
column5: as well as by developments in the financial markets.

column1: On the external side
column2: recent exchange rate developments are having a negative impact on the price competitiveness of euro area exporters
column3: but thus far this should be partly compensated for by the ongoing expansion of global demand. Overall
column4: euro area exports should therefore continue to grow. On the domestic side
column5: investment growth should benefit from the ongoing adjustment efforts of firms to enhance productivity and profitability
column6: as well as from the low level of interest rates and generally favourable financing conditions. Private consumption should receive support from real disposable income growth
column7: partly due to favourable effects on terms of trade and inflation stemming from the past appreciation of the euro.

column1: The short-term risks to this outlook remain balanced. Over longer horizons
column2: the uncertainties continue to be related to persistent external imbalances in some regions of the world and their potential repercussions on the sustainability of global economic growth. This is a challenge to be addressed by sustainable macroeconomic policies and structural reforms which foster a sound balance between savings and investment in all major partner countries
column3: enhance the production potential in the euro area and support a further expansion in trade of goods and services at the global level.

column1: With regard to price developments
column2: HICP inflation rates over the short term are still expected to fluctuate around the 2% level
column3: following a rate of 2.1% in December
column4: according to Eurostat’s flash estimate. As I have explained on previous occasions
column5: adverse food price developments
column6: the evolution of oil prices and increases in indirect taxes and administered prices have all adversely affected the short-term outlook for inflation.

column1: However
column2: in the course of this year we expect inflation rates to fall and to remain in line with price stability thereafter. This expectation is based on the assumption that wage developments will remain moderate in the context of a gradual economic recovery. Moreover
column3: the past appreciation of the euro should dampen price pressures. These views are also reflected in the available forecasts and projections. We are
column4: of course
column5: fully aware of the conditional nature of these forward-looking exercises and therefore bear in mind all elements of risk to the outlook for price stability. In the same vein
column6: we continue to closely monitor inflation expectations.

column1: Turning to the monetary analysis
column2: the strong monetary growth of the last few years means that there is significantly more liquidity available in the euro area than needed to finance non-inflationary growth. At the same time
column3: the growth of loans to the private sector has been rising over recent months
column4: benefiting from the low level of interest rates and the general improvement in the economic environment.

column1: In our view
column2: the accumulation of excess liquidity should not be of concern for price stability as long as the economic recovery is gradual. However
column3: should excess liquidity remain high once there is a significant strengthening of economic activity
column4: it could lead to inflationary pressures over the medium term. We will therefore carefully examine monetary developments as they unfold.

column1: In summary
column2: the economic analysis continues to indicate that the main scenario for price developments in the medium term is in line with price stability. This picture is confirmed by cross-checking with the monetary analysis.

column1: Concerning fiscal policies
column2: 2004 will be a crucial year for strengthening the credibility of the institutional framework and confidence in the soundness of public finances of Member States across the euro area. Together with the Treaty provisions
column3: the overall fiscal framework of the Stability and Growth Pact remains of central importance and must be fully respected. These are the foundations for trust and confidence in EMU. They are key not only to stability but also to growth
column4: and are a precondition for preserving low risk premia in financial markets. We therefore strongly urge governments and the ECOFIN Council to live up to their responsibilities and to the commitments they made last November.

column1: Finally
column2: the Governing Council strongly supports ongoing efforts by a number of governments to proceed with structural reforms – in the fiscal domain
column3: and in labour and product markets. Building on what has already been implemented

column1: On the basis of our economic and monetary analysis
column2: we have concluded that there are no fundamental changes to the medium-term outlook for price stability. Accordingly
column3: the current stance of monetary policy remains appropriate and the key ECB interest rates have been kept unchanged at their low levels. Inflationary risks should be contained by somewhat more favourable import price developments
column4: while the economic recovery in the euro area should proceed in line with our expectations. We will continue to monitor carefully all developments that could affect our assessment of risks to price stability over the medium term. With regard to exchange rates
column5: we again particularly stress stability and remain concerned about excessive exchange rate moves.

column1: Let me now explain our decision in more detail.
Starting with the economic analysis
column2: the latest data on euro area production as well as survey evidence on business confidence remain consistent with ongoing growth around the turn of the year.

column1: Looking ahead
column2: the external environment of the euro area should continue to develop favourably. In particular
column3: robust real GDP growth in our major trading partners’ economies can be expected to support foreign demand for euro area goods and services
column4: while export growth may be dampened somewhat by the decline in price competitiveness.

column1: The conditions for an improvement in domestic demand are also favourable. Investment activity should not only profit from global trends in demand
column2: but also from companies’ efforts to enhance productivity and profitability
column3: from the low level of interest rates and from generally favourable financing conditions. Growth in private consumption
column4: which has so far remained rather subdued
column5: can also be expected to recover in line with an increase in real disposable income. This assessment is reflected in all available forecasts from official and private sources and seems to be confirmed by developments in financial markets.

column1: Looking at the risks to this outlook
column2: there are no new factors to be taken into account. Over the shorter term
column3: risks remain balanced. Over longer horizons
column4: uncertainties relate to the persistent imbalances in some regions of the world and their potential repercussions on the sustainability of global economic growth. This calls for sustainable macroeconomic policies and structural reforms which foster a sound balance between savings and investment in all major partner countries
column5: which enhance the production potential in the euro area and which support a further expansion in trade of goods and services at the global level.

column1: Turning to price developments
column2: we have seen a fall in the HICP inflation rate for December to 2.0%. The same rate was estimated by Eurostat for January. In the course of this year
column3: inflation rates should fall below 2% and remain in line with price stability thereafter. While US dollar-denominated global commodity prices have been on an upward trend over recent months
column4: the past appreciation of the euro is dampening their effects on domestic prices. Moreover
column5: we continue to expect wage developments to remain moderate in the context of high rates of unemployment and a gradual economic recovery. Recent data on labour costs seem to broadly confirm the assessment of a levelling-off of wage increases. On the whole
column6: inflationary pressure remains limited – an assessment that is confirmed by all available forecasts. Given the conditional nature of any forward-looking evaluation
column7: it is of course important to bear in mind all elements of risk to the outlook for price stability and to monitor inflation expectations closely.

column1: Turning to the monetary analysis
column2: annual M3 growth has continued to moderate slowly over recent months. This can be explained by the still cautious reallocation of portfolios by economic agents and the effects of generally low interest rates on the growth of very liquid assets. At the same time
column3: the growth of loans to the private sector reflects the effects of both low interest rates and an improvement in the economic environment.

column1: The strong monetary growth over the past few years means that there is significantly more liquidity available in the euro area than needed to finance non-inflationary growth. Whether or not the accumulated excess liquidity will translate into inflationary pressures over the medium term depends on the extent to which past portfolios shifts are reversed and on the future strength of economic growth. Should excess liquidity persist
column2: it could lead to inflationary pressures over the medium term.

column1: In summary
column2: the economic analysis continues to indicate that the main scenario for price developments in the medium term is in line with price stability. Cross-checking with the monetary analysis does not alter this picture.

column1: With regard to fiscal policies
column2: there are several important issues that warrant close attention. First
column3: the implementation of fiscal policies should be in line with the commitments made late last year. In this connection
column4: a thorough assessment of the new Stability Programmes of Member States is currently under way. All parties involved need to live up to their responsibilities and commitments. Sound public finances support a stable macroeconomic framework
column5: which in turn enhances confidence and promotes investment
column6: growth and employment in the euro area.

column1: Second
column2: as regards the Stability and Growth Pact
column3: the Governing Council shares the concerns of the European Commission regarding the conclusions of the ECOFIN Council in November last year. The Commission is the guardian of the Treaty and the ECB respects the Commission’s decision to seek legal clarity. Furthermore
column4: we do not see a need to change the Treaty and
column5: in our view
column6: the Stability and Growth Pact in its current form is appropriate. We are in agreement with the Commission that the implementation of the Stability and Growth Pact could be further improved
column7: in particular in terms of the analysis of structural imbalances and the strengthening of incentives for sound fiscal policies during good economic times. Clarity and enforceability of the fiscal framework should be enhanced.

column1: A stable macroeconomic framework is necessary to enhance our growth potential
column2: but it alone is not sufficient. Boosting employment
column3: fostering labour productivity and making the best use of technological and scientific progress in the context of an ageing society all require structural reforms – in the fiscal domain as well as in financial
column4: product and labour markets. The Lisbon Strategy provides the appropriate blueprint for progress. The responsibility for its implementation
column5: however
column6: lies with governments
column7: parliaments and social partners. The Governing Council strongly supports ongoing efforts in a number of countries to proceed with structural reforms. At the same time
column8: we fully share the view that additional
column9: sustained efforts are required
column10: as recently reiterated by the Commission in its progress report on the implementation of the Lisbon Strategy and the priorities for 2004. It is a major challenge to convince the public at large that everybody would benefit – in terms of growth
column11: more and better jobs
column12: and higher incomes – if the reforms needed were indeed implemented.

column1: Overall
column2: the Governing Council confirmed its previous assessment of a favourable outlook for price stability in the euro area over the medium term. Against this background
column3: we concluded that the current stance of monetary policy remains appropriate. The key ECB interest rates have therefore been left unchanged at their low levels. column1: Let me now turn to the details of our economic analysis. According to Eurostat
column2: in the fourth quarter of 2003 real GDP in the euro area grew by 0.3% quarter on quarter
column3: following growth of 0.4% in the third quarter. These data confirm that a gradual recovery in economic activity in the euro area took place in the second half of 2003. More recent indicators point to moderate economic growth also in early 2004. While growth has been relatively modest so far
column4: both external and domestic factors give reason to expect a strengthening of the recovery through 2004 and beyond.

column1: On the external side
column2: all recent indications confirm that global economic growth in 2004 will be robust and broadly based across different regions of the world. Overall
column3: euro area exports should grow significantly this year and next.

column1: On the domestic side
column2: the conditions for a recovery in private demand are in place. Over recent months there have been signs of a stabilisation in investment. According to Eurostat
column3: fixed capital investment grew again in the last quarter of 2003
column4: after recording three successive quarter-on-quarter declines. Corporate earnings have generally improved in the euro area
column5: following a protracted restructuring of corporate balance sheets over the last few years. The financing conditions faced by corporations in the euro area are very favourable at present. All of these factors should support a further recovery in investment.

column1: There are also reasons to expect a gradual increase in consumption growth during this year
column2: following the subdued developments of last year. In the short term
column3: growth in real disposable income is supported by lower import prices and tax cuts
column4: while later on the gradual improvement in labour market conditions should become an additional factor supporting income growth and confidence. The financial situation of households in the euro area is sound
column5: not least in comparison with a number of other industrial economies
column6: and there is no financial impediment to a pick-up in private consumption.

column1: For all these reasons
column2: our main scenario of a continued gradual recovery in the course of 2004 and 2005 remains valid. This view is shared by available forecasts and projections
column3: and is also broadly reflected in financial market developments.

column1: We continue to see the risks to this scenario as broadly balanced. However
column2: there are uncertainties related to euro area private consumption and the persistent imbalances in some regions of the world and their potential repercussions on the sustainability of global economic growth.

column1: Turning to price developments
column2: according to the Eurostat flash estimate
column3: the annual HICP inflation rate declined to 1.6% in February 2004
column4: from 1.9% in January. This fall was mainly due to base effects stemming from energy prices
column5: as a sharp increase in oil prices which occurred in early 2003 dropped out of the calculation of the annual rate in February 2004. Over the coming months
column6: volatility in annual inflation rates is likely to be observed
column7: mainly due to further base effects from energy prices as well as to increases in indirect taxes. Related to this
column8: annual inflation rates are likely to edge up again temporarily in the second quarter of 2004.

column1: Looking beyond short-term fluctuations in the most volatile components of the HICP
column2: we expect inflation to remain in line with price stability. At the current juncture
column3: we see little upward pressure on inflation. Given the anticipated gradual nature of the recovery in economic activity and the high level of unemployment in the euro area
column4: wage developments should remain moderate.
