column1: Turning to the monetary analysis
column2: M3 growth has moderated over recent months. However
column3: it appears that the reallocation of economic agents' portfolios into longer-term assets is proceeding rather cautiously. In this respect
column4: the generally low level of interest rates continues to support the demand for liquid assets. The low level of interest rates also supports the growth of loans to the private sector.

column1: The high liquidity in the euro area needs to be assessed with caution. Its effects on inflation over the medium term will greatly depend on the extent and pace of the future reversal of past portfolio shifts and on the future strength of economic growth. Should excess liquidity persist
column2: it could lead to inflationary pressures over the medium term.

column1: To sum up
column2: the economic analysis continues to indicate that the main scenario for price developments in the coming years is in line with price stability. Cross-checking with the monetary analysis does not alter this picture for the time being.

column1: With regard to fiscal policies
column2: we noted the progress in fiscal consolidation envisaged in countries' stability programmes. Nonetheless
column3: there continues to be reason for concern. In some countries
column4: contrary to their commitments
column5: adjustment efforts are insufficient to mitigate the risk of excessive deficits. Moreover
column6: several countries do not plan to attain sound budgetary positions by the end of their respective programme horizons
column7: despite favourable growth prospects. This would risk a repetition of the policy errors of the last economic upswing
column8: when insufficient consolidation efforts and tax cuts without adequate expenditure restraint laid the foundations for the recent fiscal difficulties.

column1: All countries would benefit from the strengthening of the sustainability of their public finances
column2: especially in the expected upward phase of the cycle
column3: by eliminating imbalances over the coming years and avoiding or correcting as soon as possible excessive deficits. Moreover
column4: the determined implementation of comprehensive structural reforms
column5: on both the expenditure side and the revenue side
column6: will bring additional medium-term rewards in the form of higher growth and more sustainable public finances. Such consolidation and reform strategies are needed to secure a sound macroeconomic environment in the euro area.

column1: The euro area also requires further structural reforms in financial
column2: product and labour markets. The Lisbon Strategy provides the appropriate blueprint for progress. We welcome that the forthcoming spring meeting of the European Council is set to give renewed impetus to the Lisbon agenda
column3: speed up the pace of reforms
column4: and strengthen the effectiveness of the decision-making process. Structural reforms will have enormous benefits for the citizens of the euro area. These reforms are crucial for sustained non-inflationary growth and employment
column5: and they are therefore also important for maintaining social cohesion in the long run.

column1: Confidence among European citizens in the future is vital for a stronger economic recovery and sustained growth. The Governing Council recognises that the still low level of consumer confidence is related to prevailing uncertainties
column2: including the debate about the appropriate path for structural reforms in many countries of the euro area. It is also partly linked to the continued perception by European citizens of higher inflation than measured by official indices.

column1: The Governing Council notes that inflation is now back at a level consistent with price stability. column2: together with further progress in the implementation of necessary structural reforms
column3: are the key to stronger confidence
column4: and they create the conditions for increased consumption and investment and thus for growth and job creation.

column1: The Vice-President and I will now report on the outcome of today’s meeting of the Governing Council of the ECB.
On the basis of our regular economic and monetary analysis
column2: we have not changed our assessment that the current stance of monetary policy remains in line with the maintenance of price stability over the medium term. Accordingly
column3: the key ECB interest rates have been left unchanged. The low level of interest rates also provides ongoing support to the economic recovery in the euro area. We will continue to monitor carefully all developments that could affect our assessment of risks to price stability over the medium term.

column1: Let me now provide a more detailed explanation of our decision
column2: turning first to the economic analysis. With regard to real GDP growth
column3: it appears that the recovery in the euro area has continued into 2004
column4: following quarter-on-quarter growth rates of 0.3-0.4% in the second half of 2003. Recently released data on production and demand as well as confidence indicators have been mixed
column5: implying some short-term uncertainty
column6: while preliminary information available after the tragic events in Madrid on 11 March does not suggest a major impact on confidence. We will continue to monitor the situation closely. On balance
column7: there is currently no evidence challenging the assessment of continued
column8: though modest
column9: real GDP growth in the euro area over the short term.

column1: More fundamentally
column2: the conditions remain in place for the recovery to continue in 2004 and to strengthen over time. First
column3: global economic growth is robust and broadly based
column4: both geographically and across sectors
column5: thereby providing a positive external environment for the euro area. In this context
column6: we expect euro area exports to grow significantly this year and next
column7: despite some past losses in price competitiveness.

column1: Second
column2: on the domestic side
column3: investment should be helped by favourable financing conditions
column4: an improvement in corporate earnings and spillover effects from global demand trends. Some signs of an improvement in fixed capital investment are already discernible in the Eurostat data for the fourth quarter of last year. As regards private consumption
column5: growth in real disposable income should lead to increased spending
column6: in particular because there are no financial constraints for households which would pose obstacles to higher expenditure. Over time this should also be fostered by an improvement in employment and employment expectations.

column1: This is our assessment and it is supported by the available forecasts and projections. Obviously
column2: any such forward-looking evaluation is conditional and subject to risks. At this juncture
column3: risks are primarily related to the persistent imbalances in some regions of the world and the weakness of private consumption in the euro area. Concerning private consumption

Ensuring clarity about the content and timing of these reforms and a better understanding of their benefits to all citizens would make a very important contribution to supporting household confidence.

column1: 2004-05-06;2;"Ladies and gentlemen
column2: it is a pleasure to welcome you to our press conference here in Helsinki
column3: where the Governing Council of the European Central Bank met today for the ninth time outside Frankfurt. I would like to thank acting Governor Matti Louekoski for his invitation and very kind hospitality
column4: as well as the staff of Suomen Pankki – Finlands Bank for a perfectly organised meeting. We deeply regret that Mr Matti Vanhala had to resign from his position and we wish him all the best.

column1: Let me now report on the outcome of today’s meeting. On the basis of our regular economic and monetary analyses
column2: we continue to expect that price stability will be maintained over the medium term. Accordingly
column3: we did not change our assessment of the monetary policy stance and left the key ECB interest rates at their current low levels. The low interest rates across the entire maturity spectrum are also supporting the economic recovery in the euro area. As always
column4: we will continue to monitor carefully all developments that could affect our assessment of risks to price stability over the medium term.

column1: Allow me to elaborate on our decision
column2: turning first to the economic analysis. Regarding the current situation and the very short-term outlook
column3: the conjunctural indicators available still provide mixed evidence. All in all
column4: they suggest that the recovery of real economic activity in the euro area has continued into 2004
column5: albeit at a modest pace. Most recent information has been more encouraging
column6: with the latest euro area survey data offering more positive signals with regard to the beginning of the second quarter.

column1: While the latest positive signals need to be confirmed by future developments
column2: they underpin the expectation of the gradual recovery in the euro area continuing and strengthening over time. The conditions for such a recovery are in place.

column1: First
column2: global economic growth continues to be robust and world trade has strengthened. The global economic upturn is broadly based
column3: both geographically and across sectors
column4: and thus provides a favourable external environment for the euro area. In this context
column5: we expect euro area exports to grow significantly this year and next. Second
column6: favourable financing conditions
column7: improvements in corporate efficiency and earnings and the strength of global demand should help investment. Growth in real disposable income should support private consumption
column8: especially since households appear not to face financial constraints that might impede stronger spending. Over time
column9: consumer spending should also be supported by an improvement in labour market conditions.

column1: These considerations underpin our confidence in a continuation of the economic recovery
column2: an expectation which is mirrored by available forecasts and projections. It is also in line with financial market developments over the past few weeks. Obviously
column3: any forward-looking assessment is subject to risks and uncertainties. On the external side
column4: the adverse terms-of-trade effects of recent rises in oil and other commodity prices pose risks at shorter horizons
column5: while the persistence of global imbalances implies some uncertainties over the medium term. On the domestic side
column6: uncertainties surrounding fiscal policy and structural reforms in some euro area countries seem to have contributed to preventing a more vigorous improvement in consumer confidence. A continued commitment to and greater clarity about the content and timing of these crucial reforms
column7: supported by a better understanding of their necessity and benefits for all citizens
column8: would help to resolve this uncertainty and thereby mitigate the associated risks for the euro area economy.

column1: Turning to price developments
column2: annual HICP inflation rates will exhibit some short-term volatility over the coming months
column3: as we already indicated on the occasion of previous meetings of the Governing Council. According to Eurostat’s flash estimate
column4: annual HICP inflation was 2.0% in April
column5: after 1.7% in March. While no detailed information is available as yet
column6: the recent rise in annual inflation rates is likely to mainly reflect a strong base effect in the energy component resulting from the marked decline of oil prices a year ago. Moreover
column7: recent oil price increases have exerted additional upward pressure. As these factors will also play a role in the next few months
column8: inflation rates of 2% or somewhat above are possible over the short term. Despite these recent
column9: less positive developments
column10: over longer horizons we expect inflation rates to remain in line with price stability. In particular
column11: wage developments should remain moderate. The latest data on wage growth in the fourth quarter of 2003 lend support to this view.

column1: Our outlook for price developments is in line with available forecasts and projections. However
column2: at the current juncture
column3: the increase in commodity prices in general
column4: and oil prices in particular
column5: may pose an upside risk to price stability. It will therefore remain important to pay close attention to inflation expectations.

column1: Moving on to the monetary analysis
column2: annual M3 growth has moderated only slowly since the summer of 2003. While there is evidence of continued portfolio shifts out of M3 into longer-term assets
column3: the pace of this adjustment remains modest. Both monetary and credit growth continue to be supported by the historically low level of interest rates in the euro area and may also reflect the improvement in the economic environment over the last few quarters.

column1: Given the continued strength of monetary growth
column2: liquidity conditions remain ample in the euro area. The impact of this high level of liquidity on inflation over the medium term will depend on future developments in the economy and financial markets. Should excess liquidity persist
column3: it could lead to inflationary pressures over the medium term.

column1: To sum up
column2: the economic analysis indicates that the main scenario for the outlook for price developments over the medium term is in line with price stability. Cross-checking with the monetary analysis does not alter this view at the current juncture.

column1: As usual
column2: I also wish to make a few remarks regarding other policies in the euro area. With regard to fiscal policies
column3: the Governing Council sees increased reasons for concern. On the basis of the latest Commission forecasts
column4: the average euro area budgetary position is not expected to improve much this year or next. A growing number of countries are likely to report significant imbalances
column5: while fiscal consolidation efforts might fall short of commitments. It is essential that all countries concerned undertake credible measures to address these concerns. Such measures should be part of a comprehensive reform strategy. This would underpin the ongoing economic upswing by boosting confidence in sound public finances and by improving the prospects for future economic growth. The Governing Council welcomes the decision by the Commission to request more consolidation efforts from a number of countries.

column1: Turning to structural reforms
column2: the Governing Council reaffirms its view that such reforms are essential if the euro area’s growth potential is to expand substantially. In particular
column3: both our employment rate and our labour productivity growth need to increase significantly. Following our discussions here in Finland
column4: let me stress that this requires a strengthened technological and scientific base and its application in the euro area as a whole
column5: fostered by major efforts to enhance the human capital of our economy. In this context

column1: Let me now turn to today’s monetary policy discussion.
In summary
column2: we noted that the economic recovery has strengthened over recent months. At the same time
column3: we have also witnessed stronger inflationary pressures over the short term. Nevertheless
column4: we are still of the view that the medium-term outlook remains in line with price stability. Accordingly
column5: we left the key ECB interest rates unchanged. The low level of interest rates continues to support the economic recovery. We will remain vigilant with regard to all developments which could affect the risks to price stability over the medium term.

column1: I shall now explain our assessment in more detail.
In the context of our economic analysis
column2: the latest data releases confirm that the economic recovery in the euro area is under way. According to Eurostat
column3: real GDP grew by 0.6% quarter on quarter in the first quarter of this year
column4: and quarterly real GDP growth for the fourth quarter of last year was revised upwards from 0.3% to 0.4%. The more pronounced pace of real GDP growth mainly reflected both stronger private consumption and buoyant exports. Latest survey data still provide mixed signals with regard to the underlying strength of the recovery but remain fully consistent with ongoing growth in the current quarter.

column1: Looking ahead
column2: the conditions for a continuation of the recovery remain in place. Economic growth outside the euro area continues to be strong and should promote export growth. On the domestic side
column3: investment should benefit from the positive global environment as well as from the favourable financing conditions. Improvements in corporate efficiency and higher profits are also supporting business investment. Moreover
column4: private consumption should gradually recover from the stagnation witnessed during most of 2003
column5: broadly in line with growth in real disposable income which
column6: with the usual lag
column7: should be further underpinned by an increase in employment growth later on.

column1: Accordingly
column2: we expect an ongoing recovery in euro area economic growth over the coming quarters
column3: leading to a broader and stronger upswing in the course of next year. This is also reflected in the Eurosystem staff projections
column4: which envisage euro area real GDP growth of between 1.4% and 2.0% on average in 2004
column5: rising to between 1.7% and 2.7% in 2005. Available forecasts from international and private organisations convey a broadly similar picture.

column1: With regard to this scenario
column2: there are risks and uncertainties in both directions. On the one hand
column3: the current rather robust pace of economic growth outside the euro area
column4: the recent development in private consumption as well as some survey data imply a potential for stronger growth dynamics
column5: particularly in the short term. On the other hand
column6: high oil prices could pose a downside risk. Over a longer horizon
column7: concerns also remain about the persistence of global imbalances.

column1: Concerning prices
column2: recent oil price developments have created considerable upward pressure on consumer prices. According to Eurostat’s flash estimate
column3: annual HICP inflation was 2.5% in May
column4: partly due to base effects
column5: after standing at 2.0% in April. Markets expect oil prices to decline gradually from recent peaks. If they were to remain at their recent high levels
column6: it is to be expected that inflation rates would continue to be higher than previously anticipated and stay above 2% for longer than just a few months ahead. When assessing price trends over the medium term
column7: however
column8: the outlook remains favourable. In particular
column9: overall import price developments should remain moderate and inflationary pressure from wages and unit labour costs should be contained. Both factors should help to bring annual rates of consumer price inflation back to below 2% in 2005.

column1: These views are in line with the Eurosystem staff projections
column2: which put average annual HICP inflation at between 1.9% and 2.3% in 2004 and between 1.1% and 2.3% in 2005. They are also broadly consistent with recently released forecasts by international and private organisations. These forecasts and projections are subject to a number of risks and uncertainties. Concerns relate in particular to oil price developments. Moreover
column3: there is insufficient knowledge today about future changes in indirect taxes and administered prices; information on these items typically becomes available only towards the end of the year. Against this background
column4: the potential risk for second-round effects via wages needs to be monitored closely. Finally
column5: there has been an increase in measures of long-term inflation expectations derived from financial market indicators. While these indicators should be interpreted with caution
column6: the recent upward trend calls for particular vigilance.

column1: Moving on to the monetary analysis
column2: we have seen increasing evidence of a normalisation of the portfolio behaviour of private investors. As a consequence
column3: annual M3 growth has fallen quite significantly over recent quarters. Still
column4: the low level of interest rates continues to fuel monetary growth and the amount of excess liquidity remains high in the euro area. In an economic upswing
column5: the persistence of excess liquidity could lead to inflationary pressures over the medium term.

column1: To sum up
column2: the economic analysis indicates that the main scenario for the outlook for price developments over the medium term remains in line with price stability. However
column3: short-term pressures on inflation have increased recently and some upside risks need to be taken into account. Cross-checking with the monetary analysis also supports the case for vigilance with regard to the materialisation of risks to price stability.

column1: Given the signs that the economic recovery will continue
column2: it is particularly important that fiscal policies and structural reforms play their part in improving the economic fundamentals of the euro area. It is regretful that recent fiscal developments have not been helpful in this respect. A growing number of countries are reporting significant imbalances and fiscal consolidation efforts fall disappointingly short of commitments. In order to strengthen confidence in a sustainable upswing
column3: it is now essential that clarity about the future course of consolidation of fiscal policies is re-established in all countries concerned. This requires credible measures with an emphasis on structural expenditure reform so that imbalances are redressed
column4: tax/benefit systems become more growth-friendly and social security systems are put on a sound financial footing. These measures
column5: together with a revived momentum towards effectively implementing structural reforms in labour and product markets
column6: would provide very valuable support to the current economic upswing.

We said that our overall analysis of the situation was such that we judged it inopportune to go in the direction that had been suggested at the time
column4: and I would say that most of what we said proved to be well-founded. I have said what I had to say on oil and I do not want to repeat myself. We believe that the combination of past decisions – which we sometimes took against strong advice to the contrary – and vigilance – which is
column5: as we say
column6: of the essence now – will permit us to deliver what it is our duty to deliver. And again we are judged by yourselves
column7: by market participants and by all observers. We have very important responsibilities and we are subject to the scrutiny of all.

column1: I never embark on dialogues with various governments. We have a responsibility for 306 million inhabitants and for taking into account their superior interests. I would only say that the Eurogroup is very important for us. The Eurogroup is the executive branch counterpart – and certainly I would not speak of a “counterweight” since I don’t think it is appropriate at all
column2: but of a “counterpart” to the European Central Bank and the Eurosystem. We have also the Commission
column3: which plays a very important role in Europe as you know. We invite the President of the Eurogroup and the Commissioner every fortnight to participate in the Governing Council
column4: not to vote of course
column5: but to be there – to be present. This is a very
column6: very frequent occasion on which we can meet. I won’t comment any more on that. The Eurogroup certainly has very important responsibilities and these responsibilities are decisive for the European Economic and Monetary Union – EMU. It is not only a monetary union
column7: it is an economic and monetary union
column8: which is one of the reasons why we consider so important the fiscal side of the coin and on the Stability and Growth Pact.

column1: On this very important question
column2: which is the Constitution
column3: we all rely very much on the wisdom of the Irish Presidency
column4: and I will not comment on the details of what the Irish Presidency is preparing. That is really its responsibility. I was
column5: myself
column6: in Dublin recently. I had the privilege of being invited by our colleague John Hurley and I took advantage of my stay to be received by Bertie Ahern
column7: the Prime Minister

column11: not only in the short term

column1: On the second question
column2: we urged the oil producers to take account of the situation and be responsible so that the present episode that we have been witnessing for the last few days and weeks would be transitory. The decision that has been taken is a step in the right direction and I do not want to comment any more on that. As regards the uncertainties and risks for the growth and credibility of this working assumption of a gradual recovery
column3: which is materialising
column4: I do not want to say more than I have already said. Of course
column5: the main issue in the eyes of a great number of observers is certainly the oil issue. But we have other elements in the euro area and
column6: as I have said
column7: some are going in the direction of more buoyant growth. I have to remind you that
column8: in the first part of the year
column9: most of you here were more pessimistic about what you thought was materialising. The first quarter has been better in this respect than most observers expected. So we have to be prudent and cautious. There are uncertainties and risks in both directions and that is why we have to be very vigilant and alert
column10: and keen to get all new information and to introduce this new information into our own assessments. That is why we keep our options open. That is why we do not have a bias. Again I remind you that the magnetic needle of our compass is – for all the reasons I have explained – price stability.

column1: I do not want to comment again on that issue because I think I am giving a status to these projections that would not necessarily be the real appropriate status that they have in our own monetary policy strategy. But we did have such analyses and you can imagine what the various consequences of various possible scenarios would be.

We do not claim to be oil specialists and we rely very much on analyses provided by a number of specialised entities. What I say in this domain is true for all others. We are in a world of a high uncertainty. In that uncertain environment what counts is that you take decisions that are wise and robust
column2: namely that they are as optimal as possible
column3: having worked through various possible representations of an extremely complex reality that cannot be summed up with any level of pertinence by a single mathematical economic model. It is very important to restate that we are pragmatic. We will respond to the changing reality as this reality materialises. Our own goal is to maintain price stability. I personally do not exclude any scenario. We could have this scenario you are mentioning as well as others. We are not dogmatic and we do not pretend that we are extra-lucid. But what we can say is that we urge the oil producers and all partners to maintain the highest possible level of responsibility in the present circumstances. Everybody knows what the consequences of sustained high prices are. But our own responsibility is to ensure price stability
column4: namely to avoid the secondary rounds. That is what is decisive. That is where we concentrate our own action as a central bank.

column2: the Vice-President and I will now report on the outcome of today’s meeting of the Governing Council of the ECB.

column1: On the basis of the regular economic and monetary analyses
column2: we have confirmed our assessment of last month. While somewhat stronger inflationary pressure is likely to persist over the short term
column3: the outlook still remains in line with price stability over the medium term. Therefore
column4: the Governing Council decided to retain its monetary policy stance
column5: leaving the key ECB interest rates unchanged. By historical standards
column6: interest rates are low
column7: both in nominal and in real terms
column8: also lending support to economic activity. The Governing Council will remain vigilant with regard to all developments which could affect the risks to price stability over the medium term.

column1: Let me now explain our assessment in more detail
column2: turning first to the economic analysis.

column1: Following quarterly real GDP growth of 0.6% in the first quarter of this year
column2: the latest data releases confirm that the economic recovery in the euro area is continuing. All in all
column3: the latest indicators of output and expenditure
column4: as well as the most recent survey data
column5: remain consistent with ongoing growth in real activity during the second quarter.

column1: Looking ahead
column2: we remain confident that the recovery of economic activity will continue. The conditions for a broadening and strengthening of the recovery are in place. On the external side
column3: economic growth outside the euro area remains strong
column4: which should promote euro area exports. On the domestic side
column5: investment should benefit from the positive external environment and the favourable financing conditions within the euro area. As corporate restructuring gathers pace and business efficiency advances
column6: the resulting improvements in profits should further underpin business investment. Moreover
column7: the recovery of private consumption should proceed in line with increases in real disposable income and the anticipated subsequent strengthening of employment growth. Available forecasts from international and private organisations paint a broadly similar picture of the outlook for the euro area. The expectation of a continued economic recovery is also in line with recent developments in financial markets.

column1: Of course
column2: this scenario of an ongoing economic recovery may be influenced by a number of factors working in opposite directions. On the upside
column3: euro area growth in the first quarter was stronger than anticipated and this momentum may strengthen shorter-term dynamics. Ongoing robust growth in the global economy could also lead to stronger than expected activity in the euro area. On the downside
column4: despite having declined somewhat
column5: oil prices remain at high levels and may
column6: largely through their impact on the euro area’s terms of trade
column7: dampen growth. Furthermore
column8: over longer horizons
column9: there are concerns relating to the persistence of global imbalances.

column1: Turning to price developments
column2: there is a need to distinguish between short-term developments and the medium-term trend when assessing risks to price stability. Over the short term
column3: oil prices continue to exert upward pressure on the general price level. According to Eurostat’s flash estimate
column4: annual HICP inflation was 2.4% in June
column5: having stood at 2.5% in May. Although oil prices have fallen over the last weeks
column6: markets expect them to remain high for some time. Were this to occur
column7: inflation rates would most likely remain above 2% for longer than previously expected.

column1: Looking beyond the short term
column2: however
column3: the outlook remains consistent with price stability
column4: provided that wages develop moderately
column5: in line with the latest evidence available. Nevertheless
column6: there are some upside risks to price stability. The strength of global economic dynamism may continue to exert upward pressure on commodity prices
column7: including oil prices. Moreover
column8: following rather strong increases in the past
column9: the further evolution of indirect taxes and administered prices is difficult to incorporate into any forward-looking assessment at this point in time
column10: because such information usually becomes available only later in the year. Against this background
column11: the potential risk of second-round effects via wage and pricing behaviour needs to be monitored closely. Social partners can make an important contribution to facilitating the maintenance of price stability by focusing on the medium-term outlook for price developments rather than on currently observed rates of inflation. This would also be conducive to fostering employment growth. Finally
column12: measures of long-term inflation expectations derived from financial market indicators remain relatively high. While these indicators should be interpreted with caution
column13: their development calls for particular vigilance.

column1: Moving to the monetary analysis
column2: the overall picture remains unchanged from our previous assessment. Annual M3 growth rates have fallen over recent months. While this decline partly reflects base effects
column3: the portfolio decisions of firms and households are also returning to normal as financial uncertainties have receded. Indeed
column4: there are signs that savings are increasingly being allocated to long-term assets outside M3 rather than to liquid monetary assets. However
column5: despite the recent moderation of annual M3 growth
column6: there remains substantially more liquidity in the euro area than is needed to finance non-inflationary growth. While a significant part of the excess liquidity has accumulated as a result of past portfolio shifts
column7: low interest rates have also fuelled the build-up of liquid assets. The low level of interest rates also supports credit growth. The stock of excess liquidity
column8: if it persists
column9: may pose an upside risk to price stability over the medium term.

column1: To sum up
column2: the economic analysis indicates that the medium-term outlook for price developments remains in line with price stability
column3: while ongoing close monitoring is necessary. Cross-checking with the monetary analysis supports this conclusion
column4: including the case for continued vigilance with regard to the materialisation of upside risks to price stability.

column1: The Governing Council also discussed a number of issues relating to economic policies in the euro area. First
column2: as regards fiscal policies
column3: it is now of the highest priority that all countries concerned re-establish their commitment to consolidation in order to avoid past mistakes of unbalanced policies in a recovery period. Indeed
column4: the recovery offers the opportunity to put public finances on a sounder track. This requires a strict control of expenditure in the implementation of this year’s budget and a comprehensive reform strategy as a basis for next year’s fiscal planning. Credible expenditure-based reforms are needed to sustain budgetary consolidation and promote the soundness of social security systems
column5: thereby strengthening confidence in the short term and economic growth prospects in the medium term.

column1: Maintaining the existing institutional framework and implementing it consistently is essential to safeguard the soundness of public finances and the macroeconomic environment. In the view of the Governing Council
column2: the Stability and Growth Pact should not be changed
column3: even though its implementation within the current framework could be improved further.

column1: A second issue we have discussed in depth over recent weeks has been the need to clearly step up the pace of structural reforms in the labour and product markets. In this connection
column2: the Governing Council expressed concern about growth in euro area labour productivity having been on a downward trend since the mid-1990s. While this partly reflects improvements in employment
column3: it is also the consequence of sub-optimal progress in fostering overall economic efficiency. Reaping the benefits of the technological advances and efficiency gains associated with producing and using new information and communication technologies requires
column4: in particular
column5: the removal of structural rigidities. In this respect
column6: stimulating further product market competition
column7: particularly in the services sectors
column8: and facilitating industrial restructuring could speed up innovation and the adoption of the new technologies. At the same time
column9: strengthening and spreading technological advances across the individual sectors of the euro area economy must go hand in hand with increased efforts to enhance human capital and adjust educational systems to the changing needs of the labour market.

column1: Since the mid-1990s
column2: somewhat stronger average employment growth has partly compensated for the negative impact of lower productivity gains on overall output growth. However
column3: despite past improvements in employment
column4: the labour supply and its utilisation in the euro area remain low on international comparison. A relatively smaller proportion of the working-age population participates in the labour market
column5: a higher proportion of those participating is unemployed and those who are employed work
column6: on average
column7: far fewer hours per year than elsewhere. Hence
column8: there is a need for further policy changes in the euro area that underpin the labour supply and its utilisation and thereby raise the medium-term growth prospects
column9: so as to preserve average living standards in the face of an ageing population.

column1: We are now at your disposal for questions.";0;"We have not judged particularly the situation of any particular member economy of the euro area
column2: so I have no particular judgement on Germany. Of course
column3: everything that goes in the direction of flexibility
column4: everything that goes in the direction of reinforcing the overall productivity in the euro area goes in the right direction. Part of the difference that has been observed in terms of growth potential between the euro area economy and other economies in the world is clearly associated with the fact that progress in labour productivity was less substantial than has been observed elsewhere. So
column5: again
column6: if those reforms are going in the direction of more productivity
column7: more efficiency
column8: more competitiveness
column9: they are going in the right direction.

column1: First
column2: again
column3: I repeat – and you will pardon me if I say something I said already here – we have an economic analysis and then a monetary analysis
column4: and then we have a judgement on the balance of risks for price stability. The judgement we have on the gradual recovery proceeding is something which is part of our own economic analysis
column5: which again has an impact on the balance of risks for price stability. So
column6: on the judgement we have on growth
column7: I would say that what we are observing now and what we have observed during the last months
column8: goes in the direction of a confirmation of our working assumption of a gradual recovery. And we have a number of elements to substantiate that
column9: particularly the fact that the private sector
column10: private observers
column11: have more or less revised upwards their overall judgement on growth in this economy
column12: and particularly in the present year 2004. That being said
column13: our judgement on the balance of risks for price stability is – for all the reasons I have explained – balanced. We do not change our monetary policy stance because our judgement is that it is balanced and that for the medium term we are in line with our definition of price stability. We have no bias and we are vigilant. And that would be my best summing-up of the mood of this Governing Council meeting: we have no bias
column14: we are vigilant.

column1: We all have responsibility
column2: all over the world. Certainly across the Atlantic the Federal Reserve has a very important responsibility
column3: and it is not my responsibility to elaborate on that. We have our own responsibility: the US is the US and the euro area is the euro area! We are in different universes with different fundamentals and different episodes in the business cycle. Furthermore
column4: we are both responsible for price stability in these different universes. So we are not influenced in any way by what has been decided across the Atlantic or what has been decided in the past across the Channel
column5: or what has been decided elsewhere in the world. Because of our own analysis of the present situation in the euro area
column6: we have not changed our monetary policy stance. Again
column7: on the basis of European judgement and diagnosis we have no bias and we remain vigilant. Do not forget that we are responsible for inflationary expectations in the medium and long run. These inflationary expectations in the medium and long run are anchored by us
column8: by our credibility. They are priced in the various market interest rates – both medium and long term – and the very good financial environment that we are providing to the European economy relies crucially much on our own credibility to deliver price stability.

column1: I hope so; transparency is the rule of the game. If we had a bias we would say that we had a bias. It is clear that there are risks: you have exactly the same figures
column2: the same data
column3: you know the environment
column4: you see that the present level of CPI is 2.4 when it was 2.5 last month
column5: you know our definition of price stability of less than but close to 2%. Everything we have as far as our own analysis is concerned is telling us that all things being equal – and
column6: of course
column7: do not forget that we are living in a universe where there is a lot of uncertainty – in the short term inflation will probably be higher than 2% until the end of the year and even higher than 2% for part of the first semester of next year. So we have to take that into account and that is part of the situation. We also have to say that in the medium term we consider that price stability will be in line with our own definition
column8: but it is obvious that we have to take into account a number of risks and that is the reason why vigilance is warranted. But I repeat: we have no bias.

column1: Again
column2: we have to follow the situation very carefully
column3: because as you know the evolution of unit labour costs is absolutely decisive as regards the evolution of inflation. It is the combination of labour productivity and nominal increases in wages and salaries which make up the unit labour costs. I would like to insist on that: it is absolutely clear that unit labour costs are a crucial indicator of future inflation and a crucial indicator of competitiveness. We are in a universe where market economies function on the basis of comparisons between the competitiveness of corporate businesses and economies in general. So
column4: to conclude I would say that I have no particular concerns but that vigilance in this area is warranted. As regards the monetary policy stance and the overall attitude of the Governing Council
column5: I would say again: no bias – vigilance.

column1: I will not comment on that
column2: I do not see how there could be a counterweight to the ECB. The ECB is independent
column3: as you know
column4: and the independence of the ECB is warranted by the present Treaty and by the Constitution. So I would interpret such ideas as aiming at having the best functioning possible of the executive branches within their own constituencies and of the Commission itself. The Commission has a very close association with the executive branches and with the Council
column5: as well as other institutions
column6: such as the Parliament. We are in the realm of responsibility of the Council
column7: the Commission. For obvious reasons
column8: namely because we have an extremely clear Treaty
column9: it does not infringe
column10: in any respect
column11: on the ECB’s own realm of responsibility and independence.

column1: On the first point
column2: again
column3: I have to be extremely clear: we have no bias
column4: full stop. What does that mean? That means that we look at the situation regularly
column5: every month
column6: we have our own sequencing of analysis and I do not signal to you that we are likely to do anything in the future. It is as simple as that. Every month we look at the situation and we will see what happens. Nobody is master of the future. But as this stage
column7: clearly
column8: we do not signal anything. As regards the labour market changes
column9: globalisation and the impact on global inflation
column10: it is clear that the forces of globalisation have played a very important role in keeping inflation low globally over the last few years. It is also true that we have had some indications
column11: at the global level
column12: of some inflationary pressure: you have the price of oil and you have the price of commodities in general. So you have a number of signals that we are going in the direction of the upside risks for price stability. I do not want to elaborate more on that but it is extremely visible and it is clear that the world is very complex and that you have a combination of forces that are pushing inflation at a global level down and others that are pushing inflation up. It is very fortunate that we have a global recovery. This is quite buoyant and therefore exerts pressure upwards.

column1: First of all
column2: the BIS is an international institution which is important
column3: with a close relationship
column4: as you know
column5: with central banks and which is there precisely to ask pertinent questions or to suggest further deliberations in important areas at the global level because it is a fully international institution. And I am very happy myself to participate in meetings in Basel under the auspices of the BIS
column6: in particular the G10 meeting
column7: the global economy meeting which we organise every two months. That being said
column8: the question is stimulating. I trust that the question is not too much addressed to the ECB in your mind. But it is a theoretical question of great importance. Are we symmetric? Are we asymmetric? How do you deal with this very important question of asset inflation? What kind of responsibility do we have ourselves as central bankers when taking account of asset inflation? You know that we are reflecting a lot on that
column9: that this institution has developed a special understanding and vision
column10: and that we are a little bit original in the constituency of central banks the world over. We consider that on top of the possible interaction between asset inflation and possible bubbles and the monetary policy oriented towards price stability
column11: which is the rule of the game for all central banks
column12: we are keen ourselves on having a monetary analysis. And we trust that it is a way not only to better anchor inflationary expectations
column13: because in the long run inflation is a monetary phenomenon
column14: but also a way of perhaps taking more closely into account phenomena like asset inflation and bubbles because they are fed by monetary expansion. So we trust that perhaps – I say perhaps
column15: I am cautious
column16: I am prudent – our monetary policy concept is well-suited to this particular responsibility that is part of the overall BIS remark.

column1: It is a direct question. Only three comments. First comment: there is a consensus in Europe
column2: as extraordinary as it might appear
column3: on what you said
column4: on the fact that it would be extremely opportune to embark on structural reforms and to do things that some other economies have already been doing over the past years. That consensus crystallised in 2000 in the so-called Lisbon diagnosis and Lisbon agenda
column5: so the problem is not whether we are being listened to or not being listened to. We all agree on the necessity of these structural reforms and the problem is to implement those structural reforms
column6: which is being done in some countries before your eyes
column7: and before the eyes of the Governing Council
column8: but which is obviously not very easy because of the sentiment of perhaps part of the population because of the fact that public opinion in general probably has yet to understand why it would be extremely important to make those reforms if we want growth

column10: but there is no doubt that we all agree on the direction to be taken. You mentioned one particular country. I could have mentioned other countries myself. For instance
column11: I could have mentioned Ireland
column12: which is in the euro zone and is certainly a success story in terms of growth
column13: in terms of GDP per capita and in terms of job creation
column14: and again it is in the euro zone. Outside Europe
column15: I could have mentioned Australia
column16: which is a country that has introduced a lot of structural reforms on the basis very largely of a political consensus
column17: and also of a social consensus
column18: and these reforms are paying off also very well. There is a growing number of examples which prove that it is true that those structural reforms are delivering.

column1: Frankly speaking
column2: it seems to me that all the criticism about the absence of transparency of the ECB can be taken with a grain of salt. Do you know another central bank that holds a press conference immediately after the decision of the monetary policy council? Do you know another central bank that produces four or five full pages assessing the situation
column3: expressing the diagnosis
column4: not in two paragraphs but in a more detailed way? Do you remember that

column7: not only do we try to be as transparent as possible but also we

column12: all that being said
column13: I cannot invent a bias where we have none
column14: and change for your pleasure the assessment of my colleagues in the Governing Council. We try to do our best. We are under the control of public opinion. We are under the control of markets. We are under the control of savers and investors
column15: and not only in Europe but the world over. On the basis of our credibility they are managing trillions of euro

And I mention this again because it is very important: we shipped to the euro area the yield curve that was the best yield curve available before the euro area was set up. That has made it possible to generalise for 306 million inhabitants a level of market interest rates that was previously the privilege of only a fraction of those 306 million inhabitants. To the extent that we started from scratch
column17: this relied entirely upon the credit of stability that was given to us on the basis of our credibility. The credibility of the institution. The credibility
column18: perhaps
column19: of the transparent interaction with you and
column20: through you
column21: with the full body of observers
column22: savers and investors. And also the credibility of our monetary policy concept
column23: which – at the beginning – was perhaps criticised a little but it is now less and less criticised
column24: it seems to me.

column1: First of all
column2: on the particular cases which were mentioned previously
column3: I avoided mentioning any particular economy – we are looking at the 306 million citizens – but I said that anything that goes in the direction of more flexibility
column4: more adaptability to an environment which is extraordinarily demanding in terms of competitiveness
column5: also goes in the direction of growth and job creation
column6: of prosperity and diminishing unemployment. So we would strongly support across the entire euro area anything that goes in the direction of more flexibility. As regards unit labour costs they are a combination of productivity progress on the one hand
column7: and of nominal wage and salary increases on the other hand. Having highly competitive unit labour costs is extremely important. As regards this institution

column1: It is perfectly legitimate for you to ask a series of questions which have a tendency to identify one element taken out of context to see whether it plays an important role or not – I take it that this is the aim of your question? What we do is to integrate all elements. We are in a very

column3: whether this equation relates our policy to exchange rates or whether it relates our policy to fiscal position or to wage and salary increases. We operate in a universe where we have to take account of everything and make a synthesis out of everything we have
column4: to be sure that our decisions are robust and that they really take account of everything
column5: including the uncertainty
column6: which is part of our very comprehensive deliberations. And then we take a decision

column10: again
column11: that our judgement is made on the basis of the euro area
column12: we judge the situation here on the basis of all data and figures that are here and we are not under any influence. We are in a symmetrical position – I assume that the Federal Reserve would not respond by saying “Yes

column16: and this is what we try to do here.

column1: We noted that the information which has become available in recent months indicates that the economic recovery in the euro area has maintained its momentum and should remain firm in the coming quarters. We have also witnessed somewhat higher inflation rates
column2: mainly due to developments in oil prices. At present
column3: our judgement is that although some upside risks to price stability exist
column4: the overall prospects remain in line with price stability over the medium term. Accordingly
column5: we have retained our monetary policy stance and left the key ECB interest rates unchanged. The level of interest rates is very low by historical standards
column6: both in nominal and in real terms
column7: lending support to economic activity. We will remain vigilant with regard to all developments which could imply risks to price stability over the medium term.

column1: I shall now explain our assessment in more detail
column2: turning first to the economic analysis.

column1: The latest data releases confirm that the economic recovery in the euro area is continuing. According to Eurostat’s flash estimate
column2: real GDP grew by 0.5% quarter on quarter in the second quarter of this year
column3: having recorded a 0.6% increase in the first quarter. These growth rates are the strongest in the euro area for some time. The latest indicators of output and demand remain consistent with ongoing growth in real activity
column4: increasingly supported by domestic demand
column5: also in the third quarter of 2004.

column1: Looking ahead
column2: the conditions for a continuation of the recovery remain in place. Economic growth outside the euro area continues to be robust overall
column3: even if subject to temporary fluctuations
column4: and should continue to support euro area export growth. On the domestic side
column5: investment should benefit from the positive global environment and the very favourable financing conditions. Improvements in corporate efficiency and higher profits are also supporting business investment. Moreover
column6: private consumption should continue its gradual recovery
column7: broadly in line with growth in real disposable income which
column8: with the usual lag
column9: should be further underpinned by an increase in employment growth later on.

column1: Against this background
column2: we expect the economic recovery in the euro area to continue and to become more broadly based over the coming quarters
column3: leading to a somewhat stronger upswing in the course of 2005. This is also reflected in the ECB staff projections
column4: which will be published today. They envisage euro area real GDP growth of between 1.6% and 2.2% on average in 2004
column5: rising to between 1.8% and 2.8% in 2005. These growth rates are close to estimates for long-run potential growth and
column6: for both years

column1: Overall

column1: Let me now report on the outcome of today’s meeting. As regards economic growth
column2: while some uncertainty has recently arisen concerning the expected strengthening of activity
column3: the economic recovery in the euro area is ongoing. Looking at price developments
column4: high oil prices have had a visible direct impact on inflation rates this year. However
column5: the risk of second-round effects still seems to be contained

column7: we have left the key ECB interest rates unchanged. This means that the level of interest rates continues to be very low by historical standards
column8: in both nominal and real terms. Strong vigilance is warranted with regard to all developments which could imply risks to price stability over the medium term.

column9: there is scope for a recovery in euro area private consumption
column10: in line with growth in real disposable income.

column2: in particular to the extent that second-round effects stemming from wage and price-setting behaviour materialise. It is therefore of the utmost importance to avoid inappropriate reactions
column3: as observed in past episodes of strong oil price increases. A further upward risk relates to the future development of indirect taxes and administered prices. These upside risks call for ongoing vigilance
column4: which is a necessary condition for keeping medium to long-term inflation expectations in line with our definition of price stability.

column4: especially of the most liquid assets included in the narrow aggregate M1.

column3: which is mainly the result of past portfolio shifts

column5: particularly at a time when confidence and economic activity were strengthening
column6: inflationary risks would rise. In addition

column1: Let me also address the current evidence on fiscal developments
column2: where the latest budgetary notifications are a source of concern. While some countries will maintain a sound budgetary position
column3: a significant number of euro area countries are expected to record deficits near to or above 3%. The aggregate euro area fiscal deficit-to-GDP ratio is expected to increase somewhat

column7: towards structural reform
column8: innovation and competitiveness. This would very much support the Lisbon agenda and thereby promote economic growth

We consider the Pact as key to ensuring macroeconomic stability on a sustainable basis. It is a framework which is necessary to preserve sound fiscal policies in the euro area
column4: for which strict surveillance and effective peer pressure on national budget policies are indispensable.

column1: It is of vital importance to the credibility of the budgetary surveillance that the reliable compilation and timely reporting of government finance statistics is ensured. This should be done in a manner that is consistent and stable over time and homogeneous across countries. The procedures must not be vulnerable to political and electoral cycles
column2: as stated by the ECOFIN Council. Countries should consider the quality and integrity of their statistics as a priority matter.

column1: Finally
column2: let me report on the detailed discussion we had today on employment and unemployment developments in the euro area. Two observations stand out when we look at the period of relatively slow real GDP expansion since early 2001. First
column3: after an initial rise
column4: the euro area unemployment rate has remained broadly unchanged since early 2003. And second
column5: there seems to have been a relatively limited negative impact on employment growth over the past few years. The following factors might help to explain this pattern. While the period of slow growth has been relatively long from a historical perspective

2004-11-04;2;Ladies and gentlemen
column2: the Vice-President and I will now report on the outcome of today’s meeting of the Governing Council of the ECB.

column1: Persistently high and rising oil prices have had a visible direct impact on consumer prices this year
column2: and inflation is likely to remain significantly above 2% in the coming months. This is a worrisome development
column3: but there is no strong indication as yet that medium-term inflationary pressures are building up in the euro area. In particular
column4: wage growth appears to remain limited
column5: in the context of ongoing moderate real GDP growth and weak labour markets. Against this background
column6: we have decided to leave the key ECB interest rates unchanged at their present levels
column7: which are very low by historical standards. However
column8: there are upside risks to price stability over the medium term. Strong vigilance is therefore warranted with regard to all developments which could increase such risks.

column1: I shall now explain our assessment in more detail
column2: turning first to the economic analysis. The economic recovery started in the second half of 2003
column3: and we saw positive developments in the first half of 2004. Although short-term indicators have become more mixed
column4: the basic determinants of economic activity remain consistent with continuing economic growth in 2005. On the external side
column5: we see some moderation taking place following a period in which the world economy has experienced its strongest dynamism in many years. Nevertheless
column6: euro area exports should continue to benefit from positive global demand conditions in 2005. On the domestic side
column7: investment should be supported by the global environment
column8: the very favourable financing conditions in the euro area
column9: improved earnings and greater corporate efficiency gained through business restructuring. Furthermore
column10: scope exists in the euro area as a whole for private consumption to strengthen
column11: particularly once labour market prospects improve more visibly.

column1: However
column2: this outlook is surrounded by continuing uncertainty
column3: in particular stemming from recent developments in oil markets. On the one hand
column4: the magnitude and nature of this shock differ from earlier experiences
column5: when oil price rises were much stronger and mainly due to supply constraints. In addition
column6: the oil intensity of production is significantly lower in the euro area. On the other hand
column7: recent oil price increases constitute a nonetheless sizeable adverse shock to the euro area economy. If oil prices were to remain at current levels
column8: or even increase further
column9: they would dampen the strength of the recovery both inside and outside the euro area. Under certain conditions
column10: a smoother absorption of the oil price shock can be ensured: in particular
column11: second-round effects in wage and price-setting must continue to be avoided
column12: and fiscal authorities should refrain from taking measures which would prolong the necessary adjustment process.

column1: With regard to consumer prices
column2: annual inflation increased to 2.5% in October
column3: according to Eurostat’s flash estimate. This was a strong increase
column4: after the decline to 2.1% in September from 2.3% in August
column5: and shows that oil price developments have had a sizeable direct impact on the euro area HICP in recent weeks. Moreover
column6: the oil price shock may feed through the economy and generate further indirect effects
column7: as indicated by developments in producer prices.

column1: Looking further ahead
column2: however
column3: the information available so far does not suggest that stronger underlying inflationary pressures are building up in the euro area. Wage increases have remained limited since the last quarter of 2003
column4: and this trend is expected to persist in the context of ongoing moderate growth and weak labour markets.

column1: Nevertheless
column2: a number of upward risks to the outlook for price stability have emerged over recent months. Risks are mainly associated with oil price developments
column3: possible renewed increases in indirect taxes and administrative prices
column4: and potential second-round effects stemming from wage and price-setting behaviour.

column1: Further indications for the medium-term outlook are provided by the monetary analysis. The downward trend in annual M3 growth in the first half of this year appears to have come to a halt in recent months. The shorter-term dynamics of M3 have strengthened and its annual growth rates are rising. These developments reflect the stimulative effect of the historically low level of interest rates in the euro area on monetary expansion. Demand for the most liquid components of M3 contained in the narrow aggregate M1 is particularly strong. The low level of interest rates is also fuelling private sector demand for credit. In particular
column2: the growth rate of loans for house purchase continues to rise and is now approaching double digits. Yet loan demand is becoming more broadly based
column3: and the annual growth of loans to non-financial corporations is also picking up.

column1: Given the continued strength of M3 growth over the past few years
column2: there remains substantially more liquidity in the euro area than is needed to finance non-inflationary growth. This could pose inflationary risks in the future if the excess liquidity is not progressively reduced as a result of reverse portfolio shifts. Moreover
column3: persistently high excess liquidity and strong credit growth could become a source of unsustainable asset price increases
column4: particularly in property markets.

column1: To sum up
column2: the economic analysis suggests that underlying inflationary pressures are still contained
column3: but a number of medium-term upside risks to price stability need to be monitored closely. It is particularly important that these do not affect long-term inflation expectations. Cross-checking with the monetary analysis continues to support the case for strong vigilance with regard to the materialisation of risks to price stability.

column1: I would now like to make a few remarks on fiscal policies. Most countries have presented their budget plans for 2005. In some cases there are encouraging signs that Member States are planning to correct excessive deficits or make progress towards close-to-balance or in-surplus budgetary positions. However
column2: there are other cases where there are significant risks that commitments under the Stability and Growth Pact will not be met
column3: or where imbalances are on the rise and new breaches of the 3% reference value might occur. It is therefore imperative that 2005 budgets prioritise consolidation where this is necessary. Moreover
column4: it is of vital importance that the reliable compilation and timely reporting of government finance statistics are ensured. Appropriate budgetary targets and compliance with fiscal commitments and reporting requirements will help to build confidence
column5: support the economic upswing and prepare for the impact of population ageing.

column1: As regards the European fiscal framework
column2: the Governing Council remains convinced that improvements in the implementation of the Stability and Growth Pact are possible and would be beneficial. In this regard
column3: the European Commission’s proposals for improving the implementation of the preventive arm of the Pact are useful. At the same time
column4: the Governing Council warns against changes to the Pact and
column5: in particular
column6: the excessive deficit procedure. It considers the credibility of the 3% deficit limit essential to anchoring expectations of fiscal discipline. Moreover
column7: strict surveillance and effective peer pressure on national budget policies are indispensable to preserving sound fiscal policies.

column1: Finally
column2: I would also like to take this opportunity to reiterate the need for progress on structural reform. Fiscal consolidation plans should be part of a structural reform agenda that favours growth
column3: competitiveness and employment. As regards labour and product markets
column4: the mid-term review of the Lisbon agenda – now being prepared for the European Council meeting in March 2005 – is a major opportunity to increase momentum in these fields. Structural reforms are crucial to a better performing EU economy
column5: i.e. an economy with higher potential growth
column6: more employment opportunities and greater resilience to shocks. Efforts to accelerate key economic reforms are now more important than ever.

column1: We are now at your disposal for questions.";0;"My colleagues and I discussed that first question a lot today. Each of us participated in the discussion and we weighed up the balance of risks to price stability. You know that the needle of our compass is price stability. And we incorporate absolutely all elements
column2: including
column3: of course
column4: our judgement on the strength of the economy as regards its impact on this needle of the compass of price stability. We had a lot of views. The weight of the upward risks to price stability was assessed. It is clear that we see these upside risks to price stability augmenting. That is absolutely clear. And it is the reason why we consider the posture of strong vigilance to be the appropriate posture
column5: strong vigilance to clearly communicate to all economic agents that we will not let secondary effects materialise. We are there to ensure that there are no secondary effects. And that is the message of today’s Governing Council.

column1: On the exchange rates I would only say that we all signed the Washington communiqué: the Secretary of the US Treasury and the President of the Federal Reserve System
column2: as well as European counterparts
column3: including myself. It captures the present sentiment of the G7 community. Thus we all signed

That was then captured in the Boca Raton communiqué and in the following G7 communiqué of Washington that I was just quoting in response to the previous question. But there is a continuity in this sentiment.
I told you that I stick to what I said on excess volatility. This is a continuous position

column1: In reply to your first question
column2: we will publish our new projections as you know in a month’s time and then you will know what the new staff projections are. At the present time
column3: I would say that what is clear to me is that the present pick-up of the CPI which we are observing will continue for some months and will perhaps even increase. So I warn you that there is the likelihood
column4: as far as we understand the consequences and
column5: I would say
column6: the passing-through of the oil price impact that we will probably see. So that is very clear and I warn you in advance. Then
column7: it will continue for some months next year and then we think that at a certain moment we will go back down to our definition of price stability. The passing-through of this oil shock will take place over time
column8: but of course will not be permanent. I remain very prudent and cautious and I will not respond to the question on the average of next year. It depends so much on the oil price itself and what is likely or unlikely to happen and I don’t want to make any projections. The working assumption when I was mentioning the profile that I had in mind is that the price of oil would remain at the same level. You know that in the same G7 meeting that I was mentioning
column9: we also called for appropriate conditions for a decrease in the price of oil and it is our sentiment that the present level is not in line with what would be advisable in all respects. So we will see what happens
column10: but we strive to get a more appropriate – I would say – supply and demand “encounter” in order to have prices that would be lower and more in line with what is desirable for the global economy.

column1: In reply to your second question
column2: it is absolutely clear that under a working assumption that the price of oil remains at the present level and may even rise further
column3: which is a possibility that we hate but that we have mentioned
column4: clearly the impact on inflation is upward and the impact on growth is downward. So under this assumption it is absolutely clear that downward risks for growth are there and are rising. That is absolutely clear and I would say that in some respects it is an arithmetic consequence of the transfer of revenue associated with the pick-up in the price of oil from oil-consuming economies to oil-producing economies. That is absolutely clear.

column1: On the first question
column2: I am very clear and I don’t want to repeat again the fact that excessive volatility and disorderly moves in the exchange markets are undesirable. I said that and I repeat that and I say it so clearly that I take it that there is no need to repeat it again.

column1: On house loans
column2: we have mentioned in a number of recent meetings of the Governing Council that when we analyse the counterparts of M3
column3: we see credit to the economy which is quite dynamic. Within this
column4: credit to households is pretty dynamic and is now close to two-digit figures. It is also clear that we are observing in certain economies
column5: not in all economies and certainly not in our economy as a whole
column6: a phenomenon of asset inflation in the real estate sector which has to be examined very carefully. But again it is not a phenomenon that we are observing in the euro area as a whole
column7: only in a number of economies.

column1: On the dollar I already said what I had to say if you permit me. On the twin deficits it’s absolutely clear that the unanimous sentiment of the Governing Council is that we have a lack of savings in the US. We don’t disagree with the US on that. As you know
column2: it is a joint diagnosis which is made by both our US friends and ourselves that there is a lack of savings in the US. The correction of this lack of savings is
column3: I would say
column4: the “homework” of the US
column5: while we have our own homework
column6: which is structural reforms and making our economy more flexible and more resilient. On both sides of the Atlantic we have assets and liabilities and we all agree on these: our own assets are that we are balanced and we are financing our own investment with our own savings
column7: while the US is not; by contrast
column8: the assets of the US are that they have a very flexible and a very resilient economy and I would say they are permanently proving that in the present conditions of the global economy. So
column9: all that being said
column10: in our own analysis it is very important that the US progressively

column1: As regards whether or not the ECB is a truly European institution
