column2: the Vice-President and I will now report on the outcome of today’s meeting of the Governing Council of the ECB.

column1: All in all
column2: the short-term outlook for inflation remains worrisome
column3: but our assessment of price developments over the medium term is unchanged. At the current juncture oil price developments are having a sizeable impact on consumer prices in the euro area
column4: while there is no significant evidence that stronger underlying domestic inflationary pressures are building up. Accordingly
column5: we have left the key ECB interest rates unchanged at their historically low levels. At the same time
column6: we recognise the existence of upside risks to price stability over the medium term. Continued vigilance is of the essence with regard to those risks.

column1: I shall now explain our assessment in more detail
column2: turning first to the economic analysis. After the positive developments in the first half of 2004
column3: economic growth has moderated in the second half. In the third quarter of the year
column4: real GDP growth is estimated to have been only 0.3% quarter on quarter
column5: after 0.7% and 0.5% in the previous two quarters. According to Eurostat
column6: the contribution of net exports turned negative
column7: reflecting in particular high import growth
column8: and private consumption was subdued
column9: probably dampened by higher oil prices. At the same time
column10: investment growth increased and inventories were built up. The available survey information for October and November points to ongoing growth in the fourth quarter
column11: albeit at a more moderate pace than in the first half of this year.

column1: The conditions remain in place for economic growth to proceed. On the external side
column2: while global growth is showing some signs of moderation
column3: it nonetheless is expected to remain robust. Euro area exports should continue to benefit from global demand conditions. On the domestic side
column4: investment should be supported further by the very favourable financing conditions in the euro area
column5: improved earnings and greater corporate efficiency gained through business restructuring. Finally
column6: scope exists for private consumption to strengthen
column7: particularly if uncertainties surrounding the extent and pace of fiscal consolidation and structural reforms are reduced.

column1: Accordingly
column2: we expect a gradual recovery in euro area activity over the next two years
column3: with somewhat more moderate growth rates due to the impact of oil prices. This is also reflected in the Eurosystem staff projections. Euro area real GDP growth is projected to be between 1.6% and 2.0% on average in 2004
column4: between 1.4% and 2.4% in 2005 and between 1.7% and 2.7% in 2006. Available forecasts from international and private sector organisations convey a broadly similar picture.

column1: Downside risks to these projections stem in particular from potentially unfavourable developments in the oil market. In order to limit such risks
column2: second-round effects in wage and price-setting must be avoided and fiscal authorities should refrain from taking measures which would prolong or distort the necessary adjustment process. Moreover
column3: the degree of competition in the euro area energy sector is an important factor in allowing higher oil prices to be absorbed without significant distortions. Further progress in increasing competition in this sector would be highly beneficial.

column1: Turning to consumer prices
column2: annual HICP inflation was 2.2% in November
column3: according to Eurostat’s flash estimate
column4: down from 2.4% in October. Over the coming months
column5: inflation rates of above 2% are likely to persist
column6: and some temporary further increase from current levels cannot be excluded. Looking further ahead
column7: however
column8: the information available so far indicates that HICP inflation would fall below 2% in the course of 2005 if no further adverse shocks occurred and it does not suggest that stronger underlying inflationary pressures are building up in the euro area. Wage increases have remained contained over recent quarters and
column9: in the context of ongoing moderate growth and weak labour markets
column10: this trend should continue in the future. Producer prices are rising
column11: but this remains concentrated on energy and intermediate goods
column12: which should limit the pass-through.

column1: These views are also embodied in the Eurosystem staff projections. Average annual HICP inflation is projected to lie between 2.1% and 2.3% in 2004. As the impact of recent oil price increases and the effects of previous indirect tax and administered price rises gradually dissipate
column2: annual HICP inflation is projected to be between 1.5% and 2.5% in 2005 and 1.0% and 2.2% in 2006. These projections are broadly consistent with forecasts recently released by international and private sector organisations.

column1: Several upside risks need to be taken into account. Concerns relate in particular to future oil price developments and
column2: more generally
column3: to the potential risk of second-round effects in wage and price-setting throughout the economy. Further developments in indirect taxes and administered prices also need to be monitored closely.

column1: Further insight into the outlook for price developments
column2: at medium to longer-term horizons
column3: is provided by the monetary analysis. The latest monetary data confirm that the downward trend in annual M3 growth observed from the middle of 2003 has not continued in recent months and has even reversed.

column1: Over the course of 2004
column2: monetary dynamics have been driven by two opposing forces. On the one hand
column3: the historically very low level of interest rates in the euro area has stimulated M3 dynamics
column4: in particular demand for the most liquid components of M3 contained in the narrow aggregate M1. On the other hand
column5: portfolio allocation behaviour has tended to normalise over the past year following the exceptionally strong preference for liquidity observed during the period of heightened economic and financial uncertainty between 2001 and mid-2003. However
column6: investors’ preference for liquid assets seems to have remained greater than would typically be expected at the current stage of the economic cycle
column7: possibly due to the fact that the economic and financial uncertainties in recent years have been relatively strong and protracted.

column1: The very low level of interest rates is also fuelling private sector demand for credit. In particular
column2: the demand for loans for house purchase has continued to be robust
column3: supported also by strong house price dynamics in several euro area countries. Growth in loans to non-financial corporations has picked up further in recent months.

column1: As a result of the persistently high growth in M3 over the past few years
column2: there remains substantially more liquidity in the euro area than is needed to finance non-inflationary economic growth. This could pose risks to price stability over the medium term.

column1: To sum up
column2: the economic analysis suggests that underlying domestic inflationary pressures are contained
column3: but a number of medium-term upside risks to price stability need to be monitored closely. Cross-checking with the monetary analysis supports the case for continued vigilance with regard to the materialisation of risks to price stability over the medium term. It is of the essence to avoid any spillover from short-term consumer price developments to long-term inflation expectations.

column1: As regards fiscal policies
column2: forthcoming budgets and stability programmes should send strong and confidence-building signals
column3: namely that sound public finances and growth-friendly structural adjustments in public finances are being pursued. Concerning the European institutional framework
column4: the Stability and Growth Pact and the excessive deficit procedure are the key fiscal cornerstones of EMU. These must remain firm. The Pact and the excessive deficit procedure should be fully respected in their current form
column5: while their implementation could be improved
column6: in particular as regards the preventive arm of the Pact.

column1: Finally
column2: let me support the calls expressed in the report of the High Level Group chaired by Wim Kok to renew the impetus in the Lisbon process and to sharpen its focus. In this context
column3: we restate our strong support for all efforts on the part of governments
column4: parliaments and social partners implementing the reform agenda and focusing on those reforms that will support employment growth
column5: foster investment and stimulate innovation and productivity. Progress in this direction will not only enhance the underlying growth potential of the euro area economy over the medium term but will also help to bolster consumer and business confidence over a shorter horizon.

column1: While short-term inflationary pressures persist

column2: the conditions remain in place for economic growth to proceed. On the external side

column4: investment should be supported by the very favourable financing conditions in the euro area
column5: improved corporate earnings and greater business efficiency as firms continue to restructure. Moreover
column6: private consumption is likely to evolve in line with the development of real disposable income. Consumption would also be supported if uncertainties surrounding the extent and pace of fiscal consolidation and structural reform in the euro area were reduced.

column1: In the context of what is a broadly favourable outlook for price developments over the medium term
column2: upside risks to price stability need to be taken into account. Given past oil price rises
column3: there is a continued need to avoid second-round effects in wage and price-setting throughout the economy. Responsibility on the part of social partners remains very important. Moreover
column4: developments in indirect taxes and administered prices require close monitoring.

column1: Turning to the monetary analysis
column2: the latest data confirm our previous assessment. Monetary and credit growth strengthened in the second half of 2004
column3: largely as a consequence of the prevailing low level of interest rates. Given the strength of monetary dynamics over the past few years
column4: there remains significantly more liquidity in the euro area than is required to finance non-inflationary growth. Overall
column5: the monetary analysis points to upside risks to price stability over the medium to longer term. At the same time
column6: the combination of high excess liquidity and strong credit growth could in some countries become a source of unsustainable price increases in property markets.

column1: To sum up
column2: the economic analysis suggests that underlying domestic inflationary pressures are contained but upside risks to price stability over the medium term need to be monitored closely. In this context
column3: it is crucial that there is no spillover from current short-term developments in consumer price inflation to long-term inflation expectations. Cross-checking with the monetary analysis supports the case for continued vigilance with regard to the materialisation of risks to price stability over the medium term.

column1: With regard to both fiscal policies and structural reforms
column2: the governments and institutions of the European Union will have to confront many important challenges in the course of 2005.

column1: Foremost among these challenges is the need to strengthen public finances by correcting excessive deficits swiftly and returning to a path of vigorous fiscal consolidation. Moreover
column2: throughout the European Union there is a need to address the considerable challenges that population ageing poses to existing pension and social security systems.

column1: There is also a need to now bring the ongoing discussions surrounding the European fiscal framework to a convincing conclusion which builds trust and confidence. The existing fiscal framework enshrined in the Treaty and the Stability and Growth Pact is a cornerstone of Economic and Monetary Union and thus of central importance for anchoring expectations of fiscal discipline. The Governing Council is convinced that improvements in the implementation of the Pact are possible. At the same time
column2: it reiterates its position that it would be counterproductive to change the Regulations
column3: dilute the 3% deficit limit or weaken the excessive deficit procedure.

column1: Turning to structural policies
column2: the forthcoming mid-term review of the Lisbon agenda provides an opportunity to give renewed impetus to structural reform in the euro area
column3: as called for by the recently published Kok Report. We strongly support a reform agenda which focuses on raising employment growth
column4: fostering investment and stimulating innovation and productivity. Progress in this direction will not only enhance the underlying growth potential of the euro area economy over the medium term
column5: but will also help to bolster consumer and business confidence over a shorter horizon.

column1: Further insight into the outlook for price developments at medium to longer-term horizons is provided by the monetary analysis. column1: On the whole
column2: we continue to see no significant evidence of underlying domestic inflationary pressures building up in the euro area. Accordingly
column3: we have left the key ECB interest rates unchanged. These interest rates are at historically low levels and are making an important contribution to the economic recovery. At the same time
column4: upside risks to price stability over the medium term exist. These require continued vigilance on the part of the Governing Council.

column1: I shall now explain our assessment in more detail
column2: turning first to the economic analysis. According to Eurostat’s flash estimate
column3: real GDP in the euro area grew at a quarter-on-quarter rate of 0.2% in the fourth quarter of 2004. In addition
column4: third-quarter real GDP growth was revised down to 0.2%. This overall outcome for the second half of last year was disappointing. However
column5: the composition of demand growth in the fourth quarter also offered some positive signs with regard to the underlying trend. The strengthening of domestic demand and
column6: in particular
column7: consumption may point to the recovery in economic activity in the euro area regaining some momentum.

column1: There are a number of reasons why the weaker real GDP growth in the second half of 2004 could be a transitory phenomenon. On the external side
column2: growth in the world economy remains strong
column3: supporting euro area exports. On the domestic side
column4: investment is expected to continue to benefit from very favourable financing conditions
column5: robust earnings and greater business efficiency. Consumption growth should benefit from anticipated developments in real disposable income.

column1: Accordingly
column2: we expect continued economic growth in 2005 and 2006. This assessment is also reflected in the new ECB staff projections
column3: which will be published today. Euro area real GDP growth is projected by the ECB’s staff to be
column4: on average
column5: between 1.2% and 2.0% in 2005 and between 1.6% and 2.6% in 2006. These projections are lower than those published in December 2004
column6: reflecting the weaker economic developments in late 2004. Available forecasts from international and private sector organisations convey a broadly similar outlook.

column1: The picture emerging from the projections contains a number of risks. On the external side
column2: high and volatile oil prices and persistent global imbalances pose downside risks to growth. As regards exchange rates
column3: we confirm our position – expressed when the euro rose sharply – that such moves are unwelcome and undesirable for economic growth. On the domestic side
column4: there are uncertainties surrounding the evolution of consumption
column5: while the very favourable financing conditions and the recovery in corporate earnings could lead to higher investment growth than currently projected.

column1: Turning to consumer prices
column2: annual HICP inflation declined quite substantially in January 2005
column3: falling to 1.9% from 2.4% in December 2004. This was largely a result of base effects from developments in indirect taxes and administered prices in some countries. In February
column4: according to Eurostat´s flash estimate
column5: annual HICP inflation was 2.0%.

column1: In the coming months
column2: annual inflation rates are likely to fluctuate around 2%. Looking further ahead
column3: there is no evidence that stronger underlying domestic inflationary pressures are building up in the euro area. Over recent quarters
column4: wage increases have remained moderate. In the context of moderate economic growth
column5: this trend should continue.

column1: These views are also embodied in the ECB staff projections. Average annual HICP inflation is projected by the staff to lie between 1.6% and 2.2% in 2005 and between 1.0% and 2.2% in 2006. These projections are broadly unchanged from the Eurosystem staff projections published in December 2004 and consistent with forecasts recently released by international and private sector organisations.
Several upside risks to these projections need to be taken into account
column2: notably future oil price developments. Developments in indirect taxes and administered prices may also again surprise on the upside. Furthermore
column3: continued vigilance is required regarding the potential risk of past price increases leading to second-round effects in wage and price-setting throughout the economy. In this respect
column4: developments in longer-term inflation expectations need to be monitored closely.

column1: Further insight into the outlook for price developments at medium to longer-term horizons is provided by the monetary analysis. The latest monetary data confirm the strengthening of M3 growth observed since mid-2004. This increasingly reflects the stimulative effect of the historically very low level of interest rates in the euro area. As a result of the persistently strong growth in M3 over the past few years
column2: substantially more liquidity in the euro area exists than is needed to finance non-inflationary economic growth. This could pose risks to price stability over the medium term and warrants vigilance.

column1: The exceptionally low level of real interest rates is also further stimulating private sector demand for credit. Growth in loans to non-financial corporations has continued to pick up in recent months. Moreover
column2: demand for loans for house purchase has continued to be robust
column3: contributing to strong house price dynamics in some regions of the euro area.

column1: To sum up
column2: the economic analysis confirms that underlying domestic inflationary pressures remain contained
column3: while medium-term upside risks to price stability exist and will be monitored closely. Cross-checking with the monetary analysis supports the case for continued vigilance with regard to the materialisation of risks to price stability over the medium term.

column1: Turning to fiscal policies
column2: the Governing Council notes that
column3: while some progress with fiscal consolidation and the correction of excessive deficits is envisaged in euro area countries’ updated stability programmes
column4: further consolidation in a number of countries is needed. In particular
column5: several countries do not plan to pursue an appropriately ambitious adjustment path and are not targeting close-to-balance or in-surplus budgetary positions by the end of the programme horizon. In addition
column6: in some cases
column7: fiscal targets are based on rather favourable growth assumptions and on insufficiently specified measures.

column1: With respect to the Stability and Growth Pact
column2: discussions now need to be brought to a convincing conclusion with an outcome that safeguards fiscal discipline. The credibility of the excessive deficit procedure needs to be fully preserved. This is not only fundamental for macroeconomic stability and cohesion in the euro area but also for confidence and growth prospects in all Member States.

column1: In this regard
column2: the Governing Council welcomes the decision by the ECOFIN Council
column3: based on a recommendation by the European Commission
column4: to move
column5: for the first time
column6: to the next procedural step in the excessive deficit procedure and to give notice
column7: in accordance with Treaty Article 104(9)
column8: to Greece. The Governing Council also takes the view that the extension of the deadline
column9: from 2005 to 2006
column10: for correcting the excessive deficit pushes the room for interpretation of the rules and procedures to the limit. It is now indispensable for Greece to take effective action to correct its severe fiscal imbalances.

column1: As regards structural developments
column2: the euro area has seen relatively low trend productivity growth since the mid-1990s. An analysis of the determinants of productivity shows that lower productivity growth in the euro area has been partly related to higher employment due to greater participation of lower-skilled labour. Sustained wage moderation and some progress in labour market reforms aimed at increasing labour market participation appear to have partially shifted production towards a more intensive use of labour.

column1: There are also indications that the slower pace of productivity growth observed in the euro area since the mid-1990s reflects an insufficient use of new productivity-enhancing technologies. While productivity growth has increased in sectors that produce information and communication technologies or provide related services
column2: it has declined in many other areas of the economy. This points to structural rigidities in the euro area that prevent or hinder the fast and effective dissemination of new technologies and improved production processes across the economy.

column1: Against this background
column2: structural reforms that stimulate innovation
column3: investment and productivity
column4: and promote the use of new productivity-enhancing technologies are crucial. Stimulating product market competition
column5: facilitating restructuring and improving human capital through adequate educational systems and “on-the-job” training are likely to speed up productivity gains from the use of new technologies.

column1: All in all
column2: we have not changed our assessment of risks to price stability over the medium term. So far
column3: we have seen no significant evidence of underlying domestic inflationary pressures building up in the euro area. Accordingly
column4: we have left the key ECB interest rates unchanged. Both nominal and real interest rates are at exceptionally low levels
column5: lending ongoing support to economic activity. However
column6: upside risks to price stability over the medium term remain and continued vigilance is therefore of the essence.

column1: I shall now explain our assessment in more detail
column2: turning first to the economic analysis. Recent data and survey indicators on economic activity have been mixed. In general they point to ongoing economic growth at a moderate pace over the short term
column3: with no clear signs as yet of a strengthening in underlying dynamics.

column1: Looking further ahead
column2: the conditions remain in place for moderate economic growth to continue. Global growth remains solid
column3: providing a favourable environment for euro area exports. On the domestic side
column4: investment is expected to continue to be supported by very favourable financing conditions
column5: improved profits and greater business efficiency. Consumption growth should develop in line with real disposable income growth. However
column6: at the same time
column7: persistently high oil prices in particular pose downside risks to growth.

column1: Turning to consumer prices
column2: Eurostat’s flash estimate for annual HICP inflation was 2.1% in March
column3: unchanged from February. In the coming months
column4: annual inflation rates are likely to remain somewhat above 2%
column5: although the exact figure will depend largely on how oil prices develop. Looking further ahead
column6: so far we have seen no significant evidence of underlying domestic inflationary pressures building up in the euro area. Wage increases have remained contained over recent quarters and
column7: in the context of moderate economic growth and weak labour markets
column8: this trend is likely to continue for the time being.

column1: However
column2: upside risks to price stability remain. Given recent oil price rises
column3: it is once again paramount that second-round effects stemming from wage and price-setting throughout the economy are avoided. It is particularly important that the social partners assume their responsibilities in this respect. In addition
column4: developments in longer-term inflation expectations need to be monitored closely.

column1: The monetary analysis provides further insight into the outlook for price developments at medium to longer-term horizons. While the latest monetary and credit data show some moderation in the pace of monetary expansion
column2: they confirm that the stimulative effect of the low level of interest rates has remained the dominating force. In addition
column3: the fact that monetary dynamics continue to be driven mainly by the most liquid components suggests that excess liquidity may entail risks of upward inflationary pressures in the medium to longer term. Furthermore
column4: strong monetary and credit growth indicates the need to carefully monitor whether risks are building up in the context of strong house price increases in some regions of the euro area.

column1: To sum up
column2: the economic analysis confirms that underlying domestic inflationary pressures remain contained
column3: while there continue to be medium-term upside risks to price stability which need to be monitored closely. Cross-checking with the monetary analysis supports the case for continued vigilance with regard to the materialisation of such risks.

column1: Turning to fiscal policies
column2: recent information provides a mixed picture and continues to raise concerns. Although public finances remain sound in a few euro area countries and fiscal consolidation is progressing slowly in others
column3: in several countries fiscal perspectives are worrying
column4: as imbalances are not projected to decline
column5: as planned earlier

2005-05-04;2;Ladies and gentlemen

column1: Let me now report on the outcome of today’s meeting

column1: On the basis of our regular economic and monetary analyses
column2: we continue to see no significant evidence of a build-up of underlying domestic inflationary pressures in the euro area. Accordingly
column3: we have left the key ECB interest rates unchanged. The exceptionally low level of interest rates across the entire maturity spectrum provides considerable support to economic activity in the euro area. At the same time
column4: continued vigilance with regard to upside risks to price stability is warranted.

column1: Allow me to elaborate on our decision
column2: turning first to the economic analysis. Regarding the current situation and the short-term outlook for economic activity
column3: recent data and survey indicators are
column4: on balance
column5: on the downside. Some of the downward risks to economic growth identified earlier
column6: in particular those related to persistently high oil prices
column7: appear to have partially materialised over the past few months.

column2: when looking beyond the short term
column3: conditions remain in place for stronger real GDP growth. On the external side
column4: euro area exports should continue to be supported by foreign demand. On the domestic side
column5: investment should benefit from the very favourable financing conditions
column6: the robust corporate earnings currently being observed and ongoing improvements in corporate efficiency. Consumption growth should evolve broadly in line with expected developments in disposable income. Downside risks to economic growth continue to be related to oil price developments and global imbalances.

column1: Turning to price developments
column2: according to Eurostat’s flash estimate
column3: annual HICP inflation was 2.1% in April
column4: unchanged from March. Over the coming months
column5: annual HICP inflation rates are likely to remain around these levels. Wage increases have remained contained over recent quarters and
column6: in the context of moderate economic growth and weak labour markets
column7: this trend should continue for the time being. Overall
column8: when looking ahead
column9: we see no significant evidence of underlying domestic inflationary pressures building up in the euro area so that inflation rates should develop in line with price stability.

column1: However
column2: there continue to be upside risks to price stability
column3: relating mainly to oil price developments and their potential to lead to second-round effects stemming from wage and price-setting behaviour. In order to avoid this

column1: As regards the monetary analysis
column2: monetary and credit growth remain strong despite some moderation over the recent past. These developments mainly reflect the stimulative effect of the low level of interest rates in the euro area. As monetary dynamics over the past year have mainly been driven by developments in the most liquid components of M3
column3: this continues to signal upside risks to price stability in the medium to longer term.

column1: To sum up
column2: the economic analysis suggests that underlying domestic inflationary pressures remain contained. However
column3: upside risks to price stability over the medium term need to be monitored closely. Cross-checking with the monetary analysis supports the case for continued vigilance with regard to the materialisation of such risks. Against this background
column4: longer-term inflation expectations need to be monitored closely.

column1: As regards fiscal policies
column2: recent information and forecasts suggest little progress in reducing fiscal imbalances in the euro area. A timely and full implementation of consolidation commitments is essential. This will strengthen the confidence of investors and consumers in the soundness of economic policies. At the same time
column3: it is essential to implement
column4: in a strict and timely manner
column5: the revised Stability and Growth Pact procedures
column6: which are soon to enter into force
column7: so as to underpin the credibility of the EU fiscal framework.

column1: The Governing Council has repeatedly argued in favour of structural reforms to improve the potential for higher economic growth in the euro area. Authorities are aware of the structural obstacles and have taken important measures to address them
column2: but continued reforms will be needed in order to keep up with the unavoidable challenges arising from an ongoing deepening in the division of labour at the global level
column3: rapid technological change and population ageing. It is important to explain to the general public that these reforms will progressively deliver higher growth and lead to more job creation
column4: and that
column5: as a result
column6: our societies will be better off. Over recent years
column7: uncertainties surrounding the structural reform agenda in some euro area countries appear to have hindered the necessary improvement in the confidence of consumers and entrepreneurs. A clear commitment to implementing the reforms and the explanation of their benefits will help to reduce such uncertainties and thereby make a considerable contribution to improving the economic outlook for the euro area.

And it is because we are credible in terms of our own delivery of price stability that we are benefiting from these very low medium and long-term market rates. 2005-07-07;2;Ladies and gentlemen

column1: The Governing Council of the ECB expresses its deep sympathy and its total solidarity with the British people and the Bank of England in these dreadful circumstances. We have observed a minute of silence in memory of the victims of these terrorist attacks and we convey our sincere condolences to the British people and the Bank of England.
The Vice?President and I will now report on the outcome of today’s meeting of the Governing Council of the ECB
column2: which was also attended by Commissioner Almunia.

column1: On the basis of our regular economic and monetary analyses
column2: we have concluded that the monetary policy stance is appropriate
column3: given the current outlook for price stability over the medium term. Accordingly
column4: we have decided to leave the key ECB interest rates unchanged. Across the maturity spectrum
column5: interest rates in the euro area are low by historical standards
column6: in both nominal and real terms
column7: and thus lend ongoing support to economic activity. The Governing Council will continue to monitor carefully all factors that might affect this assessment and remains vigilant with respect to the emergence of risks to price stability over the medium term.

column1: Allow me to explain our assessment in greater detail.
In the context of our economic analysis
column2: recent indicators of economic activity in the euro area have
column3: on balance
column4: confirmed that growth has remained subdued. High and rising oil prices in particular appear to have weighed on demand and confidence. On the basis of current information
column5: the growth rate in the second quarter of this year is expected to be lower than the first quarter growth rate of 0.5%
column6: quarter on quarter. Available data are still mixed
column7: with some of the most recent indicators showing a slight improvement
column8: but there are no signs as yet that a more sustained recovery in economic activity has already started. At the same time
column9: looking beyond the short term
column10: there continues to be reason to expect a gradual improvement in economic activity in the euro area. On the domestic side
column11: investment should benefit from the very favourable financing conditions
column12: the robust growth of corporate earnings currently observed and ongoing improvements in corporate efficiency. Consumption growth should evolve broadly in line with expected developments in disposable income. On the external side
column13: ongoing growth in global demand and improvements in euro area price competitiveness should support euro area exports. This assessment is in line with available forecasts and projections.

column1: This baseline scenario for growth continues to be surrounded by a good deal of uncertainty. On balance
column2: risks to economic growth lie on the downside and are notably related to the persistence of high oil prices
column3: the low level of confidence prevailing in the euro area and global imbalances.

column1: Turning to price developments
column2: annual HICP inflation was 2.1% in June
column3: according to Eurostat’s flash estimate
column4: compared with 1.9% in May. Over the next few months annual HICP inflation rates are expected to fluctuate around current levels and may not fall below 2% for the remainder of 2005. This outlook mainly reflects recent developments in oil prices
column5: which were seen as an upside risk in the context of the June 2005 Eurosystem staff inflation projections. However
column6: wage increases have remained contained over recent quarters and
column7: in the context of moderate economic growth and weak labour markets
column8: this trend should continue for the time being. Overall
column9: we continue to see no significant evidence of underlying domestic inflationary pressures building up in the euro area.

column1: At the same time
column2: upside risks to this scenario for inflation warrant close monitoring. These risks relate mainly to oil price developments and their potential to lead to second-round effects stemming from wage and price-setting behaviour. It is important that the social partners continue to meet their responsibilities. Moreover
column3: uncertainties about future developments in administrative prices and indirect taxes need to be taken into account when assessing currently available inflation projections.

column1: Looking at inflation prospects over medium to longer horizons
column2: our assessment is also based on the results of our monetary analysis. In line with developments since mid-2004
column3: monetary and credit growth in the euro area remain strong. The stimulating impact of the low level of interest rates has remained the dominant factor driving monetary developments
column4: as reflected in the strength of M1 growth and the dynamism of loans to the private sector. Liquidity remains ample by all plausible measures. Overall
column5: monetary developments support the case for vigilance with regard to upward risks to price stability over medium to long-term horizons.

column1: To sum up
column2: the economic analysis confirms that domestic inflationary pressures over the medium term remain contained in the euro area
column3: while oil price developments in particular imply some upward revisions to the main scenario for price developments. The monetary analysis identifies risks to price stability over the longer term. Overall
column4: cross-checking the information from the two pillars suggests a need for ongoing vigilance in order to maintain inflation expectations in line with price stability. In fact
column5: by keeping medium-term inflation expectations firmly anchored at levels consistent with price stability
column6: monetary policy is making a significant contribution towards a recovery in economic growth.

column1: Prudent fiscal policies could provide considerable support for confidence in the euro area. The discussions on revising the Stability and Growth Pact regulations have been concluded and rigorous implementation is now key to ensuring an effective framework for fiscal policy coordination and discipline. This is all the more true as current and projected fiscal deficits in several euro area countries still need to be addressed with rigour. In a number of cases these deficits not only imply a rising debt ratio
column2: but also leave no safety margin for short-term budgetary relief in the event of adverse developments. In this context
column3: as significant revisions of past deficit and debt figures have been reported for a few countries
column4: let me also reiterate previous calls by the Governing Council for the reliable compilation and timely reporting of government finance statistics.

column1: Finally
column2: let me conclude with a few words on structural reform. As we have stressed repeatedly
column3: a decisive and comprehensive set of measures aimed at achieving a more dynamic and competitive European economy with flexible labour and product markets is urgently needed. The primary objective of such measures is to deal with the ongoing challenges from globalisation
column4: rapid technological change and ageing populations and
column5: overall
column6: to ensure greater resilience to shocks. These challenges are not specific to the euro area. Successful structural reforms would
column7: however
column8: also contribute to fostering the adjustment processes within the euro area. In particular
column9: they would allow those member countries with a weaker record in terms of economic growth and employment creation to perform better in the future. As regards existing growth and inflation differentials within the euro area
column10: there is clear evidence that the dispersion of inflation and real GDP growth rates in the euro area is not materially different from that of the United States and it does not show any signs of having increased since 1999. However
column11: in cases where differences are not due to catching-up processes or temporary factors
column12: structural reforms are even more necessary to enhance economic performance and flexibility in the adjustment process.

column1: We are now at your disposal for questions.

column1: Reflecting not on a short-term basis but on a slightly longer-term basis
column2: we believe that growth will be more dynamic. That is also the judgement being made by all European and international
column3: public and private observers; so we are not original in that respect. But we see good reasons why that should be the case and why it is not only our conclusion
column4: but also that of global observers. That being said
column5: we also say – and I have said this before – that we have real downside risks for the three reasons I have been mentioning: oil price increases
column6: which are of course something that is certainly important
column7: global imbalances
column8: and the level of confidence. You know to what extent we are committed
column9: being faithful to our mandate
column10: to doing everything we can to consolidate
column11: preserve and enhance confidence in all “constituencies” of the euro area; not only the abstract “economic agents”
column12: but households and entrepreneurs. We trust that we have a responsibility in this respect.

column1: You are used to hearing from me why we trust that what we do is what we should do; and that what we do is the best we can do for growth and job creation in Europe. I do not want to identify any newspaper or media. In various media I have read various pieces of good advice
column2: some going in totally the other direction. And from time to time advice going in both directions in the same media
column3: as is perhaps normal in the very vivid opinion-based democracies of Europe and the world. So
column4: we have a lot of good advice: to increase rates
column5: to decrease rates
column6: or to stick to the present level. But
column7: again
column8: my reasoning is the following: our mandate under the Treaty is to deliver price stability. There is no doubt anywhere that we are and will remain faithful to our mandate. We owe that to the people of Europe who consider price stability to be something which is extremely important. In a number of economies and countries the sentiment of the people is even that there are more price increases than we believe
column9: more than is calculated at the national or European levels. This sentiment has to be taken into account.

column1: We are credible in delivering price stability according to our definition. That is the reason why the inflationary expectations are well anchored in line with our definition of price stability. In our surveys
column2: we are at the level of 1.9%. When your definition is less than but close to 2%
column3: it is difficult to do better than 1.9%. And the break-even inflation that we are extracting from index-linked bonds
column4: by all means
column5: is also in line with the fact that financial markets inflationary expectations are also fully in line with our definition of price stability. The fact that our financial environment incorporates inflation expectations in line with our definition is one of the reasons
column6: not the only reason
column7: but one of the reasons why we are currently observing the lowest level of the ten-year rate that has been observed in Europe for a 100 years. If we were less credible
column8: we would have higher inflationary expectations. And then
column9: all other things being equal
column10: market interest rates would be higher. So that is why we think that
column11: by being faithful to our mandate
column12: we are delivering what is necessary for growth and job creation. I say that with the information that we have today
column13: with the anchoring of inflationary expectations that we have today and with all the information that is available to you and to us. Things could be different tomorrow. We are pragmatic people. But today
column14: clearly

column1: On the basis of our regular economic and monetary analyses
column2: we have concluded that the monetary policy stance remains appropriate
column3: given the current outlook for inflation rates over the medium term. The prevailing exceptionally low level of both nominal and real interest rates across the entire maturity spectrum provides considerable support to economic activity in the euro area. At present our judgement is that
column4: although upside risks to price stability exist
column5: we continue to see no significant evidence of a build-up in underlying inflationary pressures in the euro area. However
column6: not least in view of the risk of second-round effects from ongoing oil price increases
column7: the Governing Council continues to monitor the development of inflation expectations very closely. At present
column8: particular vigilance with regard to upside risks to price stability is warranted.

column1: Allow me to explain our assessment in greater detail
column2: turning first to the economic analysis. According to Eurostat’s flash estimate
column3: real GDP grew at a quarter-on-quarter rate of 0.3% in the second quarter of 2005
column4: compared with 0.4% in the first quarter according to the latest data releaseEconomic activity thus continued to grow moderately in the euro area. The most recent survey indicators have
column5: on balance
column6: been supportive to the view that economic growth could improve in the second half of 2005
column7: while higher oil prices continue to weigh on demand and confidence.

column1: On the external side
column2: ongoing growth in global demand and improvements in euro area price competitiveness should support euro area exports. On the domestic side
column3: investment should benefit from very favourable financing conditions
column4: the robust growth of corporate earnings and ongoing improvements in corporate efficiency. Consumption growth should gradually rise
column5: broadly in line with expected developments in disposable income.

column1: This assessment is broadly consistent with the new ECB staff projections
column2: which will be published today. Euro area real GDP is projected by staff to grow at rates of between 1.0% and 1.6% in 2005 and between 1.3% and 2.3% in 2006. Recent forecasts from international and private sector organisations give a similar picture. In comparison with the June Eurosystem staff projections
column3: the ranges projected for real GDP growth in 2005 and 2006 have been revised downwards slightly
column4: reflecting both the downward revision of growth data for the first quarter of this year and the effects of higher oil prices.

column1: On balance
column2: risks to the economic growth projections continue to lie on the downside
column3: and relate to higher oil prices
column4: low consumer confidence and concerns about global imbalances.

column1: Turning to price developments
column2: annual HICP inflation was 2.1% in August according to Eurostat’s flash estimate
column3: compared with 2.2% in July. Over the next few months
column4: annual HICP inflation rates are expected to fluctuate around current levels
column5: mainly due to recent developments in oil prices. Looking further ahead
column6: ECB staff project average annual HICP inflation to lie between 2.1% and 2.3% in 2005 and between 1.4% and 2.4% in 2006. The latest projections constitute considerable upward revisions to the Eurosystem staff inflation projections published in June
column7: reflecting the fact that oil prices have once again increased by more than was suggested earlier by forward rates. At the same time
column8: wage increases have remained contained over recent quarters; the projections are based on the assumption that this trend will prevail for the time being given the current labour market situation. Overall
column9: we continue to see no significant evidence of underlying domestic inflationary pressures building up in the euro area.

column1: Risks to this new baseline inflation scenario are on the upside and relate to potential further rises in oil prices
column2: administered prices and indirect taxes. More fundamentally
column3: the main risks to the inflation outlook stem from potential second-round effects in wage and price-setting behaviour triggered by ongoing oil price rises. In this respect
column4: it is key that the social partners continue to meet their responsibilities. Against this background
column5: we will continue to monitor wage developments and inflation expectations very closely. Ongoing vigilance is required in order to ensure that longer-term inflation expectations remain well-anchored in the euro area.

column1: Turning to the monetary analysis
column2: the latest data confirm the strong monetary and credit growth which has been observed since mid-2004. The monetary dynamics are driven by the prevailing low level of interest rates
column3: as reflected in the robust growth of the more liquid components of M3. Low interest rates are also fuelling credit expansion
column4: with the strengthening of the demand for loans broadly based across the private sector. The growth of mortgage borrowing remains very strong. In this context
column5: price dynamics in the housing markets need to be monitored closely. The liquidity situation in the euro area remains ample by all plausible measures
column6: indicating risks to price stability over medium to longer horizons.

column1: To sum up: recent oil price developments have pushed up the inflation projections for the year ahead
column2: while medium-term domestic inflationary pressures still remain contained in the euro area. However
column3: the balance of risks to the baseline inflation scenario is tilted to the upside. Cross-checking the economic analysis with the monetary analysis confirms the need for particular vigilance in order to keep medium-term inflation expectations firmly anchored at levels consistent with price stability. By achieving this
column4: monetary policy is making a significant contribution towards a recovery in economic growth.

column1: Fiscal policies will make their best contribution to stability
column2: growth and confidence if prevailing imbalances are tackled as part of determined and well-designed reform programmes. A rigorous implementation of the revised Stability and Growth Pact would reinforce the credibility of reform plans and boost expectations of a sound fiscal and growth situation. Against this background
column3: it is regrettable that the pace of fiscal consolidation remains too slow. In some countries
column4: targets for correcting excessive deficits are at risk. Moreover
column5: due to a very generous application of the new rules of the Pact
column6: countries which have recently breached the 3% deficit limit are being granted relatively long periods to correct the situation. The Governing Council therefore urges Member States to step up consolidation efforts where needed and to implement the revised rules in a manner that supports these efforts and deters future slippages.

column1: As regards structural reforms
column2: the European Commission has recently presented the “Community Lisbon Programme” and a list of measures at the EU level to relaunch the Lisbon strategy. The programme focuses on enhancing knowledge and innovation in order to strengthen growth
column3: on making Europe a more attractive place to invest and work
column4: and on creating more and better jobs. It includes
column5: for example
column6: measures to further open EU markets and to simplify the regulatory framework within which business operates. The Community Lisbon Programme will be complemented by the introduction of national action plans for growth and jobs
column7: which the Member States will present this autumn. Progress at both the Community and the Member State level is crucial to addressing the economic challenges facing the EU.

column2: the Vice-President and I are very pleased to welcome you to the press conference here in Athens. The Governing Council has
column3: today
column4: met for the 12th time outside Frankfurt
column5: meaning that it has now met once in each of the euro area member countries. I would particularly like to thank Governor Garganas for his kind hospitality and express our special gratitude to the staff of the Bank of Greece for the perfect organisation.

column1: Let me now report on the outcome of today’s meeting
column2: which was also attended by the President of the Eurogroup
column3: Prime Minister Juncker
column4: and Commissioner Almunia.

column1: On the basis of our regular economic and monetary analyses
column2: despite renewed upward pressure on prices stemming mainly from oil market developments
column3: we have concluded that the monetary policy stance still remains appropriate. Accordingly
column4: we have decided to leave the key ECB interest rates unchanged. At the same time
column5: strong vigilance with regard to upside risks to price stability is warranted. It is essential that the increase in the current inflation rate does not translate into higher underlying inflationary pressures in the euro area. Strong vigilance is also called for in the light of ample liquidity in the euro area. Across the maturity spectrum
column6: interest rates in the euro area remain very low in both nominal and real terms
column7: and thus lend ongoing support to economic activity. For this support to continue
column8: it is of the essence that inflation expectations remain firmly anchored at levels consistent with price stability.

column1: Allow me to explain our assessment in greater detail
column2: starting with the economic analysis.

column1: Real GDP has been growing at a quarter-on-quarter rate of 0.4% and 0.3% over the first two quarters of 2005
column2: dampened in particular by higher oil prices. In line with our staff projections
column3: recent survey indicators
column4: on balance
column5: support the view that economic growth could gradually pick up from the second half of this year onwards. On the external side
column6: ongoing growth in global demand should support euro area exports. On the domestic side
column7: investment should benefit both from continuously favourable financing conditions and from the robust growth of corporate earnings. Consumption should gradually recover
column8: broadly in line with expected developments in real disposable income.

column1: This outlook for economic activity remains subject to downward risks
column2: relating mainly to oil prices
column3: concerns about global imbalances and weak consumer confidence. Temporarily
column4: further uncertainty arose as to the economic effects of the recent hurricanes in the United States
column5: which assessments
column6: in the meantime
column7: have generally suggested to be limited and short-term.

column1: Turning to price developments
column2: recent increases mainly in oil prices have pushed headline inflation rates to levels significantly in excess of 2%. According to Eurostat’s flash estimate
column3: annual HICP inflation was 2.5% in September
column4: compared with 2.2% in the previous two months
column5: and it is likely that HICP inflation will remain elevated in the short term. In interpreting this jump in the annual inflation rate
column6: it is key to make a clear distinction between temporary
column7: short-term factors on the one hand
column8: and those of a more lasting nature on the other.

column1: While no detailed information on developments in the components of HICP in September is available as yet
column2: it appears that oil price increases have again played an important role
column3: this time exacerbated by a much stronger increase in petrol prices owing to exceptional capacity constraints at refineries following the two hurricanes in the United States. If a gradual normalisation in this market segment is confirmed
column4: an unwinding of the sharp increases in spreads between oil prices and refined products could materialise. Hence
column5: these increases may be only temporary.

column1: However
column2: there is currently no indication that oil prices will moderate significantly in the foreseeable future. Rather
column3: markets expect oil prices to remain at high levels
column4: driven mainly by buoyant global demand and
column5: to some extent
column6: by fragilities on the supply side. Accordingly
column7: this scenario underlies our forward-looking assessment of price developments.

column1: Crucially
column2: what matters is how these developments affect the outlook for price stability over the medium term. For the time being
column3: there continues to be no clear evidence of domestic inflationary pressures building up in the euro area. In particular
column4: wage increases have remained contained over recent quarters and
column5: with labour markets weak
column6: this should continue for the time being. Our main scenario
column7: therefore
column8: remains one of elevated inflation rates over the short term
column9: with a gradual decline thereafter.

column1: Upside risks to this scenario have
column2: however
column3: increased. These relate to ongoing uncertainties surrounding oil market developments
column4: to a potentially stronger pass-through than has so far been observed
column5: on account of higher oil prices being passed on to consumers via the domestic production chain
column6: and to potential second-round effects in wage and price-setting behaviour
column7: all of which play an important role in our assessment for price stability over the medium term. In addition
column8: possible further increases in administered prices and indirect taxes have to be taken into account. Accordingly
column9: strong vigilance is required in order to ensure that longer-term inflation expectations for the euro area remain well-anchored.

column1: The monetary analysis provides further insight into inflation prospects over medium to longer horizons. Money and credit have continued to grow robustly in the euro area over the past few months
column2: with the annual rate of M3 growth now exceeding 8%. The strength of monetary growth has been increasingly driven primarily by the prevailing low level of interest rates. In recent months
column3: the short-term dynamics of M3 have gained further momentum and the growth of borrowing
column4: in particular mortgage loans
column5: remains very strong. In this context
column6: price dynamics in a number of housing markets need to be monitored closely. Strong monetary and credit growth
column7: in the context of an already ample liquidity situation in the euro area
column8: points to risks to price stability over medium to longer horizons.

column1: To sum up
column2: the economic analysis indicates that oil and petrol price increases
column3: in particular
column4: imply upward revisions to the outlook for short-term price developments. Some of these increases can be expected to be of a temporary nature
column5: while others are likely to be more lasting. Domestic inflationary pressures over the medium term still remain contained in the euro area
column6: but significant upside risks have to be taken into account. Moreover
column7: the monetary analysis identifies upside risks to price stability over the medium to longer term.

column1: Overall
column2: cross-checking the information from the two pillars confirms the need for strong vigilance in order to maintain inflation expectations in line with price stability. By keeping medium-term inflation expectations firmly anchored at levels consistent with price stability
column3: monetary policy is making a significant ongoing contribution towards a recovery in economic growth.

column1: As regards fiscal policies in the euro area
column2: most recent information continues to provide a very mixed picture. Some countries report significant imbalances
column3: while others continue to maintain sound fiscal positions. Preparations for 2006 budgets are in their final stages in most euro area countries. It is essential that forthcoming budgets reflect the need for fiscal consolidation that both progresses at the appropriate pace and is embedded in a well-designed and comprehensive reform strategy. This would help to support confidence within the euro area by strengthening expectations of sustainable and growth-friendly public finances and by enhancing the credibility of the reformed Stability and Growth Pact. As for the impact of high oil prices on public finances
column4: consolidation of budgets must be continued. Let me also recall the latest G7 statement
column5: which affirms that subsidies and artificial price caps that constrain the price of oil and oil products have an adverse effect on the global market and should be avoided.

column1: In the context of its regular discussions about structural reform issues
column2: the Governing Council focused on unit labour cost (ULC) developments within the euro area
column3: which play an important role in determining inflation and competitiveness patterns across the euro area countries. Since the inception of EMU
column4: several euro area countries have experienced significantly larger cumulative increases in their ULCs than the euro area average. On the other hand
column5: some countries have exhibited cumulative ULC developments significantly below the euro area average.

column1: It must be understood that some differences in ULC growth rates are a natural feature of a well-functioning monetary union
column2: as these may reflect catching-up processes or necessary adjustments to past shocks. In this respect
column3: the flexibility within the euro area may well have been underestimated in its early phase of existence.

column1: At the same time
column2: there is no room for complacency. In some euro area countries
column3: wage developments have substantially and persistently exceeded labour productivity growth
column4: leading to relatively strong ULC developments over a prolonged period of time
column5: higher inflationary pressures and losses in competitiveness. This may be
column6: at least partially
column7: due to wage rigidities
column8: such as an explicit or de facto indexation of nominal wages to prices or high reservation wages determined by the level of unemployment benefits
column9: and to a lack of competition in some sectors.

column1: In the context of external shocks
column2: such as sharp increases in oil prices
column3: there is an even greater need for speeding-up structural reforms. Together with the completion of the EU internal market
column4: such reforms would support ULC developments that are conducive to price stability and would further smooth the functioning of adjustment mechanisms in the euro area
column5: thereby strengthening the foundations for sustained growth in output and employment.

column1: On the basis of our regular economic and monetary analyses
column2: taking into account ongoing upward pressure on prices stemming mainly from energy price developments
column3: we have concluded that the monetary policy stance still remains appropriate. Accordingly
column4: we have decided to leave the key ECB interest rates unchanged. At the same time
column5: strong vigilance with regard to the upside risks to price stability is warranted. Strong vigilance is also called for in the light of ample liquidity and buoyant monetary and credit growth in the euro area. It is of the essence that the increase in current inflation rates does not translate into inflationary pressures over the medium term and to ensure that inflation expectations remain firmly anchored at levels consistent with price stability. Across the maturity spectrum
column6: interest rates in the euro area remain very low in both nominal and real terms
column7: and the current very accommodative stance of monetary policy lends considerable support to economic activity.

column1: Allow me to explain our assessment in greater detail
column2: starting with the economic analysis.

column1: Although economic growth has been dampened by the marked increase in oil prices over recent quarters
column2: it appears that the euro area economy has shown considerable resilience to this shock
column3: supported also by responsible wage-negotiating behaviour. Moreover
column4: the latest indicators suggest that economic activity is currently strengthening. This would be in line with the September ECB staff projections
column5: which indicate a gradual recovery from the second half of 2005 onwards. On the external side
column6: it is projected that ongoing growth in global demand will support euro area exports
column7: and on the domestic side
column8: that investment will benefit from continued favourable financing conditions
column9: as well as from the robust growth of corporate earnings. Consumption should gradually recover
column10: broadly in line with expected developments in real disposable income. At the same time
column11: the outlook for economic activity remains subject to downward risks
column12: relating mainly to oil prices
column13: concerns about global imbalances and weak consumer confidence.

column1: Turning to price developments
column2: recent increases in mainly energy prices have pushed headline inflation rates to levels significantly in excess of 2%. According to Eurostat’s flash estimate
column3: annual HICP inflation was 2.5% in October 2005
column4: compared with 2.6% in September and 2.2% in the two preceding months. It is likely that HICP inflation will remain elevated in the short term. As we stressed in October
column5: it is key in interpreting current inflation rates to make a clear distinction between temporary
column6: short-term factors on the one hand
column7: and those of a more lasting nature on the other. While some developments might prove to be transitory
column8: markets expect oil prices to remain at high levels
column9: driven mainly by buoyant global demand and
column10: to some extent
column11: by fragilities on the supply side. This suggests a more lasting impact of energy prices on overall price developments.

column1: This assumption underlies our forward-looking assessment of price developments. At the same time
column2: wage increases have remained contained over recent quarters and
column3: with labour markets weak
column4: this should continue for the time being. Moreover
column5: pressure from manufacturing prices remains low given strong global competition. All in all
column6: while inflation rates are expected to stay above 2% over the shorter term
column7: there continues to be no clear evidence yet of domestic inflationary pressures building up in the euro area.

column1: We remain
column2: however
column3: concerned about the medium-term upside risks to this scenario. As we stressed a month ago
column4: these relate to ongoing uncertainties surrounding oil market developments
column5: to a potentially stronger pass-through than has so far been observed
column6: on account of higher oil prices being passed on to consumers via the domestic production chain
column7: and to potential second-round effects in wage and price-setting behaviour. In addition
column8: possible further increases in administered prices and indirect taxes have to be taken into account. Hence
column9: strong vigilance is required to ensure that medium and long-term inflation expectations for the euro area remain well-anchored.

column1: The monetary analysis also points to increased upside risks to price stability over the medium to longer term. Liquidity in the euro area is very ample by all plausible measures. Moreover
column2: the strengthening of monetary growth observed since mid-2004 has gained further momentum over the past few months. Growth in the monetary aggregate M3 has been driven by its most liquid components
column3: confirming the increasingly dominant impact of the low level of interest rates. Furthermore
column4: the growth of borrowing
column5: especially mortgage loans
column6: remains very robust. In this context
column7: price dynamics in a number of housing markets need to be monitored closely.

column1: To sum up
column2: the economic analysis indicates that energy price increases
column3: in particular
column4: imply upward revisions to the outlook for short-term price developments. Some of the contributing factors can be expected to be temporary but others are likely to be more lasting. Domestic inflationary pressures over the medium term still remain contained in the euro area
column5: but significant upside risks have to be taken into account. Moreover
column6: the monetary analysis identifies increased risks to price stability over the medium to longer term. Overall
column7: cross-checking the information from the two pillars confirms that strong vigilance is warranted to keep inflation expectations in line with price stability. Only by keeping medium and long-term inflation expectations firmly anchored at levels consistent with price stability can monetary policy make a significant ongoing contribution towards a recovery in economic growth.

column1: As regards fiscal policies
column2: a number of countries have presented their 2006 budget plans. Despite some welcome progress with fiscal consolidation
column3: the outlook for countries in excessive deficit is a matter of great concern
column4: as there is a risk of consolidation not proceeding and commitments for this year and next not being met. Further delays in the correction of excessive deficits and a continued inclination to look for the most lenient way to implement the procedural steps of the revised Stability and Growth Pact risk undermining the Pact’s credibility. This must be avoided. All parties involved in the forthcoming decisions carry an important responsibility to ensure the proper functioning of the overall fiscal framework in the future. This would be the most effective way to enhance the growth prospects of the euro area and to build confidence in public finances ahead of the time when the challenges of population ageing set in. We therefore urge countries with fiscal imbalances to give priority to their timely correction and to implement the revised Pact rigorously. This will send the right signal to the public and support the credibility of the fiscal framework.

column1: As regards structural reforms
column2: we stress again the urgent need to increase the flexibility of labour and product markets in order to achieve a more dynamic and competitive European economy and to help foster the adjustment processes within the euro area. The opportunities arising from globalisation and rapid technological change can best be captured by allowing and by speeding up structural change with a view to enhancing potential growth and employment creation. This would also help to facilitate the necessary adjustment to the higher level of oil prices by further increasing energy efficiency and energy savings
column3: while avoiding distortionary measures that hamper the adjustment process.

column1: To sum up
column2: increased risks to price stability identified by the economic analysis have been cross-checked with the monetary analysis. Keeping inflation expectations firmly anchored at levels consistent with price stability will permit monetary policy to continue to make a significant contribution towards a sustainable recovery in economic growth and job creation in the euro area. column1: On the basis of our regular economic and monetary analyses
column2: we have decided to keep the key ECB interest rates unchanged following the increase of 25 basis points on 1 December 2005. The information which has become available since then supports the assessment that an adjustment of our very accommodative monetary policy stance was warranted. It remains essential to keep medium to long-term inflation expectations in the euro area solidly anchored at levels consistent with price stability. Such anchoring of inflation expectations is a prerequisite for monetary policy to make an ongoing contribution towards supporting economic growth and job creation in the euro area. Maintaining price stability over the medium term is our guiding principle
column3: and we will consistently apply it when examining new information
column4: making our judgements and taking decisions. With interest rates across the whole maturity spectrum remaining historically low in both nominal and real terms
column5: and with our monetary policy stance remaining accommodative
column6: we will continue to monitor very closely all developments with respect to risks to price stability over the medium term.

column3: real GDP growth did indeed improve in the second half of 2005
column4: as we expected. According to Eurostat’s first estimate

column7: recent economic indicators and survey data support the view that the expansion of economic activity broadly maintained its momentum in the fourth quarter of 2005 and will continue to do so in the first months of 2006
column8: notwithstanding the impact of high oil prices.

column3: in line with our staff projections and other available forecasts. On the external side
column4: the continued strength of global demand should support euro area exports. On the domestic side
column5: investment should further benefit from continued very favourable financing conditions
column6: robust corporate earnings and gains in corporate efficiency. Consumption growth should gradually rise
column7: broadly in line with expected developments in disposable income.

column3: even though it moderated further in December. This moderation can be explained in part by an apparent resumption of the unwinding of past portfolio shifts

column9: strong monetary and credit growth in a context of already ample liquidity in the euro area points to risks to price stability over the medium to longer term.

column1: To sum up
column2: the economic analysis suggests that indirect effects stemming from past oil price rises and already announced changes to administered prices and indirect taxes can be expected to have an upward impact on annual HICP inflation over the coming years. It also indicates that risks to price stability over the medium term remain on the upside. column3: which need to remain firmly anchored at levels consistent with price stability. This is a prerequisite for monetary policy to make an ongoing contribution to sustainable economic growth and job creation

column1: As regards fiscal policy
column2: recent information points to somewhat better than expected outcomes for 2005 in a number of countries and for the euro area as a whole. With the improvements in economic growth
column3: determined fiscal consolidation is now even more important. In particular
column4: countries with excessive deficits must take this opportunity to reduce their fiscal imbalances in a decisive and sustainable manner. This would strongly support the European fiscal framework as established by the Stability and Growth Pact. Delaying consolidation would be both inappropriate in the short term and risky in the longer term. Adjustment efforts should be based on credible
column5: fully specified measures as part of a comprehensive consolidation programme. Any windfall gains from higher than expected growth or other factors should be allocated to speeding up deficit reduction. This would help to prevent a repeat of past experiences
column6: when complacency in good times contributed to persistent budgetary disequilibria.

column1: On the basis of our regular economic and monetary analyses

column4: and that monetary and credit growth remains very dynamic. Against this background

Such vigilance is particularly warranted in a context of ample liquidity and still very low levels of nominal and real interest rates across the whole maturity spectrum

column7: inflation expectations must be firmly anchored.

column1: Let me now explain our assessment in more detail

column1: The data that have become available since the start of the year point to a re-acceleration of economic growth in the first quarter of 2006
column2: following the moderation observed in the last quarter of 2005. In addition
column3: the latest indicators and survey information point to continued growth in the second quarter and lend support to the scenario of a gradual broadening in economic activity as embodied in the March 2006 ECB staff projections. Business confidence is particularly buoyant
column4: which
column5: in principle
column6: bodes well for investment

column3: providing continued support for euro area exports. Investment growth should benefit from an extended period of very favourable financing conditions
column4: balance sheet restructuring
column5: and gains in earnings and business efficiency. Consumption growth should also strengthen over time
column6: in line with developments in real disposable income
column7: as the labour market situation continues to improve. This favourable outlook for economic growth is broadly in line with available forecasts from international organisations and the private sector.

column2: risks to this scenario appear broadly balanced over the shorter term

This underlines the need for further improvement in the transparency of oil markets and further investment in this sector. Concerns about global imbalances continue to prevail over longer horizons

column2: according to Eurostat’s flash estimate
column3: annual HICP inflation was 2.4% in April 2006
column4: compared with 2.2% in March and 2.3% in February. In the short term

column1: Risks to the outlook for price developments remain on the upside and include further increases in oil prices

column1: Turning to the monetary analysis
column2: in a context of ample liquidity in the euro area
column3: monetary and credit growth remains very dynamic. In particular
column4: the annual growth rate of loans to the private sector has continued to increase over recent months and has now reached double-digit levels. Credit growth has also become more broadly based across sectors
column5: with borrowing both by households – especially for house purchase – and by non-financial corporations growing more strongly. Monetary growth continues to be driven mainly by the expansion of its most liquid components. Thus the latest developments confirm that the stimulative impact of the low level of interest rates remains the dominant factor behind the current high trend rate of monetary expansion. Overall
column6: further acceleration of monetary and credit growth in this environment continues to point to upside risks to price stability over the medium to longer term. Monetary developments
column7: therefore
column8: require careful monitoring

column10: in particular
