column1: To sum up
column2: annual inflation rates are projected to remain elevated in 2006 and 2007 and the economic analysis confirms that the risks to price stability continue to lie on the upside. Some of these risks appear to have increased in view of the renewed strength of oil prices. Given strong money and credit growth in a context of already ample liquidity
column3: a cross-check of the outcome of the economic analysis with that of the monetary analysis supports the assessment that upside risks to price stability prevail over the medium to longer term. It therefore remains crucial to ensure that medium to long-term inflation expectations in the euro area are kept solidly anchored at levels consistent with price stability – a prerequisite for monetary policy to make an ongoing contribution to sustainable economic growth and job creation. Accordingly
column4: particular vigilance is of the essence in order to ensure that risks to price stability do not materialise.

column1: With respect to fiscal policies
column2: there are some signs that the implementation of the Stability and Growth Pact and commitment to the rules have improved since last year’s revision. However
column3: fiscal targets in a number of cases are rather lenient and their attainment is still subject to considerable risks. The Governing Council therefore supports any further reinforcement of fiscal consolidation efforts that also takes full advantage of a more favourable economic environment. Appropriately ambitious fiscal targets as part of a comprehensive structural reform programme would bring deficit and debt ratios down more rapidly. This is decisive in order to secure the sustainability of public finances. Such strategies would also boost confidence in the economic prospects of the euro area.

column1: As regards structural reforms
column2: the Governing Council again stresses the importance of undertaking comprehensive reforms to ensure open
column3: competitive and well-functioning labour and product markets
column4: including the promotion of wage and price flexibility and the fostering of an attractive environment for investment and innovation. The need for such reforms has again been highlighted by recent oil price developments
column5: as they would enhance the resilience of the euro area economy to external shocks. There is a broad and firm consensus that openness and flexibility are beneficial in promoting growth and employment and it is now essential to turn the agreed reform plans into actions and to strengthen them where necessary. By pushing forward with ambitious structural reforms
column6: euro area countries will also lend support to the ongoing economic recovery.

column1: At today’s meeting
column2: we decided to increase the key ECB interest rates by 25 basis points. This decision reflects the upside risks to price stability over the medium term that have been identified through both our economic and monetary analyses. The further withdrawal of monetary accommodation will thus contribute to ensuring that longer-term inflation expectations in the euro area remain solidly anchored at levels consistent with price stability. As stressed on previous occasions
column3: such anchoring is a prerequisite for monetary policy to make an ongoing contribution towards supporting economic growth and job creation in the euro area. Overall
column4: also after today’s increase
column5: the key ECB interest rates are still low by historical standards
column6: liquidity is ample and our monetary policy remains accommodative. Given the outlook for price developments and the dynamism of money and credit growth in the euro area
column7: we will continue to monitor closely all developments to ensure price stability over the medium and longer term.

column1: Allow me to explain our assessment in greater detail
column2: starting with the economic analysis.

column1: All the main indicators of economic activity that have recently become available are positive. According to Eurostat’s first estimate
column2: on a quarter-on-quarter basis
column3: real GDP grew by 0.6% in the euro area in the first quarter of 2006
column4: compared with 0.3% in the previous quarter
column5: with domestic demand making a significant contribution. The expected re-acceleration of real GDP growth in the first months of 2006 has thus materialised
column6: confirming our view that economic growth is broadening and becoming more sustained. This assessment is further supported by information on activity in the second quarter – such as various confidence surveys and indicator-based estimates – which continues to be encouraging.

column1: Looking further ahead
column2: the conditions are in place for growth in the euro area to remain close to its trend potential rate
column3: despite the impact of the rise in oil prices. Growth in the economies of the euro area’s main trading partners remains robust
column4: providing support for euro area exports. Strong investment growth is expected to continue
column5: benefiting from favourable financing conditions
column6: corporate balance sheet restructuring
column7: and gains in earnings and business efficiency. Consumption growth should continue to strengthen gradually over time
column8: in line with developments in real disposable income
column9: as the labour market situation gradually improves.

column1: This outlook is also reflected in the June Eurosystem staff macroeconomic projections
column2: which provide additional input into our analysis of the prospects for economic activity. The projections foresee average annual real GDP growth in a range between 1.8% and 2.4% in 2006
column3: and between 1.3% and 2.3% in 2007. The growth projections for 2006 are broadly unchanged from the ECB staff projections of March 2006
column4: while those for 2007 are slightly lower
column5: reflecting mainly the recent rise in oil prices. Most recent forecasts by international organisations and private sector institutions give a broadly similar picture. It is the Governing Council’s view that risks to these projections for economic growth are broadly balanced over the shorter term
column6: while longer-term downside risks relate mainly to potential further oil price rises
column7: global imbalances and protectionism.

column1: Turning to price developments
column2: according to Eurostat’s flash estimate
column3: annual HICP inflation increased to 2.5% in May
column4: compared with 2.4% in April and 2.2% in March. Although no detailed information is available as yet
column5: this increase probably stems from energy price developments. In the months to come and in 2007
column6: inflation rates are likely to remain above 2%
column7: the precise levels depending on future energy price developments. While the moderate evolution of labour costs in the euro area is expected to continue in 2007 – also reflecting ongoing global competitive pressures
column8: particularly in the manufacturing sector – indirect effects of past oil price increases and the announced changes in indirect taxes are expected to have a significant upward effect on inflation. Against this background
column9: it is crucial that the social partners continue to meet their responsibilities.

column1: Further input into our assessment of the outlook for price developments is provided by the June Eurosystem staff projections. Annual HICP inflation is projected to lie between 2.1% and 2.5% in 2006
column2: and between 1.6% and 2.8% in 2007. Compared with the March 2006 ECB staff projections
column3: these ranges imply a slight upward shift to the profile for HICP inflation in 2006
column4: largely reflecting the assumption of higher oil prices.

column1: In the view of the Governing Council
column2: risks to the outlook for price developments remain on the upside and include further increases in oil prices
column3: a stronger pass-through of past oil price rises into consumer prices than currently anticipated
column4: additional increases in administered prices and indirect taxes
column5: and – more fundamentally – stronger than expected wage developments due to second-round effects of past oil price increases.

column1: Turning to the monetary analysis
column2: the Governing Council again had a thorough discussion of underlying developments in money and credit. In a context of already ample liquidity and very strong monetary and credit growth
column3: the annual growth rate of loans to the private sector has increased further in recent months to reach double-digit levels. Credit growth has also been broadly based across sectors. Borrowing by households – especially for house purchase – and by non-financial corporations has been growing very strongly. At the same time
column4: monetary growth has risen further over the past few months
column5: with the annual growth rate of M3 standing at 8.8% in April.

column1: The rapid rate of monetary growth continues to be driven mainly by the expansion of its most liquid components. Thus
column2: the latest developments confirm that the stimulative impact of the low level of interest rates remains the dominant factor behind the current high trend rate of monetary expansion
column3: which signals inflationary risks over the medium to longer term. The further acceleration of monetary and credit growth in this environment of already ample liquidity points to increased upside risks to price stability at longer horizons. Monetary developments
column4: therefore
column5: require careful monitoring
column6: in particular in the light of strong dynamics in housing markets.

column1: To sum up
column2: annual inflation rates are projected to remain elevated in 2006 and 2007
column3: with risks to this outlook on the upside. Given the strength of monetary and credit growth and the ample liquidity situation
column4: a cross-check of the outcome of the economic analysis with that of the monetary analysis confirms that upside risks to price stability over the medium term prevail. A further adjustment of interest rates was therefore warranted. By acting in a timely fashion
column5: the Governing Council is helping to keep medium and long-term inflation expectations in line with price stability
column6: thereby making an ongoing contribution to sustainable economic growth and job creation. Overall
column7: our monetary policy remains accommodative and the Governing Council will continue to monitor closely all developments to ensure that risks to price stability do not materialise.

column1: With regard to fiscal policies
column2: the forecasts published recently by the Commission point to a broadly unchanged situation in the euro area in 2006 and 2007; deficit ratios are expected to remain at around the 2005 level of 2.4%
column3: while debt ratios
column4: after declining only marginally
column5: are forecast at levels still above 70% of GDP. This is disappointing against the background of the economic outlook. Most countries with an excessive deficit have not corrected their position in a timely manner. Furthermore
column6: there is a risk of consolidation delays in other countries. It is crucial to avoid the mistakes of the past
column7: when many countries failed to consolidate sufficiently in good times. The Governing Council considers that more determined progress is required towards sound public finances in a number of countries
column8: that concrete and credible measures should be implemented swiftly as part of a medium-term-oriented strategy
column9: and that it is vital to consolidate confidence in the revised Stability and Growth Pact by ensuring the sustainability of public finances in the euro area.

column1: In terms of structural reforms
column2: the Governing Council reiterates its call for the implementation of firm measures to ensure open
column3: competitive and well-functioning product and labour markets
column4: so as to foster an attractive environment for investment and innovation and to promote flexibility in wages and prices. There is a broad and firm consensus that such reforms are beneficial in promoting growth and employment and in enhancing the resilience of the euro area economy to external shocks. At the same time
column5: these reforms would further facilitate intra-euro area adjustments by reducing rigidities that contribute
column6: in some economies
column7: to wage developments that lead to high and persistent unit labour cost growth
column8: higher inflationary pressure and losses in competitiveness. Examples of such rigidities are low productivity growth due to a lack of competition in some sectors and an explicit or de facto indexation of nominal wages to prices. All in all
column9: a comprehensive set of reforms is essential to strengthen the foundations for sustained growth in output and employment across the euro area
column10: to underpin the ongoing economic recovery and to further smoothen the functioning of adjustment mechanisms in the euro area
column11: thereby facilitating the conduct of the single monetary policy.

column1: Let me now report on the outcome of our meeting
column2: which was also attended by the President of the Eurogroup
column3: Prime Minister Juncker
column4: and Commissioner Almunia.

column1: At today’s meeting
column2: we decided to increase the key ECB interest rates by 25 basis points. This decision reflects the upside risks to price stability over the medium term that we have identified through both our economic and monetary analyses. Today’s decision will contribute to ensuring that medium to longer-term inflation expectations in the euro area remain solidly anchored at levels consistent with price stability. Such anchoring is a prerequisite for monetary policy to make an ongoing contribution towards supporting sustainable economic growth and job creation in the euro area. Also after today’s increase
column3: the key ECB interest rates remain at low levels
column4: money and credit growth are strong
column5: and liquidity in the euro area is ample by all plausible measures. Our monetary policy therefore continues to be accommodative. If our assumptions and baseline scenario are confirmed
column6: it will remain warranted to further withdraw monetary accommodation. The Governing Council will therefore continue to monitor very closely all developments so as to ensure price stability over the medium and longer term.

column1: Turning first to the economic analysis
column2: the quarter-on-quarter growth rate of real GDP in the euro area for the second quarter of 2006 was confirmed at 0.9%. Moreover
column3: since our previous meeting on 31 August
column4: Eurostat has revised upwards the growth data for the two preceding quarters
column5: thereby confirming that a significant acceleration in economic expansion has taken place over the past few quarters. On the basis of the revised data
column6: economic activity has been growing at a quarterly rate of 0.7% on average over the last four quarters
column7: the unemployment rate has been on a falling trend
column8: employment growth has recovered and employment expectations overall have remained favourable. All in all
column9: the economic recovery now appears somewhat stronger than on the basis of earlier data. It has become more broadly based and is mainly supported by domestic demand. The available information on activity in the third quarter – coming from various confidence surveys and indicator-based estimates – continues to support the assessment that economic activity will grow robustly while possibly moderating somewhat.

column1: Looking ahead to the remainder of 2006 and 2007
column2: the conditions remain in place for the euro area economy to grow at solid rates around potential
column3: with some volatility in the quarterly growth rates likely to emerge around the turn of the year. Global economic activity has become more balanced across regions and is still robust
column4: thereby providing ongoing support for euro area exports. Investment is expected to remain strong
column5: benefiting from an extended period of very favourable financing conditions
column6: balance sheet restructuring
column7: accumulated and ongoing strong earnings
column8: and gains in business efficiency. Consumption growth in the euro area should also strengthen further over time
column9: in line with developments in real disposable income
column10: as employment conditions continue to improve.

column1: Risks to the outlook for economic growth are broadly balanced over the shorter term
column2: although the recent fall in oil prices – if it were to prove lasting – has the potential to lead to somewhat stronger demand and output growth than embodied in our baseline scenario for activity in the coming quarters. Over the longer term
column3: risks to growth lie on balance on the downside
column4: and relate mainly to the possibility of a renewed increase in oil prices
column5: fears of a rise in protectionist pressures
column6: especially after the suspension of the Doha round of trade talks
column7: and possible disorderly developments owing to global imbalances.

column1: As regards price developments
column2: according to Eurostat’s flash estimate
column3: annual HICP inflation fell to 1.8% in September 2006
column4: from 2.3% in August. Although no detailed breakdown is available as yet
column5: this relatively sharp decline seems to be the combined result of favourable base effects
column6: given in particular the strong rise in oil prices a year ago
column7: and the recent significant fall in oil prices. While the outlook for energy prices is uncertain
column8: on the basis of current energy prices and the higher quotations on futures markets
column9: overall inflation rates are likely to increase again towards the end of the year and in early 2007. As a consequence
column10: we expect a considerable degree of short-term volatility in the annual HICP inflation rate
column11: while the overall inflation rate will remain elevated at levels above 2% on average in 2006 and is likely to remain so in 2007.

column1: In addition
column2: risks to the outlook for price developments remain clearly on the upside. They continue to include a stronger pass-through of past oil price rises into consumer prices than currently anticipated and additional increases in administered prices and indirect taxes beyond those announced thus far. Furthermore
column3: renewed increases in oil prices cannot be excluded. More fundamentally
column4: given the favourable momentum of real GDP growth observed over the past few quarters and the positive signs from labour markets
column5: stronger than currently expected wage developments pose substantial upward risks to price stability. Against this background
column6: it is crucial that the social partners continue to meet their responsibilities
column7: in particular in the context of a more favourable environment for economic activity and employment.

column1: The monetary analysis continues to point to upside risks to price stability at medium to longer horizons. Annual M3 growth rose again to 8.2% in August and
column2: more generally
column3: the rate of monetary and credit expansion remains rapid
column4: reflecting the still low level of interest rates in the euro area. In particular
column5: loans to the private sector continue to grow at double-digit rates on an annual basis
column6: remaining broadly based across the household and corporate sectors. Taking the appropriate medium-term perspective
column7: these developments remain consistent with the persistent upward trend in the underlying rate of monetary expansion
column8: identified by the ECB’s monetary analysis since mid-2004. Moreover
column9: following several years of robust monetary growth
column10: the liquidity situation in the euro area is ample by all plausible measures. Continued strong monetary and credit growth in an environment of still ample liquidity
column11: as a result of the persistently high rate of monetary expansion over the past few years
column12: point to upside risks to price stability over the medium to longer term. Monetary developments therefore require careful monitoring
column13: particularly against the background of improved economic conditions and strong property market developments in many parts of the euro area.

column1: To sum up
column2: annual inflation rates are projected to remain elevated in 2006 and 2007
column3: with risks to this outlook remaining clearly on the upside. Given the ongoing dynamism of monetary and credit growth in an environment of already ample liquidity
column4: a cross-check of the outcome of the economic analysis with that of the monetary analysis supports the assessment that upside risks to price stability prevail over the medium term. It is essential that inflation expectations remain firmly anchored at levels consistent with price stability. If our assumptions and baseline scenario are confirmed
column5: it will remain warranted to further withdraw monetary accommodation. The Governing Council will therefore continue to monitor very closely all developments so as to ensure price stability over the medium and longer term.

column1: As regards fiscal policy
column2: euro area countries are now in the process of finalising their 2007 budgets and preparing their next stability programme updates. In the current favourable economic environment
column3: it is essential that adequate headway be made towards sound public finances
column4: implying that budget targets for 2007 should generally be more ambitious than in previous programmes. Countries in excessive deficit need to remain fully committed to bringing their deficits to below 3% within the agreed deadline via adequate and credible structural consolidation. Other countries need to make clear progress towards their medium-term objectives in line with the requirements of the Stability and Growth Pact. In all cases
column5: any revenue windfalls from faster than expected growth should be used to speed up deficit reduction or to increase surpluses. Pro-cyclical policies should be avoided and expenditure restraint is of particular importance
column6: also given the high spending ratios and taxes as compared with many other industrialised countries. Experience has shown that expenditure reform is key to successful consolidation
column7: and consolidation is essential for reducing overall public debt and for making public finances less vulnerable to the impact of ageing populations.

column1: Fiscal consolidation is likely to be most successful when coupled with comprehensive structural reforms. These are urgently needed to help to cushion the unfavourable economic effects of the projected demographic change in the euro area. The decline in the working age population will place further pressure on pension and health care systems
column2: and may have wide-ranging economic consequences. In order to support the potential economic growth of the euro area
column3: to foster macroeconomic flexibility and dynamism
column4: and to safeguard the future standard of living of our citizens
column5: labour and product market reforms are urgently needed. This will increase labour market participation and employment and strengthen innovation and the other forces driving productivity and economic growth. The ECB will play its part by continuing to maintain price stability over the medium term.

column1: 2006-11-02;2;"Ladies and gentlemen
column2: let me welcome you to our press conference and report on the outcome of today’s meeting of the ECB’s Governing Council. The meeting was also attended by Mr Heinäluoma
column3: President of the Ecofin Council
column4: and Commissioner Almunia.

column1: On the basis of our regular economic and monetary analyses
column2: we decided at today’s meeting to leave the key ECB interest rates unchanged. The information that has become available since our last meeting has further underpinned the reasoning behind our decision to increase interest rates in October. It has also confirmed that strong vigilance remains of the essence so as to ensure that medium to longer-term inflation expectations in the euro area remain solidly anchored at levels consistent with price stability. With the key ECB interest rates at still low levels
column3: money and credit growth dynamic
column4: and liquidity ample by all plausible measures
column5: our monetary policy continues to be accommodative. If our assumptions and baseline scenario continue to be confirmed
column6: it will remain warranted to further withdraw monetary accommodation. Indeed
column7: acting in a firm and timely manner remains essential to ensuring price stability over the medium term. As emphasised on previous occasions
column8: this is a prerequisite for monetary policy to make an ongoing contribution towards supporting sustainable economic growth and job creation in the euro area.

column1: Allow me to explain our assessment in greater detail
column2: turning first to the economic analysis.

column1: Eurostat’s second estimate confirmed that real GDP growth in the euro area was 0.9% quarter on quarter in the second quarter of 2006
column2: after 0.8% in the first quarter. Looking through the usual volatility of quarterly growth rates
column3: economic activity has been growing at an average quarter-on-quarter rate of 0.7% over the four quarters to mid-2006
column4: and thus faster than generally expected a year ago. On the basis of various monthly indicators of economic activity and confidence surveys
column5: available up to October
column6: the momentum of the economic expansion is expected to have continued in the second half of this year. In addition
column7: the unemployment rate has been declining
column8: employment growth has recovered and employment expectations remain favourable. All in all
column9: the assessment of a more broadly based and more self-sustaining recovery continues to be confirmed by the incoming data
column10: notwithstanding some possibility of a somewhat slower pace of quarter-on-quarter real GDP growth in the second half of this year than in the first.

column2: the conditions remain in place for the euro area economy to grow at solid rates around potential
column3: although some volatility in the quarterly growth rates is likely to emerge around the turn of the year
column4: mainly reflecting the impact of an increase in indirect taxes in a large euro area country in January 2007. Global economic activity has become more balanced across regions and remains robust
column5: thereby providing ongoing support for euro area exports. Investment is expected to remain dynamic
column6: benefiting from an extended period of very favourable financing conditions
column7: balance sheet restructuring
column8: accumulated and ongoing strong earnings
column9: and gains in business efficiency. Consumption growth in the euro area should also strengthen further over time
column10: in line with developments in real disposable income
column11: as employment conditions continue to improve.

column2: taking into account
column3: in particular
column4: the recent slowing down in the US economy on the one hand and the recent fall in oil prices on the other. The oil price decline – if it were to prove lasting – has the potential to lead to somewhat stronger demand and output growth than embodied in our current baseline scenario for activity in the coming quarters. Over the longer term
column5: risks to growth continue to lie on the downside
column6: relating mainly to the possibility of a renewed increase in oil prices
column7: fears of a rise in protectionist pressures
column8: especially after the suspension of the Doha round of trade talks

column3: after having declined to 1.7% in September from 2.3% in August. The recent decline in inflation is the combined result of favourable base effects
column4: given in particular the strong rise in oil prices a year ago
column5: and the recent significant fall in oil prices. While the outlook for energy prices remains uncertain
column6: on the basis of current energy prices and the higher quotations on futures markets
column7: inflation rates are likely to increase again in the next few months and early 2007. As a consequence
column8: we expect a high degree of short-term volatility in the annual HICP inflation rate. Looking through this volatility
column9: however
column10: HICP inflation will remain elevated at a level above 2% on average in 2006 and is likely to remain so in 2007.

column1: Risks to the outlook for price stability remain clearly on the upside. They continue to include a stronger pass-through of past oil price rises into consumer prices than currently anticipated and additional increases in administered prices and indirect taxes beyond those announced thus far. Furthermore
column2: renewed increases in oil prices cannot be excluded. More fundamentally
column3: given the favourable momentum of real GDP growth observed over the past few quarters and the ongoing improvement in labour markets
column4: stronger than currently expected wage developments pose substantial upward risks to price stability. Against this background
column5: it is crucial that the social partners continue to meet their responsibilities
column6: particularly in the context of a more favourable environment for economic activity and employment.

column1: The monetary analysis continues to point to upside risks to price stability at medium to longer horizons. Annual M3 growth rose again to 8.5% in September
column2: after having increased to 8.2% in August. Although the annual growth rate of M1 has moderated somewhat in recent months
column3: reflecting shifts into instruments with more market-related returns in a context of rising interest rates
column4: this has been more than compensated by the stronger expansion of the other components of M3.

column1: More generally
column2: the rate of monetary and credit expansion remains rapid
column3: reflecting the still low level of interest rates in the euro area and the strengthening of economic activity. In particular
column4: loans to the private sector continue to grow at double-digit rates on an annual basis
column5: their dynamism remaining broadly based across the household and corporate sectors. While the growth of household borrowing shows some signs of stabilisation
column6: albeit at very high rates
column7: the growth of borrowing by non-financial corporations continues to trend upwards and has now reached rates of over 12% on an annual basis
column8: the highest seen since the early 1990s. Thus
column9: when the counterparts of M3 are considered
column10: the main driver of strong monetary growth remains the expansion of credit to the private sector.

column1: Taking the appropriate medium-term perspective
column2: the latest developments are consistent with a continuation of the persistent upward trend in the underlying rate of monetary expansion
column3: identified by the ECB’s monetary analysis since mid-2004. Furthermore
column4: following several years of robust monetary growth
column5: the liquidity situation in the euro area is ample by all plausible measures. Continued strong monetary and credit growth in an environment of ample liquidity point to upside risks to price stability over the medium to longer term. Monetary developments therefore continue to require very careful monitoring
column6: particularly against the background of improved economic conditions and strong property market developments in many parts of the euro area.

column1: To sum up
column2: annual inflation rates are projected to remain elevated in 2006 and 2007
column3: with risks to this outlook remaining clearly on the upside. Given the ongoing marked dynamism of monetary growth in an environment of ample liquidity
column4: a cross-check of the outcome of the economic analysis with that of the monetary analysis supports the assessment that upside risks to price stability prevail over the medium to longer term. It is essential that inflation expectations remain firmly anchored at levels consistent with price stability. If our assumptions and baseline scenario continue to be confirmed
column5: it will remain warranted to further withdraw monetary accommodation. Indeed
column6: acting in a firm and timely manner remains essential to ensuring price stability over the medium term. The Governing Council will therefore exercise strong vigilance.

column1: As regards fiscal policy
column2: euro area countries have recently notified their deficit and debt figures for 2005 to the European Commission
column3: and most have reported on developments in 2006 and budget plans for 2007. While
column4: on average
column5: this information points to further
column6: albeit slow improvements in budget balances
column7: this should not give rise to complacency. It is important that commitments under the revised Stability and Growth Pact are met in all euro area countries. It is essential that budgetary consolidation is strengthened in the current economic upswing and that pro-cyclical policies are avoided. This would boost confidence among market participants and the public. To that effect any revenue windfalls from faster than expected growth should be pre-committed and used in full to speed up deficit reduction or to increase surpluses in good times. The prospects for attaining sound budgetary positions improve when consolidation plans are based on credible commitments to reduce expenditure ratios and better expenditure control mechanisms. Finally
column8: let me reiterate previous calls for high quality statistical data and sound statistical reporting
column9: which are key for the prevention and correction of budgetary imbalances.

column1: As regards structural reforms
column2: the Governing Council stressed the importance of creating a fully operational Single Market and flexible product and labour markets in order to enhance the adjustment capacity of the euro area economy and its resilience to external shocks. Liberalising product markets to allow more competition would raise incentives for firms to invest and innovate
column3: thereby raising productivity growth. Removing labour market rigidities and distortions in wage and price formation are key conditions for promoting more homogeneous cost and price competitiveness trends among euro area countries and for generating sustained output growth and job creation. In particular
column4: wage increases should be guided
column5: in general
column6: by the trend in labour productivity growth
column7: while taking full account of the present level of unit labour costs
column8: in order to preserve or restore price competitiveness. Moreover
column9: it is desirable that wage settlements move away from automatic
column10: backward-looking indexation mechanisms. The successful implementation of reforms aimed at removing rigidities and inefficiencies in euro area countries would raise potential growth and employment prospects.

I want you to remember the time when we were called upon by a number of institutions or analysts not to increase rates. We then increased rates in December of last year. It was because cross-checking with the monetary pillar was clearly indicating to us that we had to increase rates. And again
column3: a lot of observers
column4: many economists and some institutions were advising us
column5: on the basis of their own economic analyses
column6: not to do that. So once again: the monetary pillar is important for us and has played
column7: is playing and will continue to play
column8: an important role in guiding our own decisions in a pragmatic way
column9: as has always been the case. It is clear that the latest indications we have of monetary developments have not confirmed what we had seen some months ago when
column10: as you may remember
column11: M3 growth was starting to decline progressively. Let me give you the exact figures: for the evolution of M3 growth
column12: we had 8.5% in June
column13: followed by 7.8% in July when we could see that we had something which was suggesting that perhaps there was the start of a slowdown. And then we had 8.2% in August and now
column14: today

column17: we nevertheless see the influence of our monetary policy tightening
column18: because M1
column19: as you know
column20: is now somewhat less dynamic. The three last figures we have on M1 are 7.4%
column22: which suggest that the most liquid component of M3 is a little less dynamic. And this
column23: of course

column26: we have very dynamic credit growth
column27: particularly credit to the private sector
column28: households and the corporate sector. All this calls for very careful monitoring

column2: I will confirm to you that we will do what we have done in the past

column1: As regards economic activity we have had a very good – I would say more than good – first semester; indeed it has been exceptionally favourable. We have also had a favourable period over the last
column2: say
column3: four quarters. I draw your attention to the fact that this vindicates

column1: As regards the US slowdown
column2: my colleagues and I mentioned that in our own deliberations; I told you a moment ago that it was something that we had to mention. At the present time
column3: I would say that we are making the working assumption that this slowdown would be a soft slowdown. We are not making the working assumption that it could be a hard landing. I draw your attention to the fact that the direct and indirect trade impact on us – I said that in Paris – is not something which is too substantial. I quoted the figure of a 1% slowdown in the United States transmitting -0.2% for growth in the euro area
column4: taking into account the direct effect and the echo effect on the rest of the world as well. That being said
column5: it is of course linked to the fact that our trade with the United States is less important than is frequently assumed. The United Kingdom is more important for us than the United States – only to give you an example. Also to be taken into account is the fact that
column6: at the global level
column7: what we see is that the slowdown in the United States is partially or might be partially offset by continuous robust growth in a large part of the rest of the world

column1: As regards the various decisions that are taken by central banks as regards their reserve assets
column2: we take exactly the same attitude as we take with all economic agents
column3: all investors and savers the world over. We have no policy of encouraging any such holdings and no policy of discouraging them. We consider that each institution
column4: each private or public agent has to take their decision
column5: on the basis of their own analysis. What we have observed up to now has been a smooth and orderly evolution since the creation of the euro. I would say that provided it is a smooth and orderly evolution
column6: we have no reason to comment on it.

column1: As regards the second question that you asked
column2: I would say that we have quite a diverse situation from economy to economy as regards labour productivity growth. This is a way to tell each particular economy in the euro area that they have to take into account their level and evolution of unit labour costs
column3: the overall cost-competitiveness of the economy
column4: and the arbitrage between insiders and outsiders on the labour market
column5: when they devise their decisions on wages and salaries in particular. It is absolutely clear that any increase over and above what would be reasonable
column6: taking into account the labour productivity progress
column7: would hamper sustainable growth
column8: hamper job creation and contribute to more inflation. So in the interest of the country in question
column9: in the interest of the euro area itself
column10: in the interest of ensuring price stability
column11: it is advisable to follow the recommendation of a wise and sound posture.

column1: As regards VAT
column2: I don’t think we have changed the previous messages in that respect. The fact that we have mentioned VAT in Germany as influencing growth and also creating volatility associated with it was in the statement or in the questions and answers a number of times already in such press conferences. As you know

Further administered price increases are one of the risks that we are regularly quoting because we really believe that it is a threat that we have to take into account. When we look at the past
column4: it has played a significant role in the inflation that has been observed until now. We will see exactly what happens. Again
column5: it’s a risk – I hope very much that it will not materialise – but it is a risk.

column1: As regards 2007
column2: I have already said what I wanted to say. We will see exactly what our judgement is on the basis of the new projections
column3: of the new figures that we will have
column4: and of all the information that will be available. In any case
column5: it is already being very predictable that you have little doubt on what we will do next month. So don’t be too demanding

column8: we will not tell you that we will not move in the months to come because we are alert and we will do whatever is necessary to cope with risks and threats to price stability”. And the same
column9: you remember
column10: when we started increasing rates. There were a lot of requests to the effect “Why don’t you say that you will increase every month or every two months
column11: regularly?”

column1: We said “No
column2: we are alert
column3: we will see what has to be done
column4: taking into account our analysis of the situation”. With the benefit of hindsight you see that it worked very well: we happen to be very predictable; and the market has understood - it seems to me – pretty correctly what we had in mind.

column1: As regards labour productivity
column2: let us take the example of this country that you choose – you have picked up on one particular country. I said that we have had the problem of inflation
column3: we have the problem of competitiveness
column4: and we have the problem of unemployment. At the present level of unemployment it is clear that this issue is very important. There is to be taken into account the interest of those whom I would call the outsiders

It is true that the productivity progress was quite good in the past in Germany and it is equally true that unit labour costs have moved slowly in comparison with the average
column6: but it was justified by a catching-up exercise. You remember that for this particular economy
column7: after reunification
column8: cost-competitiveness was not satisfactory at all. The cost-competitiveness of this economy
column9: Germany
column10: had to catch up
column11: which is being done
column12: and is being done regularly
column13: year after year. I would say that the main argument for wage restraint would certainly be today the level of unemployment.

column1: What we have to deliver is price stability in the medium run and what I have observed in the past is that the contribution of administered prices on inflation has been substantial year after year after year – even if it seems bizarre
column2: because we should not normally have to cope with such a big contribution of administered prices. But we have to take that into account
column3: as it's undoubtedly a problem. I do not welcome
column4: in general
column5: administered price increases. And I would say that if some are augmented
column6: for example I understand pretty well why tobacco should be augmented – there is absolutely no problem there
column7: although I think that perhaps the smokers in this room would not be at all satisfied – but I would say for health reasons we can have good reason to do that. But then I would call for other prices to be reduced in order for us and for overall inflation not to be hit by these decisions. That being said
column8: it is not my job to enter into fine-tuning such decisions
column9: as they are the responsibility of the executive branches
column10: but as a general rule we do not like at all their net impact on inflation.

column1: As regards the mention of some consideration on cycles of interest rate hikes and so forth
column2: I stick to what I have said. Everything you have seen or read or heard are personal views and have absolutely nothing to do with the views of the Governing Council which I am transmitting to you right now.

column1: This is one of the most important issues that we all have to deal with. On both sides of the Atlantic we have the same shape of yield curve
column2: the same very low level of real rates
column3: and the same extremely low level of nominal rates. It is true that we have – the last time I looked at the figures – ten-year euro rates on the Bund benchmark; we had 3.72%
column4: which is extraordinarily low. The conclusion that we could draw from the yield curve as it stands is much disputed. And I would say that the majority of economists – certainly on the other side of the Atlantic but also on this side of the Atlantic too – would not say that the present slope of the yield curve means that there is a very high risk of recession. It is considered that you have to introduce a large number of other elements to conclude
column5: and I said myself that our working assumption – which is shared
column6: it seems to me
column7: by the mainstream analysis and certainly by our friends on the other side of the Atlantic
column8: in the sister institution – is that a soft slowdown is very likely. Now you will ask me how it is possible that there are such very low levels of long-term interest rates. But you have answered this question yourself
column9: saying that it is the accumulation of past liquidity. I am not sure that this a fully appropriate explanation
column10: or the only explanation. There is an element there
column11: it is clear
column12: and the fact that we have all increased rates means that – in any case – we judged that the previous monetary policy had become too accommodating at a certain moment. And we have gradually corrected that. But there is also another element which is certainly important: the creeping oil shock. For several years
column13: every year
column14: until most recently
column15: there has been an increase in the price of oil
column16: the accumulation of additional current account surpluses by oil exporters
column17: and this has created – on top of what we had observed even before the creeping oil shock
column18: on top of the global savings that existed before – an additional and significant volume of “forced savings” that are taken by the oil exporters out of the rest of the world and are creating an additional volume of capital chasing investments at a global level. This is not a normal way of looking at things
column19: as you generally have investments chasing capital rather than the reverse.

column1: When you have such capital chasing investment
column2: it creates an environment where capital is abundant
column3: and pushes down the price of risk in general. And that might explain in particular why we have such a low level of long-term rates on both sides of the Atlantic and everywhere in the world. And that would be totally independent from the long medium-term prediction by the market of what is likely to happen in the economies concerned. That being said
column4: we will see exactly what happens. We work a lot to analyse the situation
column5: to better understand the financial markets. As you know
column6: we have the feeling that this cannot last forever
column7: and that the present accumulation of the very low level of real rates
column8: the very low level of spreads
column9: the very low level of risk premium that we are observing
column10: the underestimation of risks in general – will necessarily be corrected. Our present working assumption is that there will be a soft correction – not a sharp and abrupt correction. But
column11: as I have said several times already
column12: there will be a correction.

column1: 2006-12-07;2;"Ladies and gentlemen
column2: the Vice-President and I are very pleased to welcome you to today’s press conference. Let me report on the outcome of our meeting
column3: which was also attended by the President of the Eurogroup
column4: Prime Minister Juncker
column5: and Commissioner Almunia.

column1: At today’s meeting
column2: we decided to increase the key ECB interest rates by 25 basis points. This decision reflects the upside risks to price stability over the medium term that we have identified through both our economic and monetary analyses. Today’s decision will contribute to ensuring that medium to longer-term inflation expectations in the euro area remain solidly anchored at levels consistent with price stability. Such anchoring is a prerequisite for monetary policy to make an ongoing contribution towards supporting sustainable economic growth and job creation in the euro area. After today’s increase
column3: our monetary policy continues to be accommodative
column4: with the key ECB interest rates remaining at low levels
column5: money and credit growth strong
column6: and liquidity in the euro area ample by all plausible measures. Therefore
column7: looking ahead
column8: acting in a firm and timely manner to ensure price stability in the medium term is warranted. The Governing Council will monitor very closely all developments so that risks to price stability over the medium term do not materialise.

column1: Turning first to the economic analysis
column2: according to Eurostat’s first estimate
column3: the quarter-on-quarter growth rate of real GDP in the euro area for the third quarter of 2006 was 0.5%. The data thus confirm our assessment that economic activity continued to expand robustly
column4: while moderating from the very strong rates seen in the first half of the year. Domestic demand remained the main driver of economic growth in the third quarter
column5: confirming the anticipated broadening of the recovery and pointing to the increasingly self-sustaining nature of economic expansion in the euro area. The information on economic activity from various confidence surveys and indicator-based estimates supports the assessment that robust economic growth has continued in the fourth quarter of this year.

column1: Looking ahead
column2: the conditions remain in place for the euro area economy to grow at solid rates around potential. While some volatility in the quarterly growth rates is likely to emerge around the turn of the year
column3: associated with the impact of changes in indirect taxes in a large euro area country
column4: the medium-term outlook for economic activity remains favourable. As regards the external environment
column5: economic growth has become more balanced across regions. Helped in part by lower oil prices
column6: global growth is robust
column7: thereby providing support for euro area exports. Domestic demand in the euro area is expected to maintain its relatively strong momentum. Investment should remain dynamic
column8: benefiting from an extended period of very favourable financing conditions
column9: balance sheet restructuring
column10: accumulated and ongoing strong earnings
column11: and gains in business efficiency. Consumption should also strengthen further over time
column12: in line with developments in real disposable income
column13: as employment conditions continue to improve.

column1: This outlook is also reflected in the new Eurosystem staff macroeconomic projections. The projections foresee average annual real GDP growth in a range between 2.5% and 2.9% in 2006
column2: between 1.7% and 2.7% in 2007 and between 1.8% and 2.8% in 2008. Most recent forecasts by international organisations give a broadly similar picture. In comparison with the September ECB staff projections
column3: the ranges projected for real GDP growth in 2006 and 2007 have been revised upwards
column4: largely reflecting the assumption of lower energy prices and their impact on real disposable income.

column1: In the Governing Council’s view
column2: the risks surrounding this broadly favourable outlook for economic growth over the projection horizon lie on the downside. The main risks relate to the possibility of a renewed increase in oil prices
column3: fears of a rise in protectionist pressures
column4: especially after the suspension of the Doha round of trade talks
column5: and concerns about possible disorderly developments owing to global imbalances.

column1: As regards price developments
column2: according to Eurostat’s flash estimate
column3: annual HICP inflation rose to 1.8% in November 2006
column4: from 1.6% in October and 1.7% in September. While no detailed breakdown of the November HICP data is available as of yet
column5: the lower annual HICP inflation rates recorded in the two previous months reflected mainly the significant declines in crude oil prices from August onwards
column6: as well as base effects. While the outlook for energy prices remains uncertain
column7: on the basis of the oil prices currently implied by the futures market overall inflation rates are likely to increase again in early 2007 and then hover around 2% in the course of that year
column8: also reflecting the impact of higher indirect taxes.

column1: The December Eurosystem staff projections see annual HICP inflation at between 2.1% and 2.3% in 2006
column2: between 1.5% and 2.5% in 2007 and between 1.3% and 2.5% in 2008. Most recent forecasts by international organisations give a broadly similar picture. Compared with the September 2006 ECB staff projections
column3: the ranges for 2006 and 2007 are somewhat lower
column4: largely reflecting the assumption of lower energy prices. In this context
column5: let me remind you of the conditional nature of these projections
column6: which are based on a series of technical assumptions
column7: including market expectations for short and long-term interest rates as well as for oil and non-energy commodity prices.

column1: In the Governing Council’s view
column2: the outlook for price developments remains subject to upside risks
column3: stemming in particular from a pass-through of previous oil price increases which is stronger than assumed in the baseline scenario
column4: the possibility of renewed oil price increases and additional increases in administered prices and indirect taxes beyond those announced and decided thus far. More fundamentally
column5: given the favourable momentum of real GDP growth observed over the past few quarters and the positive signs from labour markets
column6: wage developments could be stronger than currently expected. Therefore
column7: it is crucial that the social partners continue to meet their responsibilities. Wage agreements should take into account productivity developments in connection with the still high level of unemployment and positions in price competitiveness. It is also important that wage settlements move away from automatic
column8: backward-looking indexation mechanisms.

column1: Turning to the monetary analysis
column2: annual M3 growth was unchanged at 8.5% in October
column3: remaining close to the highest rates observed since the introduction of the euro
column4: which points to inflationary risks at medium to longer horizons. Increasing interest rates have exerted some influence over monetary developments in recent months
column5: although as yet mainly by triggering shifts among the components of M3 rather than constraining the expansion of M3 itself. In particular
column6: the annual growth rate of M1 has moderated somewhat
column7: reflecting shifts from overnight deposits into other components of M3 which offer more market-related returns.

column1: More generally
column2: the rate of monetary and credit expansion remains rapid
column3: reflecting the low level of interest rates and the strengthening of economic activity in the euro area. In particular
column4: loans to the private sector continue to grow at double-digit rates on an annual basis
column5: their dynamism remaining broadly based across the household and corporate sectors. In the context of rising interest rates
column6: the growth of household borrowing has shown signs of stabilisation in recent months
column7: albeit at very high growth rates. By contrast
column8: the growth of borrowing by non-financial corporations continues to trend upwards and has now reached rates of over 12% on an annual basis
column9: the highest seen since the early 1990s. Thus
column10: when the counterparts of M3 are considered
column11: the main driver of strong monetary growth remains the expansion of credit to the private sector.

column1: Taking a medium to longer-term perspective
column2: the latest developments are consistent with a continuation of the persistent upward trend in the underlying rate of monetary expansion
column3: identified by the ECB’s monetary analysis since mid-2004. Furthermore
column4: following several years of robust monetary growth
column5: the liquidity situation in the euro area is ample by all plausible measures. Continued strong monetary and credit growth in an environment of ample liquidity point to upside risks to price stability over the medium to longer term. Monetary developments therefore continue to require very careful monitoring
column6: particularly against the background of improved economic conditions and continued strong property market developments in many parts of the euro area.

column1: To sum up
column2: annual inflation rates are projected to hover around 2% in the coming two years
column3: with risks to this outlook remaining on the upside. In addition
column4: given the ongoing marked dynamism of monetary and credit growth in an environment of ample liquidity
column5: a cross-check of the outcome of the economic analysis with that of the monetary analysis supports the assessment that upside risks to price stability prevail over the medium to long term. It is essential that inflation expectations remain firmly anchored at levels consistent with price stability. Indeed
column6: acting in a firm and timely manner to ensure price stability in the medium term is warranted. The Governing Council will therefore monitor very closely all developments so that risks to price stability over the medium term do not materialise.

column1: As regards fiscal policy
column2: the European Commission’s autumn forecasts suggest that deficits will fall below 3% of GDP in most euro area countries by 2007. This is welcome. However
column3: the projected improvements in fiscal balances can only partly be attributed to substantial progress in structural consolidation
column4: as higher economic growth and revenue windfalls are playing an important role. Moreover
column5: in a number of countries with fiscal imbalances
column6: adjustment efforts still fall short of what is needed to meet their respective medium-term objectives in a timely manner and thus fulfil the requirements of the revised Stability and Growth Pact. This is of major concern. It is therefore crucial that forthcoming updates of the stability programmes not only envisage significant progress towards the correction of excessive deficits in a sustainable manner but also make sufficient headway towards safe budgetary positions in the countries concerned. For all countries it is paramount that pro-cyclical policies be avoided in the current economic upswing. More progress is also needed with fiscal structural reform as part of a comprehensive medium-term strategy to improve economic incentives and the soundness of social security systems. This would be a crucial contribution of fiscal policies to economic growth and fiscal sustainability as well as to confidence in the revised Stability and Growth Pact.

column1: As regards structural reforms
column2: the Governing Council welcomed the 2006 progress reports submitted by EU Member States on their 2005-08 national reform programmes
column3: in line with the renewed Lisbon Strategy. Although it is encouraging that many concrete reform steps are being taken or are planned
column4: there is still a considerable way to go to make the euro area a more dynamic economy
column5: which is crucial to meeting the challenges of globalisation
column6: population ageing and rapid technological change. Reform measures should foster more integrated
column7: flexible and competitive economies in the euro area
column8: thus allowing more efficient adjustment processes and a stronger resilience to shocks. These are essential conditions for the substantial benefits of the single currency to be better exploited and for the economic performance to improve in both the euro area as a whole and in each member state.

column1: I would first like to say that we are all delighted that Slovenia is joining the euro area as soon as January next year. column7: so you have to constantly keep an eye on competitiveness. These are my two main messages. Speaking of Slovenia let me mention a point which we have made already. In a single currency area

column1: On the basis of our regular economic and monetary analyses
column2: we decided at today’s meeting to leave the key ECB interest rates unchanged. The information that has become available since our last meeting has further underpinned the reasoning behind our decision to increase interest rates in March. It has also confirmed that the medium-term outlook for price stability remains subject to upside risks
column3: so that very close monitoring of all developments is warranted. Indeed
column4: it is essential to ensure that risks to price stability over the medium term do not materialise. This will contribute to ensuring that medium to longer-term inflation expectations in the euro area remain solidly anchored at levels consistent with price stability. Such anchoring is a prerequisite for monetary policy to make an ongoing contribution towards supporting sustainable economic growth and job creation in the euro area. Given the favourable economic environment
column5: our monetary policy continues to be on the accommodative side
column6: with the key ECB interest rates moderate
column7: money and credit growth vigorous
column8: and liquidity in the euro area ample by all plausible measures. Therefore
column9: looking ahead
column10: acting in a firm and timely manner to ensure price stability in the medium term is warranted.

column1: Turning first to the economic analysis
column2: recent information has underpinned our assessment of ongoing robust economic growth dynamics in the euro area. Eurostat’s second estimate has confirmed quarter-on-quarter real GDP growth in the fourth quarter of 2006 at 0.9%. Over the whole year 2006
column3: real GDP grew by 2.7% in the euro area
column4: unadjusted for the number of working days. On the basis of the latest data
column5: survey releases and various indicator-based estimates
column6: it appears that robust growth is continuing in the first half of 2007.

column1: Looking further ahead
column2: the conditions are in place for the euro area economy to grow solidly. As regards the external environment
column3: global economic growth has become more balanced across regions and
column4: while moderating somewhat
column5: remains strong. External conditions thus continue to provide support for euro area exports. Domestic demand in the euro area is also expected to maintain its relatively strong momentum. Investment should remain dynamic
column6: benefiting from an extended period of favourable financing conditions
column7: balance sheet restructuring
column8: accumulated and ongoing strong corporate earnings
column9: and gains in business efficiency. Consumption should also strengthen further over time
column10: in line with developments in real disposable income
column11: increasingly supported by employment growth and improving labour market conditions.

column1: The risks surrounding this favourable outlook for economic growth are broadly balanced over the shorter term. At longer horizons
column2: downside risks remain
column3: stemming mainly from the external side. They relate to fears of a rise in protectionist pressures
column4: the possibility of further increases in oil prices and concerns about possible disorderly developments owing to global imbalances.

column1: As regards price developments
column2: according to Eurostat’s flash estimate
column3: annual HICP inflation was 1.9% in March 2007
column4: compared with 1.8% in the first two months of the year. A detailed breakdown of the March HICP data is not yet available. Looking ahead
column5: barring further increases in oil prices
column6: last year’s volatility in energy prices will lead to significant base effects
column7: thereby affecting the profile of annual inflation rates this year. On the basis of the current level of oil prices and oil price futures
column8: annual inflation rates are likely to fall in the months to come

column1: Over the policy-relevant medium-term horizon
column2: the outlook for price developments remains subject to upside risks. These relate to the possibility of further oil price rises and additional increases in administered prices and indirect taxes beyond those announced and decided thus far. More fundamentally
column3: stronger than currently expected wage developments could pose significant upward risks to price stability
column4: not least in view of the favourable momentum in labour markets observed over the past few quarters. It is therefore crucial that the social partners continue to meet their responsibilities. In this context
column5: wage agreements should take into account price competitiveness positions
column6: the still high level of unemployment in many economies
column7: as well as productivity developments. The Governing Council monitors the wage negotiations in euro area countries with particular attention.

column1: The monetary analysis confirms the prevailing upside risks to price stability at medium to longer horizons. Annual M3 growth increased further to 10.0% in February
column2: from 9.9% in January. At the same time
column3: the annual growth rate of loans to the private sector
column4: while remaining very strong at 10.3% in February
column5: showed some further signs of moderation. Whereas in previous months this moderation reflected a decline in the growth rate of household borrowing in an environment of rising mortgage lending rates throughout the euro area and a slowing increase in house prices in some regions
column6: in February it was due to a moderation in the growth of loans to non-financial corporations. When assessing such developments
column7: it should be borne in mind that monthly figures can be influenced by temporary factors and should thus not be overstated. Indeed
column8: the strong growth in private sector credit reflects the continuation of the strong trend in the growth of borrowing by non-financial corporations seen since mid-2004.

column1: When put in perspective
column2: the latest data continue to point to vigorous dynamics in the underlying rate of broad money expansion in the euro area. The continued robust expansion of money and credit reflects the low levels of interest rates over a prolonged period of time and the strengthening of economic activity in the euro area. Rising short-term interest rates
column3: in combination with low long-term interest rates
column4: have had an impact on developments in the individual components of monetary and credit aggregates
column5: but have thus far had only a limited influence on the overall strength of monetary developments. Following several years of robust monetary growth
column6: the liquidity situation in the euro area is ample by all plausible measures. In this environment of ample liquidity
column7: the continued vigorous expansion of money and credit points to upside risks to price stability over the medium to longer term. Monetary developments therefore continue to require very careful monitoring
column8: particularly against the background of a solid expansion in economic activity and continued strong property market developments in many parts of the euro area.

column1: To sum up
column2: in assessing price trends it is important to look through any short-term volatility in inflation rates. The relevant horizon for monetary policy is the medium term. Risks to the medium-term outlook for price stability remain on the upside
column3: relating in particular to stronger than currently expected wage developments in a context of ongoing robust growth in employment and economic activity. Given the vigorous monetary and credit growth in an environment of already ample liquidity
column4: a cross-check of the outcome of the economic analysis with that of the monetary analysis supports the assessment that upside risks to price stability prevail over the medium to longer term. Accordingly
column5: the Governing Council will continue to monitor very closely all developments. Indeed
column6: it is essential to ensure that risks to price stability over the medium term do not materialise. This will support the solid anchoring of medium to longer-term inflation expectations in the euro area at levels consistent with price stability. Therefore
column7: looking ahead
column8: acting in a firm and timely manner to ensure price stability in the medium term remains warranted.

column5: to improve the quality of public finances
column6: to foster competition and integration
column7: and to promote labour market reforms. Indeed

column9: it is of the utmost importance to use the momentum of the improved economic situation and to press ahead vigorously with budgetary consolidation. Government deficit and debt-to-GDP ratios in euro area countries in 2006 have turned out to be significantly better than anticipated. But this positive outcome largely reflects buoyant tax revenues in the context of a favourable macroeconomic environment
column10: offsetting in some cases higher than planned public expenditure. The better than expected fiscal outcomes in 2006 should lead to more ambitious targets for 2007 and beyond
column11: allowing revenue windfalls to be fully allocated to deficit and debt reduction. Furthermore

column1: 2007-05-10;2;"Ladies and gentlemen

column1: On the basis of our regular economic and monetary analyses
column2: we decided at today’s meeting to leave the key ECB interest rates unchanged. The information that has become available since our last meeting has further underpinned the reasoning behind our decision to increase interest rates in March. Strong vigilance is of the essence in order to ensure that risks to price stability over the medium term do not materialise. In turn
column3: this will contribute to ensuring that medium to longer-term inflation expectations in the euro area remain solidly anchored at levels consistent with price stability. Such anchoring is a prerequisite for monetary policy to make an ongoing contribution towards supporting sustainable economic growth and job creation in the euro area. Given the favourable economic environment
column4: our monetary policy continues to be on the accommodative side
column5: with the key ECB interest rates moderate
column6: money and credit growth vigorous
column7: and liquidity in the euro area ample by all plausible measures. Therefore
column8: looking ahead
column9: acting in a firm and timely manner to ensure price stability in the medium term is warranted.

column1: Turning first to the economic analysis
column2: the latest indicators and survey data confirm that the expansion of economic activity continued in the first quarter of 2007 and remains solid and broad-based. Looking ahead
column3: the medium-term outlook for economic growth in the euro area continues to be favourable. Conditions are in place for the ongoing expansion to proceed at sustained rates. Global economic growth has become more balanced across regions and
column4: while moderating somewhat in recent quarters
column5: remains strong. External conditions thus continue to provide support for euro area exports. Domestic demand in the euro area is also expected to maintain its momentum. Investment should remain dynamic
column6: benefiting from an extended period of favourable financing conditions
column7: balance sheet restructuring
column8: strong corporate earnings and gains in business efficiency. Consumption should also strengthen further over time
column9: in line with developments in real disposable income
column10: increasingly supported by employment growth and improving labour market conditions.

column1: The risks surrounding this favourable outlook for economic growth are broadly balanced over the shorter term. At longer horizons
column2: the balance of risks remains on the downside
column3: stemming mainly from external factors. Such factors include fears of a rise in protectionist pressures
column4: the possibility of further increases in oil prices and concerns about possible disorderly developments due to global imbalances.

column1: With regard to price developments
column2: according to Eurostat’s flash estimate
column3: annual HICP inflation was 1.8% in April 2007
column4: after 1.9% in March. Looking at the coming months
column5: barring further increases in oil prices
column6: significant base effects deriving from last year’s energy price volatility will strongly influence the profile of annual inflation rates. On the basis of the current level of oil prices and oil price futures
column7: annual inflation rates are likely to fall somewhat in the months to come
column8: before rising again towards the end of the year to hover at levels around 2%.

column1: Over the policy-relevant medium-term horizon
column2: the outlook for price developments remains subject to upside risks. These relate notably to the increasing capacity utilisation in the euro area economy
column3: the possibility of further oil price rises and additional increases in administered prices and indirect taxes beyond those announced and decided thus far. More fundamentally
column4: stronger than currently expected wage developments could pose significant upward risks to price stability
column5: not least in view of the favourable momentum in labour markets observed over the past few quarters. The Governing Council is monitoring wage negotiations in the euro area countries with particular attention. It is crucial that the social partners meet their responsibilities so as to continue to avoid wage developments that would eventually lead to inflationary pressures and harm the purchasing power of all euro area citizens. In this context
column6: it is also important to point out that wage agreements should be sufficiently differentiated and take into account price competitiveness positions
column7: the still high level of unemployment in many economies and productivity developments across sectors.

column1: The monetary analysis confirms the prevailing upside risks to price stability at medium to longer horizons. The underlying rate of monetary expansion remains strong
column2: in a context of already ample liquidity. The ongoing strength of monetary expansion is reflected in the increasingly rapid growth of M3
column3: which in March reached an annual rate of 10.9%
column4: as well as in the ongoing high levels of credit growth. Monetary and credit expansion is due partly to the moderate level of interest rates and solid economic growth.

column2: inter alia
column3: by the shape of the yield curve and external factors
column4: and be subject to some degree of volatility. Looking through such transitory aspects
column5: there are
column6: however
column7: several indications that higher short-term interest rates are influencing monetary dynamics
column8: although they have not
column9: as yet
column10: significantly dampened the overall strength of these dynamics. For example

column12: M1
column13: in recent quarters

column15: the annual growth rate of loans to the private sector has shown some signs of stabilising since mid-2006
column16: albeit at double-digit levels.

column1: All in all
column2: taking into account both short-term factors and the underlying trend of the continued vigorous expansion of money and credit
column3: there are clear indications of upside risks to price stability at medium to longer-term horizons. In fact
column4: following several years of robust monetary growth
column5: the liquidity situation in the euro area is ample by all plausible measures. In this environment
column6: monetary developments continue to require very careful monitoring
column7: particularly against the background of a solid expansion in economic activity and still strong property market developments.

column1: To sum up
column2: in assessing price trends it is important to look beyond any short-term volatility in inflation rates. The relevant horizon for monetary policy is the medium term. Risks to the medium-term outlook for price stability remain on the upside
column3: relating in particular to stronger than currently expected wage developments in a context of ongoing robust growth in employment and economic activity. Given the vigorous monetary and credit growth in an environment of already ample liquidity
column4: a cross-check of the outcome of the economic analysis with that of the monetary analysis supports the assessment that upside risks to price stability prevail over the medium to longer term. Accordingly
column5: the Governing Council will continue to be strongly vigilant in order to ensure that risks to price stability over the medium term do not materialise. This will support the solid anchoring of medium to longer-term inflation expectations in the euro area at levels consistent with price stability. Therefore
column6: looking ahead
column7: acting in a firm and timely manner to ensure price stability in the medium term remains warranted.

In the view of the Governing Council
column3: this requires a rigorous implementation of 2007 budgets

column7: all countries should avoid fiscal policies that feed macroeconomic imbalances. This would allow euro area countries to prepare themselves for less favourable economic conditions.

2007-06-05;2;Ladies and gentlemen
