column1: At today’s meeting
column2: we decided to raise the key ECB interest rates by 25 basis points. This decision was taken in view of the prevailing upside risks to price stability over the medium term that we have identified through both our economic and monetary analyses. Today’s decision will contribute to ensuring that medium to longer-term inflation expectations in the euro area remain solidly anchored at levels consistent with price stability. Such anchoring is a prerequisite for monetary policy to make an ongoing contribution towards fostering sustainable economic growth and job creation in the euro area. After today’s increase
column3: given the positive economic environment in the euro area
column4: our monetary policy is still on the accommodative side
column5: with overall financing conditions favourable
column6: money and credit growth vigorous
column7: and liquidity in the euro area ample. Looking ahead
column8: acting in a firm and timely manner to ensure price stability in the medium term is warranted. The Governing Council will monitor closely all developments to ensure that risks to price stability over the medium term do not materialise.

column1: Allow me to explain our assessment in greater detail
column2: starting with the economic analysis. Incoming information clearly confirms that the euro area economy continues to expand at a pace which is significantly stronger than generally expected a year ago. With a quarter-on-quarter rate of 0.6%
column3: real GDP growth in the first quarter of 2007 was again somewhat above previous expectations. Other available information on economic activity
column4: notably various surveys of business and consumer confidence
column5: suggests that solid growth has continued into the second quarter.

column1: Looking ahead
column2: the medium-term outlook for economic activity remains favourable. The conditions are in place for the euro area economy to continue to grow at a sustained rate. As regards the external environment
column3: global economic growth has become more balanced across regions and
column4: while moderating somewhat
column5: remains robust. External conditions thus continue to provide support for euro area exports. Domestic demand in the euro area is also expected to maintain its relatively strong momentum. Investment should remain dynamic
column6: benefiting from financing conditions which remain favourable
column7: accumulated and ongoing strong corporate earnings
column8: balance sheet restructuring as well as business efficiency gains achieved over an extended period. Meanwhile
column9: consumption should be supported by developments in real disposable income
column10: as labour market conditions continue to improve.

column1: This outlook is also reflected in the new Eurosystem staff macroeconomic projections. The projections foresee average annual real GDP growth in a range between 2.3% and 2.9% in 2007 and between 1.8% and 2.8% in 2008. In comparison with the previous ECB staff projections
column2: the ranges projected for real GDP growth in 2007 are within the upper part of the ranges from March. For 2008
column3: the ranges have been revised marginally downwards
column4: following the increase in oil prices over recent months.

column1: In the Governing Council’s view
column2: the risks surrounding this favourable outlook for economic growth are broadly balanced over the shorter term. At medium to longer horizons
column3: the balance of risks remains on the downside
column4: owing mainly to external factors. These relate in particular to fears of a rise in protectionist pressures
column5: the possibility of further increases in oil prices
column6: concerns about possible disorderly developments owing to global imbalances and potential shifts in financial market sentiment.

column1: As regards price developments
column2: oil prices have risen again over recent months. Accordingly
column3: as reflected in Eurostat’s flash estimate
column4: annual HICP inflation was 1.9% in May 2007
column5: unchanged from April but somewhat higher than expected a few months ago. Looking ahead
column6: the short-term profile of annual inflation rates continues to be determined largely by current and past energy price developments
column7: as last year’s volatility in energy prices leads to significant base effects. On the basis of the current level of oil prices and oil price futures
column8: which show an upward slope
column9: annual inflation rates are likely to fall slightly in the months ahead before rising again significantly towards the end of the year.

column1: Consistent with this view
column2: Eurosystem staff projects average annual HICP inflation of between 1.8% and 2.2% in 2007 and between 1.4% and 2.6% in 2008. Compared with the March 2007 ECB staff projections
column3: the range projected for inflation in 2007 is somewhat higher
column4: largely reflecting higher oil prices. The projected range for inflation in 2008 is unchanged. In this context
column5: let me remind you of the conditional nature of these projections
column6: which are based on a series of technical assumptions
column7: including assumptions for future short and long-term interest rates that are based on market expectations derived from the yield curve
column8: as well as assumptions for oil and non-energy commodity prices.

column1: At the policy-relevant medium-term horizon
column2: risks to the outlook for price stability remain on the upside in the Governing Council’s view. These risks relate notably to the domestic side. In particular
column3: capacity utilisation in the euro area economy is increasing and labour markets are gradually improving. Accordingly
column4: there is a risk that wage developments will be stronger than expected
column5: which would pose significant upward risks to price stability. In addition
column6: pricing power in market segments with low competition may increase in such an environment. It is therefore crucial that all parties concerned meet their responsibilities. Wage agreements in particular should be sufficiently differentiated to take into account price competitiveness positions
column7: the still high level of unemployment in many economies and sector-specific productivity developments. The Governing Council stresses that wage developments should be avoided which would eventually lead to inflationary pressures and harm the purchasing power of all euro area citizens. In addition
column8: upside risks to price stability arise from increases in administered prices beyond those anticipated thus far. Finally
column9: on the external side
column10: upside risks stem from the possibility of further unexpected oil price rises.

column1: The monetary analysis confirms the prevailing upside risks to price stability at medium to longer horizons. The underlying rate of monetary expansion remains strong
column2: in a context of already ample liquidity. The ongoing strength of monetary expansion is reflected in the continued rapid growth of M3
column3: which reached an annual rate of 10.4% in April
column4: as well as the still high level of credit growth. The strong rate of monetary and credit expansion reflects
column5: in part
column6: favourable financing conditions and solid economic growth.

column1: In the short term
column2: monetary and credit developments can be affected
column3: inter alia
column4: by the shape of the yield curve and external factors
column5: and be subject to some degree of volatility. In assessing the policy-relevant underlying trends in monetary and credit growth
column6: it is important to look through such transitory aspects. Taking this perspective
column7: there are several indications that higher short-term interest rates are now influencing monetary dynamics
column8: although they have not
column9: as yet
column10: significantly dampened the overall strength of the underlying rate of monetary and credit expansion. For example
column11: increases in short-term rates have contributed to a more moderate expansion of the narrow aggregate
column12: M1
column13: in recent quarters. Equally
column14: the annual growth rate of loans to the private sector has shown some signs of stabilising since mid-2006
column15: albeit at double-digit levels. The stabilisation of loan growth is now becoming more broad-based
column16: as evidenced in recent months by developments in borrowing by non-financial corporations and by households. At the same time
column17: house price growth has come down somewhat
column18: although remaining at high levels on average in the euro area.

column1: Taking into account both short-term factors and the underlying trend of the continued vigorous expansion of money and credit
column2: there are clear indications of upside risks to price stability at medium to longer-term horizons. Following several years of robust monetary growth
column3: the liquidity situation in the euro area remains ample. In this environment
column4: monetary developments continue to require very careful monitoring
column5: particularly against the background of the expansion in economic activity and still strong property market developments.

column1: To sum up
column2: in assessing price trends it is important to look beyond any short-term volatility in inflation rates. The relevant horizon for monetary policy is the medium term. Risks to the medium-term outlook for price stability remain on the upside
column3: relating in particular to the domestic side. As capacity utilisation increases and labour markets gradually improve
column4: constraints are emerging which could lead in particular to stronger than expected wage developments. Given the vigorous monetary and credit growth in an environment of already ample liquidity
column5: a cross-check of the outcome of the economic analysis with that of the monetary analysis supports the assessment that upside risks to price stability prevail over the medium to longer term. Accordingly
column6: the Governing Council will monitor closely all developments in order to ensure that risks to price stability over the medium term do not materialise. This will support the solid anchoring of medium to longer-term inflation expectations in the euro area at levels consistent with price stability. Looking ahead
column7: acting in a firm and timely manner to ensure price stability in the medium term is warranted.

column1: As regards fiscal policy
column2: all countries should be in line with the rules and provisions of the Stability and Growth Pact. This will be crucial for the smooth functioning of Monetary Union
column3: given that the Stability and Growth Pact is an indispensable part of its institutional setting. Following the significant budgetary improvement recorded in 2006
column4: the latest available forecasts suggest a further reduction in the government deficit-to-GDP ratio of the euro area over the period 2007-08. This reflects in particular projected ongoing strong revenue collection in the context of a favourable macroeconomic outlook. However
column5: the structural improvement is more muted. The current economic “good times” should be used to rapidly redress the remaining budgetary imbalances in euro area countries as well as to accelerate the adjustment towards their medium-term objectives of sound budget positions with a focus on expenditure restraint. As agreed by the euro area finance ministers at the Eurogroup meeting in Berlin on 20 April
column6: taking advantage of the favourable cyclical conditions would enable most euro area members to achieve their medium-term objectives in 2008 or 2009
column7: and all of them should aim for 2010 at the latest. This is particularly important with a view to reducing the still high government debt ratios and preparing for the fiscal challenges arising from population ageing. In order to ensure that fiscal developments are monitored effectively
column8: the Governing Council supports all efforts by Eurostat to improve the fiscal data situation. It also welcomes the increased emphasis placed by the ECOFIN Council on measures to improve the quality of public finances and increase the efficiency of public administration.

column1: As regards structural reforms
column2: the Governing Council fully supports any efforts that enhance competition
column3: increase productivity and foster economic flexibility
column4: thus promoting higher sustainable real GDP growth and employment. In this respect
column5: we strongly back reforms focusing on reducing labour market rigidities
column6: product market barriers and administrative burdens
column7: and on stimulating technological innovation. Exploiting the complementary nature of reforms would increase their benefits in terms of long-term economic dynamism and price stability. Furthermore
column8: the importance of a successful conclusion of the Doha round of trade talks for productivity and growth in Europe should not be underestimated. In the end
column9: higher productivity growth will allow increases in real wages without negatively affecting employment
column10: thereby supporting the income growth of the euro area workforce.

column1: I think that what we have been doing since our increase of rates in December 2005 has certainly served our purpose very well. We have anchored – in line with our previous record – the inflationary expectations in line with our definition of price stability over that year and a half. We have maintained fully our credibility and we have continued to serve our primary mandate. Because we have been faithful to our primary mandate – as it is a necessary condition for sustainable growth and job creation – we have served the European economy well. Let's remember that when we increased rates in December 2005 we had a number of observers
column2: a number of institutions that were advising us not to do so. Today
column3: at the present time
column4: all of them
column5: including the IMF and the OECD
column6: are saying that we were very well-founded in that decision and in all the decisions we have been taking until now
column7: including that one. So we have eight successive increases that are considered to be wise. We have been fully vindicated in what we have been doing.

column12: too. I could mention house purchases
column13: the financing of house purchases
column14: in the same way: in April 8.6%
column15: in February 9.4%. So we see a number of elements that are interesting. I mention these and you know that our monetary pillar is based upon a broad and deep analysis of
column16: components
column17: of counterparts
column18: of sectoral breakdowns and of a deep understanding of the dynamics that are behind it. This is considered by us as important
column19: enlightening and as something which allows us to take the wisest possible decision on the basis of this binocular approach that we are very attached to.

column1: On the United States of America: I have always said that we very much rely upon the analysis of the Federal Reserve System and that we believe that their analysis is a pertinent one. For us
column2: we have always had good trust in the analysis of the Fed. It is something which I note with satisfaction.

column1: On the second question

column7: in particular
column8: we had an explicit reference to the monetary analysis. We have the same vision of the monetary analysis as being deep
column9: broad
column10: as aiming at having as profound an understanding as possible of the various dynamics that are inside the various components

column1: That was for your second question

column1: It is an issue
column2: you are absolutely right. It is an issue for the G8 summit of industrialised countries. I know the work which has been done by the German Presidency in this respect. I had a number of occasions myself to mention that the ECB was looking at this issue very carefully. As you may know

column1: Let me only say that we had already the report of the Financial Stability Forum at the level of the global economy which had been requested by the G8. The conclusions of this progress report are very interesting. I would say that we would very much subscribe to these conclusions and they are also in line with a number of national reflections. To sum up
column2: it would rely very much on the core intermediaries being the key point to ensure an improvement of the situation. So the supervisory authorities would be called upon to ensure that the core intermediaries
column3: particularly the big commercial and investment banks that are in direct contact with the hedge funds
column4: have the best risk management practices possible
column5: are correctly enlightened on all the risks they are taking and have a correct understanding and a correct information on what the hedge funds are doing. And that of course relies upon the vigilance of the supervisory authorities themselves

The core intermediaries are also called upon to reinforce considerably their call for transparency vis-à-vis hedge funds. And the hedge funds themselves are called upon to work out benchmarks on what would be the best behaviour possible as regards transparency vis-à-vis core intermediaries and transparency vis-à-vis their own investors – those individuals or entities that are giving them their capital – and a benchmark for their own internal risk management systems.

column1: At this stage
column2: I would say that it seems that there is a consensus that we should make progress along all the lines I have suggested
column3: including the call to the industry itself to work out voluntarily what these benchmarks would be. I could perhaps call that a set of principles and I am very attached personally to the voluntary principles or benchmarks for appropriate behaviour and conduct that would be devised by the industry itself. column1: It is an important question and I would give the same response as I already gave. It is good to enter when you are as fit as possible. I know that Bulgaria has done quite a lot of good work and we have to recognise that. The reforms are being pursued and real growth has been important

I think the previous decisions that were taken by the authorities of Slovakia were justified and I expect that the functioning of ERM II will continue to be as orderly as it has been in the past. column3: our Convergence Report. I will not elaborate on that

column7: if and when there is a reunification

column1: The notion of liquidity is a very complex notion. A number of market participants are mentioning liquidity to characterise the situation where they see “capital chasing investment” or “money chasing ideas”
column2: something which they note as being a little bit exceptional
column3: because in other times
column4: and perhaps in more normal times
column5: you see the contrary
column6: you see “ideas chasing money or capital”
column7: you see “investment chasing financing or capital”. This situation is clearly driven by a large number of reasons. And I do not want to elaborate too much on these reasons
column8: but publicly
column9: yesterday
column10: on the occasion of the International Monetary Conference
column11: together with Ben Bernanke and Toshihiko Fukui
column12: we had elaborated on that and I had myself said: Look
column13: you have perhaps five reasons why we are observing that ex ante savings are at a global level superior to ex ante investment. And that creates the present observation that the pricing of risks is lower than it would be in – I would say – more normal times. Among these various reasons you have certainly the fact that most emerging countries are posting big current account surpluses. You have the fact that in a number of economies
column14: not in Europe now
column15: but in a number of economies you had physical investment by corporate businesses that were lower than what would have been suggested by econometric equations based on past observations and it is certainly the case in the United States. And you had also among all those reasons the remarkable creativity that we are observing in the global financial markets as regards derivatives and the way of splitting
column16: of repackaging
column17: of reformatting risks with the consequence of enlarging formidably the scope of the investors that are risk buyers. And also a major reason would be the oil shock: the fact that we have additional forced savings that are adding up to the pot of savings that we have at a global level.

column1: All this taken into account
column2: I would say that we are – all of us
column3: because we were in very good agreement – saying that we believe that we have to pave the way for some kind of orderly and smooth adjustment associated with the reassessment of risks. We say it not to dramatise the situation
column4: but because there are very good reasons
column5: namely what we are observing today on the market. On top of that
column6: let us not forget that the real economy is performing well at a global level
column7: but it seems to us that it is our duty to say: let us calmly prepare for a smooth and orderly reassessment of risks when the time comes
column8: in order to avoid what would not be good for the real global economy
column9: namely an adjustment which would not be orderly and smooth.

column1: The answer to your first question is no and as regards your second question
column2: I already made all the comments necessary.

column1: I have said that what we consider pertinent is the overall analysis
column2: which is not attached only to one particular aggregate
column3: one particular component or one particular counterpart. We try to understand the dynamics of this complex matrix. And on the basis of our understanding of these dynamics we conclude that risks to price stability in the longer term are signalled by this overall analysis. We do not have a mechanistic approach
column4: neither in the monetary nor in the economic analysis. So
column5: in answer to your question
column6: I would say that we make a judgement on the basis of all that we see. Our judgement today is that
column7: for the longer term
column8: there are risks to price stability embedded in what we are observing
column9: even if the dynamics are very different as regards a number of counterparts.

column1: We have an understanding of the qualification of accommodation that is multi-dimensional. I said already that we do not refer to a neutral rate
column2: and that we do not refer to any such concepts. We believe that
column3: on the basis of all that we are observing
column4: it is justified to say that we are still on the accommodative side. I do not want to elaborate more on that
column5: other than to say that
column6: in any case
column7: the needle of our compass is that we make a judgement on what is necessary to counter inflationary risks at any given moment. We judge what is necessary to counter inflationary risks in various circumstances
column8: and circumstances do not cease to change. Of course there are external influences
column9: from the global economy
column10: and there are a number of domestic factors that are moving
column11: and they move in the ways that can be very significant. If I take
column12: for instance
column13: the last four quarters of the European economy – the last four quarters that are known – I was very impressed to see that now
column14: as a very significant engine of growth
column15: we have gross capital formation. I mentioned the fact that in the case of other economies
column16: perhaps
column17: this engine was not important. In our own case
column18: if I take again the last four quarters
column19: including the first quarter of this year

column1: The ECB has a mandate
column2: the mandate is given by the Treaty
column3: the mandate is to ensure price stability for 318 million people. By being credible in ensuring it in a vast continental economy which has a dimension of the order of magnitude of the United States of America
column4: we are fulfilling a necessary condition for sustainable growth and job creation in Europe
column5: in the euro area. Those who are members of ERM II are of course considerably helped by the fact that the anchor of their currency is reliable and credible.

column1: I have a feeling that all the institutions concerned
column2: commercial banks as well as investment banks
column3: as well as highly-leveraged institutions are listening to what we say. I also have the sentiment that they are very much sharing our analysis. We are certainly not isolated in developing this analysis. They have improved their own resilience
column4: it seems to me. They have improved their risk management concepts across the board. They have embarked on sophisticated stress-testing in order to complement the traditional value-at-risk computation
column5: and so forth. So
column6: I would have a relatively positive judgement on their awareness that they are living in an environment which includes risks and that it is their duty to take into account those risks and to be ready to weather a possible materialisation of those risks. I would not be negative at all in that respect. What remains true is that global finance has proved to be very resilient. The last two or three shocks that we had in recent years and months have been very rapidly absorbed by the market and we have to consider that it is also something which is important to see that when there are some shocks
column7: they are absorbed by the normal functioning of markets. There are
column8: as I said
column9: good reasons for risks to be priced as they are. What we know is that the situation is not sustainable in the long run. What we are doing together

column11: the banking supervisory authorities on the other hand
column12: as well as the industry
column13: is to be done as seriously as possible to weather the adjustment when shocks materialise. As we say in the central banks
column14: we are not paid not to worry
column15: we are paid to worry! It is our duty to signal risks
column16: and it is part of the signalling of risks that permits global finance and the global economy to be as impressive as they are. Do not forget that it is not a new phenomenon. We have an ongoing process since the crisis of the end of the 1990s

column18: since the Asian crisis
column19: since LTCM [Long-Term Capital Management hedge fund]
column20: and so forth. We have been working a lot to improve
column21: in particular
column22: risk management and I take it again that it would be equally wrong to be too complacent and to underestimate the risks and also to say nothing is being done. A lot of things are being done but it is our duty to encourage all participants
column23: including the private sector
column24: to be as active as possible in doing a good job in this respect.

2007-07-05;2;Ladies and gentlemen
column2: the Vice-President and I are very pleased to welcome you to today’s press conference. Let me report on the outcome of our meeting
column3: which was also attended by Commissioner Almunia.

column1: On the basis of our regular economic and monetary analyses
column2: we decided at today’s meeting to leave the key ECB interest rates unchanged. The information that has become available since our previous meeting has further underpinned the reasoning behind our decision to increase interest rates in June. It has also confirmed that the medium-term outlook for price stability remains subject to upside risks. Given the positive economic environment in the euro area
column3: our monetary policy is still on the accommodative side
column4: with overall financing conditions favourable
column5: money and credit growth vigorous
column6: and liquidity in the euro area ample. Looking ahead
column7: acting in a firm and timely manner to ensure price stability in the medium term remains warranted. The Governing Council will continue to monitor closely all developments to ensure that risks to price stability over the medium term do not materialise and medium to longer-term inflation expectations in the euro area remain solidly anchored at levels consistent with price stability. Such anchoring is a prerequisite for monetary policy to make an ongoing contribution towards supporting sustainable economic growth and job creation in the euro area.

column1: Allow me to explain our assessment in greater detail
column2: starting with the economic analysis. The latest data and survey releases have remained broadly positive
column3: supporting the view that economic activity in the euro area in the second quarter of 2007 continued to expand at solid rates in line with our baseline scenario.

column1: Looking ahead
column2: the medium-term outlook for economic activity remains favourable. The conditions are in place for the euro area economy to continue to grow at a sustained rate. As regards the external environment
column3: global economic growth has become more balanced across regions and
column4: while moderating somewhat
column5: remains robust. External conditions thus continue to provide support for euro area exports. Domestic demand in the euro area is also expected to maintain its relatively strong momentum. Investment should remain dynamic
column6: benefiting from overall financing conditions which remain favourable
column7: accumulated and ongoing strong corporate earnings
column8: balance sheet restructuring as well as business efficiency gains achieved over an extended period. Meanwhile
column9: consumption should be supported by developments in real disposable income
column10: as labour market conditions continue to improve.

column1: The risks surrounding this favourable outlook for economic growth are broadly balanced over the shorter term. At medium to longer horizons
column2: the balance of risks remains on the downside
column3: owing mainly to external factors. These relate in particular to fears of a rise in protectionist pressures
column4: the possibility of further increases in oil prices
column5: concerns about possible disorderly developments owing to global imbalances and potential shifts in financial market sentiment.

column1: As regards price developments
column2: as reflected in Eurostat’s flash estimate
column3: annual HICP inflation was 1.9% in June 2007
column4: unchanged from previous months. Looking ahead
column5: the short-term profile of annual inflation rates continues to be determined largely by current and past energy price developments
column6: as last year’s volatility in energy prices leads to significant base effects. On the basis of the current level of oil prices and oil price futures
column7: which show an upward slope
column8: annual inflation rates are likely to fall only slightly in the months ahead before rising again significantly towards the end of the year.

column1: At the policy-relevant medium-term horizon
column2: risks to the outlook for price stability remain on the upside. These risks relate notably to the domestic side. In particular
column3: as capacity utilisation in the euro area economy is high and labour markets continue to improve
column4: constraints are emerging which could lead in particular to stronger than expected wage developments. In addition
column5: pricing power in market segments with low competition may increase in such an environment. Such developments would pose significant upward risks to price stability. It is therefore crucial that all parties concerned meet their responsibilities. Wage agreements in particular should be sufficiently differentiated to take into account price competitiveness positions
column6: the still high level of unemployment in many economies and sector-specific productivity developments. The Governing Council stresses the importance of avoiding wage developments that would eventually lead to inflationary pressures and harm the purchasing power of all euro area citizens. In addition
column7: upside risks to price stability arise from increases in administered prices and indirect taxes beyond those anticipated thus far
column8: and the potentially procyclical stance of fiscal policy in some countries. Finally
column9: on the external side
column10: upside risks stem from the possibility of further unexpected oil price rises.

column1: The monetary analysis confirms the prevailing upside risks to price stability at medium to longer horizons. The underlying rate of monetary expansion remains strong
column2: in a context of already ample liquidity. The ongoing strength of monetary expansion is reflected in the continued rapid growth of M3
column3: which increased at an annual rate of 10.7% in May
column4: as well as the still high level of credit growth. The strong rate of monetary and credit expansion reflects
column5: in part
column6: favourable financing conditions and solid economic growth.

column1: When identifying and assessing the policy-relevant underlying trends in monetary and credit expansion
column2: it is important to look through shorter-term volatility and the effects of changes in the slope of the yield curve and external factors that are likely to prove temporary. Taking this perspective
column3: there are several indications that higher short-term interest rates are now influencing monetary dynamics
column4: although they have not
column5: as yet
column6: significantly dampened the overall strength of the underlying rate of monetary and credit expansion. For example
column7: increases in short-term rates have contributed to a more moderate expansion of the narrow aggregate
column8: M1
column9: in recent quarters. Equally
column10: the annual growth rate of loans to the private sector has shown some signs of stabilising since mid-2006
column11: albeit at double-digit levels. The stabilisation of loan growth is now becoming more broad-based
column12: and is apparent in borrowing by both non-financial corporations and households. In the latter case
column13: the stabilisation of loan growth also reflects some moderation in house price dynamics
column14: although house price growth nonetheless remains at high levels on average in the euro area.

column1: Given the continued vigour of money and credit expansion
column2: there are clear indications of upside risks to price stability at medium to longer-term horizons. Following several years of robust monetary growth
column3: the liquidity situation in the euro area remains ample. In this environment
column4: monetary developments continue to require very careful monitoring
column5: particularly against the background of the expansion in economic activity and still strong property market developments.

column1: To sum up
column2: in assessing price trends it is important to look beyond any short-term volatility in inflation rates. The relevant horizon for monetary policy is the medium term. Risks to the medium-term outlook for price stability remain on the upside
column3: relating in particular to the domestic side. As capacity utilisation is high and labour markets continue to improve
column4: constraints are emerging which could lead in particular to stronger than expected wage and profit margin developments. Given the vigorous monetary and credit growth in an environment of already ample liquidity
column5: a cross-check of the outcome of the economic analysis with that of the monetary analysis supports the assessment that upside risks to price stability prevail over the medium to longer term. Accordingly
column6: the Governing Council will monitor closely all developments in order to ensure that risks to price stability over the medium term do not materialise and medium to longer-term inflation expectations in the euro area remain solidly anchored at levels consistent with price stability. Looking ahead
column7: acting in a firm and timely manner to ensure price stability in the medium term remains warranted.

column1: As regards fiscal policy
column2: the Governing Council notes with concern the pressures emerging in a number of countries to relax previous fiscal consolidation targets. In the current overall benign economic environment
column3: it is imperative that all governments comply with the provisions of the Stability and Growth Pact on fiscal consolidation in economic “good times” and that all the countries concerned honour the commitments they made at the Eurogroup meeting in Berlin on 20 April 2007. As agreed in Berlin
column4: taking advantage of the favourable cyclical conditions would enable most euro area countries to achieve their medium-term objectives in 2008 or 2009
column5: and all of them should aim for 2010 at the latest. These pledges should be reflected in the 2008 budget plans so as to avoid repeating governments’ past failure to adjust fiscal balances in economic “good times”. At the same time
column6: the Governing Council welcomes the emphasis placed by the ECOFIN Council on measures to improve the quality and efficiency of public finances.

column1: As regards structural reforms
column2: the Governing Council fully supports all measures that improve the functioning of product
column3: labour and financial markets. In the context of the Integrated Guidelines for Growth and Jobs
column4: the EU Member States noted that a well-functioning Internal Market remains at the heart of the Lisbon agenda and that its four freedoms will reinforce the European Union’s competitiveness. The completion of the Single Market is therefore a priority for Member States
column5: in particular as regards further financial market integration
column6: the pursuit of effective competition in the energy market and the implementation of the Services Directive. Increased market competition and a reduction of cross-border barriers are beneficial for consumers since they lead to lower prices and a greater choice of products. For firms
column7: they lead to higher efficiency
column8: greater dynamism and an enhanced capacity to cope with economic shocks and to face the challenges and opportunities posed by globalisation. Following the principle of “an open market economy with free competition” is pivotal to fostering long-term economic growth and job creation
column9: increasing the resilience of the euro area to economic shocks and facilitating the maintenance of price stability in the euro area. This was confirmed at the last European Council meeting
column10: when the EU leaders agreed to annex a new protocol to the Treaties
column11: in the context of the Intergovernmental Conference. This protocol underlines the fact that an Internal Market which includes a system ensuring that competition is not distorted is indeed indispensable for the good functioning of the EU economies.

column1: As regards the IMF
column2: I take this opportunity to pay homage to Mr Rodrigo de Rato and the fantastic job that he has been doing over the years: the medium-term strategy of the IMF and the way he has coped with the modernisation and optimisation of the IMF. Regarding the appointment of the new Managing Director
column3: I will only say that it is not the responsibility of the ECB to participate in the decision-making process. I have observed that the long-standing tradition that has existed since World War II has been followed very recently in the case of its sister institution. I have also noted that all European voices have suggested sticking to this long-standing tradition. At the moment
column4: I cannot say anything else. The Governing Council of the ECB has no position on this matter.

column1: As regards your first question
column2: this issue of eliminating certain public spending from the computation of the Maastricht criteria has already been examined. This suggestion has already been made in the past and it was examined during the discussions about revising the Stability and Growth Pact in 2004. As I remember
column3: this suggestion was rejected almost unanimously at that time by members of the Eurogroup and of the ECOFIN Council
column4: because the Stability and Growth Pact is an ECOFIN instrument.

column1: As regards your question on the euro exchange rate
column2: I will say again that this is a very important domain where those who have a major responsibility
column3: such as the President of the Eurogroup – because he represents all the executive branches of the 13 countries today and the 15 tomorrow – and myself as the representative of the ECB and the Governing Council
column4: have to be very responsible. The position of this institution
column5: as agreed upon by the Governing Council
column6: and that of our major partners at the level of the G7
column7: is that we consider excess volatility and disorderly movements in exchange rates to be undesirable for economic growth. We all agree – I signed those communiqués along with Jean-Claude Juncker
column8: as well as a number of ministers and central bank colleagues – that in emerging economies with large and growing current account surpluses
column9: especially China
column10: it is desirable that their effective exchange rates move so that the necessary adjustment will occur. This is the message that we together have on China. We have signed this message and China
column11: as well as the other emerging economies in Asia
column12: knows that. After appropriate discussion in Essen and in Washington
column13: I myself noted that our Japanese colleagues
column14: both the Minister of Finance and the Governor
column15: said they believe that the Japanese economy is on a sustainable recovery path and that the exchange rates should reflect these economic fundamentals. Exchange markets should be aware of the fact that there are two-way risks in any bet. This has been said by the responsible Japanese authorities and repeated recently. I say myself that it is important that they said that. And it is important that the market gets that message. As regards the US Dollar
column16: I have also noted with others that the US authorities have said that a strong dollar was in the interests of the US economy. I will stop there and I warn in advance that all those who would like to hear more comments will be a little bit disappointed
column17: because I will stick to what I have just said
column18: which is crystal clear and reflects our current position!

column1: To your first question: any indications that could be given in respect of a possible weakening of the fiscal consolidation would be against
column2: I repeat
column3: against the decisions that have been taken by the various governments themselves
column4: against the recommendations and decisions that have been taken within the framework of the Stability and Growth Pact upon the proposal of the Commission and against the Berlin Agreement I referred to in the introductory remarks. It is clear
column5: and this is true for all countries concerned
column6: including of course France and Italy and others
column7: if such signs are given. That being said
column8: I do not want to anticipate the meeting which will take place next Monday at the level of the Eurogroup.

column1: To your second question on the structural reforms
column2: again
column3: we are totally backing structural reforms. We know that it is not easy
column4: we know that it calls for courage from the executive branches and from the parliaments and from the social partners
column5: but we are absolutely convinced that it would permit an increase in growth and job creation and in the growth potential of Europe. Anything that would weaken the path of structural reforms is in our opinion not to be recommended at all. That would certainly be the case of the example you gave. We back structural reforms and we stand ready to explain why they are necessary. We encourage and fully support the governments that are embarking on those reforms.

column1: To your third question on the growth potential of the euro area
column2: I fully confirm
column3: at this stage
column4: that the position of the Governing Council is that we have not substantiated any conclusion that would permit an increase in the present level of the growth potential that we have in mind
column5: which is around 2.25%. So I confirm the 2.25%; that was our previous assessment. Let me repeat that we are cautious. We are prudent as this concept can be approached through different methodologies
column6: but for the present situation we confirm the 2.25%.

column1: As usual
column2: with regard to what we will say in future press conferences and after future meetings of the Governing Council
column3: I will tell you what our judgement is at the next press conference and after the next meeting of the Governing Council. At this stage
column4: I said already all what I had to say on the future.

column1: As regards growth and the impact on growth
column2: it is an occasion to repeat what you already know very well
column3: namely that we are absolutely convinced
column4: as are all our colleagues
column5: that when we ensure price stability
column6: we permit sustainable growth and sustainable job creation. And that on the basis of all that we have seen since our decision in December 2005 to increase rates to counter the inflationary risks that we were noticing at that time
column7: we have been
column8: at least until now
column9: fully vindicated in the sentiment that we were helping sustainable growth and job creation. To the extent that we had been criticised from time to time for the fact that we were playing and arbitraging price stability against job creation
column10: the figures are: more than 12 million jobs were created during the eight years since the setting-up of the euro until the end of last year. And before the euro was set up
column11: in the equivalent period of eight years
column12: less than three million had been created. I could of course also embark on national data in various countries. Again
column13: I draw your attention to the fact that there is a global consensus to consider that the prerequisite for sustainable growth and job creation is that we ensure price stability and that we are credible in ensuring price stability over time
column14: because it does not suffice to ensure price stability today
column15: we are reasoning over the medium term. That is the reason why the solid anchoring of inflationary expectations through our own credibility is so important.

column1: As regards protectionism
column2: I have to say quite sadly
column3: that I have the sentiment that things have not improved in this respect. We are listing this risk as one of the important risks that would weigh down on the global economy. I have nothing to report that I would consider positive in this respect at the global level
column4: and I say that sadly
column5: because we are absolutely convinced that it is the openness of the global economy which is one of the crucial factors for global growth. We are all sharing in this global prosperity
column6: all of us
column7: whether industrialised countries
column8: emerging countries and economies and even the poorest.

column1: I said if I have something to say on behalf of the Governing Council
column2: I will find out a nice way to say it and I do not exclude at all a press briefing or a press conference or whatever
column3: I exclude nothing.

column2: oneself

column9: the place of an adjective

column1: As regards your third question on structural reforms
column2: again
column3: I do not anticipate the next meeting and meetings of the Eurogroup. There are rules and commitments that have been taken within the framework of the Stability and Growth Pact. We back the structural reforms as well as the commitments undertaken under the framework of the Stability and Growth Pact. You know how great the responsibility of the Commission is in this respect

column5: the Berlin decisions
column6: taken under the chairmanship of Peer Steinbrück by all the members
column7: all the executive branches represented by their ministers of finance.

column2: pursuant to the IGC’s detailed mandate
column3: which has been approved by the European Council
column4: the changes to be introduced by the IGC to the current treaties in our domains will cover
column5: and will be limited to
column6: all the innovations that had been agreed at the 2004 IGC. On that basis
column7: we welcome the opening of the IGC and we stand ready to contribute to it at any time during its work and to provide our sentiment on matters within the fields of competence of the ECB. We welcome what has been done and we have observed that we adhere exactly and strictly to what had been approved and accepted on the occasion of the 2004 IGC. We will publish our opinion in the Official Journal of the European Union.

column1: Regarding your second point
column2: I do not see how President Sarkozy’s attendance at the meeting could change the dialogue between the ECB and the finance ministers. It is the composition of one delegation which will be different from usual. Let us not forget that Mr Jean-Claude Juncker is himself both a member of the ECOFIN and the European Council. But it would be better to ask this question directly to Mr Juncker – as I am myself invited in the same way as Mr Juncker and Commissioner Almunia are invited to attend the Governing Council. I am not a member of the Eurogroup. I am an invitee to the Eurogroup.

column1: First let me mention the importance of this decision in principle for Cyprus and Malta to enter the euro area. The decision has been taken at the level of the Heads of State or Government. We will have the ECOFIN decision next Tuesday on a number of points and I do not wish to speak ahead of that meeting. All I will say is that we started with 11 members
column2: very soon we were 12
column3: a few years later we were 13
column4: now next January we will be 15. It is very impressive in terms of historical evolution. And
column5: having been involved in negotiating the Maastricht Treaty myself
column6: I am absolutely impressed by the fact that when we negotiated the Treaty we had in mind that we would number perhaps seven or eight
column7: or perhaps less. I remember it was said during the course of the negotiation that even if there would be only two countries the euro would have to start in order for the first crystallisation of the single currency to begin. Being 15 next year is very impressive as regards the pace of history. When you enter a single currency area you share a destiny in common. And I can never repeat that often enough because it seems to me that this is the main message. It is a very solemn commitment to be in a single currency area. You have to take into account that all that you do and all the decisions you take must be fully consistent with the fact that you are a member of a single currency area. And whether those decisions are in the realm of fiscal policy
column8: in the realm of structural reforms
column9: or in the realm of wages and salary formation and unit labour costs
column10: all national parameters have to be checked and understood within the framework of membership of the single currency area. We cannot and I cannot say that frequently enough and with sufficient force. Cyprus and Malta will share a destiny in common with the partner countries.

column1: On Cyprus
column2: I will only mention that we ourselves said in our convergence report that the issue of reunification was an open issue and our intention was not to advise against the entry of Cyprus to the euro area
column3: but to note in advance that
column4: if and when the time comes
column5: the negotiation of this reunification on the economic
column6: financial and monetary matters should itself be fully compatible with membership of the euro area
column7: with the fact that we hare a destiny in common.

column1: I confirm that what we see in the dynamics of the various components and counterparts of the monetary aggregates reflects the fact that we have increased rates
column2: for instance the rate of growth over twelve months of M1 was 7% in March
column3: 6.3% in April and 6.1% in May. In 2005 it was 10.4%. We see clearly that there has been a deceleration of the growth of M1
column4: and the main explanation for that is that we have increased short-term rates. On the contrary
column5: at the level of M3 we see a very high level of dynamism being maintained. The last figure that we have on a 12-month basis is 10.7%. Clearly we have both phenomena operating: on the one hand we have M1 decelerating visibly
column6: and on the other hand we have M3 minus M1 remaining very dynamic
column7: at least until now
column8: in part because of the previous slope of the yield curve. We will see what happens when we have a different slope of the yield curve. I remain cautious because on that point with regard to consumer credit for households
column9: the figures for February
column10: March
column11: April and May are 6.7%
column13: 6.9% and 5.9%. So we see also elements that substantiate some kind of deceleration. All that being said
column14: these are very complex phenomena and we have to remain very alert. Loans to non-financial corporations remain very dynamic and we are at the level of 12.6% of growth over the last twelve months. As you see
column15: we are observing structural transformations. The fact that we have increased rates is visible and it triggers structural transformation. Everything taken into account
column16: when we extract all the information from these data we see that in the medium to longer term the inflationary risks are on the upside
column17: and this is what I said on behalf of the Governing Council.

column1: To your first question there is a very strong global consensus – and we share this global consensus – among the industrialised world economies that central banks should have a primary mandate of price stability. Price stability is not contradictory at all with sustainable growth and job creation. On the contrary
column2: there is a very simple logical relationship
column3: whereby price stability is a prerequisite for sustainable growth and sustainable job creation. When you take your decision on how to ensure price stability
column4: you take all parameters on board – all the information that you have
column5: both domestic and international. The exchange rates are one of the data amongst many others that you take into account when you take your decision to ensure price stability. There has been a consensus since the collapse of the Bretton Woods system that we would live in a floating exchange rate system. And there is also a consensus that when we have messages to convey to observers
column6: market participants
column7: investors and savers the world over
column8: we convey them through the appropriate means
column9: which are the informal meetings of the G7. These are the rules upon which we base the functioning of the present global economy. I refer here to the principles agreed between the partners in the industrialised world
column10: and what I mentioned earlier regarding exchange rates is precisely the implementation of those principles.

column1: As regards your second question on protectionism
column2: the Governing Council of the ECB is very profoundly committed to the completion of the Single Market. The Single Market – or common market as the names were changed to emphasise that we are really speaking of an achieved Single Market – was the visionary idea of the founding fathers
column3: and we are doing nothing more than follow in the very straight tracks that were imagined by the founding fathers and that have worked so well up to now. We support the full-fledged achievement of the single market in all domains because we believe that it is a prerequisite for continued prosperity
column4: growth and job creation in Europe. In addition
column5: we advocate proceeding in the best fashion possible against protectionism at a global level
column6: and that is because we think that protectionism at a global level could be a major risk to global growth and global job creation.

column1: On your last point
column2: I do not want to give a stamp of approval to any particular computation made by any particular firm. I would only say that
column3: taking all that I have seen published it is not my intention to ship messages aiming at changing anything in what has been computed. And I mentioned both September and October because
column4: according to all that I have seen
column5: there are certain probabilities that are attached to September and other probabilities that are attached to October
column6: and
column7: on behalf of the Governing Council
column8: I do not want to change in any respect what you saw this morning in the various computations.

column1: As regards your last question we did talk about fiscal policy this morning
column2: and I already mentioned
column3: on behalf of the Governing Council
column4: our position as regards fiscal policy while presenting the Introductory Statement. We are very attached to the respect of all the rules and the commitments that have been taken. As regards what will be said at the next meeting of the Eurogroup
column5: I do not want to anticipate; it is a meeting of the Eurogroup and it will depend very much on what will be said by the various delegations – not by only one
column6: but by the various delegations that will present their own situations and intentions. These will be the reflections and the decisions of the Eurogroup
column7: amongst the executive branches
column8: on the basis of the proposal and analysis of the Commission. I do not want to anticipate the conclusion which will be drawn following the proposal of the Commission by Jean-Claude Juncker as Chairman of the Eurogroup.

column1: As regards VAT
column2: you could see yourself what has happened with the VAT decision in Germany. It undoubtedly has an impact on inflation and Germany represents approximately 30% or more of euro area GDP. France has a GDP which is a little more modest. And then you can make the computation to see the impact.

column1: It is clear that we are looking closely at everything that happens in the area of indebtedness and we see a tendency in particular for households to be more and more indebted. We also note that there are big differences from country to country and economy to economy; some are catching up with others and there is an extraordinarily rapid expansion. Others are at a more moderate pace and it is important to have an overall view because the Governing Council’s decisions are taken for the euro area as a whole.
As regards the interaction between the dynamism of credit and the dynamism of asset prices in the real estate market in particular
column2: though not only in the real estate market
column3: it is absolutely clear that there is a link. I have already noted here that we could simultaneously see the slowing down of the pace of price increases and the slowing down of the growth of outstanding credit in a number of economies that had observed a great level of buoyancy in the real estate market. It is one of the areas where we also see that what we have been doing over the last year and a half has an impact – a very welcome impact. One of our challenges in this domain is
column4: again
column5: to take decisions at the level of the euro area as a whole in an area where you have great differences from country to country. These differences will probably diminish over time. But at a time when Germany was totally depressed and a small number of economies were totally booming in terms of real estate
column6: the synthesis was a challenging one. We can now see a pick-up in Germany and a slowing down in a number of countries: I remember I could say that in Ireland when we had the outside Governing Council meeting in Dublin and we could say that also for Spain
column7: so we see something like a progressive “rapprochement”.

column1: On the first point let me say that the present responsibilities are very clear in Europe. I would not qualify the responsibilities in the rest of the world
column2: but in Europe they are very clear according to the Treaty. There is nothing new. It is exactly the same kind of concept which has existed in this country
column3: Germany
column4: for 50 years
column5: exactly the same kind of concept which has existed
column6: to my knowledge
column7: in most European countries that are members of the euro area since the independence of the central bank. It is the responsibility which has existed in my own country since January 1994. As regards the cooperation between major global partners
column8: we know how it functions in practice and it has functioned well. The messages of the G7 must be the same on both sides of the Atlantic and on both sides of Pacific to be effective. All those messages are signed by both the executive branches and by the central banks. And it was the case before the euro was set up; it has been the case since the euro was set up – nothing has changed. The only big change since the euro was set up is that in addition to the previous members you have the presence of the President of the Eurogroup and you have the presence of the President of the European Central Bank. But the communiqué is signed by my central bank colleague of the United States
column9: my colleague of the United Kingdom
column10: my colleague of Japan
column11: the colleague of Canada. And the communiqué says “ministers and governors”. I draw your attention to that. What counts in practice is that the message or messages are underwritten by both the different global partners and the different authorities in each major economy: monetary authorities and executive branches. In exceptional circumstances this message can be strong. That is the way the world functions at the moment. This does not mean that we do not have challenges. This does not mean that we do not have a lot of issues. But it is the methodology that we have been applying since we have been in this universe of the floating exchange system since the beginning of the 1970s. And in Europe the arrangement we have is an arrangement anchored in the Treaty
column12: and it is fully in line with the European tradition.

column1: As regards Slovakia
column2: we do not have a position of the Governing Council on Slovakia and I do not want to comment on question marks that one might have
column3: which are fully legitimate. At this stage we do not have a Governing Council position on Slovakia and I strongly encourage Slovakia to embark resolutely on a convergence programme that would be as active and responsible as possible.

column1: 2007-09-06;2;"Ladies and gentlemen
column2: let me welcome you to our press conference and report on the outcome of today’s meeting of the ECB’s Governing Council. The meeting was also attended by the President of the Eurogroup
column3: Prime Minister Juncker
column4: and Commissioner Almunia.

column1: On the basis of our regular economic and monetary analyses
column2: we decided at today’s meeting to leave the key ECB interest rates unchanged. The information that has become available since our previous meeting has confirmed that the medium-term outlook for price stability remains subject to upside risks
column3: as identified by both our economic and monetary analyses. Incoming macroeconomic data also confirm the strong fundamentals of the euro area economy and support a favourable medium-term outlook for real GDP growth. Against this background
column4: our monetary policy stance is still on the accommodative side with
column5: inter alia
column6: money and credit growth vigorous in the euro area. At the same time

column1: Allow me to explain our assessment in greater detail

column4: compared with 0.7% in the previous quarter. However

column6: economic growth during the first half of 2007
column7: as a whole
column8: was in line with potential growth. Data on activity in the third quarter – from various confidence surveys and indicator-based estimates – remain favourable overall and support the assessment that real GDP is growing at sustained rates. In particular
column9: the latest data on unemployment are favourable and the levels of all confidence indicators to August were high. Global economic activity is expected to remain robust
column10: as the likely slowdown in the United States is expected to be largely offset by the continued strong growth in emerging markets. This will continue to provide support to euro area exports and investment. In addition
column11: consumption growth in the euro area should strengthen further over time
column12: in line with developments in real disposable income
column13: as employment conditions improve further. That said

column4: the range projected for real GDP growth in 2007 has been revised slightly downwards
column5: mainly reflecting the assumptions of somewhat higher oil prices and slightly tighter market financing conditions due to higher average risk premia.

column3: there are several indications that increases in short-term interest rates over recent quarters have influenced monetary developments. For example

column2: the continued vigour of underlying monetary and credit expansion points to upside risks to price stability over the medium to longer term. Monetary developments therefore continue to require very careful monitoring.

column2: which was also attended by Commissioner Almunia.

column1: On the basis of our regular economic and monetary analyses
column2: we decided at today’s meeting to leave the key ECB interest rates unchanged. The information that has become available since our previous meeting has confirmed that the outlook for price stability over the medium term is subject to upside risks. Against this background
column3: and with money and credit growth vigorous in the euro area
column4: our monetary policy stands ready to counter upside risks to price stability
column5: as required by our primary objective. The fundamentals of the euro area economy support a favourable medium-term outlook for economic activity. In particular
column6: corporate earnings and profitability have been sustained
column7: employment growth has been robust and unemployment has fallen. However
column8: given the financial market volatility and the reappraisal of risk seen in recent weeks
column9: this assessment is surrounded by heightened uncertainty. In view of the only limited range of new economic data that have become available since our meeting in early September
column10: particular caution needs to be exercised when assessing any potential impact of the financial market developments on the real economy. Hence
column11: it remains necessary to gather additional information and examine new data before drawing further conclusions for monetary policy in the context of our medium-term-oriented monetary policy strategy focused on maintaining price stability. Accordingly
column12: the Governing Council will monitor very closely all developments. On the basis of our assessment
column13: and by acting in a firm and timely manner
column14: we will ensure that risks to price stability over the medium term do not materialise and that medium and long-term inflation expectations remain firmly anchored in line with price stability
column15: thereby favouring an environment conducive to sustained economic growth
column16: well-functioning markets and job creation. Providing such an anchor for medium and long-term inflation expectations is all the more important at times of financial market volatility and increased uncertainty. As regards the financial markets
column17: we will continue to pay great attention to developments over the period to come.

column1: Allow me to explain our assessment in greater detail
column2: starting with the economic analysis. On the basis of the available data
column3: it appears that the sustained real economic growth experienced in the euro area in the first half of 2007 has continued through the summer. This is also reflected in available forecasts for real GDP growth for the third and fourth quarters of 2007. While financial market volatility appears to have contributed to a decline in euro area consumer and business confidence indicators in September
column4: these indicators remain above their historical averages and continue to point to ongoing sustained growth during the second half of 2007.

column1: Looking further ahead
column2: available forecasts for 2008 continue to confirm our main scenario of real GDP growing at around trend potential. This scenario is based on the expectation that global economic activity will remain robust
column3: with the moderation of economic growth in the United States largely offset by the continued strength of emerging market economies. This will provide ongoing support to euro area exports and investment. Consumption growth in the euro area should also contribute to economic growth
column4: in line with developments in real disposable income
column5: as employment conditions remain supportive. That said
column6: in view of the potential impact of increased financial market volatility and the re-pricing of risk on the real economy
column7: the uncertainties surrounding this broadly favourable outlook for economic activity have increased.

column1: On balance
column2: risks to the outlook for growth are judged to lie on the downside. These downside risks relate mainly to the potential for a broader impact from the ongoing reappraisal of risk in financial markets on confidence and financing conditions
column3: concerns about protectionist pressures and possible disorderly developments owing to global imbalances
column4: as well as further oil and commodity price rises.

column1: As regards price developments
column2: according to Eurostat’s flash estimate
column3: the annual HICP inflation rate increased strongly to 2.1% in September 2007
column4: from 1.7% in August. As we have already indicated on previous occasions
column5: we are now entering a period during which unfavourable effects from energy prices will have a strong impact on annual HICP inflation rates. Owing mainly to such effects
column6: as a result of the marked decline in energy prices a year ago combined with the recent substantial increase in oil prices
column7: we expect the inflation rate to remain significantly above 2% in the remaining months of 2007 and in early 2008
column8: before moderating again. Largely as a consequence of capacity constraints and relatively tight labour market conditions
column9: inflation is expected to be around 2% on average in 2008.

column1: Risks to the outlook for price developments remain on the upside. They continue to include the possibility of further increases in the prices of oil and agricultural products as well as additional increases in administered prices and indirect taxes beyond those announced thus far. Taking into account the existence of capacity constraints
column2: the favourable momentum of real GDP growth observed over the past few quarters and the positive signs from labour markets
column3: stronger than currently expected wage developments may occur
column4: and an increase in the pricing power in market segments with low competition could materialise. Such developments would pose upward risks to price stability. It is therefore crucial that all parties concerned meet their responsibilities.

column1: The monetary analysis confirms the prevailing upside risks to price stability at medium to longer-term horizons. A broad assessment of the monetary data supports the view that the underlying rate of money and credit growth remains strong. However
column2: the August annual growth rate of close to 12% in the monetary aggregate M3 as well as the annual growth rate of loans to non-financial corporations
column3: which reached a record level of more than 14% in August
column4: may have been influenced by a number of temporary or special factors
column5: such as the flattening of the yield curve and the recent financial market volatility
column6: and may therefore overstate the underlying rate of money and credit expansion.

column1: A broad assessment of underlying trends in money and credit growth is particularly important during the current period of financial market volatility
column2: as the latter may influence the short-term behaviour of private agents and thereby affect monetary developments. Thus
column3: monetary and credit data can offer an important insight into how financial institutions
column4: households and firms have responded to the financial market volatility. Indeed
column5: previous episodes of heightened financial market uncertainty have been associated with large portfolio shifts into safe and liquid monetary assets. For the time being
column6: however
column7: there is still little evidence in the monetary data for such shifts since the rise in financial market volatility in early August
column8: while it cannot be excluded that the flow of bank loans to the non-financial corporate sector in August partly reflects the re-intermediation of some financing onto bank balance sheets. Further data will be required to develop a more complete view of the impact of the financial market volatility on bank balance sheets
column9: financing conditions and money and credit growth.

column1: Overall
column2: the continued vigour of underlying monetary and credit expansion points to upside risks to price stability over the medium to longer term. Monetary developments therefore continue to require very careful monitoring so as to detect underlying trends on the one hand and to better understand shorter-term dynamics on the other. This will provide a more complete picture of the response of the private sector to the increased volatility in financial markets.

column1: To sum up
column2: a cross-check of the information identified under the economic analysis with the outcome of the monetary analysis has confirmed the existence of upside risks to price stability over the medium term
column3: against the background of good economic fundamentals in the euro area. Accordingly
column4: and with money and credit growth vigorous in the euro area
column5: our monetary policy stands ready to counter upside risks to price stability
column6: as required by our primary objective. At the same time
column7: given the heightened level of uncertainty
column8: additional information is needed before further conclusions for monetary policy can be drawn. Consequently
column9: the Governing Council will monitor very closely all developments. On the basis of our assessment
column10: and by acting in a firm and timely manner
column11: we will ensure that risks to price stability over the medium term do not materialise and that medium and long-term inflation expectations remain firmly anchored in line with price stability
column12: which is all the more important in the current context. As regards the financial markets
column13: we will continue to pay great attention to developments over the period to come.

column1: Turning to fiscal policy
column2: the Governing Council is increasingly concerned about a weakening in structural fiscal consolidation efforts and the delaying of decisive action to address fiscal imbalances. Against this background
column3: all euro area countries concerned are urged to meet the commitments made in the context of the Stability and Growth Pact to structurally improve their fiscal balances. The commitment made in the Eurogroup to reach medium-term budgetary objectives in 2008 or 2009
column4: and by 2010 at the latest
column5: must also be respected by all euro area countries. Those countries that have already achieved sound fiscal positions need to abstain from pro-cyclical fiscal policies. Sound fiscal policies will also make an important contribution to maintaining confidence at a time of heightened uncertainty in financial markets.

column1: With regard to structural reforms
column2: the Governing Council fully supports efforts to enhance competition
column3: increase productivity and foster market flexibility. While the services sector is a particularly important area for reform
column4: further efforts are also needed to improve the functioning of the agricultural markets. Against the background of a marked increase in international food commodity prices
column5: further liberalisation and reforms in the EU agricultural markets would help to enhance their efficiency and benefit European consumers through lower prices. The successful conclusion of the Doha round of world trade negotiations should also help to improve the functioning of global trade in general and of agricultural markets in Europe and worldwide in particular.

column1: Allow me to explain our assessment in greater detail
column2: starting with the economic analysis. On the basis of the available data
column3: it appears that the sustained real economic growth experienced in the euro area in the first half of 2007 has continued through the third quarter
column4: as reflected in the data for industrial production and retail sales that have been released since our meeting in early October. While financial market volatility seems to have contributed to a decline in euro area consumer and business confidence indicators in the past few months

column6: the fundamentals of the euro area remain sound

column8: robust employment growth and falling unemployment to levels not seen for 25 years.

column1: Available forecasts for 2008 continue to confirm our main scenario of real GDP growing at around trend potential. This scenario is based on the expectation that the global economy will remain resilient
column2: with the slowdown of economic growth in the United States partly offset by the sustained strength of emerging market economies. column3: in line with developments in real disposable income
column4: as continued employment growth provides supportive conditions. That said

column6: the level of uncertainty surrounding this broadly favourable outlook for economic activity remains high.

column1: On balance
column2: risks to the outlook for growth are judged to lie on the downside. These downside risks relate mainly to the potential for a broader impact from the ongoing reappraisal of risk in financial markets on confidence and financing conditions
column3: further oil and commodity price rises

column2: according to Eurostat’s flash estimate

column9: in particular

column3: as well as unanticipated increases in administered prices and indirect taxes. Moreover

column5: the favourable momentum of real GDP growth observed over the past few quarters

column9: the explicit or de facto indexation of nominal wages to prices should be reduced and ultimately eliminated.

column1: The monetary analysis confirms the prevailing upside risks to price stability at medium to longer-term horizons. column3: even taking into account these special factors

Monetary developments therefore continue to require very careful monitoring so as to detect underlying trends on the one hand and to better understand shorter-term dynamics on the other. column9: may have been strongly affected.

column2: tentatively suggesting that there is no impairment in credit supply. However

column4: financing conditions and money and credit growth.

column2: the Governing Council welcomes the ECOFIN Council’s agreement to strengthen the preventive arm of the Stability and Growth Pact. column2: the Governing Council stresses that a key effect of well-designed structural reforms is a sustainable improvement in the employment and income situation of workers and households. column1: On the basis of our regular economic and monetary analyses
