column2: while the slowdown in the economies of some of the euro area’s major trading partners is likely to have an impact on euro area real GDP growth in 2008
column3: both domestic and foreign demand are expected to support ongoing growth. This assessment is broadly in line with available forecasts from private and public-sector sources. The euro area economy does not have major imbalances Profitability has been sustained and unemployment rates have fallen to levels not seen for 25 years. As a result of the improved economic conditions and wage moderation

column5: in line with real disposable income

column4: concerns about protectionist pressures and the possibility of disorderly developments due to global imbalances.

column4: we will monitor very closely all developments. The Governing Council remains committed to preventing second-round effects and the materialisation of upside risks to price stability over the medium term. It is paramount that medium and long-term inflation expectations remain firmly anchored in line with price stability. Reflecting its mandate
column5: such anchoring is of the highest priority to the Governing Council.

column1: With respect to fiscal policies
column2: a discretionary fiscal loosening in EU countries should be avoided. There is ample evidence that activist fiscal policies were not effective in stabilising European economies but rather led to sustained increases in the ratios of government expenditure and debt to GDP. Allowing the free operation of automatic stabilisers in countries with strong fiscal positions and safeguarding the long-term sustainability of public finances are the best contributions that fiscal policy can make to macroeconomic stability. Countries with fiscal imbalances are urged to make further progress with consolidation
column3: in line with the requirements of the Stability and Growth Pact. There is a clear risk that some countries will fail to comply with the provisions of the preventive arm of the Pact
column4: thereby undermining its credibility.

column1: Structural reforms help economies to adjust to adverse shocks
column2: foster productivity growth and increase employment and competition
column3: thereby also helping to reduce inflationary pressures. In particular
column4: enhancing competition in the services sectors and network industries
column5: as well as applying adequate measures in the EU agricultural market
column6: would be conducive to price stability in the euro area.

column1: As regards your third question I will not comment on vigilance in the other direction. No comment. You had another question?

column1: On the first question
column2: as you know
column3: we have a very clear concept
column4: which is that we are never pre-committed and we are always alert at any time and always ready to take the decision that would permit price stability to be delivered. column1: As regards your third question as you know
column2: there is a difference between the ECB and a number of other central banks

column4: which is that because we had merged at the origin the concepts of a large number of national central banks

column2: we have rules as regards the ratings of these instruments

column1: I said what I said. And I also said that we were unanimous in considering that keeping rates unchanged today

column3: will allow us to deliver price stability in the medium run. And that is the point because it is our mandate.

column1: As regards monetary policy
column2: I will let you be the judge of what the appropriate qualification is. Again
column3: what we have always done
column4: since the very beginning
column5: has been to take decisions which will allow us to deliver price stability in the medium term in constantly changing circumstances. And as I have said
column6: we are in a multi-dimensional situation which requires all elements to be taken into account. As regards the other questions that you had?

column1: Again
column2: I do not comment on the exchange rate here
column3: as you know. What I would say is that we have no reason to change our perception of growth potential

column6: a clear view on what the present medium-term trend is. I would say
column7: however
column8: that the information and data we have – including those data which are

column10: less flattering than had perhaps been expected – certainly confirm that growth is ongoing. And how does this ongoing growth compare with growth potential? I would say that it is close to potential

column1: On your first question: As I have just said
column2: we are constantly alert and we never pre-commit in the medium term. So I will only say that in the months to come
column3: which will be characterised by a very high level – an unusually high level – of uncertainty
column4: we will continue to do all that is necessary in order to deliver price stability in the medium term and solidly anchor inflation expectations. We will see what happens. A lot of things can happen on all sides. We could have new developments in this ongoing turbulent episode. We could have bad or good surprises coming from the rest of the world. The question of whether or not
column5: and to what extent
column6: the emerging world will offset the slowdown in the US economy is still open. We will have the evolution of the wage negotiations I was talking about
column7: which are important. We will have the evolution of the price-setting that we are observing. And we are in a universe where it would be very naive to claim that you knew in advance everything that could happen. What is certain is that we have an anchor. We have only one needle in our compass
column8: as I have always said
column9: which is that we have to deliver price stability in the medium term. And we measure very carefully by all means – and they are numerous – the anchoring of inflation expectations
column10: which we consider to be absolutely essential not only in order to deliver price stability in the medium run

column14: as I have told you
column15: we considered

column4: fewer instruments and fewer tools available than they would have liked

column9: that institutions are being bailed out. Institutions are regularly making losses

column1: Again
column2: predictability for us lies in the fact that

As regards the question on the private sector

column26: then
column27: of course

column4: and the work of the Financial Stability Forum

column1: As regards our fiscal position
column2: again
column3: I said that for monetary policy we have different economies
column4: different features
column5: structural features of the economy and different shocks that we have to cope with. One important difference between the US and Europe which I have to underline – at least at the level of the single economy
column6: with a single currency
column7: the 320 million people that are making up the euro area – is that we are balanced. We are financing our investment with our savings and we have no domestic or external imbalances. We are balanced. In the US

column11: it means something much more important as a proportion of GDP in our own case than in the United States of America. So
column12: again
column13: when you look at the precise situation on both sides of the Atlantic
column14: you see that you have to take everything into account. We have to take into account the Stability and Growth Pact. It is not just a matter of the Commission
column15: which is the guardian of the Stability and Growth Pact. The Stability and Growth Pact has been decided by the governments themselves. We did not sign the Stability and Growth Pact. It is not the Commission that signed the Stability and Growth Pact. It has been signed by the governments: the unanimous governments of the European Union and
column16: of course
column17: the euro area.

column1: I will say that I have enormously appreciated the fact that the Secretary of the Treasury and Ben Bernanke said that a strong dollar was in the interests of the United States of America.
I never subscribe myself to the theory of decoupling. I always said that we were in a world which was interdependent and that
column2: all things being equal of course
column3: if any component of the world goes up or down it has an influence on all the other components. We are ourselves influencing the rest of the world very much; the European Union is the first commercial entity of the world. The euro area is a very important commercial entity and from that standpoint we are very much at the level of the United States of America
column4: so through the trade channel we have both
column5: I would say
column6: a great influence. I think that those who were speaking of decoupling had in mind that you could have simultaneously in the world for instance a business cycle which would be very much on the downside in the United States and a business cycle which would continue to be on the upside in the emerging world
column7: particularly in emerging Asia.
column8: But that in my opinion doesn’t mean decoupling because it’s clear that
column9: all things being equal
column10: if the US had not gone down quite strongly
column11: then of course the emerging Asia would have gone up even more. It is clear that all elements that we have in mind are confirming that the downside evolution of the real economy in the US is likely even if we have to be totally pragmatic and depending on facts and figurs. And we will see what happens and what we have today is that China
column12: India and the Asian countries continue to have very significant dynamism
column13: and the offsetting of the US slowdown could be partially or more than partially be done by Asia. But at this stage I really think that decoupling is not an appropriate word. We have to take absolutely all elements into account.

column1: As regards your second question on the insurers again
column2: you remember we always considered in this press conference that what we were observing was an ongoing market correction with episodes of turbulence and episodes of high levels of volatility and that it was an ongoing correction across a very large array of different markets. column3: before the start of the turbulences and that I reported to you concerning the fact that we had in a large array of different markets an underpricing of risks
column4: a level of volatility
column5: a level of spreads

column11: also for your information

column10: from that standpoint
column11: remarkably successful. And I want to insist on that

column1: I would say that
column2: on both sides of the Atlantic
column3: again
column4: we are used to observers and remarks and so forth. I trust that we are doing what is necessary. There is a good criteria
column5: which is to see exactly what you do in terms of anchoring medium term inflationary expectations

2008-03-06;2;Ladies and gentlemen
column2: the Vice-President and I are very pleased to welcome you to our press conference. Let me report on the outcome of our meeting
column3: which was also attended by Mr Bajuk
column4: President of the ECOFIN Council
column5: and Commissioner Almunia.

column1: On the basis of our regular economic and monetary analyses
column2: we decided at today’s meeting to leave the key ECB interest rates unchanged. The latest information has confirmed the existence of strong short-term upward pressure on inflation. It has also confirmed the assessment that there are upside risks to price stability over the medium term
column3: in a context of very vigorous money and credit growth. The economic fundamentals of the euro area are sound. Incoming macroeconomic data point to moderating but ongoing real GDP growth. column1: 2008-05-08;2;"Ladies and gentlemen
column2: the Vice-President and I are very pleased to welcome you to today’s press conference here in Athens. I would like to thank Governor Garganas for his kind hospitality and to express our special gratitude to his staff for the excellent organisation of the meeting of the Governing Council.

column1: Let me report on the outcome of our meeting
column2: which was also attended by Commissioner Almunia.

column1: On the basis of our regular economic and monetary analyses
column2: we decided at today’s meeting to leave the key ECB interest rates unchanged. Inflation rates have risen significantly since the autumn
column3: owing mainly to increases in energy and food prices. As we have said on previous occasions
column4: inflation rates are expected to remain high for a rather protracted period of time
column5: before gradually declining again. The latest information confirms our assessment that upside risks to price stability prevail over the medium term
column6: in a context of continuing very vigorous money and credit growth. At the same time
column7: the economic fundamentals of the euro area are sound
column8: and incoming macroeconomic data continue to point to moderate but ongoing real GDP growth. However
column9: the level of uncertainty resulting from the turmoil in financial markets remains unusually high and tensions still persist. Against this background
column10: we emphasise that maintaining price stability in the medium term is our primary objective in accordance with our mandate. The firm anchoring of medium to longer-term inflation expectations is of the highest priority. The Governing Council remains strongly committed to preventing second-round effects and the materialisation of upside risks to price stability over the medium term. We believe that the current monetary policy stance will contribute to achieving our objective. We will continue to monitor very closely all developments over the coming weeks.

column1: Allow me to explain our assessment in greater detail
column2: starting with the economic analysis.

column1: The latest data and survey information on economic activity confirm previous expectations of moderate but ongoing growth in the first half of 2008. In particular
column2: industrial production data for the first months of the year showed resilience
column3: while economic sentiment generally continued to soften. Overall
column4: the euro area economy has sound fundamentals and does not suffer from major imbalances.

column1: In line with available forecasts
column2: both domestic and foreign demand are expected to support ongoing real GDP growth in the euro area in 2008
column3: albeit to a lesser extent than during 2007. While moderating
column4: growth in the world economy is expected to remain resilient
column5: benefiting in particular from strong growth in emerging economies. This should continue to support euro area external demand. Meanwhile
column6: investment growth in the euro area should provide ongoing support to economic activity
column7: as capacity utilisation remains solid and profitability in the non-financial corporate sector has been sustained. At the same time
column8: employment and labour force participation have increased significantly and unemployment rates have fallen to levels not seen for 25 years. This supports real disposable income and thus consumption growth
column9: although purchasing power is being dampened by the impact of higher energy and food prices.

column1: The uncertainty surrounding this outlook for economic growth remains high
column2: and downside risks prevail. In particular
column3: risks relate to the potential for the financial market turbulence to have a more negative impact on the real economy than previously anticipated. Moreover
column4: downside risks stem from the dampening impact on consumption and investment of further unanticipated increases in energy and food prices. Risks also arise from protectionist pressures and the possibility of disorderly developments owing to global imbalances.

column1: With regard to price developments
column2: annual HICP inflation has remained above 3% for the past six months. According to Eurostat’s flash estimate
column3: it was 3.3% in April 2008. This outturn confirms the ongoing strong short-term upward pressure on inflation
column4: resulting largely from sharp increases in energy and food prices at the global level in recent months.

column1: Looking ahead
column2: on the basis of current futures prices for these commodities
column3: the annual HICP inflation rate is likely to remain significantly above 2% in the coming months
column4: moderating only gradually over the course of 2008. Accordingly
column5: we are currently experiencing a rather protracted period of high annual rates of inflation. In order to ensure that current high inflation rates remain temporary
column6: it is imperative that they do not become entrenched in longer-term expectations or lead to broadly based second-round effects in wage and price-setting.

column1: The risks to the outlook for inflation over the medium term remain clearly on the upside. These risks include the possibility of further rises in energy and food prices
column2: as well as of increases in administered prices and indirect taxes beyond those foreseen thus far. Most importantly
column3: there is a risk that price and wage-setting behaviour could add to inflationary pressures. In particular
column4: the pricing power of firms
column5: notably in market segments with low competition
column6: may prove stronger than currently expected. Moreover
column7: higher than expected wage growth may emerge
column8: taking into account high capacity utilisation
column9: tight labour market conditions and the risk of second-round effects owing to the high level of current inflation rates.

column1: Against this background
column2: it is imperative that all the parties concerned
column3: in both the private and the public sector
column4: meet their responsibilities. Wage-setting needs to take into account productivity developments
column5: the still high level of unemployment in many economies
column6: and price competitiveness positions. Moderate labour cost increases are particularly necessary in countries which have lost price competitiveness in recent years. Second-round effects stemming from the impact of higher energy and food prices on price and wage-setting behaviour must be avoided. In this context
column7: the Governing Council is concerned about the existence of schemes in which nominal wages are indexed to consumer prices. Such schemes involve the risk of upward shocks in inflation leading to a wage-price spiral
column8: which would be detrimental to employment and competitiveness in the countries concerned. The Governing Council therefore calls for such schemes to be avoided. The Governing Council is monitoring wage negotiations in the euro area with particular attention. In the view of the Governing Council
column9: continued responsible wage agreements are of key importance in order to preserve price stability in the medium term and thereby the purchasing power of all euro area citizens.

column1: The monetary analysis confirms the prevailing upside risks to price stability at medium to longer-term horizons. Annual M3 growth remained very vigorous at 10.3% in March
column2: supported by the continued strong growth of MFI loans to the private sector. At the same time
column3: annual M1 growth continued to moderate in March
column4: reflecting higher short-term interest rates which encouraged further shifts from overnight into time deposits. While the impact of the flat yield curve and other temporary factors suggest that annual M3 growth currently overstates the underlying pace of monetary expansion
column5: nonetheless
column6: even after taking such effects into account
column7: a broad-based assessment of the latest data confirms that the underlying rate of money and credit growth remains strong.

column1: The growth of household borrowing has moderated over recent months
column2: reflecting the impact of higher short-term interest rates and cooling housing markets in several parts of the euro area. However
column3: the growth of loans to non-financial corporations has remained very robust. While some future moderation can be expected in the light of tightening financing conditions and slower economic growth
column4: bank borrowing by euro area non-financial corporations grew at an annual rate of 15.0% in the year to March 2008
column5: and the flow of loans in recent months has been strong.

column1: For the time being
column2: there is little evidence that the financial market turbulence seen since early August 2007 has strongly influenced the development of broad money and loans. Continued strong loan growth to non-financial corporations suggests that the availability of bank credit to euro area firms has not been significantly impaired by the financial turmoil thus far. Further data and analysis will be required in order to obtain a more complete picture of the impact of the financial market developments on banks’ balance sheets
column3: financing conditions and money and credit growth.

column1: To sum up
column2: a cross-check of the outcome of the economic analysis with that of the monetary analysis clearly confirms the assessment that upside risks to price stability prevail over the medium term
column3: in a context of very vigorous money and credit growth and with no significant signs of supply constraints on bank loans. The economic fundamentals of the euro area are sound
column4: and incoming macroeconomic data continue to point to moderate but ongoing real GDP growth. However
column5: the level of uncertainty resulting from the turmoil in financial markets remains high. Against this background
column6: we emphasise that the firm anchoring of medium to longer-term inflation expectations is of the highest priority to the Governing Council. We believe that the current monetary policy stance will contribute to achieving this objective. The Governing Council remains strongly committed to preventing second-round effects and the materialisation of upside risks to price stability over the medium term. We will continue to monitor very closely all developments over the coming weeks.

column1: Regarding fiscal policies
column2: the latest forecast by the European Commission points to a rise in the euro area general government deficit ratio in 2008
column3: followed by a further small increase in 2009. This deterioration in part reflects a less favourable economic environment and a likely reversal of windfall revenues accrued in past years. However
column4: it also reflects a standstill in fiscal consolidation and new deficit-increasing measures in a number of countries with fiscal imbalances
column5: including some with high deficits. For several countries
column6: the attainment of the country-specific medium-term objectives by 2010 at the latest
column7: which is the commitment made by euro area governments in Berlin in April 2007
column8: is clearly at risk. In these countries

column1: I published my Annual Report on 22 April and so my views are clearly expressed there. Nevertheless
column2: because this report is in Greek and I assume that you did not read it
column3: I will give you an outline of what our views are there and my views in particular. I think the challenge for Greece is to maximize the benefits of participation in a monetary union by making further progress along the path of reforms. It is for Greece particularly important to bring down the relatively high inflation rate in order to improve its competitive position. We have persistently had an inflation rate above that of the euro area average since we adopted the euro. And to achieve this objective it is particularly important to continue on a sustainable and credible path of fiscal consolidation and to improve further fiscal performance by reducing further Greece’s high government debt ratio. And of course
column4: and this is another issue on which my views are well known
column5: in this country at any rate
column6: I believe that public finance in this country should have sufficient room for manoeuvre in order to better cope with expected substantial increases in age-related expenditure
column7: because Greece is faced with one of the worst problems of an ageing population
column8: which will have serious consequences for both healthcare and pension system expenditure. And it is important of course both in the public and private sectors to attain moderate labour cost developments. I have been criticised for that because people believe that we suggest a wage freeze or a cut in wages – we do not. We suggest labour moderation; we suggest that labour cost developments should take into account productivity growth
column9: labour market conditions and developments in competitor countries. This is a standard position of the Governing Council
column10: if I may say so Mr President
column11: and of the Bank of Greece all these years. Attention must also focus on other coming structural constraints on economic growth and job creation. There is an issue of fostering labour force participation and the strengthening of competition in product markets. Product markets are not functioning properly in Greece in many sectors
column12: and this will help keep profit margins consistent with price stability. And an improvement in the functioning of labour markets is also very important
column13: particularly in Greece.

column1: Let me say again that
column2: as far as the Governing Council is concerned
column3: what I said today on behalf of the Governing Council was that it is imperative that all the parties concerned in both the private and public sectors meet their responsibilities. Wage-setting needs to take into account productivity developments

We can make a clear distinction between those economies which recognised that prices had changed – and that had to be recognised and accepted – and those who thought that they could protect their economies from the real transfer: the second had very poor results in comparison with the first. And the second oil shocks tell exactly the same story. The mass unemployment in Europe started with the inappropriate response of several economies to the first and second oil shock. That is something which has been very well documented. But there was a question for Lucas.

column1: I should first say that there have been a number of positive developments over the past few years. Greece has experienced robust economic growth and has made further progress towards fiscal consolidation and structural adjustment. On the negative side
column2: the weak feature of the Greek economy has been the low degree of competitiveness
column3: as measured by a variety of indicators. And the persistence of significant divergences in unit labour cost increases over a number of years has had adverse implications for the inflation increase
column4: as well as for the country’s competitiveness position. The cumulative loss of competitiveness over several years is reflected in the widening of the current account deficit
column5: which has reached very high levels as a percentage of GDP and may not be sustainable. So far

column7: and were this to happen
column8: the adverse effects of the external imbalances on activity and employment would be felt more. So what is important – and what I’m saying is very much in line with what was said earlier on by President Trichet and Governor Garganas – is the pursuit of policies that will strengthen competitiveness
column9: which
column10: as you suggested
column11: first of all involves further structural reforms in order to foster higher productivity growth and strengthen competition in markets. Moderate labour cost increases are also necessary and are particularly important in helping to restore competitiveness over time. A combination of policies in labour and product markets
column12: in order to strengthen competition
column13: foster productivity growth and ensure wage moderation should be pursued so as to increase competitiveness. I think this is the path to take in the years to come.

column1: 2008-06-05;2;"Ladies and gentlemen
column2: the Vice-President and I are very pleased to welcome you to our press conference. This week we celebrated the tenth anniversary of the ECB
column3: marking an important milestone in the development of this institution and of the single monetary policy. On that occasion I expressed my sincere thanks to all those who have helped to build a solid foundation for the euro. Let me also extend these thanks to you who play such an important role in transmitting our decisions and explanations to the financial markets and to the public at large.

column1: We will now report on the outcome of today’s meeting of the Governing Council
column2: which was also attended by the President of the Eurogroup
column3: Prime Minister Juncker.

column1: On the basis of our regular economic and monetary analyses
column2: we decided at today’s meeting to leave the key ECB interest rates unchanged. At the same time
column3: we noted that risks to price stability over the medium term have increased further. Inflation rates have risen significantly since the autumn of last year
column4: owing mainly to strong increases in energy and food prices. HICP inflation is now expected to remain high for a more protracted period than previously thought. Upside risks to price stability over the medium term are also confirmed by the continuing very vigorous money and credit growth and the absence of significant constraints on bank loan supply up to now. At the same time
column5: the economic fundamentals of the euro area are sound. Against this background
column6: we emphasise that maintaining price stability in the medium term is our primary objective in accordance with our mandate. The Governing Council is monitoring very closely all developments. It is in a state of heightened alertness. By acting in a firm and timely manner
column7: we will prevent second-round effects and ensure that risks to price stability over the medium term do not materialise. It is our strong determination to secure a firm anchoring of medium and long-term inflation expectations in line with price stability.

column1: Allow me to explain our assessment in greater detail
column2: starting with the economic analysis.

column1: At a quarter-on-quarter rate of 0.8%
column2: real GDP growth in the first quarter of 2008 was well above expectations. In part
column3: this strength reflected temporary factors
column4: notably the unusually mild winter in many parts of Europe
column5: which appears to have boosted construction activity. However
column6: the high growth rate in the first quarter might be partly offset in the second. It is therefore more appropriate
column7: in order to avoid being misguided by highly volatile quarterly results
column8: to evaluate the first two quarters of 2008 together.

column1: In line with available forecasts
column2: both domestic and foreign demand are expected to support ongoing real GDP growth in the euro area in 2008
column3: albeit to a lesser extent than during 2007. While moderating
column4: growth in the world economy is expected to remain resilient
column5: benefiting in particular from continued robust growth in emerging economies. This should support euro area external demand. The fundamentals of the euro area economy remain sound
column6: and the euro area does not suffer from major imbalances. Against this background
column7: we expect investment growth in the euro area to provide ongoing support to economic activity
column8: as capacity utilisation remains solid and profitability in the non-financial corporate sector has been sustained. Moreover
column9: employment and labour force participation have increased significantly
column10: and unemployment rates have fallen to levels not seen for 25 years. These developments support disposable income
column11: although purchasing power is being dampened by the impact of higher energy and food prices.

column1: This outlook is also reflected in the June 2008 Eurosystem staff macroeconomic projections. The projections foresee average annual real GDP growth in a range between 1.5% and 2.1% in 2008 and between 1.0% and 2.0% in 2009. In comparison with the March ECB staff projections
column2: the current range projected for real GDP growth in 2008 is within the upper part of the range published in March 2008
column3: mainly as a consequence of the better than expected outcome in the first quarter. For 2009
column4: the range has been adjusted downwards
column5: following the increase in commodity prices over recent months. The year-on-year growth rates which I have just mentioned need to be interpreted with particular caution on this occasion. While the annual rates suggest that growth may be weaker in 2009 than in 2008
column6: they mask the fact that on a quarterly basis real GDP growth is projected to reach a trough in 2008
column7: before gradually recovering thereafter. In order not to draw the wrong conclusions about the growth dynamics implied in the staff projections it is important to keep this distinction in mind.

column1: In the Governing Council’s view
column2: the uncertainty surrounding this outlook for economic growth remains high
column3: and downside risks prevail. In particular
column4: risks continue to relate to the potential for the financial market turbulence to have a more negative impact on the real economy than anticipated. Moreover
column5: downside risks stem from the dampening impact on consumption and investment of further unanticipated increases in energy and food prices. Risks also arise from concerns about the emergence of protectionist pressures and the possibility of disorderly developments owing to global imbalances.

column1: With regard to price developments
column2: annual HICP inflation has remained above 3% for the past seven months. According to Eurostat’s flash estimate
column3: it was 3.6% in May 2008. This confirms the more persistent current upward pressures on euro area inflation
column4: resulting largely from sharp increases in energy and food prices at the global level in recent months.

column1: Looking ahead
column2: on the basis of current futures prices for these commodities
column3: the annual HICP inflation rate is likely to remain above 3% for some time to come
column4: before moderating only gradually in 2009. We are thus currently experiencing a protracted period of high annual rates of inflation
column5: which is likely to be more persistent than previously anticipated.

column1: Consistent with this view
column2: the Eurosystem staff projections foresee average annual HICP inflation at between 3.2% and 3.6% in 2008 and between 1.8% and 3.0% in 2009. Compared with the March 2008 ECB staff projections
column3: the ranges projected for inflation in 2008 and 2009 are markedly higher
column4: reflecting mainly higher oil and food prices and increasingly inflationary pressures in the services sector.

column1: In this context
column2: it is important to recall the conditional nature of the Eurosystem staff projections. They are based on a number of assumptions which are of a purely technical nature and unrelated to policy intentions. In particular
column3: the technical assumptions for short-term interest rates are taken from market expectations as at mid-May. Moreover
column4: it should be noted that the projections are based on the assumption that the recent dynamism in oil and non-oil commodity prices will diminish over the projection horizon
column5: in line with futures prices. A further crucial assumption is that there will be no broad-based second-round effects on wages.

column1: In the Governing Council’s view
column2: at the policy-relevant medium-term horizon risks to the outlook for prices remain clearly on the upside and have increased further These risks include notably the possibility of further increases in energy and food prices
column3: as well as of increases in administered prices and indirect taxes beyond those foreseen thus far. It is also a strong concern that price and wage-setting behaviour could add to inflationary pressures. The pricing power of firms
column4: particularly in market segments with low competition
column5: such as parts of the services sector
column6: may prove stronger than currently expected. Moreover
column7: higher than expected wage growth may emerge
column8: taking into account high capacity utilisation
column9: tight labour market conditions and the risk of second-round effects. The Governing Council is monitoring wage negotiations and price-setting behaviour in the euro area with particular attention.

column1: Against this background
column2: it is imperative to secure that medium to longer-term inflation expectations remain firmly anchored in line with price stability. All parties concerned
column3: in both the private and the public sector
column4: must meet their responsibilities. Wage-setting needs to take into account productivity developments
column5: the still high level of unemployment in many economies
column6: and price competitiveness positions. Moderate labour cost increases are particularly necessary in countries which have lost price competitiveness in recent years. Broadly based second-round effects stemming from the impact of higher energy and food prices on price and wage-setting behaviour must be avoided. In this context
column7: the Governing Council is concerned about the existence of schemes in which nominal wages are indexed to consumer prices. Such schemes involve the risk of upward shocks in inflation leading to a wage-price spiral
column8: which would be detrimental to employment and competitiveness in the countries concerned. The Governing Council therefore calls for such schemes to be avoided.

column1: The monetary analysis confirms the prevailing upside risks to price stability at medium to longer-term horizons. Annual M3 growth remained very vigorous in April
column2: supported by the continued strong growth of MFI loans to the private sector. While the impact of the flat yield curve and other temporary factors suggest that annual M3 growth continues to overstate the underlying pace of monetary expansion
column3: nonetheless
column4: even after taking such effects into account
column5: a broad-based assessment of the latest data confirms that the underlying rate of money and credit growth remains strong.

column1: Annual M1 growth has continued to moderate in recent months
column2: reflecting higher short-term interest rates which have encouraged further shifts from overnight into time deposits. The moderation in the growth of household borrowing also reflects the dampening impact of higher short-term interest rates
column3: as well as cooling housing markets in several parts of the euro area. However
column4: the growth of loans to non-financial corporations has remained very robust. While some moderation can be expected in the future in the light of tightening financing conditions and slower economic growth
column5: bank borrowing by euro area non-financial corporations grew at an annual rate of 14.9% in April 2008
column6: and the flow of loans in recent months has been strong.

column1: The monetary analysis has helped to support the necessary medium-term orientation of monetary policy in the face of the ongoing financial turmoil. From this perspective
column2: the monetary analysis points to upside risks to price stability at longer horizons. Moreover
column3: a thorough assessment of the monetary counterparts suggests that
column4: as yet
column5: the availability of bank credit to households and non-financial corporations has not been significantly affected by the turmoil.

column1: To sum up
column2: a cross-check of the outcome of the economic analysis with that of the monetary analysis clearly confirms the assessment that upside risks to price stability prevail over the medium term
column3: in a context of very vigorous money and credit growth and the absence of significant constraints on bank loan supply up to now. In fact
column4: we noted that risks to price stability over the medium term have increased further. The economic fundamentals of the euro area are sound
column5: and incoming macroeconomic data continue to point to moderate but ongoing real GDP growth. Against this background
column6: the Governing Council is monitoring very closely all developments. It is in a state of heightened alertness. By acting in a firm and timely manner
column7: we will prevent second-round effects and ensure that risks to price stability over the medium term do not materialise. Securing a firm anchoring of medium and long-term inflation expectations in line with price stability is of the essence.

column1: Regarding fiscal policy

2008-07-03;2;Ladies and gentlemen

column1: On the basis of our regular economic and monetary analyses
column2: we decided at today’s meeting to increase the key ECB interest rates by 25 basis points. This decision was taken to prevent broadly based second-round effects and to counteract the increasing upside risks to price stability over the medium term. HICP inflation rates have continued to rise significantly since the autumn of last year. They are expected to remain well above the level consistent with price stability for a more protracted period than previously thought. Moreover
column3: continued very vigorous money and credit growth and the absence thus far of significant constraints on bank loan supply in a context of ongoing financial market tensions confirm our assessment of upside risks to price stability over the medium term. At the same time
column4: while the latest data confirm the expected weakening of real GDP growth in mid-2008 after exceptionally strong growth in the first quarter
column5: the economic fundamentals of the euro area are sound. Against this background and in full accordance with our mandate
column6: we emphasise that maintaining price stability in the medium term is our primary objective and that it is our strong determination to keep medium and long-term inflation expectations firmly anchored in line with price stability. This will preserve purchasing power in the medium term and continue to support sustainable growth and employment in the euro area. On the basis of our current assessment
column7: the monetary policy stance following today’s decision will contribute to achieving our objective. We will continue to monitor very closely all developments over the period ahead.

column1: Allow me to explain our assessment in greater detail
column2: starting with the economic analysis. Information that has become available since the June press conference confirms our previous expectation of rather weak real GDP growth in the second quarter of 2008
column3: in part as a technical counter-reaction to the strong quarter-on-quarter increase of 0.8% in the first quarter. As we have stressed previously
column4: the quarterly growth rates for the first half of this year have been subject to strong temporary and compensatory factors
column5: notably weather-related effects on the profile of construction activity. Therefore
column6: in order to assess the underlying momentum of euro area economic activity and to avoid being misguided by highly volatile quarterly outturns
column7: it is necessary to evaluate the first two quarters of 2008 together. Interpreted on this basis
column8: the information available remains broadly in line with our expectation of moderate ongoing growth.

column1: Looking ahead
column2: both domestic and foreign demand are expected to support real GDP growth in the euro area in 2008
column3: albeit to a lesser extent than during 2007. While moderating
column4: growth in the world economy is expected to remain resilient
column5: benefiting in particular from continued robust growth in emerging economies. This should support euro area external demand. As regards domestic developments
column6: the fundamentals of the euro area economy remain sound and the euro area does not suffer from major imbalances. In this context
column7: investment growth in the euro area should continue to support economic activity
column8: as rates of capacity utilisation remain elevated and profitability in the non-financial corporate sector has been sustained. Moreover
column9: employment rates and labour force participation have increased significantly in recent years
column10: and unemployment rates have fallen to levels not seen for 25 years. However
column11: these developments
column12: which support household disposable income and consumption
column13: are unlikely to fully compensate the loss of purchasing power caused by higher energy and food prices.

column1: In the view of the Governing Council
column2: the uncertainty surrounding this outlook for economic activity remains high
column3: owing not least to the very high levels of commodity prices
column4: and downside risks prevail. In particular
column5: risks stem from the dampening impact on consumption and investment of further unanticipated increases in energy and food prices. Moreover
column6: downside risks continue to relate to the potential for the ongoing financial market tensions to affect the real economy more adversely than anticipated. Concerns about the emergence of protectionist pressures and the possibility of disorderly developments owing to global imbalances also imply downside risks to the outlook for economic activity.

column1: With regard to price developments
column2: annual HICP inflation has remained well above the level consistent with price stability since last autumn
column3: reaching 3.7% in May 2008 and – according to Eurostat’s flash estimate – 4.0% in June. This worrying level of inflation rates results largely from sharp increases in energy and food prices at the global level in recent months.

column1: Looking ahead
column2: on the basis of current futures prices for these commodities
column3: the annual HICP inflation rate is likely to remain well above 2% for quite some time
column4: moderating only gradually in 2009. We are thus currently experiencing a protracted period of high annual rates of inflation
column5: which is likely to be more persistent than anticipated some months ago.

column1: Risks to price stability at the policy-relevant medium-term horizon remain clearly on the upside and have increased further over the past few months. These risks include notably the possibility of further increases in energy and food prices. There is also a very strong concern that price and wage-setting behaviour could add to inflationary pressures via broadly based second-round effects. The Governing Council is monitoring price-setting behaviour and wage negotiations in the euro area with particular attention. Furthermore
column2: there are potential upside risks from unanticipated rises in indirect taxes and administered prices.

column1: Against this background
column2: it is imperative to ensure that medium to longer-term inflation expectations remain firmly anchored at levels in line with price stability. The shift in relative prices and the related transfer of income from commodity-importing countries to commodity-exporting countries have to be accepted. They require a change in the behaviour of companies and households. Therefore
column3: broadly based second-round effects stemming from the impact of higher energy and food prices on price and wage-setting behaviour must be avoided. All parties concerned
column4: in both the private and the public sector
column5: must meet their responsibilities in this regard. In this context
column6: the Governing Council is concerned about the existence of schemes in which nominal wages are indexed to consumer prices. Such schemes involve the risk of upward shocks in inflation leading to a wage-price spiral
column7: which would be detrimental to employment and competitiveness in the countries concerned. The Governing Council therefore calls for such schemes to be avoided.

column1: The monetary analysis confirms the prevailing upside risks to price stability at medium to longer-term horizons. In line with our monetary policy strategy
column2: we take the view that the sustained underlying strength of monetary and credit expansion in the euro area over the past few years has created upside risks to price stability. Over recent quarters
column3: these risks appear to have become manifest as inflation has trended upwards. Against this background
column4: the continued strength of monetary dynamics represents an important signal of the risks to price stability over the medium term that we have been addressing through our actions since end-2005
column5: including today’s move.

column1: More specifically
column2: annual M3 growth has remained very vigorous in recent months
column3: supported by the continued strong growth of MFI loans to the private sector. Although annual M3 growth of still above 10% overstates the underlying pace of monetary expansion
column4: owing to the impact of the flat yield curve and other temporary factors
column5: nonetheless
column6: even after taking such effects into account
column7: a broad-based assessment of the latest data confirms that the underlying rate of money and credit growth remains strong.

column1: The current structure of yields has triggered substitution both within and into the broad monetary aggregate M3
column2: leading to a pronounced decline in annual M1 growth and very rapid increases in time deposits. At the same time
column3: higher short-term interest rates have served to moderate the growth of household borrowing
column4: although cooling housing markets in several parts of the euro area have also played a substantial role in this regard. However
column5: the growth of bank loans to non-financial corporations has remained very robust despite the rises in short-term rates. While some moderation can be expected in the future in the light of tightening financing conditions and more moderate economic growth
column6: bank borrowing by euro area non-financial corporations grew at an annual rate of 14.2% in May 2008
column7: and the flow of loans in recent months has been strong.

column1: Not least in the face of the ongoing tensions in financial markets
column2: the monetary analysis helps to support the necessary medium-term orientation of monetary policy by focusing attention on the upside risks to price stability prevailing at medium to longer horizons. Moreover
column3: a thorough assessment of the money and credit data has provided an important insight into bank behaviour and financing conditions. In particular
column4: the strength
column5: maturity and sectoral composition of bank borrowing suggest that
column6: at the level of the euro area as a whole
column7: the availability of bank credit has
column8: as yet
column9: not been significantly affected by the tensions.

column1: To sum up
column2: a cross-check of the outcome of the economic analysis with that of the monetary analysis clearly confirms the assessment of increasing upside risks to price stability over the medium term
column3: in a context of very vigorous money and credit growth and the absence thus far of significant constraints on bank loan supply. At the same time
column4: the economic fundamentals of the euro area are sound
column5: and incoming macroeconomic data continue to point to moderate ongoing real GDP growth when the high volatility of growth rates in the first half of this year is taken properly into account. Against this background and in full accordance with our mandate
column6: it is imperative that we prevent broadly based second-round effects and counteract the increasing risks to price stability. We emphasise that maintaining price stability in the medium term is our primary objective and that it is our strong determination to keep medium and long-term inflation expectations firmly anchored in line with price stability
column7: thereby preserving purchasing power in the medium term and supporting sustainable growth and employment in the euro area. On the basis of our current assessment
column8: the monetary policy stance following today’s decision will contribute to achieving our objective. We will continue to monitor very closely all developments over the period ahead.

column1: Regarding fiscal policy
column2: budgetary consolidation targets are at risk in a number of euro area countries. Moreover
column3: the risk of countries’ budget deficits coming close to or even exceeding the 3% of GDP reference value has increased. The Governing Council therefore reiterates its strong support for a rigorous implementation of euro area governments’ 2008 budgets and a prudent design of fiscal policy plans for 2009
column4: in line with the agreement in the Eurogroup in May 2008. Achieving and maintaining sound structural fiscal positions is essential to ensure the sustainability of public finances as well as to create scope for the free working of automatic stabilisers in all euro area countries and thereby contribute to the smoothing of cyclical fluctuations.

column1: As regards structural reforms
column2: we reiterate our full support for all efforts to enhance competition
column3: increase productivity and foster market flexibility. In view of the marked increase in international food commodity prices
column4: removing impediments to competition at the various stages of the food supply chain in the retail and distribution sectors would benefit European consumers through lower prices. As regards labour markets
column5: let me direct your attention to the ECB’s 2008 Structural Issues Report
column6: which was recently submitted to the European Parliament. It emphasises the generally favourable labour market developments in the euro area over the last decade but equally points out the urgent need to counter the ageing-related reduction in the labour force
column7: in particular by increasing employment in all groups of society
column8: by making labour markets more flexible and by enhancing investment in education and training.

2008-08-07;2;Ladies and gentlemen
column2: the Vice-President and I are very pleased to welcome you to our press conference. We will now report on the outcome of today’s meeting of the Governing Council.

column1: On the basis of our regular economic and monetary analyses
column2: we decided at today’s meeting to leave the key ECB interest rates unchanged. The information that has become available since our previous meeting has further underpinned the reasoning behind our decision to increase interest rates in July. It has confirmed that annual inflation rates are likely to remain well above levels consistent with price stability for a protracted period of time and that risks to price stability over the medium term remain on the upside. This assessment is underpinned by continued vigorous money growth
column3: with so far no signs of significant constraints on bank loan supply. In such a context
column4: it remains crucial to avoid broadly based second-round effects in wage and price-setting. The latest economic data point to a weakening of real GDP growth in mid-2008
column5: which in part was expected after the exceptionally strong growth in the first quarter. Against this background and in full accordance with our mandate
column6: we emphasise that maintaining price stability in the medium term is our primary objective and that it is our strong determination to keep medium and long-term inflation expectations firmly anchored in line with price stability. This will preserve purchasing power in the medium term and support sustainable growth and employment. On the basis of our assessment
column7: the current monetary policy stance will contribute to achieving our objective. We will continue to monitor very closely all developments over the period ahead.

column1: Allow me to explain our assessment in greater detail
column2: starting with the economic analysis.

column1: The information on economic activity that has become available since the July press conference suggests that real GDP growth figures for mid-2008 will be substantially weaker than for the first quarter of the year. As indicated on previous occasions
column2: this represents partly a technical reaction to the strong growth seen in the first months of the year. In addition
column3: it also partly reflects a weakening in GDP growth due to factors such as slower expansion at the global level and dampening effects from high and volatile oil and food prices. In order to assess the underlying momentum of euro area economic activity and to avoid being misguided by highly volatile quarterly outturns
column4: it is necessary to look through the volatility in quarter-on-quarter growth rates and monthly indicators.

column1: Taking this perspective
column2: growth in the world economy
column3: while moderating
column4: is expected to remain relatively resilient
column5: benefiting in particular from sustained growth in emerging economies. This should support external demand for euro area goods and services. As regards domestic developments
column6: in a medium-term perspective the fundamentals of the euro area are sound and the euro area does not suffer from major imbalances. Investment growth in the euro area has provided ongoing
column7: though moderating
column8: support to economic activity. Moreover
column9: employment and labour force participation have increased significantly
column10: and unemployment rates remain low in historical terms. However
column11: these developments
column12: which support household disposable income and consumption
column13: are unlikely to fully compensate the loss of purchasing power caused by higher energy and food prices.

column1: In the view of the Governing Council
column2: the uncertainty surrounding this outlook for economic activity remains high
column3: owing to
column4: among other things
column5: the very high and volatile levels of commodity prices and the ongoing tensions in financial markets. Overall
column6: downside risks prevail. In particular
column7: risks stem from the dampening impact on consumption and investment of further unanticipated increases in energy and food prices. Moreover
column8: downside risks continue to relate to the potential for the financial market tensions to affect the real economy more adversely than currently anticipated. The possibility of disorderly developments owing to global imbalances also implies downside risks to the outlook for economic activity
column9: as do concerns about the emergence of protectionist pressures. In this respect
column10: the failure of the recent negotiations in the context of the World Trade Organization’s Doha round on trade liberalisation is a major setback.

column1: With regard to price developments
column2: annual HICP inflation has remained considerably above the level consistent with price stability since last autumn
column3: reaching 4.0% in June 2008 and
column4: according to Eurostat’s flash estimate
column5: 4.1% in July. This worrying level of inflation rates results largely from both direct and indirect effects of past sharp increases in energy and food prices at the global level. At the same time
column6: while labour productivity growth has decelerated
column7: there are some indications that labour cost growth has been rising in recent quarters.

column1: Looking ahead
column2: on the basis of current futures prices for commodities
column3: the annual HICP inflation rate is likely to remain well above a level consistent with price stability for quite some time
column4: moderating only gradually in 2009.

column1: Risks to price stability at the policy-relevant medium-term horizon remain clearly on the upside and have increased over the past few months. These risks include notably the possibility of further increases in energy and food prices and of increasing indirect effects on consumer prices. There is a very strong concern that price and wage-setting behaviour could add to inflationary pressures via broadly based second-round effects. The Governing Council is monitoring price-setting behaviour and wage negotiations in the euro area with particular attention. Furthermore
column2: there are potential upside risks from unanticipated rises in indirect taxes and administered prices.

column1: Against this background
column2: it is imperative to ensure that medium to longer-term inflation expectations remain firmly anchored at levels in line with price stability. The shift in relative prices and the related transfer of income from commodity-importing countries to commodity-exporting countries require a change in the behaviour of companies and households. Therefore
column3: broadly based second-round effects stemming from the impact of higher energy and food prices on price and wage-setting behaviour must be avoided. All parties concerned
column4: in both the private and the public sector
column5: must meet their responsibilities in this regard. In this context
column6: the Governing Council has repeatedly expressed its concern about the existence of schemes in which nominal wages are indexed to consumer prices. Such schemes involve the risk of upward shocks in inflation leading to a wage-price spiral
column7: which would be detrimental to employment and competitiveness in the countries concerned. The Governing Council therefore calls for such schemes to be avoided.

column1: The monetary analysis confirms the prevailing upside risks to price stability at medium to longer-term horizons. In line with our monetary policy strategy
column2: we take the view that the sustained underlying strength of monetary and credit expansion in the euro area over the past few years has created upside risks to price stability. Over recent quarters
column3: these risks appear to have become manifest as inflation has trended upwards.

column1: Not least in the face of the ongoing tensions in financial markets
column2: the monetary analysis helps to support the necessary medium-term orientation of monetary policy by focusing attention on the upside risks to price stability prevailing at medium to longer horizons. While the growth of broad money and credit aggregates is now showing some signs of moderation
column3: also reflecting the policy measures taken since 2005 to address upside risks to price stability
column4: the strong underlying pace of monetary expansion points to continued risks to price stability over the medium term.

column1: The current yield curve has led to very rapid increases in time deposits and to a substantial decline in annual M1 growth. Such effects and other temporary factors must be taken into account in assessing monetary developments. Overall
column2: a broad-based analysis of the data
column3: taking the appropriate medium-term perspective
column4: confirms the underlying strength of money growth.

column1: One of the main factors leading to this conclusion is the still high growth of MFI loans to the private sector
column2: which is underpinning the robust nature of monetary growth. The pace
column3: maturity and sectoral composition of bank borrowing suggest that
column4: at the level of the euro area as a whole
column5: the availability of bank credit has
column6: as yet
column7: not been significantly affected by the ongoing financial tensions. Higher short-term interest rates and housing market weakness in several parts of the euro area have dampened the growth of household borrowing over the past few years. By contrast
column8: and notwithstanding tighter financing conditions and moderating economic growth
column9: the expansion of bank credit to non-financial corporations thus far remains very robust.

column1: To sum up
column2: a cross-check of the outcome of the economic analysis with that of the monetary analysis clearly confirms the assessment of increasing upside risks to price stability over the medium term. Annual inflation rates are likely to remain well above levels consistent with price stability
column3: and monetary aggregates continue to grow vigorously
column4: with so far no signs of significant constraints on bank loan supply. The latest economic data point to a weakening of real GDP growth in mid-2008
column5: which in part was expected after the exceptionally strong growth in the first quarter. Against this background
column6: it remains crucial to avoid broadly based second-round effects in wage and price-setting. In full accordance with our mandate
column7: we emphasise that maintaining price stability in the medium term is our primary objective and that it is our strong determination to keep medium and long-term inflation expectations firmly anchored in line with price stability
column8: thereby preserving purchasing power in the medium term and supporting sustainable growth and employment in the euro area. On the basis of our assessment
column9: the current monetary policy stance will contribute to achieving our objective. We will continue to monitor very closely all developments over the period ahead.

column2: there are risks that some countries will not achieve their fiscal targets this year. In this situation a rigorous implementation of budget plans and the avoidance of expenditure slippage are of crucial importance. Budget plans for 2009
column3: which are currently being finalised in a number of countries

column2: measures which reduce adjustment costs and promote moderate unit labour cost growth are of the utmost importance
column3: particularly in the current climate of high inflation and slowing real GDP growth. These include the removal of impediments to competition in the services sector in general

column6: more specifically. Equally

2008-09-04;2;Ladies and gentlemen
column2: the Vice-President and I are very pleased to welcome you to our press conference. We will now report on the outcome of today’s meeting of the Governing Council
column3: which was also attended by Commissioner Almunia.

column1: On the basis of our regular economic and monetary analyses
column2: at today’s meeting we decided to leave the key ECB interest rates unchanged. The information that has become available since the last meeting has confirmed that annual inflation rates are likely to remain well above levels consistent with price stability for a protracted period of time and that upside risks to price stability over the medium term prevail. While the growth of broad money and credit aggregates is now showing some signs of moderation
column3: the still strong underlying pace of monetary expansion points to continued upside risks to price stability over the medium term. The latest economic data also confirm the weakening of real GDP growth in mid-2008. This reflects partly an expected technical reaction to the strong growth seen in the first quarter as well as dampening effects from global and domestic factors
column4: including direct and indirect effects from high commodity prices. In this environment
column5: it remains imperative to avoid broad-based second-round effects in price and wage-setting. In full accordance with our mandate
column6: we emphasise that maintaining price stability in the medium term is our primary objective and that we are resolute in our determination to keep medium and long-term inflation expectations firmly anchored in line with price stability. This will preserve purchasing power in the medium term and support sustainable growth and employment. On the basis of our assessment
column7: the current monetary policy stance will contribute to achieving our objective. We will continue to monitor very closely all developments over the period ahead.

column1: Allow me to explain our assessment in greater detail
column2: starting with the economic analysis.

column1: According to Eurostat’s first estimate
column2: following strong quarterly growth of 0.7% in the first quarter
column3: euro area real GDP contracted by 0.2% in the second quarter of 2008. In terms of quarter-on-quarter growth
column4: private consumption declined by 0.2% and there was a perceptible weakness in investment
column5: which fell by 1.2%. Growth in both euro area imports and exports declined by 0.4%.

column1: Taking into account all available information
column2: the euro area economy is currently experiencing an episode of weak activity characterised by high commodity prices weighing on consumer confidence and demand
column3: as well as by dampened investment growth. We expect this episode to be followed by a gradual recovery. In particular
column4: if persistent
column5: the fall in oil prices from their peak in July will help strengthen real disposable income
column6: with the level of employment remaining high and the unemployment rate low by historical standards. Moreover
column7: growth in the world economy is expected to remain relatively resilient
column8: benefiting mainly from sustained growth in emerging economies. This should support external demand for euro area goods and services and thereby investment.

column1: This outlook is also reflected in the September 2008 ECB staff macroeconomic projections for the euro area. The exercise projects average annual real GDP growth in a range between 1.1% and 1.7% in 2008
column2: and between 0.6% and 1.8% in 2009. In comparison with the June Eurosystem staff projections
column3: real GDP growth figures for 2008 and 2009 are lower.

column1: In the view of the Governing Council
column2: the uncertainty surrounding this outlook for economic activity is particularly high at the current juncture and
column3: generally
column4: downside risks prevail. Risks stem particularly from renewed increases in energy and food prices
column5: which could dampen consumption and investment. Moreover
column6: downside risks continue to relate to the potential for the financial market tensions to affect the real economy more adversely than currently foreseen. The possibility of disorderly developments owing to global imbalances also implies downside risks to the outlook for economic activity
column7: as do concerns about rising protectionist pressures.

column1: With regard to price developments
column2: annual HICP inflation has remained considerably above the level consistent with price stability since last autumn
column3: standing at 3.8% in August according to Eurostat’s flash estimate
column4: after 4.0% in June and July 2008. This worrying level of inflation is largely the result of both the direct and indirect effects of past surges in energy and food prices at the global level. Moreover
column5: wage growth has been picking up in recent quarters
column6: at a time when labour productivity growth has decelerated
column7: resulting in sharp increases in unit labour costs.

column1: Looking ahead
column2: on the basis of current commodity futures prices
column3: the annual HICP inflation rate is likely to remain well above levels consistent with price stability for quite some time
column4: moderating only gradually during the course of 2009. Consistent with this view
column5: the September ECB staff projections foresee average annual HICP inflation at between 3.4% and 3.6% in 2008
column6: and between 2.3% and 2.9% in 2009. The higher inflation projections for 2008 and 2009 mainly reflect higher energy prices and
column7: to a lesser extent
column8: higher food and services prices than assumed previously.

column1: In this context
column2: it is important to recall the conditional nature of the ECB staff projections. They are based on a number of assumptions that are of a purely technical nature and unrelated to policy intentions. In particular
column3: the technical assumptions for short-term interest rates reflect market expectations as at mid-August. Moreover
column4: it should be noted that the projections are based on the assumption that oil and non-oil commodity prices
column5: while remaining at elevated levels
column6: will exhibit greater stability over the projection horizon than has been the case in recent months
column7: in line with prevailing futures prices.

column1: It is the Governing Council’s view that
column2: at the policy-relevant medium-term horizon
column3: there are upside risks to the outlook for price developments. These risks include the possibility of renewed increases in commodity prices and of previous rises having further and stronger indirect effects on consumer prices. There is particularly a very strong concern that the emergence of broad-based second-round effects in price and wage-setting behaviour could add significantly to inflationary pressures. Moreover
column4: the upside risks to price stability could be aggravated by unexpected rises in indirect taxes and administered prices.

column1: Against this background
column2: it is imperative to ensure that medium to longer-term inflation expectations remain firmly anchored at levels in line with price stability. Broad-based second-round effects stemming from the impact of higher energy and food prices on price and wage?setting behaviour must be avoided. The Governing Council is monitoring price-setting behaviour and wage negotiations in the euro area with particular attention. All parties concerned – in both the private and the public sectors – must meet their responsibilities in this regard. The Governing Council has repeatedly expressed its concern about the existence of schemes in which nominal wages are indexed to consumer prices. Such schemes involve the risk of upward shocks in inflation leading to a wage-price spiral
column3: which would be detrimental to employment and competitiveness in the countries concerned. The Governing Council calls for these schemes to be abolished.

column1: The monetary analysis confirms the prevailing upside risks to price stability at medium to longer-term horizons. In line with our monetary policy strategy
column2: we take the view that the sustained underlying strength of monetary and credit expansion in the euro area over the past few years has created upside risks to price stability. Over recent quarters
column3: these risks appear to have become manifest as inflation has trended upwards.

column1: Not least in the face of the ongoing tensions in financial markets
column2: the monetary analysis helps to support the necessary medium-term orientation of monetary policy by focusing attention on the upside risks to price stability prevailing at medium to longer horizons. While the growth of broad money and credit aggregates is now showing some signs of moderation
column3: reflecting the policy measures taken since 2005 to address risks to price stability
column4: the strong underlying pace of monetary expansion points to continued upside risks to price stability over the medium term.

column1: The currently flat yield curve has given rise to a substitution from longer maturity assets into monetary instruments
column2: which offer similar remuneration but greater liquidity and less risk. This substitution has led the current headline rate of M3 growth to overstate the underlying pace of monetary expansion. At the same time
column3: shifts out of overnight deposits drove the annual growth rate of M1 down further in July. These effects
column4: as well as other temporary factors
column5: must be taken into account when assessing monetary developments and their implications. A broad-based analysis of the data
column6: taking the appropriate medium-term perspective and allowing for these considerations
column7: confirms the underlying strength of money growth.

column1: In particular
column2: the pace
column3: maturity and sectoral composition of borrowing from banks suggest that
column4: at the level of the euro area as a whole
column5: the availability of bank credit has
column6: as yet
column7: not been significantly affected by the ongoing financial tensions. This notwithstanding
column8: growth in loans now shows signs of moderation
column9: as previously anticipated
column10: with corporate demand for credit slowing. At the same time
column11: the growth of loans to households continues to follow the downward trend observed over the past few years
column12: as a result of higher short-term interest rates and housing market weakness in several parts of the euro area.

column1: To sum up
column2: a cross-check of the outcome of the economic analysis with that of the monetary analysis clearly confirms the assessment of upside risks to price stability over the medium term. The information that has become available since the last meeting of the Governing Council has confirmed that annual inflation rates are likely to remain well above levels consistent with price stability for a protracted period of time. The growth of broad money and credit aggregates is now showing some signs of moderation
column3: but the still strong underlying pace of monetary expansion points to continued risks to price stability over the medium term. The latest economic data also confirm the weakening of real GDP growth in mid-2008. This reflects partly an expected technical reaction to the strong growth seen in the first quarter as well as dampening effects from global and domestic factors
column4: including direct and indirect effects from high commodity prices. Against this background
column5: it remains imperative to avoid broad-based second-round effects in wage and price-setting. In full accordance with our mandate
column6: we emphasise that maintaining price stability in the medium term is our primary objective and that we are resolute in our determination to keep medium and long-term inflation expectations firmly anchored in line with price stability
column7: thereby preserving purchasing power in the medium term and supporting sustainable growth and employment in the euro area. On the basis of our assessment
column8: the current monetary policy stance will contribute to achieving our objective. We will continue to monitor very closely all developments over the period ahead.

column1: Regarding fiscal policy
column2: budget plans for 2009 should fully reflect existing policy commitments. This implies that euro area countries with relatively large fiscal deficits need to specify much more ambitious and concrete consolidation measures
column3: especially on the expenditure side. Countries that have already achieved their medium-term budgetary objectives need to ensure that they maintain sound structural fiscal positions. At the current juncture
column4: the steady pursuit of stability-oriented fiscal policies would help to contain inflationary pressures and provide the required budgetary room for manoeuvre to allow automatic stabilisers to contribute to smoothing the business cycle.

column1: Turning to structural policies
column2: measures that reduce adjustment costs and promote moderate unit labour cost growth are of the utmost importance in the current economic circumstances. While this is crucial in all euro area countries
column3: it is particularly pressing in those that have experienced a significant loss of cost and price competitiveness over recent years and where unemployment has already started to rise. Moreover
column4: fostering productivity through enhanced investment in innovation and education enlarges the scope for increases in real incomes in the longer run.

column1: As regards ABSs
column2: we have decided to apply to asset-backed securities a uniform haircut of 12% for all residual maturities and all coupon types. So 12% across the board. I have to mention that we are not
