column1: 2008-10-02;2;"Ladies and gentlemen
column2: the Vice-President and I are very pleased to welcome you to our press conference. We will now report on the outcome of today’s meeting of the Governing Council
column3: which was also attended by Commissioner Almunia.

column1: On the basis of its regular economic and monetary analyses
column2: at today’s meeting the Governing Council decided to leave the key ECB interest rates unchanged. We discussed extensively the recent intensification of the financial market turmoil and its possible impact on economic activity and inflation
column3: recognising the extraordinarily high level of uncertainty stemming from latest developments. In this context
column4: we stressed the crucial importance of keeping inflation expectations firmly anchored in line with our objective. Price stability fosters an efficient allocation of resources
column5: contains inflation risk premia and longer-term financing costs
column6: and preserves the purchasing power of our currency. In so doing
column7: it supports sustainable growth and employment and contributes to financial stability. The most recent data clearly confirm that economic activity in the euro area is weakening
column8: with contracting domestic demand and tighter financing conditions. At the same time
column9: annual inflation rates are likely to remain well above levels consistent with price stability for some time. With the weakening of demand
column10: upside risks to price stability have diminished somewhat
column11: but they have not disappeared. While the still strong underlying pace of monetary expansion points to upside risks to price stability over the medium term
column12: the growth of broad money and credit aggregates is showing some further signs of moderation. It is imperative to avoid broad-based second-round effects in price and wage-setting. All parties concerned face exceptional challenges and are called upon to meet their responsibilities Accordingly
column13: we confirm that we remain determined to secure price stability in the medium term and will continue to monitor very closely all developments over the period ahead.

column1: Allow me to explain our assessment in greater detail
column2: starting with the economic analysis.

column1: When analysing current developments in economic activity
column2: it needs to be stressed that we face an extraordinarily high degree of uncertainty
column3: in large part stemming from the recent intensification of the financial market turmoil. This complicates any assessment of the near to medium-term economic prospects. As the world economy as a whole is feeling the adverse effects of the intensified and prolonged financial market turmoil
column4: the most recent data clearly confirm that economic activity in the euro area is weakening
column5: with contracting domestic demand and tighter financing conditions. The fall in oil prices from their peak in July and ongoing growth in emerging market economies might support a gradual recovery in the course of 2009.

column1: In the view of the Governing Council
column2: the economic outlook is subject to increased downside risks
column3: mainly stemming from a scenario of ongoing financial market tensions affecting the real economy more adversely than currently foreseen. Other downside risks relate to the possibility of renewed increases in highly volatile energy and food prices
column4: disorderly developments owing to global imbalances and rising protectionist pressures.

column1: With regard to price developments
column2: annual HICP inflation has remained considerably above the level consistent with price stability since last autumn
column3: standing at 3.6% in September according to Eurostat’s flash estimate
column4: after 3.8% in August. This still worrying level of inflation is largely the consequence of both the direct and indirect effects of past surges in energy and food prices at the global level. Moreover
column5: wage growth has been picking up rather strongly in recent quarters
column6: in spite of a weaker growth momentum and at a time when labour productivity growth has decelerated. This resulted in a sharp increase in the year-on-year unit labour cost – to 3.4% – in the second quarter of this year
column7: after several years of more moderate increases in the order of 1-1½%.

column1: Looking ahead
column2: on the basis of current commodity futures prices
column3: annual HICP inflation rates are likely to remain well above levels consistent with price stability for some time
column4: moderating gradually during the course of 2009. At the policy-relevant medium-term horizon
column5: taking into account the weakening in demand
column6: upside risks to price stability have diminished somewhat
column7: but they have not disappeared. They include the possibility of previous commodity price rises having further and stronger indirect effects on consumer prices
column8: as well as a renewed increase in commodity prices. In particular
column9: there is a very strong concern that the emergence of broad-based second-round effects in price and wage-setting behaviour could add significantly to inflationary pressures. Moreover
column10: unexpected rises in indirect taxes and administered prices could occur.

column1: Against this background
column2: it is imperative to ensure that medium to longer-term inflation expectations remain firmly anchored at levels in line with price stability. This is all the more the case in an environment of very high uncertainty. Broad-based second-round effects stemming from the impact of past energy and food price increases on price and wage-setting behaviour must be avoided. The Governing Council is monitoring price-setting behaviour and wage negotiations in the euro area with particular attention. We have repeatedly expressed our concern about the existence of schemes in which nominal wages are indexed to consumer prices. Such schemes involve the risk of upward shocks in inflation leading to a wage-price spiral
column3: which would be detrimental to employment and competitiveness in the countries concerned. The Governing Council calls for these schemes to be abolished.

column1: Turning to the monetary analysis
column2: we need to recognise that the latest monetary data refer to the end of August and thus do not yet embody the impact of the recent intensification of the financial market turmoil. Further data on this impact will be carefully evaluated. As a general observation
column3: previous episodes suggest that financial market tensions can have a relatively limited impact on monetary developments
column4: but they have also been associated with large portfolio shifts and thus have exerted significant influence on monetary data.

column1: While the still strong underlying pace of monetary expansion points to upside risks to price stability over the medium term
column2: data up to August show that the growth of broad money and credit aggregates moderated over the past few months
column3: reflecting the monetary policy decisions taken since 2005 to address risks to price stability. As a more detailed examination shows
column4: the flat yield curve and the structure of bank deposit rates have led to a number of substitution effects. First
column5: there has been a substitution from longer-term maturity assets into instruments covered by M3
column6: which offer similar remuneration but greater liquidity and less risk. As a consequence
column7: the annual growth rate of M3 probably overstates the underlying pace of monetary expansion. Second
column8: there have been substitution effects within M3. In contrast to the dynamic developments in M3
column9: annual M1 growth has fallen to very low levels. This reflects relatively attractive interest rates for time deposits
column10: which have increased the opportunity cost of holding cash or overnight deposits.

column1: Although
column2: at the level of the euro area as a whole
column3: the availability of bank credit has
column4: as yet
column5: not been significantly affected by the ongoing financial tensions
column6: the gradual moderation of growth in loans continued in the August data
column7: as previously anticipated
column8: with corporate demand for credit slowing. At the same time
column9: the growth of loans to households continues to follow the downward trend observed over the past few years
column10: as a result of higher short-term interest rates and housing market weakness in several parts of the euro area.

column1: To sum up
column2: we discussed extensively the recent intensification of the financial market turmoil and its possible impact on economic activity and inflation
column3: recognising the extraordinarily high level of uncertainty stemming from latest developments. In this context
column4: we stressed how crucial it is for monetary policy to keep inflation expectations firmly anchored in line with our objective. Price stability fosters an efficient allocation of resources
column5: contains inflation risk premia and longer-term financing costs
column6: and preserves the purchasing power of our currency. In so doing
column7: it supports sustainable growth and employment and contributes to financial stability. The most recent data clearly confirm that economic activity in the euro area is weakening
column8: with contracting domestic demand and tighter financing conditions. The cross-check of the outcome of the economic analysis with that of the monetary analysis clearly confirms that annual inflation rates are likely to remain well above levels consistent with price stability for some time and
column9: when taking into account the weakening of demand
column10: that upside risks to price stability have diminished somewhat
column11: but they have not disappeared. While the still strong underlying pace of monetary expansion points to upside risks to price stability over the medium term
column12: the growth of broad money and credit aggregates is showing some further signs of moderation. It is imperative to avoid broad-based second-round effects in price and wage-setting. All parties concerned face exceptional challenges and are called upon to meet their responsibilities Accordingly
column13: we confirm that we remain determined to secure price stability in the medium term and will continue to monitor very closely all developments over the period ahead.

column1: Regarding fiscal policy
column2: in the current situation of continuing economic uncertainty
column3: it is essential that governments abide by the rules of the Stability and Growth Pact and ensure the sustainability of public finances. Maintaining sound public finances will enable governments to let automatic stabilisers operate freely and thus contribute to smoothing the economic cycle and to supporting private sector confidence.

column1: Turning to structural policies
column2: measures that foster competition and flexibility and promote moderate unit labour cost growth are of the utmost importance in the current economic circumstances. While moderate unit labour cost growth is crucial in all euro area countries
column3: it is particularly pressing in those that have experienced a significant loss of cost and price competitiveness over recent years and where unemployment has already started to rise. Moreover
column4: labour market reforms fostering employment and investment and promoting skills
column5: innovation and efficiency remain essential to support growth and real incomes in the longer term.

column1: We are now at your disposal for questions.";0;"You are correct in your understanding of our judgement. We are observing a slowdown in the euro area economy and I said that this has contributed to alleviating somewhat the upside risks to price stability. They have not disappeared. In particular

column3: as well as all price-setters

column1: On your first question

column13: as a group

column20: which is the mark of deflation. column23: the Channel and the Pacific.

column1: Regarding frontloading
column2: we do exactly what we think is appropriate when we think that it is necessary. We have just taken decisions that are clearly very important: two 50 basis point reductions in rates in less than one month. We have never done that before

column1: As regards the commercial paper issue
column2: as you know
column3: from the very beginning of the euro

column1: As regards your first question

column8: one-month

column4: different levels of flexibility
column5: many different features. You cannot say that two economies are alike

column9: exceptionally uncertain and challenging. I think it is important that we take up our own responsibilities

column1: I think that of the many reasons why we are observing this bust phenomenon
column2: which has followed a boom phenomenon – we have to be fully aware that after the boom you have the bust; these are two sides of the same coin – you certainly have an absence of discipline at a global level. I am not thinking of any particular economy
column3: but I think that
column4: among the lessons to be drawn from the present episode in global finance and the global economy
column5: we have to take into account the need to introduce –through different means
column6: a new framework
column7: perhaps peer surveillance
column8: perhaps other means – a way of avoiding the persistence of very large imbalances
column9: both domestic and external. That is certainly something we are all aiming at addressing. This is easy to say
column10: and much more difficult to introduce in the global economy with the real functioning of the global economic and financial system. I think that this is one of the issues that we have to reflect upon. And this is a long-term consideration. I am not suggesting that the fine-tuning of the present situation through fiscal stimulus would be part of it. This is a totally different question
column11: a totally different issue
column12: one which leads back to the consideration of Bretton Woods itself.

column1: This is one of the issues that we are looking at very carefully. It is associated with the strong encouragement that I gave a moment ago for commercial banks to live up to their responsibilities. It is clearly not normal to ensure large supply of liquidity
column2: which
column3: at the end of the day
column4: ends up in our deposit window. So we are reflecting on the best way of improving this.

column1: I won’t mention any particular instrument. Perhaps the encouragement – the strong encouragement – that I mentioned earlier will work. This is my working assumption at this stage
column2: but I’m not ruling anything out!

column1: This is the first time that we have had a very large episode of financial turbulence in the industrialised world itself
column2: at the heart of the industrialised world
column3: and we are particularly attentive to that. But we had previously great difficulties in the emerging world – for instance in the 1980s
column4: when we had entire continents which were broke and bankrupt. I myself was Chairman of the Paris Club at the time
column5: and at that time we had to cope with 52 countries defaulting simultaneously. There we had to see how to organise – or not – the rescheduling of their debt
column6: because they had defaulted depending on the qualification of the conditionality that they were embarking on with the help of the IMF. We have forgotten that we have had very difficult episodes
column7: not to mention the Asian crisis
column8: which was also very dramatic. In most cases
column9: you can see that there is something which is lacking in the global framework – an appropriate level of surveillance; surveillance ensuring greater discipline. And it is true for everyone. It is true for the industrialised world; it’s true for the emerging world. So
column10: how do you do that? How do you reintroduce a level of discipline which seems indispensable in order to avoid problems at a global level? This is an open question. I won’t say that it’s easy to answer
column11: but it has to be addressed. Otherwise
column12: we will have more problems.

column1: As regards Europe
column2: what the Governing Council of the ECB says is very simple: you apply the Stability and Growth Pact. Follow all the rules as they are. You don’t change the rules. You don’t change the Stability and Growth Pact. We are lucky enough to have a framework which is one of the pillars is EMU: Economic and Monetary Union. Monetary Union is the euro. We know what that is. We have a single currency and single monetary policy decisions that I am explaining at the moment. And we have an economic union. The core of the economic union is very much the Stability and Growth Pact. I would sum up our position in this way
column3: and the President of the Eurogroup has publicly said exactly the same. We stick to the Stability and Growth Pact – all of its provisions as crafted in the last reform by national governments. It’s as simple as that.

column1: Why would it be bad for the rate cuts to be passed on?
We are decreasing our own rates. It should normally be something that they would appreciate. If they pass on the rate cut
column2: it will be neutral. They would be passing on the rate cut that we ourselves have triggered. It’s clear that the decisions which have been taken – not Ireland in particular; all of the governments that have taken bold decisions – are decisions which have been taken in extraordinary circumstances to allow commercial banks and the financial system in general to function much more normally. These are bold decisions
column3: obviously
column4: taken for very good reasons. And we ourselves are echoing these decisions. It means an additional effort
column5: in terms of risk taken by Governments. And this is one of the reasons why I am saying that commercial banks should take full account of the fact that it is not just us. Governments too have taken bold decision. And these should be seen for what they are
column6: namely decisions that increase the risks for the governments themselves and therefore decrease the risks for the banks.

column1: We are back to what I said earlier. We really consider that commercial banks have to live up to their responsibilities. What we are observing as regards the spreads on the market today illustrate the fact that
column2: collectively
column3: they have not yet done this. We do not want to have an economy which is a planned economy. We are in an economy which is a market economy and has to function as a market economy. But they have
column4: collectively
column5: to understand that they are in a different universe. I do not think that the index should necessarily be changed: we should instead see the EURIBOR going down to a level that takes into account all the decisions that have been taken.

column2: since our last meeting
column3: the evidence that inflationary pressures are diminishing further has increased and

column5: inflation rates are expected to be in line with price stability over the policy-relevant horizon
column6: supporting the purchasing power of incomes and savings. The decline in inflation rates is due mainly to the fall in commodity prices and the significant slowdown in economic activity. Largely related to the effects of the intensification and broadening of the financial turmoil

column8: while the underlying pace of monetary expansion has remained strong

column1: Allow me to explain our assessment in greater detail
column2: starting with the economic analysis.

column1: Since September
column2: there has been an intensification and broadening of the financial market turmoil. Tensions have increasingly spilled over from the financial sector to the real economy
column3: and the world economy as a whole is feeling their adverse effects. In the euro area
column4: a number of the downside risks to economic activity that were identified previously have materialised
column5: leading in the third quarter to a contraction of 0.2% in real GDP growth
column6: on a quarterly basis
column7: according to Eurostat’s first estimate. Available survey data and the monthly indicators for October and November suggest that economic activity has weakened further during the fourth quarter of 2008.

column1: Looking further ahead
column2: on the basis of our current analysis and assessment
column3: we see global economic weakness and very sluggish domestic demand persisting in the next few quarters. According to the December 2008 Eurosystem staff macroeconomic projections for the euro area
column4: a subsequent recovery should then gradually take place
column5: supported by the fall in commodity prices and assuming that the external environment improves and the financial tensions weaken. Eurosystem staff project annual real GDP growth of between 0.8% and 1.2% for 2008
column6: between -1.0% and 0.0% for 2009
column7: and between 0.5% and 1.5% for 2010. These figures represent substantial downward revisions relative to the previous ECB staff projections for 2008 and 2009 published in September. Forecasts by international organisations have also been revised downwards and are broadly in line with the December 2008 Eurosystem staff projections.

column1: In the view of the Governing Council
column2: the economic outlook remains surrounded by an exceptionally high degree of uncertainty. Risks to economic growth lie on the downside. They relate mainly to the potential for a more significant impact on the real economy of the turmoil in financial markets
column3: as well as concerns about protectionist pressures and possible disorderly developments owing to global imbalances.

column1: It is crucial that all parties concerned make their contribution to lay sound foundations for a sustainable recovery. For this to materialise as early as possible
column2: it is of the utmost importance to maintain discipline and a medium-term perspective in macroeconomic policy-making. This is the best way to support confidence. The significant measures announced by governments to deal with the financial turmoil should be implemented swiftly so as to help ensure trust in the financial system and to prevent constraints on credit supply to companies and households.

column1: With regard to price developments
column2: annual HICP inflation has declined substantially since July. According to Eurostat’s flash estimate
column3: HICP inflation was 2.1% in November
column4: after 3.2% in October and 4.0% in July. The significant decline in headline inflation since the summer mainly reflects the considerable easing in global commodity prices over the past few months
column5: which more than offsets the impact of the sharp rise in unit labour costs in the first half of this year.

column1: Looking forward
column2: lower commodity prices and weakening demand lead us to conclude that inflationary pressures are diminishing further. The annual HICP inflation rate is expected to continue to decline in the coming months and to be in line with price stability over the policy-relevant horizon. Depending primarily on future developments in oil and other commodity prices
column3: a faster decline in HICP inflation cannot be excluded around the middle of next year
column4: mainly due to base effects. However
column5: also due to base effects
column6: inflation rates could increase again in the second half of the year
column7: so that any sharp fall in HICP inflation should be short-lived and is therefore not relevant from a monetary policy perspective.

column1: Consistent with this assessment
column2: the December 2008 Eurosystem staff projections foresee annual HICP inflation of between 3.2% and 3.4% for 2008 and declining to between 1.1% and 1.7% for 2009. For 2010
column3: HICP inflation is projected to lie between 1.5% and 2.1%. The HICP inflation projections for 2008 and 2009 have been revised downwards substantially in relation to the September 2008 ECB staff projections
column4: reflecting mainly the large declines in commodity prices and the impact of weakening demand on price developments. In this context
column5: let me remind you of the conditional nature of these projections
column6: which are based on a series of technical assumptions
column7: including market expectations for short and long-term interest rates
column8: as well as futures prices for oil and non-energy commodities. In addition
column9: the projections are based on the expectation of a decline in wage pressure over the projection horizon. Forecasts from international organisations give a broadly similar picture.

column1: Looking through the shorter-term volatility in headline HICP inflation rates
column2: risks to price stability at the policy-relevant horizon are more balanced than in the past. Unexpected further declines in commodity prices could put downward pressure on inflation
column3: while upside risks to price stability could materialise particularly if the recent fall in commodity prices were to reverse or if domestic price pressures turn out to be stronger than assumed. It is therefore crucial that price and wage-setters fully live up to their responsibilities.

column1: Turning to the monetary analysis
column2: various estimates of underlying broad money growth point to a sustained but moderating rate of monetary expansion in the euro area. Monetary trends therefore support the view that inflationary pressures are diminishing further
column3: with some risks remaining on the upside in the medium to longer term.

column1: It should be recognised that the intensification of the financial market turmoil since mid-September marks a potential watershed in the evolution of monetary developments. The most recent money and credit data indicate that this intensification has had a significant impact on the behaviour of market participants. Thus far
column2: such developments have largely taken the form of substitution among components of the broad aggregate M3
column3: rather than sharp changes in the evolution of M3 itself.

column1: The latest available data
column2: namely up to the end of October
column3: reveal a continued moderation of the growth rate of loans to the non-financial private sector. At the same time
column4: for the euro area as a whole
column5: there were no significant indications of a drying up in the availability of loans. The annual growth rate of loans to households also moderated further
column6: in line with the weakening of economic and housing market prospects and tighter financing conditions. The data do signal an impact of the intensification of the financial turmoil on bank behaviour. Looking forward
column7: more data and further analysis are necessary to form a robust judgement.

column1: To sum up
column2: there is increased evidence that inflationary pressures are diminishing further and inflation rates are expected to be in line with price stability over the policy-relevant horizon
column3: supporting the purchasing power of incomes and savings. The decline in inflation rates is due mainly to the fall in commodity prices and the significant slowdown in economic activity largely related to the global effects of the financial turmoil. A cross-check of the outcome of the economic analysis with that of the monetary analysis supports this view. While the underlying pace of monetary expansion has remained strong
column4: it has continued to decelerate further. Hence
column5: when considering all available information and analysis
column6: the Governing Council decided to reduce the key ECB interest rates by a further 75 basis points. All in all
column7: the level of uncertainty remains exceptionally high. The Governing Council will continue to keep inflation expectations firmly anchored in line with its medium-term objective. In so doing
column8: it supports sustainable growth and employment and contributes to financial stability. Accordingly
column9: we will continue to monitor very closely all developments over the period ahead.

column1: Regarding fiscal policies
column2: the Governing Council considers it crucial that discipline and a medium-term perspective are maintained
column3: taking fully into account the consequences of any shorter-term action on fiscal sustainability. It is of the utmost importance that the public’s confidence in the soundness of fiscal policies is preserved
column4: with the rules-based EU fiscal framework being fully applied and its integrity being fully preserved. The provisions of the Treaty of Nice and the Stability and Growth Pact require a medium-term perspective and allow for the necessary flexibility. Automatic fiscal stabilisers are relatively large in the euro area and provide a powerful source of fiscal support to a weakening economy. Where room for manoeuvre exists
column5: additional budgetary measures could be effective if they are timely
column6: targeted and temporary.

column1: Turning to structural policies
column2: the ongoing period of weak economic activity and high uncertainty about the economic outlook imply the need to strengthen the resilience and flexibility of the euro area economy. Product market reforms should foster competition and speed up effective restructuring. Labour market reforms should help to facilitate appropriate wage-setting
column3: as well as labour mobility across sectors and regions. The current situation should therefore be seen as a catalyst to foster the implementation of necessary domestic reforms in line with the principle of an open market economy with free competition.

column1: We will now report on the outcome of today’s meeting of the Governing Council

column1: On the basis of its regular economic and monetary analyses
column2: the Governing Council decided to reduce the interest rate on the main refinancing operations of the Eurosystem by a further 50 basis points
column3: bringing the total reduction since 8 October 2008 to 225 basis points. Today’s decision takes into account that inflationary pressures have continued to diminish
column4: owing in particular to the further weakening in the economic outlook. Looking forward
column5: we continue to expect inflation rates in the euro area to be in line with price stability over the policy-relevant medium-term horizon
column6: thereby supporting the purchasing power of incomes and savings. After today’s decision we consider risks to price stability over the medium term to be broadly balanced. This takes into account the latest economic data releases and survey information
column7: which add clear further evidence to the assessment that the euro area is experiencing a significant slowdown
column8: largely related to the effects of the intensification and broadening of the financial turmoil. Both global demand and euro area demand are likely to be dampened for a protracted period. Monetary expansion is moderating further
column9: supporting the assessment that inflationary pressures and risks are diminishing. All in all
column10: the level of uncertainty remains exceptionally high. The Governing Council will continue to keep inflation expectations firmly anchored in line with its medium-term objective of inflation rates below
column11: but close to
column12: 2%. This supports sustainable growth and employment and contributes to financial stability. Accordingly
column13: we will continue to monitor very closely all developments over the period ahead.

column1: Allow me to explain our assessment in greater detail
column2: starting with the economic analysis. Since September 2008 the financial market turmoil has intensified and broadened. Tensions have increasingly spilled over from the financial sector into the real economy. As a result
column3: economic activity throughout the world
column4: including in the euro area
column5: has weakened further. In particular
column6: foreign demand for euro area exports has declined
column7: and euro area domestic activity has contracted in the face of weaker demand prospects and tighter financing conditions. The survey data and monthly indicators for November and December that have become available since our last meeting clearly point to a further weakening of economic activity around the turn of the year
column8: indicating the materialisation of previously identified downside risks to activity.

column1: Looking further ahead
column2: on the basis of our current analysis and assessment
column3: we continue to see global economic weakness and very sluggish domestic demand persisting in the coming quarters as the impact of the financial tensions on activity continues. At the same time
column4: we expect the fall in commodity prices to support real disposable income in the period ahead. Furthermore
column5: the euro area should over time reap the full benefit from the effects of policy measures announced over recent weeks

column1: In the view of the Governing Council
column2: this outlook for the economy remains surrounded by an exceptionally high degree of uncertainty. Overall
column3: risks to economic growth remain clearly on the downside. They relate mainly to the potential for a stronger impact on the real economy of the turmoil in financial markets
column4: as well as to concerns about the emergence and intensification of protectionist pressures and to possible adverse developments in the world economy stemming from a disorderly correction of global imbalances.

column1: It is crucial that all parties concerned make their contribution to lay sound foundations for a sustainable recovery. For this to materialise as early as possible
column2: it is of the utmost importance to maintain discipline and a medium-term perspective in macroeconomic policy-making
column3: pursuing a stability-oriented and sustainable approach. This is the best way to preserve and enhance confidence. The significant measures being implemented by governments to deal with the financial turmoil should help to ensure trust in the financial system and to ease constraints on credit supply to companies and households.

column1: With regard to price developments
column2: annual HICP inflation has declined substantially since the middle of 2008
column3: when it peaked at 4.0%. HICP inflation was 1.6% in December
column4: after 2.1% in November. As we have emphasised on previous occasions
column5: the significant decline in headline inflation in the second half of 2008 reflects mainly the sharp falls in global commodity prices over the past few months.

column1: Looking forward
column2: lower commodity prices and weakening demand confirm that inflationary pressures in the euro area are diminishing. Owing mainly to base effects stemming from the past behaviour of energy prices
column3: headline annual inflation rates are projected to decline further in the coming months
column4: possibly reaching very low levels at mid-year. However
column5: also owing to base effects stemming from past energy price developments
column6: inflation rates are expected to increase again in the second half of the year. Hence it is likely that HICP inflation rates will fluctuate sharply during 2009. Such short-term volatility is
column7: however
column8: not relevant from a monetary policy perspective. Looking over the policy-relevant
column9: medium-term horizon
column10: annual HICP inflation is expected to be in line with price stability. This assessment is supported by available indicators of inflation expectations for the medium term.

column1: Risks to price stability over the medium term are broadly balanced. Unexpected further declines in commodity prices or a stronger than expected slowdown in the economy could put downward pressure on inflation
column2: while upside risks to price stability could materialise particularly if the recent fall in commodity prices were to reverse or if domestic price pressures turn out to be stronger than assumed. It is therefore crucial that price and wage-setters fully live up to their responsibilities.

column1: Turning to the monetary analysis
column2: the latest evidence confirms a moderating rate of monetary expansion in the euro area. Monetary trends therefore support the view that inflationary pressures and risks are diminishing.

column1: In analysing monetary developments it should be recognised that the intensification of the financial market turmoil since mid-September has the potential to affect the evolution of monetary aggregates significantly. Recent money and credit data indicate that this has already had a substantial impact on the behaviour of market participants. Both the broad aggregate M3 and
column2: in particular
column3: the components of M3 that are most closely related to the ongoing financial tensions – such as holdings of money market funds – have shown high month-to-month volatility of late. Overall
column4: however
column5: looking to the extent possible through this volatility
column6: the rate of broad money growth continues to moderate in line with the trend established over the past 18 months
column7: with the intensification of financial tensions since September leading to significant substitution among the components of M3
column8: rather than
column9: at least so far
column10: sharp changes in the trend of M3 itself.

column1: Turning to the evolution of bank loans
column2: the tightening of financing conditions resulting from the intensification of the financial tensions has contributed to a slowdown in the flow of monetary financial institution (MFI) loans to the non-financial private sector in recent months. More data and further analysis are necessary to form a robust judgement about the severity and scope of credit constraints and their possible implications for economic activity.

column1: On the basis of its regular economic and monetary analyses
column2: the Governing Council decided today to reduce the key ECB interest rates by a further 50 basis points. This decision brings the total reduction in the interest rate on the main refinancing operations of the Eurosystem since 8 October 2008 to 275 basis points.

column1: Overall
column2: inflation rates have decreased significantly and are now expected to remain well below 2% over 2009 and 2010. This outlook for inflation is due to the fall in commodity prices and diminishing domestic price and cost pressures
column3: reflecting the severe downturn in economic activity. Indeed
column4: recent economic data releases and survey information add further evidence to our assessment that both global and euro area demand are likely to be very weak in 2009. Over the course of 2010
column5: the economy is expected to gradually recover. At the same time
column6: available indicators of inflation expectations over the medium to longer term remain firmly anchored in line with the Governing Council’s aim of keeping inflation at rates of below
column7: but close to
column8: 2% over the medium term. A cross-check with the outcome of the monetary analysis confirms that inflationary pressure has been diminishing. After today’s decision we expect price stability to be maintained over the medium term
column9: supporting the purchasing power of euro area households. The Governing Council will continue to ensure a firm anchoring of medium-term inflation expectations
column10: which supports sustainable growth and employment and contributes to financial stability. Accordingly
column11: we will monitor very closely all developments over the period ahead.

column1: Let me now explain our assessment in greater detail
column2: starting with the economic analysis. Reflecting the impact of the financial market turmoil
column3: the world economy has weakened substantially in recent months
column4: affecting increasingly also emerging market economies. In a climate of heightened uncertainty
column5: a severe fall in world trade volumes has been accompanied by a pronounced decline in domestic demand in the euro area. As a consequence
column6: euro area real GDP contracted markedly in the fourth quarter of 2008
column7: by 1.5% on a quarterly basis
column8: according to Eurostat’s first estimate. Available data and survey indicators suggest that economic activity in the euro area remained weak in early 2009.

column1: Looking ahead
column2: the Governing Council expects that both global and domestic demand will decline in 2009 but thereafter recover gradually. This assessment is also reflected in the March 2009 ECB staff macroeconomic projections for the euro area
column3: which place annual real GDP growth in a range of -3.2% to -2.2% in 2009
column4: and between -0.7% and +0.7% in 2010. These ranges represent a downward revision of the December 2008 Eurosystem staff macroeconomic projections. In both 2009 and 2010
column5: the annual GDP growth rate will be significantly reduced by negative carry-over effects from the previous year. The projected gradual recovery in 2010 reflects the effects of the substantial macroeconomic stimulus under way as well as of the extensive policy measures that have been introduced to restore the functioning of the financial system
column6: both inside and outside the euro area. In addition
column7: the fall in commodity prices is expected to support real disposable income and consumption in the period ahead.

column1: The outlook for the economy continues to be surrounded by uncertainty. In the view of the Governing Council
column2: the risks to the economic outlook now appear to be more balanced. On the one hand

column5: stemming from the extensive macroeconomic stimulus under way and reflecting other policy measures taken. On the other hand
column6: concerns relate mainly to the potential for a stronger impact on the real economy of the turmoil in financial markets

column4: we looked at the situation from every possible angle and we took our decision by consensus. We took the decision to lower all three interest rates by 25 basis points. This means that the deposit interest rate is at 0.25%

column14: of course

This is something which needs to be known and is probably due to a combination of lower risk premia and lower liquidity premia on our own money market rates. We will continue to look at the evolution of our money market rates with great attention. It is worth remembering that

column18: I told you that we would make every effort to revive our money market and to allow it function as well as possible. Regarding the third question

column28: of course

column1: On the question of the evolution of credit
column2: I said what I had to say on behalf of the Governing Council. It is very clear. Obviously
column3: we have facts and figures before us
column4: and we have to understand better how to attribute what we are observing to the demand side and what we could attribute to the supply side. As regard supply
column5: we are doing whatever we can to keep our banking system as active as possible. I would echo all that has been said in the run-up to the important meeting
column6: the G20 which is taking place in London
column7: namely that a great number of decisions have been taken by the authorities with respect to support in the financial sphere and that it is extremely important for all those measures to be implemented as soon as possible
column8: measures that are very important for enabling the banking system to lend
column9: which is the task of the banking system. And to the extent that moral suasion is important in the present circumstances in which we find a lack of confidence wherever we look
column10: I would certainly echo what I have said before and what the Governing Council has said
column11: namely that we call on our banks to be as active lenders as possible in the present circumstances. As regards deflation
column12: we have not changed our diagnosis – we do not see any substantiation or materialisation of deflationary risk. We see ourselves in a disinflationary episode. At the moment
column13: we continue to deem our medium-term inflation expectations to be soundly anchored. That
column14: by the way
column15: is one of the most important successes of this institution. When I look at the medium term
column16: I am looking at the inflation expectations expressed in the Survey of Professional Forecasters
column17: and we will have to see what it says in a month’s time
column18: but thus far since the setting up of the euro these expectations have fluctuated between 1.7% and 2%. And the last reading that we had was 1.9%. When your definition of price stability over the medium term is less than 2%
column19: close to 2%
column20: it is difficult to find something that would be much better than this oscillation between 1.7% and 1.9%. I said on behalf of the Governing Council that the disinflationary process that we are facing and which is due predominantly to the prices of oil and commodities will continue to push the consumer price index downwards – we are currently at 0.6 %
column21: and we are likely to see it go below zero. That
column22: of course
column23: depends on the price of oil
column24: but I hope that the price of oil will not go up again. And all this is something that we should not confuse with deflation
column25: because – on the contrary – it is a factor that is expansionary
column26: because we are distributing purchasing power to our fellow citizens through lower prices of oil and commodities. That having been said
column27: we will continue to be very alert and we look permanently at our inflation expectations. We constantly look at the various indicators that we have at hand and that could substantiate the deflationary risk
column28: but we do not see materialisation of such a risk at the moment. Now I will hand over to the Vice-President.

column1: Very briefly
column2: my remarks last week consisted of two parts. I mentioned potential further non-standard measures that may be taken. As the President has already emphasised
column3: we have taken a number of non-standard measures in the past. Such measures aim at improving the functioning of credit markets and facilitating the financing of the economy. At the same time

column1: Regarding your first question
column2: I said that 1.25% was not the lowest level that we have decided ex ante. And I have nothing to add to that. We are never pre-committed. As you know
column3: we will do what we judge appropriate at any time. I said also that it would be a measured decision.

column1: As regards the OECD

column7: including those of the IMF. We will see. We are in a world which is difficult and uncertain. I would just draw your attention to something I said a month ago. When we issued our last projections
column8: I told you that of course they did not incorporate the 50 basis point decrease in interest rates that we had only just decided upon. They do not
column9: by definition
column10: incorporate the 25 basis point cut of today. So there has been a further 75 basis point reduction overall
column11: for all three of our interest rates
column12: that is now incorporated. This is one of the reasons why we said that we felt that the risks for inflation
column13: in particular
column14: were balanced
column15: because we also take into account the decisions that have been taken since the last set of projections was issued. But we have to remain extraordinarily pragmatic and humble in the presence of facts and figures in a period in which uncertainty is greater than ever.

column1: No
column2: we have certainly not changed our diagnosis at the level of the euro area as a whole and I will not comment on one particular event. I would say that it is a process. Everybody knows about the developments regarding real estate
column3: not only in Spain but in a number of other countries also. So I have nothing particular to say and we certainly have not changed our diagnosis at all because of that event.

column1: I would say on the first point that my reading of the market rates and of the expectations that can be extracted from the money market was that they saw a probability of 50% for a decrease of 50 basis points and 100% for a decrease of at least 25 basis points. So I would not say that it is as simple as you said. I would certainly echo what you said about the deposit rate
column2: although there was no real mathematical extraction of information from the market that would substantiate a 25 basis point decrease in only the deposit rate. It was more the reasoning of economists or specialist experts. They were not wrong on that particular point as we can see. And I can only tell you that we have judged that it was appropriate
column3: taking all factors into account
column4: to decrease the rate on the main refinancing operations by 25 basis points while
column5: at the same time
column6: we have not decided that this is the lowest point that could be attained. It is as simple as that. It is the result of a very in-depth discussion and weighing of the various arguments. I will only mention one of them
column7: which is that we have been quite satisfied so far with our decision to widen the de facto corridor for the very short term money market rates between the rate on the main refinancing operations and the deposit rate. And with regard to maintaining the width of this corridor
column8: which has served us very well in the recent past
column9: there was no particular or decisive reason not to continue. But this may not be true in the future. So I do not rule out the possibility that we could reduce the width of the corridor.

column1: On the non-standard measures
column2: we are already fully engaged in non-standard measures. And we were the first
column3: as perhaps you remember
column4: to embark upon very audacious and bold measures
column5: including the unlimited supply of liquidity at fixed rates. We did that to cover the end of the year in 2007
column6: with very bold decisions at the time
column7: and after the intensification of the crisis we were extremely prompt in embarking upon this unlimited supply of liquidity. We were also the first to supply liquidity at longer maturities – not only of one week but of three months and six months. And this confirms that the ECB has the capacity to adopt non-standard measures in the main area of the financing of our economy
column8: namely the 70% of the financing of the economy which goes through commercial banks
column9: according to the figures for outstanding financing. We will tell you at our next meeting how we intend to go further in terms of non-standard measures. I do not want to pre-empt in any respect what we may say then. Rest assured that we will ensure that
column10: by so doing
column11: we optimise the appropriate help that we can offer to our economy with regard to the enhanced credit support in particular.

column1: Today’s decision was “measured” in this respect.
We will meet next month as regards the non-standard measures. And as I have said
column2: we are examining carefully all elements that would allow us to be convinced at the level of the Governing Council that we are optimising what could be done
column3: and should be done
column4: in our view
column5: to enhance credit support and be sure that we have an optimised set of non-standard measures.

column1: And let me just say – and this is not a comment on those particular future decisions; it’s also a general comment – that we are extremely keen on preserving what we consider essential in the present circumstances
column2: namely the fact that this institution
column3: the ECB
column4: is an anchor of stability and confidence
column5: and that all that we do must be understood and perceived as such by our fellow citizens. You know that the confidence of our fellow citizens is the most important thing today. We have many economic difficulties in particular because our fellow citizens have lost some of their confidence. So we have to continue to be able to tell them “you can trust us; we will do all that is necessary
column6: as we have done in the past
column7: we will do what is called for in the circumstances”. Remember that we were the first – and we were criticised for it – to diagnose that we were in a very difficult situation and that we had to take bold measures. It was 9 August 2007.

column1: At the same time
column2: it is essential that we preserve their confidence that we will continue to deliver price stability in line with our definition in the medium and long run. This is an essential component of their confidence today. I’m reading the papers
column3: I’m reading articles
column4: including the popular press
column5: and I’m struck by the fact that the debate on what tomorrow and the day after tomorrow will bring for us and for our children is an open question. We have to be very careful in this respect. I say that just to give you an idea of our thinking when taking this decision. In any case
column6: when we meet after the next monetary policy meeting
column7: I will tell you what has been decided for the non-standard measures.

column1: No. Exchange rate questions are not part of what we are presently discussing. And on exchange rates

2009-05-07;2;Ladies and gentlemen
column2: the Vice-President and I are very pleased to welcome you to today’s press conference. We will now report on the outcome of today’s meeting of the Governing Council
column3: which was also attended by Commissioner Almunia.

column1: On the basis of its regular economic and monetary analyses
column2: the Governing Council decided to reduce the interest rate on the main refinancing operations of the Eurosystem by a further 25 basis points and the rate on the marginal lending facility by 50 basis points
column3: to 1.00% and 1.75% respectively. The interest rate on the deposit facility will remain unchanged at 0.25%. This decision brings the total reduction in the interest rate on the main refinancing operations of the Eurosystem since 8 October 2008 to 325 basis points.

column1: Current key ECB interest rates are appropriate taking into account all available information and analysis. In addition to the reductions in interest rates
column2: the Governing Council decided today to proceed with its enhanced credit support approach. In continuity and consistency with the operations we have undertaken since October 2008
column3: and in recognition of the central role played by the banking system in financing the euro area economy
column4: we will conduct liquidity-providing longer-term refinancing operations with a maturity of 12 months. The operations will be conducted as fixed rate tender procedures with full allotment. The rate for the first of these operations
column5: to be announced on 23 June 2009
column6: will be the rate on the main refinancing operations at that time. Subsequently
column7: the fixed rate may include a premium to the rate on the main refinancing operations
column8: depending on the circumstances at the time.

column1: The Governing Council has decided in principle that the Eurosystem will purchase euro-denominated covered bonds issued in the euro area. The detailed modalities will be announced after the Governing Council meeting of 4 June 2009.
Furthermore
column2: the Governing Council has decided that the European Investment Bank will become an eligible counterparty in the Eurosystem’s monetary policy operations with effect from 8 July 2009 and under the same conditions as any other counterparty.

column1: These decisions have been taken to promote the ongoing decline in money market term rates
column2: to encourage banks to maintain and expand their lending to clients
column3: to help to improve market liquidity in important segments of the private debt security market
column4: and to ease funding conditions for banks and enterprises.

column1: Today’s decisions take into account the expectation that price developments will continue to be dampened by the substantial past fall in commodity prices and the marked weakening of economic activity in the euro area and globally. The latest economic data and survey information suggest tentative signs of a stabilisation at very low levels
column2: after a first quarter which was significantly weaker than expected. The world economy
column3: including the euro area
column4: is still undergoing a severe downturn
column5: with the prospect of both external and domestic demand remaining very weak over 2009 before gradually recovering in the course of 2010. This assessment incorporates a number of adverse developments which are likely to materialise over the coming months
column6: such as a further deterioration in labour markets. At the same time
column7: available indicators of inflation expectations over the medium to longer term remain firmly anchored in line with the Governing Council’s aim of keeping inflation rates at levels below
column8: but close to
column9: 2% over the medium term. The outcome of the monetary analysis confirms that inflationary pressure has been diminishing
column10: as money and credit growth have further decelerated in recent months. Against the background of these developments
column11: after today’s decisions we expect price stability to be maintained over the medium term
column12: thereby supporting the purchasing power of euro area households.

column1: Let me now explain our assessment in some more detail
column2: starting with the economic analysis. Reflecting the impact of the financial market turmoil
column3: economic activity continued to weaken in the euro area in the course of the first quarter of 2009
column4: in parallel with the ongoing downturn in the world economy. This weakening in the first quarter appears to have been significantly more pronounced than projected in March. More recently
column5: there have been some tentative signs in survey data of a stabilisation
column6: albeit at very low levels. Overall
column7: economic activity is likely to be very weak for the remainder of this year
column8: before gradually recovering in the course of 2010. In particular
column9: the substantial fall in commodity prices since the summer of 2008 is supporting real disposable income and thus consumption. In addition
column10: external as well as domestic demand should increasingly benefit from the effects of the significant macroeconomic stimulus under way as well as from the measures taken so far to restore the functioning of the financial system both inside and outside the euro area.

column1: Taking all these measures and their effects into account
column2: as well as the pronouncedly negative growth in the first quarter of this year and the most recently published forecasts by public institutions
column3: the risks to this outlook remain broadly balanced. On the downside
column4: there are concerns that the turmoil in financial markets could have a stronger impact on the real economy
column5: as well as that protectionist pressures could intensify and that there could be adverse developments in the world economy stemming from a disorderly correction of global imbalances. At the same time
column6: there may be stronger than anticipated positive effects due to the decrease in commodity prices and to the policy measures taken.

column1: Annual HICP inflation was
column2: according to Eurostat’s flash estimate
column3: 0.6% in April
column4: unchanged from March. As explained on earlier occasions
column5: the decline in inflation since last summer primarily reflects the sharp fall in global commodity prices over this period. Moreover
column6: signs of a more broad-based reduction in inflationary pressure are increasingly emerging. Looking ahead
column7: base effects stemming from past energy price movements will play a significant role in the shorter-term dynamics of the HICP. Accordingly
column8: we expect to see headline annual inflation rates declining further and temporarily remaining at negative levels for some months around mid-year. Thereafter
column9: annual inflation rates are expected to increase again. Such short-term dynamics are
column10: however
column11: not relevant from a monetary policy perspective. Looking further ahead
column12: HICP inflation is likely to remain positive and below 2% in 2010
column13: with price developments being dampened by ongoing sluggish demand in the euro area and elsewhere. Available indicators of inflation expectations over the medium to longer term remain firmly anchored in line with the Governing Council’s aim of keeping inflation rates at levels below
column14: but close to
column15: 2% over the medium term.

column1: The risks surrounding this outlook are broadly balanced. They relate in particular to the risks to the outlook for economic activity as well as to risks to commodity prices.
Turning to the monetary analysis
column2: the latest data confirm the continued deceleration in the pace of underlying monetary expansion. This is signalled
column3: for instance
column4: by the concurrent further declines in the annual growth rates of M3 to 5.1% and of loans to the private sector to 3.2%. The deceleration supports the assessment of diminishing inflationary pressures in the medium term.

column1: Month-on-month developments in M3 and its components have remained volatile
column2: with data for March showing a contraction in most of the respective outstanding amounts. This may partly reflect market participants’ investment responses to the past reduction in the key ECB interest rates
column3: which has reduced the remuneration of short-term deposits and marketable instruments and fostered corresponding shifts in the allocation of funds not only within M3 but also to instruments outside M3.

column1: The outstanding amount of MFI loans to the private sector contracted further in March
column2: reflecting mainly a negative flow of lending to non-financial corporations. The reduced amount of financing is again related mainly to loans with shorter maturities
column3: while the net flow of loans with longer maturities remained positive. The decline in short-term lending is likely to reflect to a large extent lower demand in the wake of a sharp deterioration in economic activity and business prospects at the start of the year. Interest rates on short-term and floating rate bank loans to households and non-financial corporations have declined significantly over recent months
column4: indicating that the transmission of monetary policy impulses to the economy continues. Overall
column5: the latest money and credit data support the assessment that both banks and money-holding sectors are reducing their highly leveraged positions built up in past years.

column1: To sum up
column2: the Governing Council’s decisions today take into account the expectation that price developments will continue to be dampened by the substantial past fall in commodity prices and the marked weakening of economic activity in the euro area and globally. The latest economic data and survey information suggest tentative signs of a stabilisation at very low levels
column3: after a first quarter which was significantly weaker than expected. The world economy
column4: including the euro area
column5: is still undergoing a severe downturn
column6: with the prospect of both external and domestic demand remaining very weak over 2009 before gradually recovering in the course of 2010. This assessment incorporates a number of adverse developments which are likely to materialise over the coming months
column7: such as a further deterioration in labour markets. At the same time
column8: available indicators of inflation expectations over the medium to longer term remain firmly anchored in line with the Governing Council’s aim of keeping inflation rates at levels below
column9: but close to
column10: 2% over the medium term. A cross-check with the outcome of the monetary analysis confirms that inflationary pressure has been diminishing
column11: as money and credit growth have further decelerated in recent months. Against the background of these developments
column12: after today’s decisions we expect price stability to be maintained over the medium term
column13: thereby supporting the purchasing power of euro area households.

column1: All in all
column2: since the intensification of the financial crisis in September 2008
column3: the Eurosystem has taken a series of measures that are unprecedented in nature
column4: scope and timing. As a consequence
column5: we have observed a clear decline in key money market interest rates that euro area banks typically use as benchmarks to reset floating rate loans and price new short-term loans. This in turn has led to sharp declines in rates for such loans to households and non-financial corporations. As the transmission of monetary policy works with lags
column6: our policy action will progressively feed through to the economy in full. Hence
column7: with all the measures taken
column8: monetary policy has provided ongoing support for households and corporations.

column1: The Governing Council will ensure that
column2: once the macroeconomic environment improves
column3: the measures taken can be quickly unwound and the liquidity provided absorbed so that any threat to price stability over the medium to longer term can be effectively countered in a timely fashion. Indeed
column4: as has been stressed many times
column5: the Governing Council will continue to ensure a firm anchoring of medium-term inflation expectations. Such anchoring is indispensable to supporting sustainable growth and employment and contributes to financial stability. Accordingly
column6: we will continue to monitor very closely all developments over the period ahead.

column1: Regarding fiscal policies
column2: the latest projections for euro area countries point to continued revisions to budget balance estimates and forecasts. Higher budget deficits and the fiscal impact of financial sector support measures will lead to significantly higher government debt-to-GDP ratios. In addition
column3: updated projections by the Economic Policy Committee of the EU show that most countries face a challenging task in dealing with the budgetary costs of an ageing population. Therefore
column4: it is paramount that countries make a strong and credible commitment to a path of consolidation in order to return to sound fiscal positions
column5: respecting fully the provisions of the Stability and Growth Pact. This will preserve the public’s trust in the sustainability of public finances and will support both the recovery and long-term economic growth. The credibility of fiscal consolidation commitments will be strengthened if they are part of national policy frameworks oriented to the medium term.

column1: Turning to structural policies
column2: it is crucial that the focus is now on strengthening the adjustment capacity and flexibility of the euro area economy in line with the principle of an open market economy. This calls for an accelerated implementation of labour market reforms to facilitate appropriate wage-setting and labour mobility across sectors and regions as well as product market reforms to foster competition and speed up restructuring.
