column1: 2009-12-03;2;"Ladies and gentlemen
column2: the Vice-President and I are very pleased to welcome you to our press conference today. We will now report on the outcome of today’s meeting of the Governing Council
column3: which was also attended by Commissioner Almunia.

column1: Based on its regular economic and monetary analyses
column2: the Governing Council decided to leave the key ECB interest rates unchanged. The current rates remain appropriate. Taking into account all the information and analyses that have become available since our meeting on 5 November 2009
column3: price developments are expected to remain subdued over the policy-relevant horizon. The latest information also confirms the expected improvement in economic activity in the second half of this year
column4: with euro area real GDP growth returning to positive territory in the third quarter of 2009. However
column5: some of the factors supporting the recovery at present are of a temporary nature. The Governing Council expects the euro area economy to grow at a moderate pace in 2010
column6: recognising that the recovery process is likely to be uneven and that the outlook remains subject to high uncertainty. The outcome of the monetary analysis confirms the assessment of low inflationary pressure over the medium term
column7: as money and credit growth continues to slow down. All in all
column8: we expect price stability to be maintained over the medium term
column9: thereby supporting the purchasing power of euro area households. Medium to longer-term inflation expectations remain firmly anchored in line with the Governing Council’s aim of keeping inflation rates below
column10: but close to
column11: 2% over the medium term.

column1: At today’s meeting we also decided to continue conducting our main refinancing operations (MROs) as fixed rate tender procedures with full allotment for as long as is needed – and at least until the third maintenance period of 2010 ends on 13 April. We will continue to use this tender procedure in our special-term refinancing operations with a maturity of one maintenance period
column2: which will continue for at least the first three maintenance periods of 2010. Moreover
column3: we decided that the rate in the last 12-month longer-term refinancing operation
column4: to be allotted on 16 December 2009
column5: will be fixed at the average minimum bid rate of the MROs over the life of this operation. Finally
column6: as regards longer-term refinancing operations in the first quarter of 2010
column7: we decided to carry out the last six-month longer-term refinancing operation on 31 March 2010. This operation will be carried out using a full allotment fixed rate tender procedure
column8: as will the regular monthly three-month longer-term refinancing operations already announced for the first quarter of 2010.

column1: Further operational details on these decisions can be found in a press release that will be posted on our website after this press conference.
The improved conditions in financial markets have indicated that not all our liquidity measures are needed to the same extent as in the past. With these decisions
column2: the Eurosystem continues to provide liquidity support to the banking system of the euro area for an extended period at very favourable conditions and to facilitate the provision of credit to the euro area economy.

column1: Let me now explain our assessment in greater detail
column2: starting with the economic analysis. Economic activity in the euro area improved further in the third quarter of 2009
column3: with real GDP growth returning to positive territory following five quarters of contraction. According to Eurostat’s first estimate
column4: real GDP increased by 0.4 % quarter on quarter. Available survey data suggest that the recovery is continuing during the fourth quarter of 2009. At present
column5: the euro area is benefiting from the inventory cycle and a recovery in exports
column6: as well as from the significant macroeconomic stimulus under way and the measures adopted to restore the functioning of the financial system. However
column7: a number of the supporting factors are of a temporary nature and activity is likely to be affected for some time to come by the ongoing process of balance sheet adjustment in the financial and the non-financial sector
column8: both inside and outside the euro area. For this reason
column9: the euro area economy is expected to grow only at a moderate pace in 2010
column10: and the recovery process is likely to be uneven.

column1: Eurosystem staff project annual real GDP growth of between -4.1% and -3.9% in 2009
column2: between +0.1% and +1.5% in 2010
column3: and between +0.2% and +2.2% in 2011. The range for 2010 has been revised upwards compared with the September 2009 ECB staff macroeconomic projections. Forecasts by international organisations are broadly in line with the December 2009 Eurosystem staff projections.

column1: The Governing Council continues to view the risks to this outlook as broadly balanced. On the upside
column2: there may be stronger than anticipated effects stemming from the extensive macroeconomic stimulus being provided and from other policy measures taken. Confidence may also improve further and foreign trade may recover more strongly than projected. On the downside
column3: concerns remain relating to a stronger or more protracted than expected negative feedback loop between the real economy and the financial sector
column4: renewed increases in oil and other commodity prices
column5: the intensification of protectionist pressures and the possibility of disruptive market movements related to the correction of global imbalances.

column1: With regard to price developments
column2: as expected
column3: euro area annual HICP inflation has turned positive again after five months of negative rates. According to Eurostat’s flash estimate
column4: it stood at +0.6% in November
column5: up from -0.1% in October. The rise mainly reflects upward base effects stemming from the drop in global commodity prices a year ago. Inflation is expected to rise further in the near term
column6: mainly owing to upward base effects in the energy and food components. Looking further ahead
column7: inflation is expected to remain moderate over the policy-relevant horizon
column8: with overall price
column9: cost and wage developments staying subdued in line with a slow recovery in demand in the euro area and elsewhere. In this context
column10: it is important to re-emphasise that inflation expectations over the medium to longer term remain firmly anchored in line with the Governing Council’s aim of keeping inflation rates below
column11: but close to
column12: 2% over the medium term.

column1: Consistent with this assessment
column2: the December 2009 Eurosystem staff projections foresee annual HICP inflation of 0.3% in 2009
column3: between 0.9% and 1.7% in 2010
column4: and between 0.8% and 2.0% in 2011. Compared with the September 2009 ECB staff projections
column5: the inflation projections for 2010 remain largely unchanged. Available forecasts from international organisations provide a broadly similar picture.

column1: Risks to this outlook remain broadly balanced. They relate
column2: in particular
column3: to the outlook for economic activity and the evolution of commodity prices. Furthermore
column4: increases in indirect taxation and administered prices may be stronger than currently expected owing to the need for fiscal consolidation in the coming years.

column1: Turning to the monetary analysis
column2: the data for October confirm the ongoing decline in the annual growth rates of M3 and loans to the private sector
column3: to 0.3% and -0.8% respectively. These concurrent declines continue to support the assessment of a moderate underlying pace of monetary expansion and low inflationary pressures over the medium term. At the same time
column4: the annual growth rate of M1 was 11.8% in October 2009
column5: down from 12.8% in September
column6: mainly reflecting a base effect.

column1: The current decline in the annual growth rates of monetary aggregates is influenced by a number of special factors and is thereby likely to overstate the deceleration in the underlying pace of monetary expansion. First
column2: base effects associated with the intensification of the financial turmoil in autumn 2008 have had a downward effect on the annual growth rate of M3 in the past two months. Second
column3: and more fundamentally
column4: the steep slope of the yield curve provides an incentive to shift funds out of M3 into longer-term deposits and securities
column5: thereby dampening M3 growth. The current constellation of interest rates also continues to trigger shifts of funds within M3
column6: as the narrow spread between the rates on different short-term deposits reduces the opportunity costs of holding the most liquid assets contained in M1.

column1: The annual growth rate of bank loans to the non-financial private sector turned somewhat more negative in October. In the case of loans to households
column2: the latest data provide further confirmation of a levelling-off at low rates of growth. As regards loans to non-financial corporations
column3: it is worthwhile to note that the growth of loans to enterprises typically picks up with some lag compared with the cycle in economic activity. In this respect
column4: the still subdued levels of production and trade
column5: as well as the ongoing uncertainty surrounding the business outlook
column6: are likely to dampen firms’ demand for bank financing also in the coming months
column7: especially for short-term loans. At the same time
column8: overall financing conditions continue to improve
column9: which should support the demand for loans in the period ahead. Banks are currently faced with the challenge of managing the size and structure of their overall balance sheets
column10: and at the same time ensuring the availability of credit to the non-financial sector. Against the background of their improved liquidity situation and access to market financing
column11: banks should address this challenge by taking appropriate measures to strengthen further their capital bases and
column12: where necessary
column13: take full advantage of government support measures for recapitalisation.

column1: To sum up
column2: the current rates remain appropriate. Taking into account all the information and analyses that have become available since our meeting on 5 November 2009
column3: price developments are expected to remain subdued over the policy-relevant horizon. The latest information also confirms the expected improvement in economic activity in the second half of this year
column4: with euro area real GDP growth returning to positive territory in the third quarter of 2009. However
column5: some of the factors supporting the recovery at present are of a temporary nature. The Governing Council expects the euro area economy to grow at a moderate pace in 2010
column6: recognising that the recovery process is likely to be uneven and that the outlook remains subject to high uncertainty. Cross-checking the outcome of the economic analysis with that of the monetary analysis confirms the assessment of low inflationary pressure over the medium term
column7: as money and credit growth continues to slow down. All in all
column8: we expect price stability to be maintained over the medium term
column9: thereby supporting the purchasing power of euro area households.

column1: With all the measures we have taken in response to the intensification of the financial crisis
column2: we have supported both the availability of liquidity to the banking sector and the recovery of the euro area economy. As the transmission of monetary policy works with lags
column3: we expect that our policy action will continue to progressively feed through to the economy. We will continue our enhanced credit support to the banking system
column4: while taking into account the ongoing improvement in financial market conditions and avoiding distortions associated with maintaining non-standard measures for too long. Looking ahead
column5: the Governing Council will gradually phase out
column6: at the appropriate time
column7: the extraordinary liquidity measures that are not needed to the same extent as in the past. In order to counter effectively any threat to price stability over the medium to longer term
column8: the liquidity provided will be absorbed when necessary. In this way
column9: the Governing Council will continue to ensure a firm anchoring of medium-term inflation expectations. Such anchoring is indispensable to supporting sustainable growth and employment and contributing to financial stability. Accordingly
column10: we will continue to monitor very closely all developments over the period ahead.

column1: As regards fiscal policies
column2: we re-emphasise how important it is for governments to develop
column3: communicate and implement ambitious fiscal consolidation strategies in a timely manner. These strategies must be based on realistic output growth assumptions and focus on structural expenditure reforms
column4: not least with a view to coping with the budgetary burden associated with an ageing population. As agreed by the ECOFIN Council on 2 December 2009
column5: governments need to set out concrete and quantifiable adjustment measures that will lead to a sustainable correction of fiscal imbalances. Several countries will have to start consolidation in 2010
column6: and all others in 2011 at the latest.

column1: With regard to structural reforms
column2: most estimates indicate that the financial crisis has reduced the productive capacity of our economies
column3: and will continue to do so for some time to come. In order to support sustainable growth and employment
column4: labour market flexibility and more effective incentives to work will be needed. Furthermore
column5: policies that enhance competition and innovation are also urgently needed to speed up restructuring and investment and to create new business opportunities. An appropriate restructuring of the banking sector should also play an important role. Sound balance sheets
column6: effective risk management
column7: and transparent as well as robust business models are key to strengthening banks’ resilience to shocks
column8: thereby laying the foundations for sustainable economic growth and financial stability.

column3: we believe that the decisions we have taken are appropriate. We do not see any harm for any part of the environment in what we have been doing. I have nothing to add to what I have already said. Let me repeat: we were unanimous in taking our decision.

column1: As you know
column2: the main tasks of the ESRB will be to identify and assess systemic risks and to issue risk warnings and recommendations in order to address these risks if they are considered to be significant. However
column3: the responsibility for the implementation of these recommendations will rest either with national authorities – supervisory or economic – or
column4: depending on the recommendation
column5: with the European Commission or the European Supervisory Authorities. If the macro-prudential recommendations of the ESRB are not implemented in an effective and timely manner
column6: the mission of the macro-prudential supervision will not be fully accomplished. So
column7: implementation is key. It is absolutely essential that the macro-prudential recommendations are translated into effective action if we are going to accomplish the ultimate objective of the new framework for macro-prudential supervision
column8: which is to prevent or at least to minimise the likelihood of future crises and to strengthen the resilience of the financial system. Mechanisms should be in place to ensure the translation of the macro-prudential recommendations into effective action.

column1: On the issue of independence
column2: I think it is very important that the ESRB and the members of the Board perform their tasks in the interest of the Union in order to prevent and mitigate systemic risks. This can be done most effectively if these tasks are carried out in full independence
column3: just as we perform our own tasks at the ECB. The current legal text – the regulation that has been agreed by the Council – provides for this independence. So my point was to underline the importance of ensuring the independence for the Board in carrying out its tasks.

column1: If the question was that you were wondering whether this will create a problem for the Governing Council of the ECB
column2: the independence of the Governing Council and of the ECB is guaranteed by the Maastricht Treaty and there can
column3: therefore
column4: be absolutely no influence
column5: in any respect
column6: on our own duty as regards delivering price stability. That is crystal clear.

column1: And it is also crystal clear that the objectives of the ESRB in no way conflict with the objectives of the ECB.
As regards the Eurosystem staff projections
column2: we are very much in agreement with the assessment of the major institutions
column3: so I don’t think there is a significant difference. Perhaps some private sector projections are significantly better
column4: but this is not necessarily the case in general. In any case
column5: we consider that there is still a high level of uncertainty
column6: and we consider the risks to be broadly balanced. The Governing Council considers that the level of uncertainty depends in particular on whether confidence improves further. Let’s not forget that the recession stemmed from a very dramatic evaporation of confidence. As regards risks to the upside the global economy – and therefore foreign trade – could be more dynamic than is presently foreseen or projected. We also have the effects of the policy decisions that have been taken and
column7: as I have said
column8: are not necessarily fully taken into account in the projections because of their lags. But we also have a number of very significant risks on the downside
column9: which are
column10: in our view
column11: balancing the risks on the upside. I would say that the possible increases in oil prices and commodity prices certainly constitute a very large downside risk. We consider that protectionist pressures are still looming
column12: and they would constitute a very adverse element. And you also have the adverse feedback loop between the real sector and the financial sector
column13: taking into account the magnitude of the recession
column14: which could perhaps have been underestimated in the projections. But again
column15: taking everything into account
column16: we have risks that are broadly balanced
column17: together with a high level of uncertainty. We are now in positive territory with a likely bumpy road ahead. Let’s remain alert.

column1: First of all
column2: we have said that interest rates are appropriate. I was very clear on that. We consider that at the moment it is important not to signal anything on interest rates. In that respect
column3: the message from us is clear: we are engaging in the progressive
column4: timely
column5: gradual phasing out of the non-conventional measures and this is something which accompanies and reflects what we are observing in the market. We are not signalling anything in terms of hardening our monetary policy. In taking these decisions we are reflecting the fact that some of the exceptional non-standard measures (i.e. enhanced credit support) that we have implemented in order to cope with an exceptional situation are progressively working and are no more needed. We are accompanying these progressive improvements. That is exactly the way we are looking at it.

column7: if boom is followed by bust

2010-01-14;2;Ladies and gentlemen
column2: the Vice-President and I are very pleased to welcome you to our first press conference in 2010. Let me take this opportunity to wish you all a Happy New Year. We will now report on the outcome of today’s meeting of the Governing Council
column3: which was also attended by Commissioner Almunia.

column1: Based on its regular economic and monetary analyses
column2: the Governing Council decided to leave the key ECB interest rates unchanged. The current rates remain appropriate. Taking into account all the information and analyses that have become available since our meeting on 3 December 2009
column3: price developments are expected to remain subdued over the policy-relevant horizon. The latest information has also confirmed that towards the end of 2009 euro area economic activity continued to expand. However
column4: some of the factors supporting the growth in real GDP are of a temporary nature. Overall
column5: the Governing Council expects the euro area economy to grow at a moderate pace in 2010
column6: recognising that the recovery process is likely to be uneven and that the outlook remains subject to uncertainty. The outcome of the monetary analysis confirms the assessment of low inflationary pressure over the medium term
column7: given the ongoing parallel decline in money and credit growth. All in all
column8: we expect price stability to be maintained over the medium term
column9: thereby supporting the purchasing power of euro area households. Medium to longer-term inflation expectations remain firmly anchored in line with the Governing Council’s aim of keeping inflation rates below
column10: but close to
column11: 2% over the medium term.

column1: Let me now explain our assessment in greater detail
column2: starting with the economic analysis. Following the 0.4% quarter-on-quarter increase in real GDP in the third quarter of 2009
column3: the latest information confirms that towards the end of last year economic activity in the euro area continued to expand. The euro area has been benefiting from a turn in the inventory cycle and a recovery in exports
column4: as well as from the significant macroeconomic stimulus under way and the measures adopted to restore the functioning of the financial system. However
column5: a number of the supporting factors are of a temporary nature. Furthermore
column6: there is likely to be a drag on activity for some time to come on account of the ongoing process of balance sheet adjustment in the financial and non-financial sectors
column7: both inside and outside the euro area. In addition
column8: low capacity utilisation rates are likely to dampen investment
column9: and unemployment in the euro area is expected to increase somewhat further
column10: thereby lowering consumption growth. For these reasons
column11: the euro area economy is expected to grow only at a moderate pace in 2010 and the recovery process could be uneven.

column1: The Governing Council continues to view the risks to this outlook as broadly balanced. On the upside
column2: there may be stronger than anticipated effects stemming from the extensive macroeconomic stimulus being provided and from other policy measures taken. Confidence may also improve further
column3: and the global economy as well as foreign trade may recover more strongly than projected. On the downside
column4: concerns remain relating to a stronger or more protracted than expected negative feedback loop between the real economy and the financial sector
column5: renewed increases in oil and other commodity prices
column6: the intensification of protectionist pressures and the possibility of disruptive market movements related to the correction of global imbalances.

column1: With regard to price developments
column2: as expected
column3: euro area annual HICP inflation increased further in December 2009 to stand at 0.9%
column4: after 0.5% in November. The rise mainly reflects upward base effects stemming mostly from the drop in global energy prices a year ago. Inflation is expected to remain around 1% in the near term. Looking further ahead
column5: inflation is expected to remain moderate over the policy-relevant horizon
column6: with overall price
column7: cost and wage developments staying subdued in line with a slow recovery in demand in the euro area and elsewhere. In this context
column8: it is important to emphasise
column9: once again
column10: that inflation expectations over the medium to longer term remain firmly anchored in line with the Governing Council’s aim of keeping inflation rates below
column11: but close to
column12: 2% over the medium term.

column1: Risks to this outlook remain broadly balanced. They relate
column2: in particular
column3: to the outlook for economic activity and the evolution of commodity prices. Furthermore
column4: increases in indirect taxation and administered prices may be stronger than currently expected owing to the need for fiscal consolidation in the coming years.

column1: Turning to the monetary analysis
column2: both the annual growth rates of M3 and loans to the private sector were negative in November
column3: standing at -0.2% and -0.7% respectively. The concurrent declines to historically low growth rates recorded in these two series over the past months support the assessment of a decelerating underlying pace of monetary expansion and low inflationary pressures over the medium term. Looking ahead
column4: M3 and credit growth are likely to remain very weak or negative for some time to come.

column1: The decline in actual monetary growth is likely to overstate the deceleration in the underlying pace of monetary expansion. This is due to the continued steep slope of the yield curve
column2: which explains shifts of funds out of M3 into longer-term deposits and securities. At the same time
column3: the interest rate constellation continues to foster divergent developments in the main components of M3
column4: as the narrow spreads between the rates on different short-term bank deposits reduce the opportunity costs of shifting funds from
column5: for instance
column6: short-term time deposits into overnight deposits. As a result
column7: M1 continued to grow at a robust annual rate of 12.6% in November
column8: when annual M3 growth turned negative.

column1: The negative annual growth of bank loans to the private sector conceals a return to positive annual rates of growth in the case of loans to households
column2: while the annual growth of loans to non-financial corporations became more negative. Such divergence remains in line with business cycle regularities
column3: with turning points in the growth of loans to enterprises typically lagging those in economic activity. In the case of households
column4: the latest data provide further confirmation of a levelling-off at low rates. In the case of non-financial corporations
column5: the decline in loans continues to reflect mainly a strong net redemption of loans with a shorter maturity
column6: while lending and borrowing at longer maturities remained positive. The subdued levels of production and trade
column7: as well as the ongoing uncertainty surrounding the business outlook
column8: will probably continue to dampen firms’ demand for bank financing in the months to come. In the meantime
column9: financing conditions for enterprises have improved over recent months in terms of the cost of both bank credit and market financing. In this respect
column10: the continued negative flows in short-term bank loans to non-financial corporations observed in recent months may partly reflect better possibilities for substitution with different sources of longer-term financing.

column1: Banks have continued to reduce the size of their overall balance sheets
column2: mainly through downsizing the assets held vis-à-vis other banks. The challenge remains to adjust the size and structure of balance sheets while ensuring the availability of credit to the non-financial sector. To address this challenge
column3: banks should use the improved funding conditions to strengthen further their capital bases and
column4: where necessary
column5: take full advantage of government support measures for recapitalisation.

column1: To sum up
column2: the current key ECB interest rates remain appropriate. Taking into account all the information and analyses that have become available since our meeting on 3 December 2009
column3: price developments are expected to remain subdued over the policy-relevant horizon. The latest information has also confirmed that towards the end of 2009 euro area economic activity continued to expand. However
column4: some of the factors supporting the growth in real GDP are of a temporary nature. Overall
column5: the Governing Council expects the euro area economy to grow at a moderate pace in 2010
column6: recognising that the recovery process is likely to be uneven and that the outlook remains subject to uncertainty. A cross-check of the outcome of the economic analysis with that of the monetary analysis confirms the assessment of low inflationary pressure over the medium term
column7: given the ongoing parallel decline in money and credit growth. All in all
column8: we expect price stability to be maintained over the medium term
column9: thereby supporting the purchasing power of euro area households. Medium to longer-term inflation expectations remain firmly anchored in line with the Governing Council’s aim of keeping inflation rates below
column10: but close to
column11: 2% over the medium term.

column1: We will continue our enhanced credit support to the banking system
column2: while taking into account the ongoing improvement in financial market conditions and avoiding distortions associated with maintaining non-standard measures for too long. The Governing Council will also continue to implement the gradual phasing-out of the extraordinary liquidity measures that are not needed to the same extent as in the past. In order to counter effectively any threat to price stability over the medium to longer term
column3: the liquidity provided will be absorbed when necessary. Accordingly
column4: we will continue to monitor very closely all developments over the period ahead.

column1: As regards fiscal policies
column2: many euro area governments are faced with high and sharply rising fiscal imbalances. The very large government borrowing requirements carry the risk of triggering rapid changes in market sentiment
column3: leading to less favourable medium and long-term market interest rates. This
column4: in turn
column5: would dampen private investment and thereby weaken the foundations for sustained growth. Moreover
column6: high levels of public deficit and debt would place an additional burden on monetary policy and undermine the credibility of the provisions of both the Treaty on European Union and the Stability and Growth Pact as a key pillar of Economic and Monetary Union. The Governing Council therefore calls upon governments to decide and implement in a timely fashion ambitious fiscal exit and consolidation strategies based on realistic growth assumptions
column7: with a strong focus on expenditure reforms. Tax cuts should only be considered over the medium term
column8: when countries have regained sufficient room for budgetary manoeuvre. In this regard
column9: current government commitments to start consolidation in 2011 at the latest and to go well beyond the structural benchmark for adjustment of 0.5% of GDP per annum represent the minimum requirement for all euro area countries. The success of fiscal adjustment strategies will also depend
column10: crucially
column11: on appropriate national budgetary rules and institutions and requires transparent budgetary procedures
column12: as well as reliable and complete government finance statistics.

column1: Turning to structural reforms
column2: an appropriate restructuring of the banking sector should play an important role. Sound balance sheets
column3: effective risk management
column4: and transparent as well as robust business models are key to strengthening banks’ resilience to shocks
column5: thereby laying the foundations for sustainable economic growth and financial stability.

column1: The Eurosystem will submit its response to the European Commission’s public consultation on the EU 2020 strategy
column2: which is designed as a successor to the current Lisbon strategy. To address future challenges
column3: the EU 2020 strategy should focus on raising potential growth and creating high levels of employment through well-functioning labour and product markets
column4: sound financial systems and sustainable fiscal policies. The aim is to achieve a highly competitive social market economy
column5: as spelled out in the Treaty.

column1: On the first question
column2: as you know
column3: we have enormous difficulties ahead of us. We did our job properly in the past because we took very bold decisions and avoided depression. It is extremely important that all the economic agents realise the seriousness of the situation we would have had without the rapidity and the boldness of the decisions taken by the ECB and other central banks or the decisions of our governments. We avoided that
column4: but we still had a big recession and a lot of problems. We are called upon to reform the financial system. I have to say that the work which has been done by all of us
column5: – I’m speaking in particular of the ECB’s Governing Council as a whole and of a number of members of the Governing Council in various positions

And I would say that the G20 has been extremely important in enlarging global governance as well as in working out a consensus on the methodology and goals for drawing the lessons from the crisis. But again
column7: this is no time for complacency. We have a very hard job ahead of us. I have already told you that we cannot afford to have a financial system which is as fragile in the future as it has proved to be in the past. Our democracies in particular would not accept that. And
column8: in my opinion
column9: would not stand ready to do in the future what they have accepted to do in the past. So we are obliged to find appropriate ways for making the system more resilient.

column1: Let me now explain our assessment in greater detail

column9: but close to

column5: where necessary

column1: As regards fiscal policies
column2: it is now essential that governments reduce budget imbalances and correct excessive deficits by the agreed deadlines. In a number of euro area countries
column3: fiscal consolidation will start this year and in all others corrective measures will need to be in place by 2011 at the latest. Fiscal consolidation will need to exceed substantially the annual structural adjustment of 0.5% of GDP set as a minimum requirement by the Stability and Growth Pact
column4: and there is a need to fully define and implement credible fiscal adjustment strategies. This requires determined efforts
column5: notably on the part of countries with high government deficit and debt-to-GDP ratios
column6: not least in view of the expected rising budgetary costs associated with an ageing population. A strong focus on expenditure reforms is needed. The Governing Council welcomes the statement on Greece made by the Heads of State and Government of the euro area countries on 25 March. We fully support the intention to strengthen surveillance of economic and budgetary risks and the instruments for their prevention as well as the excessive deficit procedure. We also welcome the decision to work on a robust crisis resolution framework. Progress in these fields should aim to support the sustainability of public finances and promote the smooth functioning of EMU.

column2: the agreements reached at the European Council on 25 and 26 March on the Europe 2020 strategy should help to reinforce job creation
column3: competitiveness and sustainable growth. To this end
column4: policies should now focus on increasing competition

column6: sufficient wage flexibility and a reinforcement of incentives to work are required
column7: in order to avoid higher structural unemployment over the coming years. In the same vein
column8: an appropriate restructuring of the banking sector remains essential. Sound balance sheets
column9: effective risk management and transparent
column10: robust business models are key to strengthening banks’ resilience to shocks and to ensuring adequate access to finance
column11: thereby laying the foundations for sustainable growth and financial stability.

column2: the Governing Council has decided to keep the minimum credit threshold for marketable and non-marketable assets in the Eurosystem collateral framework at investment-grade level (i.e. BBB-/Baa3) beyond the end of 2010

The detailed haircut schedule will be based on a number of parameters which are specified in the press release to be published after today’s press conference.

column1: Let me now explain our assessment in greater detail

column5: on a quarterly basis

column7: in particular
column8: dampened growth in the early part of the year

column4: in an environment of increasing demand. To address this challenge
column5: where necessary
column6: it is essential for banks to retain earnings

column1: To sum up
column2: the current key ECB interest rates still remain appropriate. We therefore decided to leave them unchanged. Taking into account all the new information and analyses which have become available since our meeting on 13 January 2011
column3: we continue to see evidence of short-term upward pressure on overall inflation
column4: mainly owing to energy and commodity prices. This has not so far affected our assessment that price developments will remain in line with price stability over the policy-relevant horizon. At the same time
column5: very close monitoring is warranted. Recent economic data confirm the positive underlying momentum of economic activity in the euro area
column6: while uncertainty remains elevated. A cross-check of the outcome of our economic analysis with that of the monetary analysis indicates that inflationary pressures over the medium to long term should remain contained. Inflation expectations remain firmly anchored in line with our aim of keeping inflation rates below
column7: but close to
column8: 2% over the medium term. The continued firm anchoring of inflation expectations is of the essence.

column1: Turning to fiscal policies
column2: it is now essential that all governments fully implement their fiscal consolidation plans in 2011. Where necessary
column3: additional corrective measures must be implemented swiftly to ensure progress in achieving fiscal sustainability. Beyond 2011
column4: countries need to specify concrete policy measures in their multi-year adjustment programmes so as to underpin the credibility of their fiscal consolidation targets. Experience shows that expenditure restraint is an important step towards achieving and maintaining fiscal soundness
column5: notably when enshrined in binding domestic policy rules. Such a commitment helps to strengthen confidence in the sustainability of public finances
column6: reduces interest rate risk premia and improves the conditions for sound and sustainable growth. The implementation of credible policies is crucial in view of ongoing financial market pressures.

column1: Substantial and far-reaching structural reforms
column2: complementing fiscal adjustment
column3: should be urgently implemented to improve the prospects for higher sustainable growth and employment. Major reforms are particularly necessary in those countries that have experienced a loss of competitiveness in the past or that are suffering from high fiscal and external deficits. Increased product market competition and labour market flexibility would further support the necessary adjustment processes in the economy. All these structural reforms should be supported by the necessary improvements in the structure of the banking sector. Sound balance sheets
column4: effective risk management and transparent
column5: robust business models remain key to strengthening banks’ resilience to shocks and to ensuring adequate access to finance
column6: thereby laying the foundations for sustainable growth and financial stability.

column1: Based on its regular economic and monetary analyses
column2: the Governing Council decided to leave the key ECB interest rates unchanged. The information which has become available since our meeting on 3 February 2011 indicates a rise in inflation
column3: largely reflecting higher commodity prices. The economic analysis indicates that risks to the outlook for price developments are on the upside
column4: while the underlying pace of monetary expansion remains moderate. Recent economic data confirm that the underlying momentum of economic activity in the euro area remains positive; however
column5: uncertainty remains elevated. The current very accommodative stance of monetary policy lends considerable support to economic activity. It is essential that the recent rise in inflation does not give rise to broad-based inflationary pressures over the medium term. Strong vigilance is warranted with a view to containing upside risks to price stability. Overall
column6: the Governing Council remains prepared to act in a firm and timely manner to ensure that upside risks to price stability over the medium term do not materialise. The continued firm anchoring of inflation expectations is of the essence.

column1: The Governing Council today also decided to continue conducting its main refinancing operations (MROs) and the special-term refinancing operations with a maturity of one maintenance period as fixed rate tender procedures with full allotment for as long as necessary
column2: and at least until the end of the sixth maintenance period of 2011 on 12 July 2011. Furthermore
column3: the Governing Council decided to conduct the three-month longer-term refinancing operations (LTROs) to be allotted on 27 April
column4: 25 May and 29 June 2011 as fixed rate tender procedures with full allotment. The rates in these three-month operations will be fixed at the average rate of the MROs over the life of the respective LTRO.

column2: the provision of liquidity and the allotment modes will be adjusted as appropriate
column3: taking into account the fact that all the non-standard measures taken during the period of acute financial market tensions are
column4: by construction
column5: temporary in nature. Accordingly
column6: the Governing Council will continue to monitor all developments over the period ahead very closely.

column1: Let me now explain our assessment in greater detail
column2: starting with the economic analysis. Following the 0.3% quarter-on-quarter increase in euro area real GDP in both the third and the fourth quarter of 2010
column3: recent statistical releases and survey-based evidence continue to confirm the positive underlying momentum of economic activity in the euro area at the beginning of 2011. Looking ahead
column4: euro area exports should continue to be supported by the ongoing recovery in the world economy. At the same time
column5: taking into account the relatively high level of business confidence in the euro area
column6: private sector domestic demand should increasingly contribute to growth
column7: benefiting from the very accommodative monetary policy stance and the measures adopted to improve the functioning of the financial system. However
column8: the recovery in activity is expected to be dampened somewhat by the process of balance sheet adjustment in various sectors.

column1: This assessment is also reflected in the March 2011 ECB staff macroeconomic projections for the euro area
column2: which foresee annual real GDP growth in a range between 1.3% and 2.1% in 2011 and between 0.8% and 2.8% in 2012. Compared with the December 2010 Eurosystem staff macroeconomic projections
column3: the lower ends of these ranges have been shifted upwards
column4: reflecting better prospects for the global economy – and thus for euro area exports – as well as for domestic demand. The March 2011 ECB staff projections are broadly in line with forecasts by international organisations.

column1: In the Governing Council’s assessment
column2: the risks to this economic outlook are broadly balanced in a context of elevated uncertainty. On the one hand
column3: global trade may continue to grow more rapidly than expected
column4: thereby supporting euro area exports. Moreover
column5: strong business confidence could provide more support to domestic economic activity in the euro area than is currently expected. On the other hand
column6: downside risks relate to the ongoing tensions in some segments of the financial markets and their potential spillover to the euro area real economy. Downside risks also relate to further increases in commodity prices
column7: in particular in view of renewed geopolitical tensions
column8: and to protectionist pressures and the possibility of a disorderly correction of global imbalances.

column1: With regard to price developments
column2: euro area annual HICP inflation was 2.4% in February 2011
column3: according to Eurostat’s flash estimate
column4: after 2.3% in January. The increase in inflation rates in early 2011 largely reflects higher commodity prices. Pressure stemming from the sharp increases in energy and food prices is also discernible in the earlier stages of the production process. It is paramount that the rise in HICP inflation does not lead to second-round effects and thereby give rise to broad-based inflationary pressures over the medium term. Inflation expectations over the medium to longer term must remain firmly anchored in line with the Governing Council’s aim of maintaining inflation rates below
column5: but close to
column6: 2% over the medium term.

column1: The March 2011 ECB staff macroeconomic projections for the euro area foresee annual HICP inflation in a range between 2.0% and 2.6% for 2011 and between 1.0% and 2.4% for 2012. In comparison with the December 2010 Eurosystem staff macroeconomic projections
column2: the ranges for HICP inflation have been shifted upwards. This is mainly due to the considerable rise in energy and food prices. It should be stressed that the projections are based on commodity price futures as of mid-February 2011
column3: and therefore do not take into account the most recent oil price increases. Moreover
column4: it needs to be emphasised that the projections assume continued moderate domestic wage and price-setting behaviour.

column1: Risks to the medium-term outlook for price developments are on the upside. They relate
column2: in particular
column3: to higher than assumed increases in energy and non-energy commodity prices. Furthermore
column4: increases in indirect taxes and administered prices may be greater than currently assumed
column5: owing to the need for fiscal consolidation in the coming years. Finally
column6: risks also relate to stronger than expected domestic price pressures in the context of the ongoing recovery in activity. Price and wage setters’ behaviour should not lead to broadly based second-round effects stemming from higher commodity prices.

column1: Turning to the monetary analysis
column2: the annual growth rate of M3 declined to 1.5% in January 2011
column3: from 1.7% in December 2010
column4: while the annual growth rate of loans to the private sector increased to 2.4% in January
column5: from 1.9% in December. Looking beyond the movements in individual months and the effects of special factors
column6: trends in broad money and loan growth confirm the assessment that the underlying pace of monetary expansion is still moderate and that inflationary pressures over the medium to longer term should remain contained. At the same time
column7: the low level of money and credit growth has thus far led to only a partial unwinding of the large amounts of monetary liquidity accumulated in the economy prior to the period of financial tensions. This liquidity may facilitate the accommodation of price pressures currently emerging in commodity markets as a result of strong economic growth and ample liquidity at the global level.

column1: Looking at M3 components
column2: annual M1 growth moderated further to stand at 3.2% in January 2011
column3: reflecting the prevailing low remuneration of overnight deposits. At the same time
column4: the yield curve steepened somewhat further at the start of the year
column5: implying that the attractiveness of short-term instruments included in M3 continues to decline compared with more highly remunerated longer-term instruments outside M3.

column1: On the counterpart side
column2: the rise in the annual growth rate of bank loans to the private sector in January was due to stronger lending to both households and non-financial corporations. The growth of loans to non-financial corporations turned positive
column3: to stand at 0.4% in January
column4: after -0.2% in December
column5: while the growth of loans to households strengthened further to 3.1%
column6: from 2.9% in December. Overall
column7: lending to the non-financial private sector has gradually strengthened over the past few quarters
column8: as the economic recovery gathered momentum.

column1: The latest data also confirm that banks have continued to expand their lending to the euro area economy
column2: while at the same time keeping the overall size of their balance sheets broadly unchanged. It is important that banks continue to expand the provision of credit to the private sector
column3: in an environment of increasing demand. To address this challenge
column4: where necessary
column5: it is essential for banks to retain earnings
column6: to turn to the market to strengthen further their capital bases or to take full advantage of government support measures for recapitalisation. In particular
column7: banks that currently have limited access to market financing urgently need to increase their capital and their efficiency.

column1: 2011-05-05;2;"Ladies and gentlemen
column2: the Vice-President and I are very pleased to welcome you to our press conference here in Helsinki. column1: Based on its regular economic and monetary analyses
column2: the Governing Council decided to keep the key ECB interest rates unchanged following the 25-basis point increase on 7 April 2011. The information that has become available since then confirms our assessment that an adjustment of the very accommodative monetary policy stance was warranted. We continue to see upward pressure on overall inflation
column3: mainly owing to energy and commodity prices. While the monetary analysis indicates that the underlying pace of monetary expansion is still moderate
column4: monetary liquidity remains ample and may facilitate the accommodation of price pressures. Furthermore
column5: recent economic data confirm the positive underlying momentum of economic activity in the euro area
column6: with uncertainty continuing to be elevated. All in all
column7: it is essential that recent price developments do not give rise to broad-based inflationary pressures. Inflation expectations in the euro area must remain firmly anchored in line with our aim of maintaining inflation rates below
column8: but close to
column9: 2% over the medium term. Such anchoring is a prerequisite for monetary policy to make an ongoing contribution towards supporting economic growth and job creation in the euro area. With interest rates across the entire maturity spectrum remaining low and the monetary policy stance still accommodative
column10: we will continue to monitor very closely all developments with respect to upside risks to price stability. Maintaining price stability over the medium term is our guiding principle
column11: which we apply when assessing new information
column12: forming our judgements and deciding on any further adjustment of the accommodative stance of monetary policy.

column1: As stated on previous occasions
column2: the provision of liquidity and the allotment modes for refinancing operations will also be adjusted when appropriate
column3: taking into account the fact that all the non-standard measures taken during the period of acute financial market tensions are
column4: by construction
column5: temporary in nature.

column1: Let me now explain our assessment in greater detail
column2: starting with the economic analysis. Following the 0.3% quarter-on-quarter increase in euro area real GDP in the fourth quarter of 2010
column3: recent statistical releases and survey-based indicators point towards a continued positive underlying momentum of economic activity in the euro area during the first quarter of 2011 and at the beginning of the second quarter. Looking ahead
column4: euro area exports should be supported by the ongoing expansion in the world economy. At the same time
column5: taking into account the high level of business confidence in the euro area
column6: private sector domestic demand should contribute increasingly to economic growth
column7: benefiting from the accommodative monetary policy stance and the measures adopted to improve the functioning of the financial system. However
column8: activity is expected to continue to be dampened somewhat by the process of balance sheet adjustment in various sectors.

column1: In the Governing Council’s assessment
column2: the risks to this economic outlook remain broadly balanced in an environment of elevated uncertainty. On the one hand
column3: global trade may continue to grow more rapidly than expected
column4: thereby supporting euro area exports. Moreover
column5: strong business confidence could provide more support to domestic economic activity in the euro area than currently expected. On the other hand
column6: downside risks relate to the ongoing tensions in some segments of the financial markets that may potentially spill over to the euro area real economy. Downside risks also relate to further increases in energy prices
column7: particularly in view of ongoing geopolitical tensions in North Africa and the Middle East
column8: and to protectionist pressures and the possibility of a disorderly correction of global imbalances. Finally
column9: there are still potential risks stemming from the economic impact on the euro area and elsewhere of the natural and nuclear disasters in Japan.

column1: With regard to price developments
column2: euro area annual HICP inflation was 2.8% in April according to Eurostat’s flash estimate
column3: after 2.7% in March. The increase in inflation rates during the first four months of 2011 largely reflects higher commodity prices. Looking ahead
column4: inflation rates are likely to stay clearly above 2% over the coming months. Upward pressure on inflation
column5: mainly from energy and commodity prices
column6: is also discernible in the earlier stages of the production process. It is of paramount importance that the rise in HICP inflation does not translate into second-round effects in price and wage-setting behaviour and lead to broad-based inflationary pressures. Inflation expectations must remain firmly anchored in line with the Governing Council’s aim of maintaining inflation rates below
column7: but close to
column8: 2% over the medium term.

column1: Risks to the medium-term outlook for price developments remain on the upside. They relate
column2: in particular
column3: to higher than assumed increases in energy prices
column4: not least on account of the ongoing political tensions in North Africa and the Middle East. More generally
column5: strong economic growth in emerging markets
column6: supported by ample liquidity at the global level
column7: may further fuel commodity price rises. Moreover
column8: increases in indirect taxes and administered prices may be greater than currently assumed
column9: owing to the need for fiscal consolidation in the coming years. Finally
column10: risks also relate to stronger than expected domestic price pressures in the context of the ongoing recovery in activity.

column1: Turning to the monetary analysis
column2: the annual growth rate of M3 increased to 2.3% in March 2011
column3: from 2.1% in February. Looking through the recent volatility in broad money growth caused by special factors
column4: M3 growth has continued to edge up over recent months. The annual growth rate of loans to the private sector remained broadly unchanged at 2.5% in March
column5: after 2.6% in February. Overall
column6: the underlying pace of monetary expansion is gradually picking up
column7: but it remains moderate. At the same time
column8: monetary liquidity accumulated prior to the period of financial market tensions remains ample and may facilitate the accommodation of price pressures in the euro area.

column1: Looking at M3 components
column2: the annual growth rate of M1 remained broadly unchanged in March
column3: while that of other short-term deposits increased. The development partly reflects the gradual increase in the remuneration of these deposits over recent months. At the same time
column4: the steep yield curve implies a dampening impact on overall M3 growth
column5: as it reduces the attractiveness of monetary assets compared with more highly remunerated longer-term instruments outside M3.

column1: On the counterpart side
column2: there has been a further slight strengthening in the growth of loans to non-financial corporations
column3: which rose to 0.8% in March
column4: after 0.6% in February. The growth of loans to households was 3.4% in March
column5: compared with 3.0% in February. Looking through short-term volatility
column6: the latest data confirm a continued gradual strengthening in the annual growth of lending to the non-financial private sector.

column1: The overall size of bank balance sheets has remained broadly unchanged over the past few months
column2: notwithstanding some volatility. It is important that banks continue to expand the provision of credit to the private sector in an environment of increasing demand. To address this challenge
column3: where necessary
column4: it is essential for banks to retain earnings
column5: to turn to the market to strengthen further their capital bases or to take full advantage of government support measures for recapitalisation. In particular
column6: banks that currently have limited access to market financing urgently need to increase their capital and their efficiency.

column1: Based on its regular economic and monetary analyses
column2: the Governing Council decided to keep the key ECB interest rates unchanged
column3: following the 25 basis point increase on 7 July 2011. While the monetary analysis indicates that the underlying pace of monetary expansion is still moderate
column4: monetary liquidity remains ample and may facilitate the accommodation of price pressures. As expected

column2: the Governing Council today also decided to conduct a liquidity-providing supplementary longer-term refinancing operation (LTRO) with a maturity of approximately six months. column3: albeit
column4: as expected

column6: the present level of consumer and business confidence in the euro area supports private sector domestic demand. However

column1: Fiscal consolidation and structural reforms must go hand in hand to strengthen confidence
column2: growth prospects and job creation. The Governing Council therefore urges all euro area governments to decisively and swiftly implement substantial and comprehensive structural reforms. This will help these countries to strengthen competitiveness
column3: increase the flexibility of their economies and enhance their longer-term growth potential. In this respect

column5: with a focus on the removal of rigidities and the implementation of measures which enhance wage flexibility. In particular
column6: we should see the elimination of automatic wage indexation clauses and a strengthening of firm-level agreements so that wages and working conditions can be tailored to firms’ specific needs. column8: where appropriate

column1: Based on its regular economic and monetary analyses
column2: the Governing Council decided to keep the key ECB interest rates unchanged. Inflation has remained elevated and incoming information has confirmed our view that inflation is likely to stay above 2% over the months ahead but to decline thereafter. At the same time
column3: the underlying pace of monetary expansion continues to be moderate. Ongoing tensions in financial markets and unfavourable effects on financing conditions are likely to dampen the pace of economic growth in the euro area in the second half of this year. The economic outlook remains subject to particularly high uncertainty and intensified downside risks. At the same time
column4: short-term interest rates remain low. It remains essential for monetary policy to maintain price stability over the medium term
column5: thereby ensuring a firm anchoring of inflation expectations in the euro area in line with our aim of maintaining inflation rates below
column6: but close to
column7: 2% over the medium term. Such anchoring is a prerequisite for monetary policy to make its contribution towards supporting economic growth and job creation in the euro area. A very thorough analysis of all incoming data and developments over the period ahead is warranted.

column1: The Governing Council has decided to conduct two longer-term refinancing operations (LTROs)
column2: one with a maturity of approximately 12 months in October and the other with a maturity of approximately 13 months in December. The operations will be conducted as fixed rate tender procedures with full allotment. The rate in both operations will be fixed at the average rate of the main refinancing operations (MROs) over the life of the respective LTRO
column3: and interest will be paid when each operation matures. These operations will be conducted in addition to the regular and special-term refinancing operations

column1: Based on our regular economic and monetary analyses
column2: we decided to keep the key ECB interest rates unchanged. The information that has become available since mid-January broadly confirms our previous assessment. Inflation is likely to stay above 2% for several months to come
column3: before declining to below 2%. Available survey indicators confirm some tentative signs of a stabilisation in economic activity at a low level around the turn of the year
column4: but the economic outlook remains subject to high uncertainty and downside risks. The underlying pace of monetary expansion remains subdued. Looking ahead
column5: it is essential for monetary policy to maintain price stability for the euro area as a whole. This ensures a firm anchoring of inflation expectations in line with our aim of maintaining inflation rates below
column6: but close to
column7: 2% over the medium term. Such anchoring is a prerequisite for monetary policy to make its contribution to supporting economic growth and job creation in the euro area. A very thorough analysis of all incoming data and developments over the period ahead is warranted.

column1: Through our non-standard monetary policy measures we will continue to support the functioning of the euro area financial sector
column2: and thus the financing of the real economy. Since the first three-year longer-term refinancing operation (LTRO) was conducted in December 2011 we have approved specific national eligibility criteria and risk control measures for the temporary acceptance in a number of countries of additional credit claims as collateral in Eurosystem credit operations
column3: which should lead to an increase in available collateral. Further details will be provided in a press release to be published today at 3.30 p.m. At the start of the current reserve maintenance period on 18 January 2012 the reserve ratio was reduced
column4: freeing up additional collateral. As stated on previous occasions
column5: all our non-standard measures are temporary in nature.

column1: Let me now explain our assessment in greater detail
column2: starting with the economic analysis. Real GDP growth in the fourth quarter of 2011 is likely to have been very weak. According to the survey data for the last two months
column3: there are tentative signs of a stabilisation in economic activity at a low level. Looking ahead
column4: we expect the euro area economy to recover very gradually in the course of 2012. The very low short-term interest rates and all the measures taken to foster the proper functioning of the euro area financial sector are lending support to the euro area economy. Moreover
column5: stress in financial markets has diminished in response to our monetary policy measures
column6: but also in response to the progress made towards a stronger euro area governance framework and intensified fiscal consolidation in several euro area countries. However
column7: subdued global demand growth
column8: the remaining tensions in euro area sovereign debt markets and their impact on credit conditions
column9: as well as the process of balance sheet adjustment in the financial and non-financial sectors
column10: continue to dampen the underlying growth momentum.

column1: This outlook is subject to downside risks. They notably relate to tensions in euro area debt markets and their potential spillover to the euro area real economy. Downside risks also relate to possible adverse developments in the global economy
column2: higher than assumed increases in commodity prices
column3: protectionist pressures and the potential for a disorderly correction of global imbalances.

column1: Euro area annual HICP inflation was 2.7% in January 2012
column2: according to Eurostat’s flash estimate
column3: unchanged from December. The average inflation rate for 2011 was 2.7%
column4: mainly driven by higher energy and other commodity prices. Looking ahead
column5: inflation is likely to stay above 2% for several months to come
column6: before declining to below 2%. This pattern reflects the expectation that
column7: in an environment of weak growth in the euro area and globally
column8: underlying price pressures in the euro area should remain limited.

column1: Risks to the medium-term outlook for price developments remain broadly balanced. On the upside
column2: they relate to higher than assumed increases in indirect taxes and administered prices
column3: as well as increases in commodity prices. The main downside risks relate to the impact of weaker than expected growth in the euro area and globally.

column1: The monetary analysis indicates that the underlying pace of monetary expansion remains subdued. The annual growth rate of M3 decreased to 1.6% in December 2011
column2: after 2.0% in November
column3: reflecting a further weakening of monetary dynamics towards the end of the year.

column1: The annual growth rates of loans to non-financial corporations and loans to households
column2: adjusted for loan sales and securitisation
column3: also decreased further in December
column4: and stood at 1.2% and 1.9% respectively. The volume of MFI loans to both sectors declined in December
column5: and this was particularly pronounced in the case of the non-financial corporate sector. In addition
column6: there are indications that bank lending conditions tightened further
column7: affecting loan supply in several euro area countries in late 2011. It is not yet possible to draw firm conclusions from these developments
column8: particularly given that the impact of the first three-year LTRO on bank funding is still unfolding and may not have been fully reflected in the most recent bank lending survey. In addition
column9: other non-standard monetary policy measures announced in December are still to be implemented. Accordingly
column10: close scrutiny of credit developments in the period ahead is essential.

column1: The soundness of bank balance sheets will be a key factor in facilitating an appropriate provision of credit to the economy over time. It is essential that the implementation of banks’ recapitalisation plans does not result in developments that are detrimental to the financing of economic activity in the euro area.
To sum up
column2: the economic analysis indicates that underlying price pressures should remain limited and risks to the medium-term outlook for price developments remain broadly balanced. A cross-check with the signals from the monetary analysis confirms this picture.

column1: A combination of structural reforms and fiscal discipline is essential for boosting confidence and delivering a favourable environment for sustainable growth. Regarding fiscal policies
column2: all euro area governments need to continue to do their utmost to ensure fiscal sustainability. It is essential that all countries adhere to the fiscal targets they announced for 2012. This should help to anchor expectations of sound fiscal policies and strengthen confidence. The rules guiding the design and implementation of national fiscal policies are being strengthened at the EU level as well as in the legal frameworks of several Member States. These are important steps in the right direction. With regard to structural reforms
column3: these are key to increasing the adjustment capacity and competitiveness of euro area countries
column4: thereby strengthening growth prospects and job creation. Notably
column5: far-reaching and ambitious reforms should be implemented to foster competition in product markets
column6: particularly in services sectors
column7: while rigidities in labour markets should be reduced and wage flexibility should be enhanced.

2012-03-08;3;Ladies and gentlemen
column2: the Vice-President and I are very pleased to welcome you to our press conference. We will now report on the outcome of today’s meeting of the Governing Council.

column1: Based on our regular economic and monetary analyses
column2: we decided to keep the key ECB interest rates unchanged. The information that has become available since the beginning of February has confirmed our previous assessment of the outlook for economic activity. Available survey indicators confirm signs of a stabilisation in the euro area economy. However
column3: the economic outlook is still subject to downside risks. Owing to rises in energy prices and indirect taxes
column4: inflation rates are now likely to stay above 2% in 2012
column5: with upside risks prevailing. Nevertheless
column6: we expect price developments to remain in line with price stability over the policy-relevant horizon. The underlying pace of monetary expansion remains subdued
column7: consistent with contained inflationary pressures over the medium term.

column1: Looking ahead
column2: we are firmly committed to maintaining price stability in the euro area
column3: in line with our mandate. To this end
column4: the continued firm anchoring of inflation expectations – in line with our aim of maintaining inflation rates below
column5: but close to
column6: 2% over the medium term – is of the essence.

column1: Over recent months
column2: a wide range of additional non-standard monetary policy measures has been implemented by the Eurosystem. These measures
column3: including in particular two three-year longer-term refinancing operations
column4: were decided upon against the background of exceptional circumstances in the last quarter of 2011. The first impact of these measures has been positive. Together with fiscal consolidation and stepped-up structural reforms in several euro area countries
column5: as well as progress towards a stronger euro area economic governance framework
column6: they have contributed to a significant improvement in the financial environment over recent months. We expect that the three-year longer-term refinancing operations will provide further support for the ongoing stabilisation in financial markets and
column7: in particular
column8: for lending activity in the euro area. All our non-standard monetary policy measures are temporary in nature. Furthermore
column9: all the necessary tools to address potential upside risks to medium-term price stability are fully available.

column1: Let me now explain our assessment in greater detail
column2: starting with the economic analysis. Real GDP contracted by 0.3% in the euro area in the fourth quarter of 2011. According to recent survey data
column3: there are signs of a stabilisation in economic activity
column4: albeit still at a low level. Looking ahead
column5: we expect the euro area economy to recover gradually in the course of this year. The outlook for economic activity should be supported by foreign demand
column6: the very low short-term interest rates in the euro area
column7: and all the measures taken to foster the proper functioning of the euro area financial sector. However
column8: the remaining tensions in euro area sovereign debt markets and their impact on credit conditions
column9: as well as the process of balance sheet adjustment in the financial and non-financial sectors
column10: are expected to continue to dampen the underlying growth momentum.

column1: This assessment is also reflected in the March 2012 ECB staff macroeconomic projections for the euro area
column2: which foresee annual real GDP growth in a range between -0.5% and 0.3% in 2012 and between 0.0% and 2.2% in 2013. Compared with the December 2011 Eurosystem staff macroeconomic projections
column3: the ranges have been shifted slightly downwards.

column1: This outlook remains subject to downside risks. They notably relate to a renewed intensification of tensions in euro area debt markets and their potential spillover to the euro area real economy. Downside risks also relate to further increases in commodity prices.
Euro area annual HICP inflation was 2.7% in February 2012
column2: according to Eurostat’s flash estimate
column3: slightly up from 2.6% in January. Looking ahead
column4: inflation is now likely to stay above 2% in 2012
column5: mainly owing to recent increases in energy prices
column6: as well as recently announced increases in indirect taxes. On the basis of current futures prices for commodities
column7: annual inflation rates should fall again to below 2% in early 2013. Looking further ahead
column8: in an environment of modest growth in the euro area and well-anchored long-term inflation expectations
column9: underlying price pressures should remain limited.

column1: The March 2012 ECB staff macroeconomic projections for the euro area foresee annual HICP inflation in a range between 2.1% and 2.7% in 2012 and between 0.9% and 2.3% in 2013. In comparison with the December 2011 Eurosystem staff macroeconomic projections
column2: the ranges for HICP inflation have been shifted upwards
column3: notably the range for 2012.

column1: Risks to projected HICP inflation rates in the coming years are seen to be still broadly balanced
column2: with upside risks in the near term mainly stemming from higher than expected oil prices and indirect tax increases. However
column3: downside risks continue to exist owing to weaker than expected developments in economic activity.

column1: The monetary analysis indicates that the underlying pace of monetary expansion remains subdued. The annual growth rate of M3 was 2.5% in January 2012
column2: up from 1.5% in December 2011. Loan growth to the private sector also remains subdued. However
column3: its annual rate (adjusted for loan sales and securitisation) picked up slightly in January to 1.5% year on year from 1.2% in December.

column1: The annual growth rates of loans to non-financial corporations and loans to households (adjusted for loan sales and securitisation) stood at 0.8% and 2.1% respectively in January. The volume of MFI loans to non-financial corporations declined only slightly in January
column2: following the pronounced decline in December. By contrast
column3: the flow of loans to households in January was positive.

column1: Following the signs of improvement in the financial environment
column2: it is essential for banks to strengthen their resilience further
column3: including by retaining earnings. The soundness of banks’ balance sheets will be a key factor in facilitating an appropriate provision of credit to the economy.

column1: To sum up
column2: the economic analysis indicates that price developments should remain in line with price stability over the medium term. A cross-check with the signals from the monetary analysis confirms this picture.

column1: Looking ahead
column2: in order to deliver a favourable environment for sustainable growth and to support confidence and competitiveness
column3: the Governing Council stresses the urgent need for governments to make further progress towards restoring sound fiscal positions and implementing the structural reform agenda. Regarding fiscal consolidation
column4: many governments in the euro area are making progress. Continuing with comprehensive fiscal consolidation and complying with all commitments remains essential. In this respect
column5: the 2012 European Semester should be used to enforce rigorously the reinforced fiscal surveillance mechanism. Equally important are structural reforms to increase the adjustment capacity and competitiveness of euro area countries and to strengthen growth prospects and job creation. In this area
column6: more progress is desirable. The Governing Council strongly welcomes the European Commission’s Alert Mechanism Report on macroeconomic imbalances and expects the proposed in-depth country reviews to actively support the reform processes under way in euro area countries.
