column2: the Vice-President and I are very pleased to welcome you to our press conference. We will now report on the outcome of today’s meeting of the Governing Council.

column1: Based on our regular economic and monetary analyses
column2: we decided to keep the key ECB interest rates unchanged. The information that has become available since the beginning of March broadly confirms our previous assessment. Inflation rates are likely to stay above 2% in 2012
column3: with upside risks prevailing. Over the policy-relevant horizon
column4: we expect price developments to remain in line with price stability. Consistent with this picture
column5: the underlying pace of monetary expansion remains subdued. Survey indicators for economic growth have broadly stabilised at low levels in the early months of 2012
column6: and a moderate recovery in activity is expected in the course of the year. The economic outlook remains subject to downside risks.

column1: Medium-term inflation expectations for the euro area economy must continue to be firmly anchored in line with our aim of maintaining inflation rates below
column2: but close to
column3: 2% over the medium term. Over the last few months we have implemented both standard and non-standard monetary policy measures. This combination of measures has contributed to a stabilisation in the financial environment and an improvement in the transmission of our monetary policy. We need to carefully monitor further developments. It is also important to keep in mind that all our non-standard monetary policy measures are temporary in nature and that all the necessary tools are available to address upside risks to medium-term price stability in a firm and timely manner.

column1: Let me now explain our assessment in greater detail
column2: starting with the economic analysis. Real GDP contracted by 0.3% in the euro area in the fourth quarter of 2011. Survey data confirm a stabilisation in economic activity at a low level in early 2012. We continue to expect the euro area economy to recover gradually in the course of the year. The outlook for economic activity should be supported by foreign demand
column3: the very low short-term interest rates in the euro area
column4: and all the measures taken to foster the proper functioning of the euro area economy. However
column5: the remaining tensions in euro area sovereign debt markets and their impact on credit conditions
column6: as well as the process of balance sheet adjustment in the financial and non-financial sectors and high unemployment in parts of the euro area
column7: are expected to continue to dampen the underlying growth momentum.

column1: Downside risks to the economic outlook prevail. They relate in particular to a renewed intensification of tensions in euro area debt markets and their potential spillover to the euro area real economy. Downside risks also relate to further increases in commodity prices.
Euro area annual HICP inflation was 2.6% in March 2012
column2: according to Eurostat’s flash estimate
column3: after 2.7% in the previous three months. Inflation is likely to stay above 2% in 2012
column4: mainly owing to recent increases in energy prices
column5: as well as recently announced rises in indirect taxes. On the basis of current futures prices for commodities
column6: annual inflation rates should fall below 2% again in early 2013. In this context
column7: we will pay particular attention to any signs of pass-through from higher energy prices to wages
column8: profits and general price-setting. However
column9: looking ahead
column10: in an environment of modest growth in the euro area and well-anchored long-term inflation expectations
column11: underlying price pressures should remain limited.

column1: Risks to the outlook for HICP inflation rates in the coming years are still seen to be broadly balanced
column2: with upside risks in the near term mainly stemming from higher than expected oil prices and indirect tax increases. Downside risks continue to exist owing to weaker than expected developments in economic activity.

column1: The monetary analysis indicates that the underlying pace of monetary expansion has remained subdued. The annual growth rate of M3 was 2.8% in February 2012
column2: compared with 2.5% in January. In both January and February we observed a strengthening in the deposit base of banks. Annual loan growth to the private sector has remained subdued
column3: with the rate (adjusted for loan sales and securitisation) moderating in February to 1.1% year on year
column4: from 1.5% in January.

column1: The annual growth rates of loans to non-financial corporations and loans to households (adjusted for loan sales and securitisation) stood at 0.6% and 1.8% respectively in February. The volume of MFI loans to non-financial corporations and households remained practically unchanged compared with the previous month.

Money and credit data up to February confirm a broad stabilisation of financial conditions and thereby the avoidance of an abrupt and disorderly adjustment in the balance sheets of credit institutions
column2: as intended by our measures. Funding conditions for banks have generally improved
column3: and there has been increased issuance activity and a re-opening of some segments of funding markets. The demand for credit remains weak in the light of still subdued economic activity and the ongoing process of balance sheet adjustment in non-financial sectors. The full supportive impact of the Eurosystem’s non-standard measures will need time to unfold and to have a positive effect on the growth of loans when demand recovers. In this context
column4: it should be noted that the second three-year longer-term refinancing operation was only settled on 1 March 2012.

column1: Following the stabilisation in the financial environment
column2: it is essential for banks to strengthen their resilience further
column3: including by retaining earnings. The soundness of banks’ balance sheets will be a key factor in facilitating both an appropriate provision of credit to the economy and the normalisation of all funding channels.

column1: To sum up
column2: the economic analysis indicates that price developments should remain in line with price stability over the medium term. A cross-check with the signals from the monetary analysis confirms this picture.

column1: In order to support confidence
column2: sustainable growth and employment
column3: the Governing Council calls upon governments to restore sound fiscal positions and implement strong structural reforms. Commitments under the Stability and Growth Pact need to be fully honoured and weaknesses in competitiveness forcefully addressed. National policy-makers need to fully meet their responsibilities to ensure fiscal sustainability
column4: to increase the adjustment capacity of product and labour markets
column5: to enhance productivity and competitiveness
column6: and to ensure the soundness of their financial system. In particular
column7: countries which have suffered losses in cost competitiveness need to ensure sufficient wage adjustment and foster productivity growth.

column1: Let me conclude by recalling that the single monetary policy naturally focuses on maintaining medium-term price stability for the euro area as a whole. It is up to national policy-makers to foster domestic developments which support the competitiveness of their economies. Both prudent fiscal policies and competitive and flexible product and labour markets are of crucial importance for the functioning of the euro area economy.

column2: it is essential for banks to strengthen their resilience further

column1: To sum up

column1: It is of utmost importance to ensure fiscal sustainability and sustainable growth in the euro area. Most euro area countries made good progress in terms of fiscal consolidation in 2011. While the necessary comprehensive fiscal adjustment is weighing on near-term economic growth
column2: its successful implementation will contribute to the sustainability of public finances and thereby to the lowering of sovereign risk premia. In an environment of enhanced confidence in fiscal balances
column3: private sector activity should also be fostered
column4: supporting private investment and medium-term growth.

column2: together with fiscal consolidation
column3: growth and growth potential in the euro area need to be enhanced by decisive structural reforms. In this context
column4: facilitating entrepreneurial activities
column5: the start-up of new firms and job creation is crucial. Policies aimed at enhancing competition in product markets and increasing the wage and employment adjustment capacity of firms will foster innovation
column6: promote job creation and boost longer-term growth prospects. Reforms in these areas are particularly important for countries which have suffered significant losses in cost competitiveness and need to stimulate productivity and improve trade performance.

column1: Based on our regular economic and monetary analyses
column2: we decided to keep the key ECB interest rates unchanged. While inflation rates are likely to stay above 2% for the remainder of 2012
column3: over the policy-relevant horizon we expect price developments to remain in line with price stability. Consistent with this picture
column4: the underlying pace of monetary expansion remains subdued. Inflation expectations for the euro area economy continue to be firmly anchored in line with our aim of maintaining inflation rates below
column5: but close to
column6: 2% over the medium term. At the same time
column7: economic growth in the euro area remains weak
column8: with heightened uncertainty weighing on confidence and sentiment
column9: giving rise to increased downside risks to the economic outlook.

column1: In previous months we have implemented both standard and non-standard monetary policy measures. This combination of measures has supported the transmission of our monetary policy. Today
column2: we have decided to continue conducting our main refinancing operations (MROs) as fixed rate tender procedures with full allotment for as long as necessary
column3: and at least until the end of the 12th maintenance period of 2012 on 15 January 2013. This procedure will also remain in use for the Eurosystem’s special-term refinancing operations with a maturity of one maintenance period
column4: which will continue to be conducted for as long as needed. The fixed rate in these special-term refinancing operations will be the same as the MRO rate prevailing at the time. Furthermore
column5: the Governing Council has decided to conduct the three-month longer-term refinancing operations (LTROs) to be allotted until the end of 2012 as fixed rate tender procedures with full allotment. The rates in these three-month operations will be fixed at the average rate of the MROs over the life of the respective LTRO. Keeping in mind that all our non-standard monetary policy measures are temporary in nature
column6: we will monitor further developments closely and ensure medium-term price stability for the euro area by acting in a firm and timely manner.

column1: Let me now explain our assessment in greater detail

column4: we continue to expect the euro area economy to recover gradually. However
column5: ongoing tensions in some euro area sovereign debt markets and their impact on credit conditions
column6: the process of balance sheet adjustment in the financial and non-financial sectors and high unemployment are expected to continue to dampen the underlying growth momentum.

column4: to a further increase in the tensions in several euro area financial markets and their potential spillover to the euro area real economy. Downside risks also relate to possibly renewed increases in commodity prices over the medium term.

column2: as intended by our policy measures

column2: it is essential for banks to continue to strengthen their resilience further. The soundness of banks’ balance sheets will be a key factor in facilitating both an appropriate provision of credit to the economy and the normalisation of all funding channels.

column1: To sum up
column2: the economic analysis indicates that price developments should remain in line with price stability over the medium term. A cross-check with the signals from the monetary analysis confirms this picture.

column1: Let me now make a few remarks relating to fiscal and economic policies. Significant progress has been achieved with fiscal consolidation over recent years. column1: Based on our regular economic and monetary analyses
column2: we decided to cut the key ECB interest rates by 25 basis points. Inflationary pressure over the policy-relevant horizon has been dampened further as some of the previously identified downside risks to the euro area growth outlook have materialised. Consistent with this picture
column3: the underlying pace of monetary expansion remains subdued. Inflation expectations for the euro area economy continue to be firmly anchored in line with our aim of maintaining inflation rates below
column4: but close to
column5: 2% over the medium term. At the same time
column6: economic growth in the euro area continues to remain weak
column7: with heightened uncertainty weighing on confidence and sentiment.

column1: We have implemented both standard and non-standard monetary policy measures. This combination of measures has supported the transmission of our monetary policy. All our non-standard monetary policy measures are temporary in nature and we maintain our full capacity to ensure medium-term price stability by acting in a firm and timely manner. Let me also remind you of the decision taken by the Governing Council on 22 June 2012 concerning further measures to increase collateral availability for counterparties.
Let me now explain our assessment in greater detail
column2: starting with the economic analysis. On a quarterly basis
column3: euro area real GDP growth was flat in the first quarter of 2012
column4: following a decline of 0.3% in the previous quarter. Indicators for the second quarter of 2012 point to a renewed weakening of economic growth and heightened uncertainty. Looking beyond the short term we expect the euro area economy to recover gradually
column5: although with momentum dampened by a number of factors. In particular
column6: tensions in some euro area sovereign debt markets and their impact on credit conditions
column7: the process of balance sheet adjustment in the financial and non-financial sectors and high unemployment are expected to weigh on the underlying growth momentum.

column1: The risks surrounding the economic outlook for the euro area continue to be on the downside. They relate
column2: in particular
column3: to a renewed increase in the tensions in several euro area financial markets and their potential spillover to the euro area real economy. Downside risks also relate to possibly renewed increases in energy prices over the medium term.

column1: Euro area annual HICP inflation was 2.4% in June 2012
column2: according to Eurostat’s flash estimate
column3: unchanged from the previous month. On the basis of current futures prices for oil
column4: inflation rates should decline further in the course of 2012 and be again below 2% in 2013. Over the policy?relevant horizon
column5: in an environment of modest growth in the euro area and well?anchored long-term inflation expectations
column6: underlying price pressures should remain moderate.

column1: Taking into account today’s decisions
column2: risks to the outlook for price developments continue to be broadly balanced over the medium term. The main downside risks relate to the impact of weaker than expected growth in the euro area. Upside risks pertain to further increases in indirect taxes
column3: owing to the need for fiscal consolidation
column4: and higher than expected energy prices over the medium term.

column1: Turning to the monetary analysis
column2: the underlying pace of monetary expansion has remained subdued
column3: with short-term developments displaying some volatility. The increase in the annual growth rate of M3 to 2.9% in May
column4: up from 2.5% in April and close to the 3.0% observed in March
column5: mainly reflected a reversal of the outflows in April from overnight deposits belonging to non-monetary financial intermediaries (particularly investment funds). In addition to an increased preference for deposits with shorter maturities
column6: these factors have also shaped M1 developments
column7: with the annual growth rate increasing from 1.8% in April to 3.3% in May.

column1: The annual growth rate of loans to the private sector (adjusted for loan sales and securitisation) declined to 0.4% in May (from 0.8% in April). Annual growth rates for loans to both non?financial corporations and households (adjusted for loan sales and securitisation) also decreased in May
column2: to 0.2% and 1.3% respectively
column3: with negative monthly loan flows to non-financial corporations. To a large extent
column4: subdued loan growth reflects the current cyclical situation
column5: heightened risk aversion
column6: and the ongoing adjustment in the balance sheets of households and enterprises which weigh on credit demand.

column1: Looking ahead
column2: it is essential for banks to continue to strengthen their resilience where it is needed. The soundness of banks’ balance sheets will be a key factor in facilitating both an appropriate provision of credit to the economy and the normalisation of all funding channels.

column1: To sum up
column2: taking into account today’s decisions
column3: the economic analysis indicates that price developments should remain in line with price stability over the medium term. A cross-check with the signals from the monetary analysis confirms this picture.

column1: Let me now make a few remarks relating to other policies. We welcome the European Council conclusions of 29 June 2012 to take action to address financial market tensions
column2: restore confidence and revive growth. We agree that Economic and Monetary Union needs to be put on a more solid basis for the future and that sustainable growth
column3: sound public finances and structural reforms to boost competitiveness remain key economic priorities. column6: the ECB is ready to serve as an agent to the EFSF/ESM in conducting market operations.

column1: The Governing Council extensively discussed the policy options to address the severe malfunctioning in the price formation process in the bond markets of euro area countries. Exceptionally high risk premia are observed in government bond prices in several countries and financial fragmentation hinders the effective working of monetary policy. Risk premia that are related to fears of the reversibility of the euro are unacceptable
column2: and they need to be addressed in a fundamental manner. The euro is irreversible.

column1: In order to create the fundamental conditions for such risk premia to disappear
column2: policy-makers in the euro area need to push ahead with fiscal consolidation
column3: structural reform and European institution-building with great determination. As implementation takes time and financial markets often only adjust once success becomes clearly visible
column4: governments must stand ready to activate the EFSF/ESM in the bond market when exceptional financial market circumstances and risks to financial stability exist – with strict and effective conditionality in line with the established guidelines.

column2: within its mandate to maintain price stability over the medium term and in observance of its independence in determining monetary policy

column9: the process of balance sheet adjustment in the financial and non-financial sectors and high unemployment are expected to weigh on the underlying growth momentum

column2: the Vice-President and I are very pleased to welcome you to our press conference. We will now report on the outcome of today’s meeting of the Governing Council.

column1: Based on our regular economic and monetary analyses
column2: we decided to keep the key ECB interest rates unchanged. Owing to high energy prices and increases in indirect taxes in some euro area countries
column3: inflation rates are likely to remain above 2% for the remainder of 2012. They are expected to fall below that level in the course of next year and to remain in line with price stability over the policy-relevant horizon. Consistent with this picture
column4: the underlying pace of monetary expansion continues to be subdued. Inflation expectations for the euro area remain firmly anchored in line with our aim of maintaining inflation rates below
column5: but close to
column6: 2% over the medium term. Economic activity in the euro area is expected to remain weak
column7: although it continues to be supported by our monetary policy stance and financial market confidence has visibly improved on the back of our decisions as regards Outright Monetary Transactions (OMTs). At the same time
column8: the necessary process of balance sheet adjustment in large parts of the financial and non-financial sectors as well as high uncertainty continue to weigh on the economic outlook. It is essential for governments to support confidence by forcefully implementing the necessary steps to reduce both fiscal and structural imbalances and to proceed with financial sector restructuring.

column1: The Governing Council remains firmly committed to preserving the singleness of its monetary policy and to ensuring the proper transmission of the policy stance to the real economy throughout the euro area. As we said before
column2: we are ready to undertake OMTs
column3: which will help to avoid extreme scenarios
column4: thereby clearly reducing concerns about the materialisation of destructive forces.

column1: Let me now explain our assessment in greater detail
column2: starting with the economic analysis. Euro area real GDP contracted by 0.2%
column3: quarter on quarter
column4: in the second quarter of 2012
column5: following flat growth in the previous quarter. As regards the second half of 2012
column6: the available indicators continue to signal weak activity. While industrial production data showed some resilience in July/August
column7: most recent survey evidence for the economy as a whole
column8: extending into the fourth quarter
column9: does not signal improvements towards the end of the year.

column1: Looking ahead to next year
column2: the growth momentum is expected to remain weak. It continues to be supported by our standard and non-standard monetary policy measures
column3: but the necessary process of balance sheet adjustment in the financial and non-financial sectors and an uneven global recovery will continue to dampen the pace of recovery. The risks surrounding the economic outlook for the euro area remain on the downside.

column1: Euro area annual HICP inflation was 2.5% in October 2012
column2: according to Eurostat’s flash estimate
column3: compared with 2.6% in September and August. On the basis of current futures prices for oil
column4: inflation rates could remain at elevated levels
column5: before declining to below 2% again in the course of next year. Over the policy-relevant horizon
column6: in an environment of modest growth in the euro area and well-anchored long-term inflation expectations
column7: underlying price pressures should remain moderate. Current levels of inflation should thus remain transitory. We will continue to monitor closely further developments in costs
column8: wages and prices.

column1: Risks to the outlook for price developments continue to be broadly balanced over the medium term. Upside risks pertain to further increases in indirect taxes owing to the need for fiscal consolidation. The main downside risks relate to the impact of weaker than expected growth in the euro area
column2: in the event of a renewed intensification of financial market tensions
column3: and its effects on the domestic components of inflation.

column1: Turning to the monetary analysis
column2: the underlying pace of monetary expansion continues to be subdued. In September the annual growth rate of M3 decreased to 2.7%
column3: from 2.8% in August. Monthly outflows from M3 reflected to some extent the reversal of portfolio shifts into the most liquid components of M3. Accordingly
column4: the annual rate of growth of M1 declined to 5.0% in September
column5: from 5.2% in August. At the same time
column6: we have observed a strengthening in the deposit base of banks in some stressed countries
column7: amid improvements in investors’ confidence in the euro area.

column1: The annual growth rate of loans to the private sector (adjusted for loan sales and securitisation) declined further to -0.4% in September
column2: from -0.2% in August. This development was mainly due to further net redemptions in loans to non-financial corporations
column3: which led to an annual rate of decline in these loans of -1.2%
column4: compared with -0.5% in August. The annual growth in MFI lending to households remained unchanged at 0.9% in September. To a large extent
column5: subdued loan dynamics reflect the weak outlook for GDP
column6: heightened risk aversion and the ongoing adjustment in the balance sheets of households and enterprises
column7: all of which weigh on credit demand. At the same time
column8: in a number of euro area countries
column9: the segmentation of financial markets and capital constraints for banks restrict credit supply. The recent results of the bank lending survey for the third quarter of 2012 underpin this assessment.

column1: The soundness of banks’ balance sheets will be a key factor in facilitating both an appropriate provision of credit to the economy and the normalisation of all funding channels
column2: thereby contributing to an adequate transmission of monetary policy to the financing conditions of the non-financial sectors in the individual countries of the euro area. It is thus essential that the resilience of banks continues to be strengthened where needed.

column1: To sum up
column2: the economic analysis indicates that price developments should remain in line with price stability over the medium term. A cross-check with the signals from the monetary analysis confirms this picture.

column1: Other economic policy areas need to make substantial contributions to ensure a further stabilisation of financial markets and an improvement in the outlook for growth. Structural reforms are crucial to boost the growth potential of euro area countries and to enhance employment. Policy action is also necessary to increase the adjustment capacity of euro area economies in order to complete the ongoing process of unwinding existing imbalances. Visible progress is being made in the correction of unit labour costs and current account imbalances. However
column2: further measures to enhance labour market flexibility and labour mobility across the euro area are warranted. Such structural measures would also complement and support fiscal consolidation and debt sustainability. As regards fiscal policies
column3: there is clear evidence that consolidation efforts in euro area countries are bearing fruit. It is crucial that efforts are maintained to restore sound fiscal positions
column4: in line with the commitments under the Stability and Growth Pact and the 2012 European Semester recommendations. Full compliance with the reinforced EU fiscal and governance framework
column5: including the rapid implementation of the fiscal compact
column6: will send a strong signal to markets and strengthen confidence in the soundness of public finances.

column1: The Governing Council takes note of the European Council conclusions on completing Economic and Monetary Union
column2: adopted on 18 October 2012. In the context of measures to achieve an integrated financial framework
column3: it welcomes in particular the objective of agreeing on the legislative framework for a Single Supervisory Mechanism (SSM) by 1 January 2013 with a view to the SSM becoming operational in the course of 2013.

column9: necessary balance sheet adjustments in financial and non-financial sectors and persistent uncertainty will continue to weigh on economic activity. Later in 2013 economic activity should gradually recover

column11: it is essential for governments to reduce further both fiscal and structural imbalances and to proceed with financial sector restructuring.

column1: In order to ensure an adequate transmission of monetary policy to the financing conditions in euro area countries
column2: it is essential to continue strengthening the resilience of banks where needed. The soundness of banks’ balance sheets will be a key factor in facilitating both an appropriate provision of credit to the economy and the normalisation of all funding channels. Decisive steps for establishing an integrated financial framework will help to accomplish this objective. A single supervisory mechanism (SSM) is one of the main building blocks. It is a crucial move towards re-integrating the banking system.

column2: the economic analysis indicates that price developments should remain in line with price stability over the medium term. A cross-check with the signals from the monetary analysis confirms this picture.

column1: Further economic policy measures and progress in the reform of European governance should help to support financial market sentiment and improve the outlook for economic growth. In this context
column2: the Governing Council looks forward to the roadmap towards genuine Economic and Monetary Union to be decided at the European Council meeting on 13-14 December 2012. Initiatives to accelerate structural reforms that help restore competitiveness are particularly important to revive the growth potential of euro area countries and to increase employment. column3: all euro area countries must ensure that their product and labour markets possess the adjustment capacity required for their smooth and effective functioning within a monetary union. Finally
column4: continued fiscal consolidation is expected to restore sound fiscal positions
column5: in line with the commitments under the Stability and Growth Pact and the 2012 European Semester recommendations. Significant progress has already been made in reducing domestic and external imbalances and in improving competitiveness. Continued policy actions on the European
column6: structural and fiscal reform fronts should be mutually reinforcing and send a strong signal to markets.

column1: In order to ensure adequate transmission of monetary policy to the financing conditions in euro area countries

column1: Based on our regular economic and monetary analyses
column2: we decided to keep the key ECB interest rates unchanged. Incoming information has confirmed our assessment which led to the cut in interest rates in early May. The underlying price pressure in the euro area is expected to remain subdued over the medium term. In keeping with this picture
column3: monetary and
column4: in particular
column5: credit dynamics remain subdued. Medium-term inflation expectations for the euro area continue to be firmly anchored in line with our aim of maintaining inflation rates below
column6: but close to
column7: 2%. At the same time
column8: recent economic sentiment survey data have shown some improvement from low levels. The accommodative stance of our monetary policy
column9: together with the significant improvements in financial markets since mid-2012
column10: should contribute to support prospects for an economic recovery later in the year. Against this overall background
column11: our monetary policy stance will remain accommodative for as long as necessary. In the period ahead
column12: we will monitor very closely all incoming information on economic and monetary developments and assess any impact on the outlook for price stability.

column1: Let me now explain our assessment in greater detail
column2: starting with the economic analysis. Real GDP contracted by 0.2% in the first quarter of 2013
column3: following a decline of 0.6% in the fourth quarter of 2012. Output has thus declined for six consecutive quarters
column4: with labour market conditions remaining weak. Recent developments in economic sentiment survey data have shown some improvement from low levels. Looking ahead to later in the year and to 2014
column5: euro area export growth should benefit from a recovery in global demand
column6: while domestic demand should be supported by the accommodative stance of our monetary policy and by the recent real income gains due to lower oil prices and generally lower inflation. Furthermore
column7: the significant improvements in financial markets seen since last summer should work their way through to the real economy
column8: as should the progress made in fiscal consolidation. At the same time
column9: the remaining necessary balance sheet adjustments in the public and private sectors will continue to weigh on economic activity. Overall
column10: euro area economic activity should stabilise and recover in the course of the year
column11: albeit at a subdued pace.

column2: which foresee annual real GDP declining by 0.6% in 2013 and increasing by 1.1% in 2014. Compared with the March 2013 ECB staff macroeconomic projections
column3: the projection for 2013 has been revised marginally downwards
column4: largely reflecting the incorporation of the latest GDP data releases. For 2014 there has been a marginal upward revision.

According to Eurostat’s flash estimate

column4: in particular
column5: accounted for by a rebound in services prices related to the unwinding of the Easter effect and an increase in food prices. More generally
column6: as stated last month

column10: inflation expectations remain firmly anchored in line with price stability.

column1: Turning to the monetary analysis
column2: recent data confirm that the underlying pace of monetary and
column3: in particular
column4: credit expansion continues to be subdued. Annual growth in broad money
column5: M3
column6: increased in April to 3.2%
column7: from 2.6% in March

column1: In order to ensure adequate transmission of monetary policy to the financing conditions in euro area countries
column2: it is essential that the fragmentation of euro area credit markets continues to decline further and that the resilience of banks is strengthened where needed. Progress has been made since last summer in improving the funding situation of banks
column3: in strengthening the domestic deposit base in stressed countries and in reducing reliance on the Eurosystem as reflected in repayments of the three-year LTROs. Further decisive steps for establishing a banking union will help to accomplish this objective. In particular
column4: the Governing Council emphasises that the future Single Supervisory Mechanism and a Single Resolution Mechanism are crucial elements for moving towards re-integrating the banking system and therefore require swift implementation.

column1: To sum up
column2: the economic analysis indicates that price developments should remain in line with price stability over the medium term. A cross-check with the signals from the monetary analysis confirms this picture.

column1: With regard to fiscal consolidation and structural reforms
column2: the Governing Council welcomes the progress made and encourages governments to continue with determined efforts. It is essential that euro area countries do not unravel their efforts to reduce government budget deficits. The new European governance framework for fiscal and economic policies should be applied in a steadfast manner. In this respect
column3: the Governing Council considers it very important that decisions by the EU Council to extend the time frame for the correction of excessive fiscal deficits should remain reserved for exceptional circumstances. At the same time
column4: it is necessary to continue
column5: where needed
column6: to take legislative action or otherwise promptly implement structural reforms. Structural reforms should
column7: in particular
column8: target competitiveness and adjustment capacities in labour and product markets
column9: thereby helping to generate employment opportunities in an environment of unacceptably high unemployment levels
column10: especially among young workers
column11: prevailing in several countries. Combined action on the fiscal and structural front should mutually reinforce fiscal sustainability and economic growth potential and thereby foster sustainable job creation.

column1: The issue of ABSs is more complicated than the others

column8: probably the smallest component of the ABS market

column5: as I said

column1: The second point concerns unemployment. The Governing Council is of the persuasion that the present levels of unemployment are the result of a combination of cyclical factors
column2: as well as structural factors. As of cyclical factors
column4: there is no doubt that the labour market in general is experiencing the combined effects of a credit crunch and the unavoidable fiscal consolidation that many of these countries have had to undertake. It is also true that

column9: however

column11: in other words globalisation
column12: does require new skills and investment in human capital

column16: in the second part of this year.

column1: Your second question was about fiscal measures. The position of the ECB is that these two-year extensions should be given in exceptional circumstances and
column2: more importantly
column3: should be coupled with a commitment to undertake structural reforms. And I’m saying this because
column4: very often
column5: these fiscal adjustments are combined with a lack of competiveness in the countries concerned. So
column6: if a country just gets a two-year extension and in two years’ time comes back with a higher deficit
column7: a higher level of debt and the same degree of competitiveness – that is to say very little – I don’t think the markets will be happy
column8: and they’ll very soon punish this country or other countries like that. The plea here is don’t get too optimistic about the present market condition; don’t interpret the present market condition as one that would allow any protracted relaxation of fiscal standards without undertaking structural reforms at the same time
column9: without increasing competiveness. That’s the message that I would have. And that’s the message in the Introductory Statement – that is what is meant.

column1: In answer to the first question
column2: we continue to experience a decrease in excess liquidity
column3: we continue to experience LTRO repayments
column4: and these repayments have currently reached approximately 60%
column5: or perhaps slightly below 60%
column6: of the net injection that took place in the early months of 2012. This is a positive sign
column7: because it shows that financial conditions are continuing to normalise and that banks do not need to rely solely on the ECB for their funding as they can get funding from other sources. For example
column8: deposits in the stressed countries have once again become a source of funding; the interbank market in the non-stressed countries is again becoming a source of funding; and so on and so forth. It is also a sign
column9: however
column10: that this liquidity is not being used in the system. So

column13: because we

column15: can gradually downsize our balance sheet without having to take any decisions that would
column16: or could
column17: create volatility. This is an automatic process that is not deflationary. It is not that credit has been cut; credit is not there yet. Finally
column18: I am sure you have not forgotten that
column19: in the early months of 2012

column21: immense were the risks that we were undertaking with these measures. Have we seen any of these risks materialise?

column1: Your first question is the key question we are always asking ourselves
column2: and not only when we meet. One answer is to ask yourself what are the drivers of this recovery
column3: which is going to be gradual as I have said many times. Currently
column4: exports are the main driver. Exports have increased in almost all countries
column5: especially in Germany
column6: Spain and Italy. The second driver is our own accommodative monetary policy
column7: which will gradually find its way through the economy. Third
column8: low inflation is increasing people’s purchasing power. The lower price of oil is also an important factor. Finally
column9: although less than in other countries
column10: such as the United States or United Kingdom
column11: you have a wealth effect coming from the improvements in financial markets and
column12: as I said before
column13: you have a lower cost of capital for investment. On the other hand
column14: you have a quite broad weakness in domestic demand and consumption
column15: particularly because of the high levels of unemployment. There is something I would like to mention that is linked to this. When you talk to healthy banks that do not need to be recapitalised
column16: you ask them why they are not lending more. The answer you get is that the net rate of return
column17: adjusted for the risk of lending
column18: is not high enough for them to lend. We have made a significant contribution to increasing the net rate of return
column19: because it includes funding rates
column20: which have gone down. But the perception of macroeconomic risk is still there
column21: and that is a question of time.

column1: On the second question
column2: one reason why banks do not lend is risk aversion
column3: which is both micro
column4: with respect to their clients
column5: and macro
column6: with respect to the general economic environment and the high uncertainty that still prevails in some parts of the euro area. Of course
column7: I take for granted that there are sectors of economic activity in certain countries
column8: such as construction in Spain
column9: which needed to be downsized anyway. So
column10: you have a certain amount of deleveraging taking place
column11: for one reason or another
column12: in various parts of the euro area
column13: and that is encouraging. The second point is about banks being recapitalised. We do not want to repeat the mistakes made in 2011
column14: when we had the European Banking Authority running stress tests without a backstop being agreed by governments. I am sure you remember that in the United States it was the other way round. First
column15: they determined the backstop
column16: and then they conducted the asset quality management review and
column17: miraculously
column18: the capital needs of these banks came out exactly equal to the backstop that had been allotted. We do not have these magic powers. But we at least want to make sure that there is an explicit commitment by governments
column19: by the European Stability Mechanism and by the Eurogroup to provide a backstop
column20: in case the asset quality review undertaken by the ECB
column21: the national supervisors
column22: the third-party private sector assessor and other national supervisors
column23: which will exert peer pressure
column24: finds capital shortfalls. Let me quickly add two things. First
column25: I think the situation has changed significantly in the past two or three years
column26: and for the better. Banks have raised capital and substantially reduced their leverage
column27: which is not what we expected three or four years ago. In fact
column28: the current situation is different to how we had imagined it would be two
column29: three
column30: four years ago. Second
column31: before using a backstop there are many ways for a bank to recapitalise itself. First
column32: you have supervisory action. Second
column33: you can go to the markets. Third
column34: you can merge. You can do many other things before you use the backstop
column35: but it is extremely important
column38: if you have a capital shortfall that cannot be addressed by all these measures
column39: it can be addressed by the backstop. This is vital

column1: On the second point

column3: we have looked at that
column4: but we won’t pre-commit. I’m not going to tell you what we will do next month or in two months’ time

In answering the first question

What we are going to do is – and I think we did say it clearly – we are going to have an asset quality or balance sheet review of the banks that are going to be taken under this Single Supervisory Mechanism. We have agreed on having this review done by the ECB the national supervisor

column4: having consequences on volatility and interest rates all along the yield curves
column5: and we will certainly look at that in our monetary policy decisions

column1: Well
column2: not really.

column1: First
column2: on deflation: the price path that has been foreseen by the staff projections is lower than the price path foreseen in previous staff projections
column3: both for this and next year. This is mostly due to a decrease in the price of oil. If you discount oil and food
column4: you see that the difference between the two price paths
column5: of the previous and of today’s projections
column6: is much smaller. Second: is there deflation? We must first ask ourselves what deflation is. Deflation is a protracted fall in prices across different commodities
column7: sectors and countries. In other words
column8: it is a generalised protracted fall in prices
column9: with self-fulfilling expectations. Therefore
column10: it has explosive downward dynamics. We do not see anything like that in any country. Also
column11: when we look at which prices are falling
column12: we see that the fall in prices is actually limited to certain categories of goods and – when discounting oil and food
column13: as I said before – these decreases are due to less regulation
column14: for example
column15: or to the introduction of technologies which increase productivity. Of course
column16: the falling price of oil is very important because now we really have to understand whether it is a structural fall in price
column17: i.e. whether it is going to stay because of the shale gas in the United States and elsewhere (as apparently it is not only in the United States)
column18: or whether it is something transitory. Also
column19: monetary policy has to look beyond volatility which
column20: as I think I said in the introductory statement
column21: is going to continue to be present in price developments – so do not be surprised if you see bumps in the price paths in the months ahead
column22: because there is going to be volatility there. But you have to look through volatility and you need to ask yourself how inflation expectations are behaving. There you see that inflation expectations remain firmly anchored
column23: and this is the case whether looking at the inflation expectations derived from the financial markets or those from the surveys. The Survey of Professional Forecasters (SPF) shows that inflation expectations have been anchored at 1.9% for 15 years
column24: since the creation of the ECB. So
column25: all in all
column26: we do not see deflation. Furthermore
column27: we would certainly consider any deflation very seriously because it is a threat to our ability to pursue our objective of maintaining price stability. If we were to see deflation
column28: we would have to sit down and think carefully
column29: but we do not see it. In addition
column30: some of these changes I hinted at are actually changes in relative prices
column31: so they are positive. They show that there is real adjustment taking place
column32: which can be seen in the export levels
column33: which have gone up in some of the stressed countries.

column1: Well
column2: I am not sure I get the point
column3: but I think I get it. First
column4: the fact that inflation is low is not
column5: by itself
column6: bad; with low inflation
column7: you can buy more stuff. Second

Now that is not growth-friendly and it is not growth-friendly because it happens in parts of the world where taxes are already very

And then what adjustments are needed in order to achieve this objective? The encouraging thing is that we see that most countries
column16: if not all of them
column17: are in this process
column18: which of course is very painful
column19: and I don’t think I miss one opportunity to make sure that you all know how aware of this we all are in the ECB.";0;0;13;http://www.ecb.europa.eu/press/pressconf/2013/html/is130606.en.html

column1: 2013-07-04;3;"Ladies and gentlemen
column2: the Vice-President and I are very pleased to welcome you to our press conference. We will now report on the outcome of today’s meeting of the Governing Council
column3: which was also attended by the Commission Vice-President
column4: Mr. Rehn.

column1: Based on our regular economic and monetary analyses
column2: we decided to keep the key ECB interest rates unchanged. Incoming information has confirmed our previous assessment. Underlying price pressures in the euro area are expected to remain subdued over the medium term. In keeping with this picture
column3: monetary and
column4: in particular
column5: credit dynamics remain subdued. Inflation expectations for the euro area continue to be firmly anchored in line with our aim of maintaining inflation rates below
column6: but close to
column7: 2% over the medium term. At the same time
column8: recent confidence indicators based on survey data have shown some further improvement from low levels. Our monetary policy stance is geared towards maintaining the degree of monetary accommodation warranted by the outlook for price stability and promoting stable money market conditions. It thereby provides support to a recovery in economic activity later in the year and in 2014. Looking ahead
column9: our monetary policy stance will remain accommodative for as long as necessary. The Governing Council expects the key ECB interest rates to remain at present or lower levels for an extended period of time. This expectation is based on the overall subdued outlook for inflation extending into the medium term
column10: given the broad-based weakness in the real economy and subdued monetary dynamics. In the period ahead
column11: we will monitor all incoming information on economic and monetary developments and assess any impact on the outlook for price stability.

column1: Let me now explain our assessment in greater detail
column2: starting with the economic analysis. Real GDP declined by 0.3% in the first quarter of 2013
column3: following a contraction of 0.6% in the last quarter of 2012. At the same time
column4: labour market conditions remain weak. Recent developments in cyclical indicators
column5: particularly those based on survey data
column6: indicate some further improvement from low levels. Looking ahead to later in the year and to 2014
column7: euro area export growth should benefit from a gradual recovery in global demand
column8: while domestic demand should be supported by the accommodative monetary policy stance as well as the recent gains in real income owing to generally lower inflation. Furthermore
column9: notwithstanding recent developments
column10: the overall improvements in financial markets seen since last summer should work their way through to the real economy
column11: as should the progress made in fiscal consolidation. This being said
column12: the remaining necessary balance sheet adjustments in the public and private sectors will continue to weigh on economic activity. Overall
column13: euro area economic activity should stabilise and recover in the course of the year
column14: albeit at a subdued pace.

column1: The risks surrounding the economic outlook for the euro area continue to be on the downside. The recent tightening of global money and financial market conditions and related uncertainties may have the potential to negatively affect economic conditions. Other downside risks include the possibility of weaker than expected domestic and global demand and slow or insufficient implementation of structural reforms in euro area countries.
As stated in previous months
column2: annual inflation rates are expected to be subject to some volatility throughout the year owing particularly to base effects. According to Eurostat’s flash estimate
column3: euro area annual HICP inflation was 1.6% in June 2013
column4: up from 1.4% in May. This increase reflected an upward base effect relating to energy price developments twelve months earlier. However
column5: underlying price pressures are expected to remain subdued over the medium term
column6: reflecting the broad-based weakness in aggregate demand and the modest pace of the recovery. Medium-term inflation expectations remain firmly anchored in line with price stability.

column1: The risks to the outlook for price developments are expected to be still broadly balanced over the medium term
column2: with upside risks relating to stronger than expected increases in administered prices and indirect taxes
column3: as well as higher commodity prices
column4: and downside risks stemming from weaker than expected economic activity.

column1: Turning to the monetary analysis
column2: recent data confirm the subdued monetary and
column3: in particular
column4: credit dynamics. Annual growth in broad money (M3) decreased in May to 2.9%
column5: from 3.2% in April. Moreover
column6: annual growth in M1 decreased to 8.4% in May

column1: On the other question about collateral
column2: let me first state with some emphasis that the decisions we have taken do not weaken the Eurosystem’s collateral framework. The objective of these decisions was to have a consistent treatment of all classes of eligible collateral. To have consistent treatment means to enhance risk equivalence across all eligible assets. Let me give you two examples. First
column3: on asset-backed securities (ABSs)
column4: we now have lower haircuts than before because the transparency and standardisation of this asset class has significantly improved. This is also because of the ineligibility of mixed-pool ABSs and close-links provisions and servicing provisions. There are lots of technical reasons why this asset class would deserve a lower haircut. At the same time
column5: the single-A requirement remains more stringent than for the other asset classes
column6: as it is defined on a second-best-rating basis. The second-best triple-B ABSs remain acceptable in the temporary framework only. That is one example. Another example is: we looked at covered bonds and there we distinguish now between retained ones that are more risky and therefore deserve a higher haircut and non-retained ones that are less risky and therefore have a lower haircut. Now
column7: this had overall a minimal impact on the overall collateral and we will certainly review it at a proper time. At the country level
column8: we estimate that the actual impact has been at most around 1%. Now
column9: you have to judge this negative impact – and you are right
column10: it went in this direction – against the positive impact that previous decisions had as far as some stressed countries are concerned. You have to look at it in a dynamic way across the overall set of decisions. Let me just mention some of those decisions. In December 2011 we lowered the rating requirement at issuance for some ABSs and we introduced the additional credit claims. In June 2012 we eased again the conditions for ABSs. In September 2012 we allowed ABS loans and credit claims in other currencies. You have to judge the most recent decisions in the context of the previous decisions which have broadened the collateral and the classes and eased the treatment of assets eligible as collateral. I think that is the way to look at this.

column10: and confidence indicators up to August confirm the expected gradual improvement in economic activity from low levels. Our monetary policy stance continues to be geared towards maintaining the degree of monetary accommodation warranted by the outlook for price stability and promoting stable money market conditions. It thereby provides support to a gradual recovery in economic activity. Looking ahead

column4: governments should not unravel their efforts to reduce deficits and put debt ratios on a downward path. column1: Based on our regular economic and monetary analyses
column2: we decided to keep the key ECB interest rates unchanged. Incoming information and analysis have further underpinned our previous assessment. Underlying price pressures in the euro area are expected to remain subdued over the medium term. In keeping with this picture
column3: monetary and
column4: in particular
column5: credit dynamics remain subdued. Inflation expectations for the euro area continue to be firmly anchored in line with our aim of maintaining inflation rates below
column6: but close to
column7: 2% over the medium term. At the same time
column8: real GDP growth in the second quarter was positive
column9: after six quarters of negative output growth
column10: and confidence indicators up to September confirm the expected gradual improvement in economic activity from low levels. Our monetary policy stance continues to be geared towards maintaining the degree of monetary accommodation warranted by the outlook for price stability and promoting stable money market conditions. It thereby provides support to a gradual recovery in economic activity. Looking ahead
column11: our monetary policy stance will remain accommodative for as long as necessary
column12: in line with the forward guidance provided in July. The Governing Council confirms that it expects the key ECB interest rates to remain at present or lower levels for an extended period of time. This expectation continues to be based on an unchanged overall subdued outlook for inflation extending into the medium term
column13: given the broad-based weakness in the economy and subdued monetary dynamics. In the period ahead
column14: we will monitor all incoming information on economic and monetary developments and assess any impact on the medium-term outlook for price stability. With regard to money market conditions
column15: we will remain particularly attentive to developments which may have implications for the stance of monetary policy and are ready to consider all available instruments.

column1: Let me now explain our assessment in greater detail
column2: starting with the economic analysis. Following six quarters of negative output growth
column3: euro area real GDP rose
column4: quarter on quarter
column5: by 0.3% in the second quarter of 2013
column6: also supported by temporary factors related to unusually adverse weather conditions in some euro area countries earlier this year. Developments in industrial production data point to somewhat weaker growth at the beginning of the third quarter
column7: while survey-based confidence indicators up to September have improved further from low levels
column8: overall confirming our previous expectations of a gradual recovery in economic activity. Looking ahead
column9: output is expected to recover at a slow pace
column10: in particular owing to a gradual improvement in domestic demand supported by the accommodative monetary policy stance. Euro area economic activity should
column11: in addition
column12: benefit from a gradual strengthening of external demand for exports. Furthermore
column13: the overall improvements in financial markets seen since last summer appear to be gradually working their way through to the real economy
column14: as should the progress made in fiscal consolidation. In addition
column15: real incomes have benefited recently from generally lower inflation. This being said
column16: unemployment in the euro area remains high
column17: and the necessary balance sheet adjustments in the public and private sectors will continue to weigh on economic activity.

column1: The risks surrounding the economic outlook for the euro area continue to be on the downside. Developments in global money and financial market conditions and related uncertainties may have the potential to negatively affect economic conditions. Other downside risks include higher commodity prices in the context of renewed geopolitical tensions
column2: weaker than expected global demand and slow or insufficient implementation of structural reforms in euro area countries.

column2: and broadly in line with expectations
column3: euro area annual HICP inflation decreased in September 2013 to 1.1%

column6: underlying price pressures are expected to remain subdued
column7: reflecting the broad-based weakness in aggregate demand and the modest pace of the recovery. Medium to long-term inflation expectations continue to be firmly anchored in line with price stability.

column1: The risks to the outlook for price developments are expected to be still broadly balanced over the medium term
column2: with upside risks relating in particular to higher commodity prices as well as stronger than expected increases in administered prices and indirect taxes
column3: and downside risks stemming from weaker than expected economic activity.

column1: Turning to the monetary analysis
column2: data for August indicate that the underlying growth of broad money (M3) and
column3: in particular
column4: credit remained subdued. Annual growth in M3 continued to be broadly stable at 2.3% in August

column1: Since the summer of 2012 substantial progress has been made in improving the funding situation of banks and
column2: in particular
column3: in strengthening the domestic deposit base in a number of stressed countries. In order to ensure an adequate transmission of monetary policy to the financing conditions in euro area countries
column4: it is essential that the fragmentation of euro area credit markets declines further and that the resilience of banks is strengthened where needed. Further decisive steps to establish a banking union will help to accomplish this objective.

column1: To sum up
column2: the economic analysis indicates that price developments should remain in line with price stability over the medium term. A cross-check with the signals from the monetary analysis confirms this picture.

column1: As regards fiscal policies
column2: euro area countries should not unravel their efforts to reduce deficits and put high government debt ratios on a downward path. The draft budgetary plans that countries will now deliver for the first time under the “two-pack” regulations need to provide for sufficiently far-reaching measures to achieve the fiscal targets for 2014. Governments must also decisively strengthen efforts to implement the needed structural reforms in product and labour markets. These reforms are required not only to help countries to regain competitiveness and to rebalance within the euro area
column3: but also to create more flexible and dynamic economies that generate sustainable economic growth and employment.

column8: in addition

column1: Turning to the monetary analysis
column2: data for October confirm the assessment of subdued underlying growth in broad money (M3) and credit. Annual growth in M3 moderated to 1.4% in October
column3: from 2.0% in September. This moderation was partly related to a base effect. Annual growth in M1 remained strong at 6.6%
column4: reflecting a preference for liquidity

column1: Since the summer of 2012 substantial progress has been made in improving the funding situation of banks. In order to ensure an adequate transmission of monetary policy to the financing conditions in euro area countries
column2: it is essential that the fragmentation of euro area credit markets declines further and that the resilience of banks is strengthened where needed. The ECB’s comprehensive assessment before it adopts its supervisory role under the single supervisory mechanism will further support this confidence-building process. Further decisive steps to establish a banking union will help to restore confidence in the financial system.

column4: but close to

column1: As regards fiscal policies

column1: Looking ahead

column3: quarter on quarter
column4: in the last quarter of 2013

column13: although labour markets have shown the first signs of improvement
column14: unemployment in the euro area remains high and
column15: overall
column16: unutilised capacity is sizeable. Moreover

column2: as well as geopolitical risks

column4: as well as weaker export growth.

column2: the possible repercussions of both geopolitical risks and exchange rate developments will be monitored closely.

column1: Since the summer of 2012

column1: 2014-08-07;3;"Ladies and gentlemen
column2: the Vice-President and I are very pleased to welcome you to our press conference. We will now report on the outcome of today’s meeting of the Governing Council.

column1: Based on our regular economic and monetary analyses
column2: we decided to keep the key ECB interest rates unchanged. The available information remains consistent with our assessment of a continued moderate and uneven recovery of the euro area economy
column3: with low rates of inflation and subdued monetary and credit dynamics. At the same time
column4: inflation expectations for the euro area over the medium to long term continue to be firmly anchored in line with our aim of maintaining inflation rates below
column5: but close to
column6: 2%. The monetary policy measures decided in early June have led to an easing of the monetary policy stance. This is in line with our forward guidance and adequately reflects the outlook for the euro area economy
column7: as well as the differences in terms of the monetary policy cycle between major advanced economies. The targeted longer-term refinancing operations (TLTROs) that are to take place over the coming months will enhance our accommodative monetary policy stance. These operations will provide long-term funding at attractive terms and conditions over a period of up to four years for all banks that meet certain benchmarks applicable to their lending to the real economy. This should help to ease funding conditions further and stimulate credit provision to the real economy. As our measures work their way through to the economy they will contribute to a return of inflation rates to levels closer to 2%.

column1: As stated previously
column2: and as a follow-up to our decision in early June
column3: we have intensified preparatory work related to outright purchases in the asset-backed securities market to enhance the functioning of the monetary policy transmission mechanism.

column1: Looking ahead
column2: we will maintain a high degree of monetary accommodation. Concerning our forward guidance
column3: the key ECB interest rates will remain at present levels for an extended period of time in view of the current outlook for inflation. Moreover
column4: the Governing Council is unanimous in its commitment to also using unconventional instruments within its mandate
column5: should it become necessary to further address risks of too prolonged a period of low inflation. We are strongly determined to safeguard the firm anchoring of inflation expectations over the medium to long term.

column1: Based on our regular economic and monetary analyses
column2: the Governing Council decided today to lower the interest rate on the main refinancing operations of the Eurosystem by 10 basis points to 0.05% and the rate on the marginal lending facility by 10 basis points to 0.30%. The rate on the deposit facility was lowered by 10 basis points to -0.20%. In addition
column3: the Governing Council decided to start purchasing non-financial private sector assets. The Eurosystem will purchase a broad portfolio of simple and transparent asset-backed securities (ABSs) with underlying assets consisting of claims against the euro area non-financial private sector under an ABS purchase programme (ABSPP). This reflects the role of the ABS market in facilitating new credit flows to the economy and follows the intensification of preparatory work on this matter
column4: as decided by the Governing Council in June. In parallel
column5: the Eurosystem will also purchase a broad portfolio of euro-denominated covered bonds issued by MFIs domiciled in the euro area under a new covered bond purchase programme (CBPP3). Interventions under these programmes will start in October 2014. The detailed modalities of these programmes will be announced after the Governing Council meeting of 2 October 2014. The newly decided measures
column6: together with the targeted longer-term refinancing operations which will be conducted in two weeks
column7: will have a sizeable impact on our balance sheet.

column1: These decisions will add to the range of monetary policy measures taken over recent months. In particular
column2: they will support our forward guidance on the key ECB interest rates and reflect the fact that there are significant and increasing differences in the monetary policy cycle between major advanced economies. They will further enhance the functioning of the monetary policy transmission mechanism and support the provision of credit to the broad economy. In our analysis
column3: we took into account the overall subdued outlook for inflation
column4: the weakening in the euro area’s growth momentum over the recent past and the continued subdued monetary and credit dynamics. Today’s decisions
column5: together with the other measures in place
column6: have been taken with a view to underpinning the firm anchoring of medium to long-term inflation expectations
column7: in line with our aim of maintaining inflation rates below
column8: but close to
column9: 2%. As our measures work their way through to the economy they will contribute to a return of inflation rates to levels closer to 2%. Should it become necessary to further address risks of too prolonged a period of low inflation
column10: the Governing Council is unanimous in its commitment to using additional unconventional instruments within its mandate.

column1: Let me now explain our assessment in greater detail

column3: euro area real GDP remained unchanged in the second quarter of this year compared with the previous quarter. While it partly reflected one-off factors
column4: this outcome was weaker than expected. With regard to the third quarter

column6: while remaining consistent with a modest expansion.

column3: the progress made in fiscal consolidation and structural reforms
column4: and lower energy prices supporting real disposable income. Furthermore

column6: the recovery is likely to continue to be dampened by high unemployment
column7: sizeable unutilised capacity
column8: continued negative MFI loan growth to the private sector
column9: and the necessary balance sheet adjustments in the public and private sectors. Looking ahead

column4: credit risk

column1: To sum up
column2: a cross-check of the outcome of the economic analysis with the signals coming from the monetary analysis led the Governing Council to decide on measures to provide further monetary policy accommodation and to support lending to the real economy.

column1: With regard to structural reforms
column2: important steps have been taken in several Member States
column3: while in others such measures still need to be legislated for and implemented. These efforts now clearly need to gain momentum to achieve higher sustainable growth and employment in the euro area. Determined structural reforms in product and labour markets as well as action to improve the business environment are warranted. As regards fiscal policies
column4: comprehensive fiscal consolidation in recent years has contributed to reducing budgetary imbalances. Euro area countries should not unravel the progress made with fiscal consolidation and should proceed in line with the Stability and Growth Pact. The Pact acts as an anchor for confidence
column5: and the existing flexibility within the rules allows the budgetary costs of major structural reforms to be addressed and demand to be supported. There is also leeway to achieve a more growth-friendly composition of fiscal policies. A full and consistent implementation of the euro area’s existing fiscal and macroeconomic surveillance framework is key to bringing down high public debt ratios
column6: to raising potential growth and to increasing the euro area’s resilience to shocks.

column5: in particular

column4: the combined monthly purchases of public and private sector securities will amount to €60 billion. column2: the Governing Council decided to change the pricing of the six remaining targeted longer-term refinancing operations (TLTROs). Accordingly

column3: we decided to keep the key ECB interest rates unchanged.

column1: Well that data is indeed quite troubling. I think if we are to run the same survey now we would probably find a better number. There has been some improvement. But it's very important to understand that our expansion in monetary policy finds its natural complement in structural reforms. Some people argue
column2: and you certainly have heard them argue in this way
column3: that accommodative monetary policy removes the incentives for governments to undertake structural reforms. It's just the other way around. Monetary policy actually accompanies -- there is a dividend from a combined expansion of monetary policy and the right structural reforms.

column2: the aging population
column3: the decline in the labour force. At the same time European Commission figures show that there is an average structural unemployment rate in the euro area of 11%. And that's an average
column4: which means that some countries and we know which
column5: have an unemployment rate of around 20% or even above 20%. And they had this high unemployment rate even before the financial crisis. That's why there is no other way than undertaking the needed structural reforms.

column2: yes
column3: structural reforms. column2: expected permanent income and therefore have an effect immediately on consumption for firms for households and on investments for firms. That's what I read in the introductory statement. So that's why there shouldn’t be any doubt about doing structural reforms.

column1: On the first question

column1: As I said the downside risks are still there
column2: but they are diminished. The issue now is to firm up this recovery and create conditions so that it's sustained through time that it's not only cyclical but becomes a structural recovery. The recovery is certainly due both to our monetary policy and that's because our monetary policy
column3: accommodative monetary policy stance
column4: which has been in place a long time before we actually did QE

column1: There is a second aspect in which the monetary
column2: even the recent monetary policy decisions have been important. You remember when we experienced this dramatic fall in oil prices there were many worries that there may not be all that pass-through into higher spending but actually the opposite could take place having negative second round effects on lower inflation. column3: and it eased the pass-through of lower oil prices into higher consumption and in due time higher investment. There is also another channel of course
column4: which is the difference in monetary policy cycles between different jurisdictions
column5: which had implications on the exchange rate. So these are the main drivers that one can see.

column1: There are also other long-term drivers less evident now. One of which is certainly the condition of the capital stock in the euro area where many
column2: many years of low investment both private and public would suggest that the years ahead should see a firming up of investments. There is another factor which would suggest that the pressure to de-lever should gradually ease if it's not eased already. And finally
column3: of course
column4: there are going to be less headwinds coming from fiscal policy consolidation than what was in place a year ago and this because of the progress that many governments have already achieved on that front.

column1: So
column2: as I said
column3: the current recovery is basically the outcome of two competing factors -- oil prices
column4: actually not competing they are complementing factors -- oil prices and our monetary policy stance. But there is one condition which makes a big difference that was not in place in 2012 when we first started creating conditions for the return of confidence in the financial markets; namely the banking system. The health check that all banks had to go through last year nowadays ensures that more accommodative monetary policy is being translated into better credit conditions
column5: which is not something we've seen before.

Now the situation seems to be different. So I think one very important reason often neglected is the better health of the banking system.

column1: And finally let me restate one thing. That this recovery is conditional upon the full implementation of our monetary policy stance
column2: so let's never forget that. Of course

column1: Well it's probably the most difficult question I got today. What I can say is that the present situation of the labour market is something that should be overcome

column3: I ask myself
column4: shouldn’t the unemployment level be an incentive to change the labour market
column5: especially since these levels are not the output
column6: or not only the output of the financial crisis. They've been high
column7: very high for many years before the financial crisis.

column1: So
column2: on top of this in the early years 2000's several countries had passed labour legislation. With a view to increasing flexibility in the labour market
column3: they passed legislation where the labour conditions of the ones who were already employed wouldn’t change at all
column4: but the new entrants would have very flexible terms of employment. So the outcome of this was a disproportionate fall of flexibility onto the young sector of the working population.

column1: This was
column2: as you can imagine
column3: especially unfortunate for a variety of reasons. One of which was that as soon as the financial crisis struck the first to lose their jobs were the young people
column4: were the youth. And that's why we still have such high levels of youth unemployment. So that has to change. We have to eliminate this sort of dual labour market condition. And we have to make sure the flexibility as its needed falls proportionately on all segments of the labour market.

column1: So first restore the conditions whereby people hire
column2: entrepreneurs
column3: companies hire people easily. Reduce the amount of time
column4: if someone loses a job
column5: reduce the amount of time he or she is unemployed. Change the educational skills

column7: you and your classmates of course. And so I think that's what's needed. And especially now
column8: that we've seemed to enter into a period of time where economic conditions are improving.

column1: Based on our regular economic and monetary analyses

column1: Our monetary policy measures have contributed to a broad-based easing in financial conditions
column2: a recovery in inflation expectations and more favourable borrowing conditions for firms and households. The effects of these measures are working their way through to the economy and are contributing to economic growth
