column4: and money and credit expansion. The full implementation of all our monetary policy measures will provide the necessary support to the euro area economy
column5: lead to a sustained return of inflation rates towards levels below
column6: but close to

column1: Let me now explain our assessment in greater detail
column2: starting with the economic analysis. In the first quarter of 2015
column3: real GDP in the euro area rose by 0.4%
column4: quarter on quarter
column5: after 0.3% in the last quarter of 2014. In recent quarters
column6: domestic demand and
column7: particularly
column8: private consumption were the main drivers behind the ongoing recovery. The latest survey data to May remain consistent with a continuation of the modest growth trend in the second quarter. Looking ahead
column9: we expect the economic recovery to broaden. Domestic demand should be further supported by our monetary policy measures and their favourable impact on financial conditions
column10: as well as by the progress made with fiscal consolidation and structural reforms. Moreover
column11: the low level of the price of oil should continue to support households’ real disposable income and corporate profitability and
column12: therefore
column13: private consumption and investment. Furthermore
column14: demand for euro area exports should benefit from improvements in price competitiveness. However
column15: economic growth in the euro area is likely to continue to be dampened by the necessary balance sheet adjustments in a number of sectors and the sluggish pace of implementation of structural reforms.

column1: This assessment is also broadly reflected in the June 2015 Eurosystem staff macroeconomic projections for the euro area
column2: which foresee annual real GDP increasing by 1.5% in 2015
column3: 1.9% in 2016 and 2.0% in 2017. Compared with the March 2015 ECB staff macroeconomic projections
column4: the projections for real GDP growth over the projection horizon remain virtually unchanged.

column1: While remaining on the downside
column2: the risks surrounding the economic outlook for the euro area have become more balanced on account of our monetary policy decisions and oil price and exchange rate developments.

column1: Inflation bottomed out at the beginning of the year. According to Eurostat’s flash estimate
column2: euro area annual HICP inflation was 0.3% in May 2015
column3: up from 0.0% in April and compared with -0.6% in January. On the basis of the information available and current oil futures prices
column4: annual HICP inflation is expected to remain low in the months ahead and to rise towards the end of the year
column5: also on account of base effects associated with the fall in oil prices in late 2014. Supported by the expected economic recovery
column6: the impact of the lower euro exchange rate and the assumption embedded in oil futures markets of somewhat higher oil prices in the years ahead
column7: inflation rates are expected to pick up further during 2016 and 2017.

column1: This assessment is also broadly reflected in the June 2015 Eurosystem staff macroeconomic projections for the euro area
column2: which foresee annual HICP inflation at 0.3% in 2015
column3: 1.5% in 2016 and 1.8% in 2017. In comparison with the March 2015 ECB staff macroeconomic projections
column4: the inflation projections have been revised upwards for 2015 and remain unchanged for 2016 and 2017.

column1: The Governing Council will continue to monitor closely the risks to the outlook for price developments over the medium term. In this context
column2: we will focus in particular on the pass-through of our monetary policy measures
column3: as well as on geopolitical
column4: exchange rate and energy price developments. We acknowledge that the staff projections are conditional on the full implementation of all our monetary policy measures in place. We also take into account that the degree of forecast uncertainty tends to increase with the length of the projection horizon.

column1: Turning to the monetary analysis
column2: recent data confirm the increase in underlying growth in broad money (M3). The annual growth rate of M3 increased to 5.3% in April 2015
column3: up from 4.6% in March. Annual growth in M3 continues to be supported by its most liquid components
column4: with the narrow monetary aggregate M1 growing at an annual rate of 10.5% in April.

column1: Loan dynamics gradually improved further. The annual rate of change of loans to non-financial corporations (adjusted for loan sales and securitisation) was -0.1% in April
column2: after -0.2% in March
column3: continuing its gradual recovery from a trough of -3.2% in February 2014. Despite these improvements
column4: the dynamics of loans to non-financial corporations remain subdued. They continue to reflect the lagged relationship with the business cycle
column5: credit risk
column6: credit supply factors
column7: and the ongoing adjustment of financial and non-financial sector balance sheets. The annual growth rate of loans to households (adjusted for loan sales and securitisation) increased further to 1.3% in April 2015
column8: after 1.1% in March. The monetary policy measures we have put in place will support further improvements both in borrowing costs for firms and households and in credit flows across the euro area.

column1: To sum up
column2: a cross-check of the outcome of the economic analysis with the signals coming from the monetary analysis confirms the need to maintain a steady monetary policy course
column3: firmly implementing the Governing Council’s monetary policy decisions. The full implementation of all our monetary policy measures will provide the necessary support to the economic recovery in the euro area and lead to a sustained return of inflation rates towards levels below
column4: but close to
column5: 2% in the medium term.

column1: Monetary policy is focused on maintaining price stability over the medium term and its accommodative stance contributes to supporting economic activity. However
column2: in order to reap the full benefits from our monetary policy measures
column3: other policy areas must contribute decisively. Given continued high structural unemployment and low potential output growth in the euro area
column4: the ongoing cyclical recovery should be supported by effective structural policies. In particular
column5: in order to increase investment
column6: boost job creation and raise productivity
column7: both the implementation of product and labour market reforms and actions to improve the business environment for firms need to gain momentum in several countries. A swift and effective implementation of these reforms
column8: in an environment of accommodative monetary policy
column9: will not only lead to higher sustainable economic growth in the euro area but will also raise expectations of permanently higher incomes. Therefore
column10: it will encourage both households to expand consumption and firms to increase investment today
column11: thus reinforcing the current cyclical economic recovery. As concerns fiscal developments
column12: reflecting mainly the cyclical recovery and the low level of interest rates
column13: the aggregate euro area general government deficit ratio is projected to decline gradually from 2.1% of GDP this year to 1.5% in 2017. The general government debt ratio is projected to decline gradually from 91.5% of GDP this year to 88.4% in 2017. Fiscal policies should support the economic recovery while remaining in compliance with the Stability and Growth Pact. Full and consistent implementation of the Pact is key for confidence in our fiscal framework.

column2: the Vice-President and I are very pleased to welcome you to our press conference. We will now report on the outcome of today’s meeting of the Governing Council. As usual

column1: Based on our regular economic and monetary analysis
column2: and in line with our forward guidance
column3: the Governing Council decided to keep the key ECB interest rates unchanged.

column1: Our asset purchase programme continues to proceed smoothly. Regarding non-standard monetary policy measures
column2: following the announced review of the public sector purchase programme’s issue share limit after the first six months of purchases
column3: the Governing Council decided to increase the issue share limit from the initial limit of 25% to 33%
column4: subject to a case-by-case verification that this would not create a situation whereby the Eurosystem would have blocking minority power
column5: in which case the issue share limit would remain at 25%.

column1: Underlying our monetary policy assessment was a review of recent data
column2: new staff macroeconomic projections and an interim evaluation of recent market fluctuations. The information available indicates a continued though somewhat weaker economic recovery and a slower increase in inflation rates compared with earlier expectations. More recently
column3: renewed downside risks have emerged to the outlook for growth and inflation. However
column4: owing to sharp fluctuations in financial and commodity markets
column5: the Governing Council judged it premature to conclude on whether these developments could have a lasting impact on the outlook for prices and on the achievement of a sustainable path of inflation towards our medium-term aim
column6: or whether they should be considered to be mainly transitory.

column1: Accordingly
column2: the Governing Council will closely monitor all relevant incoming information. It emphasises its willingness and ability to act
column3: if warranted
column4: by using all the instruments available within its mandate and
column5: in particular
column6: recalls that the asset purchase programme provides sufficient flexibility in terms of adjusting the size
column7: composition and duration of the programme.

column1: In the meantime
column2: we will fully implement our monthly asset purchases of €60 billion. These purchases have a favourable impact on the cost and availability of credit for firms and households. They are intended to run until the end of September 2016
column3: or beyond
column4: if necessary
column5: and
column6: in any case
column7: until we see a sustained adjustment in the path of inflation that is consistent with our aim of achieving inflation rates below
column8: but close to
column9: 2% over the medium term.

column1: Let me now explain our assessment of the available information in greater detail
column2: starting with the economic analysis. Real GDP in the euro area rose by 0.3% in the second quarter of 2015
column3: which was somewhat lower than previously expected. The latest survey indicators point to a broadly similar pace of real GDP growth in the second half of this year. Overall
column4: we expect the economic recovery to continue
column5: albeit at a somewhat weaker pace than earlier expected
column6: reflecting in particular the slowdown in emerging market economies
column7: which is weighing on global growth and foreign demand for euro area exports. Domestic demand should be further supported by our monetary policy measures and their favourable impact on financial conditions
column8: as well as by the progress made with fiscal consolidation and structural reforms. Moreover
column9: the decline in oil prices should provide support for households’ real disposable income and corporate profitability and
column10: therefore
column11: private consumption and investment. However
column12: economic growth in the euro area is likely to continue to be dampened by the necessary balance sheet adjustments in a number of sectors and the sluggish pace of implementation of structural reforms.

column1: This assessment is also broadly reflected in the September 2015 ECB staff macroeconomic projections for the euro area
column2: which foresee annual real GDP increasing by 1.4% in 2015
column3: 1.7% in 2016 and 1.8% in 2017. Compared with the June 2015 Eurosystem staff macroeconomic projections
column4: the outlook for real GDP growth has been revised down
column5: primarily due to lower external demand owing to weaker growth in emerging markets.

column1: The risks to the euro area growth outlook remain on the downside
column2: reflecting in particular the heightened uncertainties related to the external environment. Notably
column3: current developments in emerging market economies have the potential to further affect global growth adversely via trade and confidence effects.

column1: According to Eurostat’s flash estimate
column2: euro area annual HICP inflation was 0.2% in August 2015
column3: unchanged from June and July. Compared with the previous month
column4: this reflects a further decline in energy price inflation
column5: compensated for by higher price increases for food and industrial goods. On the basis of the information available and current oil futures prices
column6: annual HICP inflation rates will remain very low in the near term. Annual HICP inflation is expected to rise towards the end of the year
column7: also on account of base effects associated with the fall in oil prices in late 2014. Inflation rates are foreseen to pick up further during 2016 and 2017
column8: supported by the expected economic recovery
column9: the pass-through of past declines in the euro exchange rate and the assumption of somewhat higher oil prices in the years ahead as currently reflected in oil futures markets. However
column10: this increase in annual inflation rates is currently expected to materialise somewhat more slowly than anticipated thus far.

column1: This assessment is also broadly reflected in the September 2015 ECB staff macroeconomic projections for the euro area
column2: which foresee annual HICP inflation at 0.1% in 2015
column3: 1.1% in 2016 and 1.7% in 2017. In comparison with the June 2015 Eurosystem staff macroeconomic projections
column4: the outlook for HICP inflation has been revised down
column5: largely owing to lower oil prices. Taking into account the most recent developments in oil prices and recent exchange rates
column6: there are downside risks to the September staff inflation projections.

column1: In this context
column2: the Governing Council will closely monitor the risks to the outlook for price developments over the medium term. We will focus in particular on the pass-through of our monetary policy measures
column3: as well as on global economic
column4: financial
column5: commodity price and exchange rate developments.

column1: Turning to the monetary analysis
column2: recent data confirm robust growth in broad money (M3). The annual growth rate of M3 was 5.3% in July 2015
column3: compared with 4.9% in June. Annual growth in M3 continues to be increasingly supported by its most liquid components
column4: with the narrow monetary aggregate M1 growing at an annual rate of 12.1% in July
column5: compared with 11.7% in June.

column1: Loan dynamics continued to improve. The annual rate of change of loans to non-financial corporations (adjusted for loan sales and securitisation) increased to 0.9% in July
column2: up from 0.2% in June
column3: continuing its gradual recovery since the beginning of 2014. Despite these improvements
column4: the dynamics of loans to non-financial corporations remain subdued. They continue to reflect the lagged relationship with the business cycle
column5: credit risk
column6: credit supply factors
column7: and the ongoing adjustment of financial and non-financial sector balance sheets. The annual growth rate of loans to households (adjusted for loan sales and securitisation) increased to 1.9% in July 2015
column8: after 1.7% in June. Overall
column9: the monetary policy measures we have put in place since June 2014 provide clear support for improvements both in borrowing conditions for firms and households and in credit flows across the euro area.

column1: To sum up
column2: a cross-check of the outcome of the economic analysis with the signals coming from the monetary analysis indicates the need to firmly implement the Governing Council’s monetary policy decisions and to monitor closely all relevant incoming information as concerns their impact on the medium-term outlook for price stability.

column1: Monetary policy is focused on maintaining price stability over the medium term and its accommodative stance contributes to supporting economic activity. However
column2: in order to reap the full benefits from our monetary policy measures
column3: other policy areas must contribute decisively. Given continued high structural unemployment and low potential output growth in the euro area
column4: the ongoing cyclical recovery should be supported by effective structural policies. Further product and labour market reforms
column5: and particularly actions to improve the business environment
column6: including an adequate public infrastructure
column7: are vital to increase productive investment
column8: boost job creation and raise productivity. The swift and effective implementation of these reforms
column9: in an environment of accommodative monetary policy
column10: will not only lead to higher sustainable economic growth in the euro area but will also raise expectations of permanently higher incomes and accelerate the benefits of reforms
column11: thereby making the euro area more resilient to global shocks. Fiscal policies should support the economic recovery while remaining in compliance with the Stability and Growth Pact. Full and consistent implementation of the Pact is crucial for confidence in our fiscal framework.

column1: 2015-10-22;3;"Ladies and gentlemen
column2: the Vice-President and I are very pleased to welcome you to our press conference. I would like to thank Governor Bonnici for his kind hospitality and express our special gratitude to his staff for the excellent organisation of today’s meeting of the Governing Council. We will now report on the outcome of our meeting.

column1: Based on our regular economic and monetary analyses
column2: and in line with our forward guidance
column3: the Governing Council decided to keep the key ECB interest rates unchanged. As regards non-standard monetary policy measures
column4: the asset purchases are proceeding smoothly and continue to have a favourable impact on the cost and availability of credit for firms and households.

column1: The Governing Council has been closely monitoring incoming information since our meeting in early September. While euro area domestic demand remains resilient
column2: concerns over growth prospects in emerging markets and possible repercussions for the economy from developments in financial and commodity markets continue to signal downside risks to the outlook for growth and inflation. Most notably
column3: the strength and persistence of the factors that are currently slowing the return of inflation to levels below
column4: but close to
column5: 2% in the medium term require thorough analysis. In this context
column6: the degree of monetary policy accommodation will need to be re-examined at our December monetary policy meeting
column7: when the new Eurosystem staff macroeconomic projections will be available. The Governing Council is willing and able to act by using all the instruments available within its mandate if warranted in order to maintain an appropriate degree of monetary accommodation. In particular
column8: the Governing Council recalls that the asset purchase programme provides sufficient flexibility in terms of adjusting its size
column9: composition and duration. In the meantime
column10: we will continue to fully implement the monthly asset purchases of €60 billion. These purchases are intended to run until the end of September 2016
column11: or beyond
column12: if necessary
column13: and
column14: in any case
column15: until we see a sustained adjustment in the path of inflation that is consistent with our aim of achieving inflation rates below
column16: but close to
column17: 2% over the medium term.

column1: Let me now explain our assessment of the available information in greater detail
column2: starting with the economic analysis. Euro area real GDP increased by 0.4%
column3: quarter on quarter
column4: in the second quarter of 2015
column5: following a rise of 0.5% in the previous quarter. The outcome for the second quarter reflected positive contributions from both domestic demand and net exports. The most recent survey indicators point to a broadly similar pace of real GDP growth in the third quarter of the year. Overall
column6: we expect the economic recovery to continue
column7: albeit dampened
column8: in particular
column9: by weaker than expected foreign demand. Domestic demand should be further supported by our monetary policy measures and their favourable impact on financial conditions
column10: as well as by the progress made with fiscal consolidation and structural reforms. Moreover
column11: the decline in oil prices should provide support for households’ real disposable income and corporate profitability and
column12: therefore
column13: private consumption and investment. However
column14: the recovery in domestic demand in the euro area continues to be hampered by the necessary balance sheet adjustments in a number of sectors and the sluggish pace of implementation of structural reforms.

column1: The risks to the euro area growth outlook remain on the downside
column2: reflecting in particular the heightened uncertainties regarding developments in emerging market economies
column3: which have the potential to further weigh on global growth and foreign demand for euro area exports. Increased uncertainty has recently manifested itself in financial market developments
column4: which may have negative repercussions for euro area domestic demand.

column1: According to Eurostat
column2: euro area annual HICP inflation was -0.1% in September 2015
column3: down from 0.1% in August. Compared with the previous month
column4: this mainly reflects a further decline in energy price inflation. On the basis of the information available and current oil futures prices
column5: annual HICP inflation rates will remain very low in the near term. Annual HICP inflation is expected to rise at the turn of the year
column6: also on account of base effects associated with the fall in oil prices in late 2014. Inflation rates are foreseen to pick up further during 2016 and 2017
column7: supported by the expected economic recovery
column8: the pass-through of past declines in the euro exchange rate and the assumption of somewhat higher oil prices in the years ahead as currently reflected in oil futures markets. However
column9: there are risks stemming from the economic outlook and from financial and commodity market developments which could further slow down the gradual increase in inflation rates towards levels closer to 2%. These risks are being closely monitored by the Governing Council.

column1: Turning to the monetary analysis
column2: recent data confirm solid growth in broad money (M3)
column3: notwithstanding a decline in the annual growth rate of M3 to 4.8% in August 2015 from 5.3% in July. Annual growth in M3 continues to be mainly supported by its most liquid components
column4: with the narrow monetary aggregate M1 growing at an annual rate of 11.4% in August
column5: after 12.2% in July.

column1: Loan dynamics continued to improve. The annual rate of change of loans to non-financial corporations (adjusted for loan sales and securitisation) increased to 0.4% in August
column2: up from 0.3% in July
column3: pursuing its gradual recovery since the beginning of 2014. Despite these improvements
column4: developments in loans to enterprises continue to reflect the lagged relationship with the business cycle
column5: credit risk
column6: credit supply factors
column7: and the ongoing adjustment of financial and non-financial sector balance sheets. The annual growth rate of loans to households (adjusted for loan sales and securitisation) increased to 1.0% in August 2015
column8: compared with 0.9% in July. The euro area bank lending survey for the third quarter of 2015 confirms the increase in demand for bank loans
column9: supported by the general level of interest rates
column10: financing needs for investment purposes and housing market prospects. In addition
column11: credit standards eased further on loans to enterprises
column12: notably due to increasing competitive pressures in retail banking
column13: while tightening somewhat on loans to households for house purchase. Overall
column14: the monetary policy measures we have put in place since June 2014 provide clear support for improvements both in borrowing conditions for firms and households and in credit flows across the euro area.

column1: To sum up
column2: a cross-check of the outcome of the economic analysis with the signals coming from the monetary analysis indicates the need to firmly implement the Governing Council’s monetary policy decisions and to monitor closely all relevant incoming information as concerns their impact on the medium-term outlook for price stability.

column1: Monetary policy is focused on maintaining price stability over the medium term and its accommodative stance supports economic activity. However
column2: in order to reap the full benefits from our monetary policy measures
column3: other policy areas must contribute decisively. Given continued high structural unemployment and low potential output growth in the euro area
column4: the ongoing cyclical recovery should be supported by effective structural policies. In particular
column5: actions to improve the business environment
column6: including the provision of an adequate public infrastructure
column7: are vital to increase productive investment
column8: boost job creation and raise productivity. The swift and effective implementation of structural reforms
column9: in an environment of accommodative monetary policy
column10: will not only lead to higher sustainable economic growth in the euro area but will also raise expectations of permanently higher incomes and accelerate the benefits of reforms
column11: thereby making the euro area more resilient to global shocks. Fiscal policies should support the economic recovery
column12: while remaining in compliance with the EU’s fiscal rules. Full and consistent implementation of the Stability and Growth Pact is crucial for confidence in our fiscal framework. At the same time
column13: all countries should strive for a growth-friendly composition of fiscal policies.

column1: On why to fight low inflation: I've discussed this many times. Low inflation on one hand has a supporting power for real disposable income. On the other hand
column2: it increases the real value of debt. As we've seen
column3: low interest rates promote consumption and it's essential for the recovery of growth and economic activity. That's why we're fighting. But to fight low inflation doesn't mean that we want high inflation. We just want to be compliant with our mandate
column4: which is to drive inflation back to below but close to 2% in the medium term. I understand the Vice-President may want to add something on the first question.

column2: I would like to add something. Because it's the second or third time that you asked that question

column4: let me remind you that some years ago in the US there was a commission headed by an economist called Boskin to examine the measurement of inflation. And the conclusion of the Boskin Commission was that the way inflation is measured
column5: in particular the type of indexes that are used
column6: Laspeyres indexes
column7: tend to exaggerate the measurement of inflation
column8: in the case of the US by 1.5 percentage points. So

column2: and when there is a situation of high indebtedness
column3: when inflation is very low
column4: the burden of servicing the debt increases and that is very detrimental to the economy. The third point is that with very low inflation or negative inflation
column5: the real interest rate increases
column6: and when the nominal rate cannot go below zero it means that the interest rate in real terms may be above the equilibrium real interest rates that would equal savings to investment at the level of full employment. So that's another reason why negative inflation rates can be detrimental.

column1: Then there are the deflation risks – real deflation
column2: not what you implied in your question
column3: because to have negative inflation for a few months is not a deflation situation. A deflation situation is a situation of prolonged period
column4: meaning more than one year
column5: of negative inflation. And in that case you have two phenomena: you have an increase in real wages
column6: because there is rigidity in nominal wage growth to not go negative
column7: so you will constrain supply
column8: profits of firms
column9: and you hit growth. And second
column10: there is also then in such a situation a problem of consumers postponing their expenditure
column11: if deflation lasts long enough; when we are talking about real deflation
column12: not just a few months of negative inflation.

column1: Based on our regular economic and monetary analyses
column2: and after the recalibration of our monetary policy measures last month
column3: we decided to keep the key ECB interest rates unchanged and we expect them to remain at present or lower levels for an extended period of time. Regarding our non-standard monetary policy measures
column4: the asset purchases are proceeding smoothly and continue to have a favourable impact on the cost and availability of credit for firms and households.

column1: Taking stock of the evidence available at the beginning of 2016
column2: it is clear that the monetary policy measures that we have adopted since mid-2014 are working. As a result
column3: developments in the real economy
column4: credit provision and financing conditions have improved and have strengthened the euro area’s resilience to recent global economic shocks. The decisions taken in early December to extend our monthly net asset purchases of €60 billion to at least the end of March 2017
column5: and to reinvest the principal payments on maturing securities for as long as necessary
column6: were fully appropriate. They will result in a significant addition of liquidity to the banking system and will strengthen our forward guidance on interest rates.

column1: Yet
column2: as we start the new year
column3: downside risks have increased again amid heightened uncertainty about emerging market economies’ growth prospects
column4: volatility in financial and commodity markets
column5: and geopolitical risks. In this environment

column1: Let me now explain our assessment in greater detail
column2: starting with the economic analysis. Euro area real GDP growth was confirmed at 0.3%
column3: quarter on quarter
column4: in the third quarter of 2015
column5: supported mainly by private consumption
column6: while being dampened by a negative contribution from net exports. The most recent survey indicators
column7: available up to December
column8: point to ongoing real GDP growth momentum in the fourth quarter of last year. Looking ahead
column9: we expect the economic recovery to proceed. Domestic demand should be further supported by our monetary policy measures and their favourable impact on financial conditions
column10: as well as by the earlier progress made with fiscal consolidation and structural reforms. Moreover
column11: the renewed fall in oil prices should provide additional support for households’ real disposable income and corporate profitability and
column12: therefore
column13: for private consumption and investment. In addition
column14: the fiscal stance in the euro area is becoming slightly expansionary
column15: reflecting in particular measures in support of refugees. However
column16: the economic recovery in the euro area continues to be dampened by subdued growth prospects in emerging markets
column17: volatile financial markets
column18: the necessary balance sheet adjustments in a number of sectors and the sluggish pace of implementation of structural reforms.

column1: The risks to the euro area growth outlook remain on the downside and relate in particular to the heightened uncertainties regarding developments in the global economy
column2: as well as to broader geopolitical risks. These risks have the potential to weigh on global growth and foreign demand for euro area exports and on confidence more widely.

column1: Euro area annual HICP inflation was 0.2% in December 2015
column2: compared with 0.1% in November. The December outcome was lower than expected

column4: as well as lower food price and services price inflation. On the basis of current oil futures prices

column1: Turning to the monetary analysis
column2: recent data confirm solid growth in broad money (M3)
column3: with the annual rate of growth of M3 standing at 5.1% in November 2015
column4: after 5.3% in October. Annual growth in M3 continues to be mainly supported by its most liquid components
column5: with the narrow monetary aggregate M1 growing at an annual rate of 11.2% in November
column6: after 11.8% in October.

column1: Loan dynamics continued the path of gradual recovery observed since the beginning of 2014. The annual rate of change of loans to non-financial corporations (adjusted for loan sales and securitisation) increased to 0.9% in November 2015
column2: up from 0.6% in October. Developments in loans to enterprises continue to reflect the lagged relationship with the business cycle
column3: credit risk and the ongoing adjustment of financial and non-financial sector balance sheets. The annual growth rate of loans to households (adjusted for loan sales and securitisation) increased to 1.4% in November
column4: compared with 1.2% in October.

column1: The bank lending survey for the euro area for the fourth quarter of 2015 points to further improvements in demand for bank loans
column2: supported by the low level of interest rates
column3: financing needs for investment purposes and housing market prospects. Credit standards eased further on loans to enterprises
column4: notably owing to increasing competitive pressures in retail banking
column5: and reverted to a net easing on loans to households for house purchase. Overall
column6: the monetary policy measures in place since June 2014 have clearly improved borrowing conditions for both firms and households
column7: as well as credit flows across the euro area.

column1: Monetary policy is focused on maintaining price stability over the medium term and its accommodative stance supports economic activity. However
column2: in order to reap the full benefits from our monetary policy measures
column3: other policy areas must contribute decisively. Given continued high structural unemployment and low potential output growth in the euro area
column4: the ongoing cyclical recovery should be supported by effective structural policies. In particular
column5: actions to improve the business environment
column6: including the provision of an adequate public infrastructure

column1: Based on our regular economic and monetary analyses
column2: we have conducted a thorough review of the monetary policy stance
column3: in which we also took into account the new macroeconomic projections by our staff extending into the year 2018. As a result
column4: the Governing Council has decided on a set of measures in the pursuit of its price stability objective. This comprehensive package will exploit the synergies between the different instruments and has been calibrated to further ease financing conditions
column5: stimulate new credit provision and thereby reinforce the momentum of the euro area’s economic recovery and accelerate the return of inflation to levels below
column6: but close to

column1: First
column2: as regards the key ECB interest rates
column3: we decided to lower the interest rate on the main refinancing operations of the Eurosystem by 5 basis points to 0.00% and the rate on the marginal lending facility by 5 basis points to 0.25%. The rate on the deposit facility was lowered by 10 basis points to -0.40%.

column1: Second
column2: we decided to expand the monthly purchases under our asset purchase programme from €60 billion at present to €80 billion. They are intended to run until the end of March 2017
column3: or beyond
column4: if necessary
column5: and in any case until the Governing Council sees a sustained adjustment in the path of inflation consistent with its aim of achieving inflation rates below
column6: but close to
column7: 2% over the medium term. To ensure the continued smooth implementation of our asset purchases
column8: we also decided to increase the issuer and issue share limits for the purchases of securities issued by eligible international organisations and multilateral development banks from 33% to 50%.

column1: Third
column2: we decided to include investment-grade euro-denominated bonds issued by non-bank corporations established in the euro area in the list of assets that are eligible for regular purchases under a new corporate sector purchase programme. This will further strengthen the pass-through of our asset purchases to the financing conditions of the real economy. Purchases under the new programme will start towards the end of the second quarter of this year.

column1: Fourth
column2: we decided to launch a new series of four targeted longer-term refinancing operations (TLTRO II)
column3: starting in June 2016
column4: each with a maturity of four years. These new operations will reinforce the ECB’s accommodative monetary policy stance and will strengthen the transmission of monetary policy by further incentivising bank lending to the real economy. Counterparties will be entitled to borrow up to 30% of the stock of eligible loans as at 31 January 2016. The interest rate under TLTRO II will be fixed over the life of each operation

column6: the rate applied to the TLTRO II will be lower
column7: and can be as low as the interest rate on the deposit facility prevailing at the time of take-up. There will be no requirement for mandatory early repayments under TLTRO II
column8: and switches from TLTRO I will be allowed.

column1: Finally
column2: looking ahead
column3: taking into account the current outlook for price stability
column4: the Governing Council expects the key ECB interest rates to remain at present or lower levels for an extended period of time
column5: and well past the horizon of our net asset purchases.

column1: Separate press releases with further details of the measures taken by the Governing Council will be published this afternoon at 15:30 CET.
Adding to the measures taken since June 2014

column5: but close to
column6: 2% without undue delay. The Governing Council will continue to monitor very closely the evolution of the outlook for price stability over the period ahead.

column1: Let me now explain our assessment in greater detail
column2: starting with the economic analysis. Euro area real GDP growth was confirmed at 0.3%
column3: quarter on quarter
column4: in the fourth quarter of 2015
column5: supported by domestic demand
column6: while being dampened by a negative contribution from net exports. The most recent survey data point to weaker than expected growth momentum at the beginning of this year. Looking ahead
column7: we expect the economic recovery to proceed at a moderate pace. Domestic demand should be further supported by our monetary policy measures and their favourable impact on financial conditions
column8: as well as by continued employment gains benefiting from past structural reforms. Moreover
column9: the low price of oil should provide additional support for households’ real disposable income and private consumption
column10: as well as corporate profitability and investment. In addition
column11: the fiscal stance in the euro area is slightly expansionary
column12: partly reflecting measures in support of refugees. However
column13: the economic recovery in the euro area continues to be dampened by subdued growth prospects in emerging markets
column14: volatile financial markets
column15: the necessary balance sheet adjustments in a number of sectors and the sluggish pace of implementation of structural reforms.

column1: This outlook is broadly reflected in the March 2016 ECB staff macroeconomic projections for the euro area
column2: which foresee annual real GDP increasing by 1.4% in 2016
column3: 1.7% in 2017 and 1.8% in 2018. Compared with the December 2015 Eurosystem staff macroeconomic projections
column4: the outlook for real GDP growth has been revised slightly down
column5: mainly reflecting the weakened growth prospects for the global economy.

column1: The risks to the euro area growth outlook remain tilted to the downside. They relate in particular to the heightened uncertainties regarding developments in the global economy
column2: as well as to broader geopolitical risks.

column1: According to Eurostat’s flash estimate
column2: euro area annual HICP inflation was -0.2% in February 2016
column3: compared with 0.3% in January. All main HICP components contributed to this decline. Looking ahead
column4: on the basis of current futures prices for energy
column5: inflation rates are expected to remain at negative levels in the coming months and to pick up later in 2016. Thereafter
column6: supported by our monetary policy measures and the expected economic recovery
column7: inflation rates should recover further. The Governing Council will closely monitor price-setting behaviour and wage developments in the euro area
column8: paying particular attention to ensure that the current low inflation environment does not become entrenched in second-round effects on wage and price-setting.

column1: This broad pattern is also reflected in the March 2016 ECB staff macroeconomic projections for the euro area
column2: which foresee annual HICP inflation at 0.1% in 2016
column3: 1.3% in 2017 and 1.6% in 2018. In comparison with the December 2015 Eurosystem staff macroeconomic projections
column4: the outlook for HICP inflation has been revised down

column1: Turning to the monetary analysis
column2: recent data confirm solid growth in broad money (M3)
column3: with the annual rate of growth of M3 standing at 5.0% in January 2016
column4: after 4.7% in December 2015. Annual growth in M3 continues to be mainly supported by its most liquid components
column5: with the narrow monetary aggregate M1 growing at an annual rate of 10.5% in January
column6: after 10.8% in December.

column1: Loan dynamics continued the path of gradual recovery observed since the beginning of 2014. The annual rate of change of loans to non-financial corporations (adjusted for loan sales and securitisation) increased to 0.6% in January 2016
column2: up from 0.1% in December 2015. Developments in loans to enterprises continue to reflect the lagged relationship with the business cycle
column3: credit risk and the ongoing adjustment of financial and non-financial sector balance sheets. The annual growth rate of loans to households (adjusted for loan sales and securitisation) remained stable at 1.4% in January 2016. Overall
column4: the monetary policy measures in place since June 2014 have clearly improved borrowing conditions for firms and households
column5: as well as credit flows across the euro area.

column1: To sum up
column2: a cross-check of the outcome of the economic analysis with the signals coming from the monetary analysis confirmed the need for further monetary stimulus in order to secure a return of inflation rates towards levels that are below
column3: but close to
column4: 2% without undue delay.

column1: Monetary policy is focused on maintaining price stability over the medium term and its accommodative stance supports economic activity. However
column2: in order to reap the full benefits from our monetary policy measures
column3: other policy areas must contribute decisively. Given continued high structural unemployment and low potential output growth in the euro area
column4: the ongoing cyclical recovery should be supported by effective structural policies. In particular
column5: actions to raise productivity and improve the business environment
column6: including the provision of an adequate public infrastructure
column7: are vital to increase investment and boost job creation. The swift and effective implementation of structural reforms
column8: in an environment of accommodative monetary policy
column9: will not only lead to higher sustainable economic growth in the euro area but will also make the euro area more resilient to global shocks. As indicated by the European Commission
column10: the implementation of country-specific recommendations continued to be fairly limited in 2015; reform efforts thus need to be stepped up in the majority of euro area countries. Fiscal policies should support the economic recovery
column11: while remaining in compliance with the fiscal rules of the European Union. Full and consistent implementation of the Stability and Growth Pact is crucial to maintain confidence in the fiscal framework. At the same time
column12: all countries should strive for a more growth-friendly composition of fiscal policies.

Further information on the implementation aspects of the CSPP will be released after the press conference on the ECB’s website.

column1: Following our comprehensive package of decisions taken in early March
column2: broad financing conditions in the euro area have improved. The pass-through of the monetary policy stimulus to firms and households
column3: notably through the banking system
column4: is strengthening. However
column5: global uncertainties persist.

column2: it is essential to preserve an appropriate degree of monetary accommodation as long as needed in order to underpin the momentum of the euro area’s economic recovery and in order to accelerate the return of inflation to levels below
column3: but close to
column4: 2%. The Governing Council will continue to monitor closely the evolution of the outlook for price stability and
column5: if warranted to achieve its objective
column6: will act by using all the instruments available within its mandate. In the current context
column7: it is crucial to ensure that the very low inflation environment does not become entrenched in second-round effects on wage and price setting.

column2: starting with the economic analysis. Euro area real GDP increased by 0.3%
column3: quarter on quarter
column4: in the fourth quarter of 2015
column5: supported by domestic demand
column6: while being dampened by relatively weak export trends. Incoming data for the first quarter of 2016 point to ongoing output growth

column9: in particular
column10: continues to be supported by our monetary policy measures. Their favourable impact on financing conditions
column11: together with improvements in corporate profitability
column12: is benefiting investment. Moreover
column13: our accommodative monetary policy stance

column15: the fiscal stance in the euro area is slightly expansionary. At the same time
column16: the economic recovery in the euro area is still dampened by the ongoing balance sheet adjustments in a number of sectors
column17: the insufficient pace of implementation of structural reforms and subdued growth prospects in emerging markets.

column2: which should support the outlook for consumption and investment. However

column4: in particular

column1: Overall
column2: the monetary policy measures in place since June 2014 have clearly improved borrowing conditions for firms and households
column3: as well as credit flows across the euro area. The comprehensive package of new monetary policy measures adopted in March this year underpins the ongoing upturn in loan growth
column4: thereby supporting the recovery of the real economy.

column1: To sum up
column2: a cross-check of the outcome of the economic analysis with the signals coming from the monetary analysis confirmed the need to preserve an appropriate degree of monetary accommodation in order to secure a return of inflation rates towards levels that are below
column3: but close to
column4: 2% without undue delay.

column1: Monetary policy is focused on maintaining price stability over the medium term and its accommodative stance supports economic activity. As emphasised repeatedly by the Governing Council
column2: and as strongly echoed in both European and international policy discussions
column3: in order to reap the full benefits from our monetary policy measures
column4: other policy areas must contribute much more decisively
column5: both at the national and at the European levels. Structural policies are essential
column6: given continued high structural unemployment and low potential output growth in the euro area. In particular
column7: actions to raise productivity and improve the business environment

2016-06-02;3;Ladies and gentlemen
column2: the Vice-President and I are very pleased to welcome you to our press conference. column1: Based on our regular economic and monetary analyses
column2: we decided to keep the key ECB interest rates unchanged. We continue to expect them to remain at present or lower levels for an extended period of time
column3: and well past the horizon of our net asset purchases. Regarding non-standard monetary policy measures
column4: we confirm that the monthly asset purchases of €80 billion are intended to run until the end of March 2017
column5: or beyond
column6: if necessary
column7: and in any case until the Governing Council sees a sustained adjustment in the path of inflation consistent with its inflation aim. As a next step
column8: on 8 June we will start making purchases under our corporate sector purchase programme (CSPP). Moreover
column9: starting on 22 June
column10: we will conduct the first operation in our new series of targeted longer-term refinancing operations. Further information on implementation aspects of the CSPP will be released after the press conference on the ECB’s website.

column1: The comprehensive package of decisions taken in early March underpins the momentum of the euro area’s economic recovery and fosters the return of inflation to levels below
column2: but close to
column3: 2%. In particular
column4: our measures continue to ease the cost of credit and contribute to a strengthening in credit creation. The economic recovery is gradually proceeding. Additional stimulus
column5: beyond the impetus already taken into account
column6: is expected from the monetary policy measures still to be implemented and will contribute to further rebalancing the risks to the outlook for growth and inflation. In the current context
column7: it is crucial to ensure that the very low inflation environment does not become entrenched in second-round effects on wage and price setting. The Governing Council will closely monitor the evolution of the outlook for price stability and
column8: if warranted to achieve its objective
column9: will act by using all the instruments available within its mandate.

column1: Let me now explain our assessment in greater detail
column2: starting with the economic analysis. Euro area real GDP increased by 0.5%
column3: quarter on quarter
column4: in the first quarter of 2016
column5: after 0.3% in the last quarter of 2015. Growth continues to be supported by domestic demand
column6: while being dampened by weak exports. The latest data point to ongoing growth in the second quarter
column7: though possibly at a lower rate than in the first quarter. Looking ahead
column8: we expect the economic recovery to proceed at a moderate but steady pace. Domestic demand remains supported by the pass-through of our monetary policy measures to the real economy. Favourable financing conditions and improvements in corporate profitability continue to promote investment. Moreover
column9: sustained employment gains
column10: which are also benefiting from past structural reforms
column11: and still relatively low oil prices provide additional support for households’ real disposable income and private consumption. In addition
column12: the fiscal stance in the euro area is slightly expansionary. However
column13: the economic recovery in the euro area continues to be dampened by subdued growth prospects in emerging markets
column14: the necessary balance sheet adjustments in a number of sectors and a sluggish pace of implementation of structural reforms.

column1: This outlook is broadly reflected in the June 2016 Eurosystem staff macroeconomic projections for the euro area
column2: which foresee annual real GDP increasing by 1.6% in 2016 and 1.7% in 2017 and 2018. Compared with the March 2016 ECB staff macroeconomic projections
column3: the outlook for real GDP growth has been revised up for 2016 and has remained broadly unchanged for 2017 and 2018.

column1: The risks to the euro area growth outlook remain tilted to the downside
column2: but the balance of risks has improved on the back of the monetary policy measures taken and the stimulus still in the pipeline. Downside risks continue to relate to developments in the global economy
column3: to the upcoming British referendum and to other geopolitical risks.

column1: According to Eurostat’s flash estimate
column2: euro area annual HICP inflation in May 2016 was -0.1%
column3: up from -0.2% in April
column4: mainly reflecting higher energy and services price inflation. Looking ahead
column5: on the basis of current futures prices for oil
column6: inflation rates are likely to remain very low or negative in the next few months before picking up in the second half of 2016
column7: in large part owing to base effects in the annual rate of change of energy prices. Supported by our monetary policy measures and the expected economic recovery
column8: inflation rates should recover further in 2017 and 2018.

column1: This broad pattern is also reflected in the June 2016 Eurosystem staff macroeconomic projections for the euro area
column2: which foresee annual HICP inflation at 0.2% in 2016
column3: 1.3% in 2017 and 1.6% in 2018. In comparison with the March 2016 ECB staff macroeconomic projections
column4: the outlook for HICP inflation has been revised slightly up for 2016
column5: reflecting recent oil price increases
column6: and has remained unchanged for 2017 and 2018.

column1: Turning to the monetary analysis
column2: broad money (M3) continued to grow at a robust pace in April 2016
column3: with its annual rate of growth standing at 4.6%
column4: after 5.0% in March. As in previous months
column5: annual growth in M3 is mainly supported by its most liquid components
column6: with the narrow monetary aggregate M1 growing at an annual rate of 9.7% in April
column7: after 10.1% in March.

column1: Loan dynamics followed the path of gradual recovery observed since the beginning of 2014. The annual rate of change of loans to non-financial corporations (adjusted for loan sales and securitisation) stood at 1.2% in April 2016
column2: compared with 1.1% in March. Developments in loans to enterprises continue to reflect the lagged relationship with the business cycle
column3: credit risk and the ongoing adjustment of financial and non-financial sector balance sheets. The annual growth rate of loans to households (adjusted for loan sales and securitisation) remained broadly stable at 1.5% in April
column4: after 1.6% in March.

column1: The monetary policy measures in place since June 2014 have clearly improved borrowing conditions for firms and households
column2: as well as credit flows across the euro area. The comprehensive package of new monetary policy measures adopted in March this year underpins the ongoing upturn in loan growth
column3: thereby supporting the recovery of the real economy.

column1: To sum up
column2: a cross-check of the outcome of the economic analysis with the signals coming from the monetary analysis confirmed the need to preserve an appropriate degree of monetary accommodation in order to secure a return of inflation rates towards levels that are below
column3: but close to
column4: 2% without undue delay.

column1: Monetary policy is focused on maintaining price stability over the medium term and its accommodative stance supports economic activity. As emphasised repeatedly by the Governing Council
column2: and as again strongly echoed in both European and international policy discussions
column3: in order to reap the full benefits from our monetary policy measures
column4: other policy areas must contribute much more decisively
column5: both at the national and at the European levels. Structural policies are essential
column6: given continued high structural unemployment and low potential output growth in the euro area. Structural reforms are necessary in all euro area countries
column7: although specific reform needs differ across the individual economies. At this stage
column8: the focus should be on actions to raise productivity and improve the business environment
column9: including the provision of an adequate public infrastructure
column10: which are vital to increase investment and boost job creation. The enhancement of current investment initiatives
column11: including the extension of the Juncker plan
column12: and progress on the capital markets union will also contribute positively to this objective. In an environment of accommodative monetary policy
column13: the swift and effective implementation of structural reforms
column14: in line with the country-specific recommendations recently published by the European Commission
column15: will not only lead to higher sustainable economic growth in the euro area but will also make the euro area more resilient to global shocks. Fiscal policies should also support the economic recovery
column16: while remaining in compliance with the fiscal rules of the European Union. Full and consistent implementation of the Stability and Growth Pact over time and across countries is crucial to maintain confidence in the fiscal framework. At the same time
column17: all countries should strive for a more growth-friendly composition of fiscal policies.

column1: Your second question has been asked several times today. “Why don't you revise the inflation target?” Now
column2: there are two schools of thought. Some people say we should revise it downward and simply accept the fact that we'll never reach 2%
column3: and we should take 1% or 0%. And some say
column4: “Oh
column5: you should revise it upward and go to 3% or 4%
column6: because in this way you will elicit expectations that you will go up with your policies.” Now
column7: the ECB position has been basically contrary to revising the inflation objective either way
column8: and the reasons are different in different cases. The revision upward
column9: frankly
column10: would test seriously our credibility
column11: because people would actually say
column12: “How come you want to go to 3% when you're not even able to reach 1.5%?”

column1: And by the way
column2: each revision on both sides undermines the credibility of the central bank – for different reasons
column3: but it undermines the credibility of the central bank. That effect by itself would raise the risk premium
column4: and in so doing it would increase real interest rates and would go against the objective that we have of price stability but also against restoring growth. In the case of accepting a lower inflation target
column5: this effect would be immediate. We would have an immediate increase in real interest rates

column7: in the late ’90s
column8: all central banks of major monetary policy jurisdictions decided that 2% was the right objective and the right target.

column1: We've discussed these reasons on many occasions. Especially so in the monetary union. Where you lose flexibility in the exchange rate

column3: and so you need a certain cushion for carrying out these adjustments. So the reasons for keeping this objective are overwhelming
column4: and they work in both directions.

column1: 2016-07-21;3;"Ladies and gentlemen
column2: the Vice-President and I are very pleased to welcome you to our press conference. We will now report on the outcome of today’s meeting of the Governing Council
column3: which was also attended by the Commission Vice-President
column4: Mr Dombrovskis.

column1: Based on our regular economic and monetary analyses
column2: we decided to keep the key ECB interest rates unchanged. We continue to expect them to remain at present or lower levels for an extended period of time
column3: and well past the horizon of our net asset purchases. Regarding non-standard monetary policy measures
column4: we confirm that the monthly asset purchases of €80 billion are intended to run until the end of March 2017
column5: or beyond
column6: if necessary
column7: and in any case until the Governing Council sees a sustained adjustment in the path of inflation consistent with its inflation aim.

column1: Today we discussed developments since our last monetary policy meeting in early June. Following the UK referendum on EU membership
column2: our assessment is that euro area financial markets have weathered the spike in uncertainty and volatility with encouraging resilience. The announced readiness of central banks to provide liquidity
column3: if needed
column4: and our accommodative monetary policy measures
column5: as well as a robust regulatory and supervisory framework
column6: have all helped to keep market stress contained. Financing conditions remain highly supportive
column7: which contributes to a strengthening in credit creation. They continue to support our baseline scenario of an ongoing economic recovery and an increase in inflation rates.

column1: At the same time
column2: given prevailing uncertainties
column3: the Governing Council will continue to monitor economic and financial market developments very closely and to safeguard the pass-through of its accommodative monetary policy to the real economy. Over the coming months
column4: when we have more information
column5: including new staff projections
column6: we will be in a better position to reassess the underlying macroeconomic conditions
column7: the most likely paths of inflation and growth
column8: and the distribution of risks around those paths. If warranted to achieve its objective
column9: the Governing Council will act by using all the instruments available within its mandate.

column1: Let me now explain our assessment in greater detail
column2: starting with the economic analysis. Euro area real GDP increased by 0.6%
column3: quarter on quarter
column4: in the first quarter of 2016
column5: after 0.4% in the last quarter of 2015. Growth continues to be supported by domestic demand
column6: while export growth has remained modest. Incoming data point to ongoing growth in the second quarter of 2016
column7: though at a lower rate than in the first quarter. Looking ahead
column8: we continue to expect the economic recovery to proceed at a moderate pace. Domestic demand remains supported by the pass-through of our monetary policy measures to the real economy. Favourable financing conditions and improvements in corporate profitability continue to promote a recovery in investment. Sustained employment gains
column9: which are also benefiting from past structural reforms
column10: and still relatively low oil prices provide additional support for households’ real disposable income and thus for private consumption. In addition
column11: the fiscal stance in the euro area is expected to be mildly expansionary in 2016 and to turn broadly neutral in 2017 and 2018.

column1: At the same time
column2: headwinds to the economic recovery in the euro area include the outcome of the UK referendum and other geopolitical uncertainties
column3: subdued growth prospects in emerging markets
column4: the necessary balance sheet adjustments in a number of sectors and a sluggish pace of implementation of structural reforms. Against this background
column5: the risks to the euro area growth outlook remain tilted to the downside.

column1: According to Eurostat
column2: euro area annual HICP inflation in June 2016 was 0.1%
column3: up from -0.1% in May
column4: mainly reflecting higher energy and services price inflation. Looking ahead
column5: on the basis of current futures prices for oil
column6: inflation rates are likely to remain very low in the next few months before starting to pick up later in 2016
column7: in large part owing to base effects in the annual rate of change of energy prices. Supported by our monetary policy measures and the expected economic recovery
column8: inflation rates should increase further in 2017 and 2018.

column1: Turning to the monetary analysis
column2: broad money (M3) continued to increase at a robust pace in May 2016
column3: with its annual rate of growth standing at 4.9%
column4: after 4.6% in April. As in previous months
column5: annual growth in M3 was mainly supported by its most liquid components
column6: with the narrow monetary aggregate M1 expanding at an annual rate of 9.1% in May
column7: after 9.7% in April.

column1: Loan dynamics followed the path of gradual recovery observed since the beginning of 2014. The annual rate of change of loans to non-financial corporations (adjusted for loan sales and securitisation) increased to 1.4% in May 2016
column2: compared with 1.2% in April. Developments in loans to enterprises continue to reflect the lagged relationship with the business cycle
column3: credit risk and the ongoing adjustment of financial and non-financial sector balance sheets. The annual growth rate of loans to households (adjusted for loan sales and securitisation) remained broadly stable at 1.6% in May
column4: after 1.5% in April.

column1: The euro area bank lending survey for the second quarter of 2016 indicates further improvements in loan supply conditions for loans to enterprises and households and a continued increase in loan demand across all loan categories. Furthermore
column2: banks continued to report that the targeted longer-term refinancing operations had contributed to more favourable terms and conditions on loans.

column1: The monetary policy measures in place since June 2014 have significantly improved borrowing conditions for firms and households
column2: as well as credit flows across the euro area. The comprehensive package of new monetary policy measures adopted in March this year underpins the ongoing upturn in loan growth
column3: thereby supporting the recovery of the real economy. In the light of the prevailing uncertainties
column4: it is essential that the bank lending channel continues to function well.

column1: To sum up
column2: a cross-check of the outcome of the economic analysis with the signals coming from the monetary analysis confirmed the need to preserve an appropriate degree of monetary accommodation in order to secure a return of inflation rates towards levels that are below
column3: but close to
column4: 2% without undue delay.

column1: Monetary policy is focused on maintaining price stability over the medium term and its accommodative stance supports economic activity. As emphasised repeatedly by the Governing Council
column2: and as again strongly echoed in both European and international policy discussions
column3: in order to reap the full benefits from our monetary policy measures
column4: other policy areas must contribute much more decisively
column5: both at the national and at the European level. The implementation of structural reforms needs to be substantially stepped up to reduce structural unemployment and boost potential output growth in the euro area. Structural reforms are necessary in all euro area countries
column6: although specific reform needs differ across the individual economies. The focus should be on actions to raise productivity and improve the business environment
column7: including the provision of an adequate public infrastructure
column8: which are vital to increase investment and boost job creation. The enhancement of current investment initiatives
column9: including the extension of the Juncker plan
column10: progress on the capital markets union and reforms that will improve the resolution of non-performing loans will also contribute positively to this objective. In an environment of accommodative monetary policy
column11: the swift and effective implementation of structural reforms
column12: in line with the 2016 country-specific recommendations recently approved by the European Council
column13: will not only lead to higher sustainable economic growth in the euro area but will also make the euro area more resilient to global shocks. Fiscal policies should also support the economic recovery
column14: while remaining in compliance with the fiscal rules of the European Union. Full and consistent implementation of the Stability and Growth Pact over time and across countries is crucial to maintain confidence in the fiscal framework. At the same time
column15: all countries should strive for a more growth-friendly composition of fiscal policies.

column1: Based on our regular economic and monetary analyses
column2: we today conducted a comprehensive assessment of the economic and inflation outlook and our monetary policy stance. As a result
column3: the Governing Council took the following decisions in the pursuit of its price stability objective:

column1: As regards non-standard monetary policy measures
column2: we will continue to make purchases under the asset purchase programme (APP) at the current monthly pace of €80 billion until the end of March 2017. From April 2017
column3: our net asset purchases are intended to continue at a monthly pace of €60 billion until the end of December 2017
column4: or beyond
column5: if necessary
column6: and in any case until the Governing Council sees a sustained adjustment in the path of inflation consistent with its inflation aim. If
column7: in the meantime
column8: the outlook becomes less favourable
column9: or if financial conditions become inconsistent with further progress towards a sustained adjustment of the path of inflation
column10: the Governing Council intends to increase the programme in terms of size and/or duration. The net purchases will be made alongside reinvestments of the principal payments from maturing securities purchased under the APP.

column1: To ensure the continued smooth implementation of the Eurosystem’s asset purchases
column2: the Governing Council decided to adjust the parameters of the APP as of January 2017 as follows. First
column3: the maturity range of the public sector purchase programme will be broadened by decreasing the minimum remaining maturity for eligible securities from two years to one year. Second
column4: purchases of securities under the APP with a yield to maturity below the interest rate on the ECB’s deposit facility will be permitted to the extent necessary.

column1: The key ECB interest rates were kept unchanged and we continue to expect them to remain at present or lower levels for an extended period of time
column2: and well past the horizon of our net asset purchases.

column1: Today’s extension of the asset purchase programme has been calibrated to preserve the very substantial degree of monetary accommodation necessary to secure a sustained convergence of inflation rates towards levels below
column2: but close to
column3: 2% over the medium term. Together with the sizeable volume of past purchases and forthcoming reinvestments
column4: it ensures that financial conditions in the euro area will remain very favourable
column5: which continues to be crucial to achieve our objective. In particular
column6: the extension of our purchases over a longer horizon allows for a more sustained market presence and
column7: therefore
column8: a more lasting transmission of our stimulus measures. This calibration reflects the moderate but firming recovery of the euro area economy and still subdued underlying inflationary pressures. The Governing Council will closely monitor the evolution of the outlook for price stability and
column9: if warranted to achieve its objective
column10: will act by using all the instruments available within its mandate.

column1: Let me now explain our assessment in greater detail

column3: quarter on quarter
column4: in the third quarter of 2016
column5: following similar growth in the second quarter. Incoming data
column6: notably survey results
column7: point to a continuation of the growth trend in the fourth quarter of 2016. Looking further ahead
column8: we expect the economic expansion to proceed at a moderate but firming pace. The pass-through of our monetary policy measures to the real economy is supporting domestic demand and has facilitated deleveraging. Improvements in corporate profitability and very favourable financing conditions continue to promote a recovery in investment. Moreover
column9: sustained employment gains
column10: which are also benefiting from past structural reforms
column11: provide support for households’ real disposable income and private consumption. At the same time
column12: there are indications of a somewhat stronger global recovery. However
column13: economic growth in the euro area is expected to be dampened by a sluggish pace of implementation of structural reforms and remaining balance sheet adjustments in a number of sectors.

column2: which foresee annual real GDP increasing by 1.7% in 2016 and 2017
column3: and by 1.6% in 2018 and 2019. Compared with the September 2016 ECB staff macroeconomic projections
column4: the outlook for real GDP growth is broadly unchanged. The risks surrounding the euro area growth outlook remain tilted to the downside.

column7: mainly owing to base effects in the annual rate of change of energy prices. Supported by our monetary policy measures
column8: the expected economic recovery and the corresponding gradual absorption of slack

column2: broad money (M3) growth moderated in October 2016
column3: with its annual rate of growth decreasing to 4.4%
column4: after 5.1% in September. As in previous months
column5: annual growth in M3 was mainly supported by its most liquid components
column6: with the narrow monetary aggregate M1 expanding at an annual rate of 7.9% in October

column3: credit risk and the ongoing adjustment of financial and non-financial sector balance sheets
column4: the monetary policy measures put in place since June 2014 are significantly supporting borrowing conditions for firms and households and thereby credit flows across the euro area.

column1: To sum up

column4: 2% without undue delay.

column1: Monetary policy is focused on maintaining price stability over the medium term and its accommodative stance supports economic activity. As emphasised repeatedly by the Governing Council
column2: in order to reap the full benefits from our monetary policy measures

column4: both at the national and at the European level.
